Jadavpur University (JU) saw night-long rampage and vandalism on August 20, when a mob, armed with sticks and rods, allegedly stormed the campus.
The violence followed a heated altercation late on August 19 between activists from the Akhil Bharaitya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) from the university’s engineering department and members of the Left-wing student outfit, Democratic Students’ Federation (DSF), and other student organizations. The ABVP alleged that its members were assaulted and that several workers required hospitalisation. Students from the engineering faculty disputed the claim and offered a counter-account of the incident.
By midnight, an armed mob allegedly entered the campus, apparently seeking to avenge the earlier altercation. The attackers tore down and set fire to placards, festoons and flags belonging to various student organisations active on the campus. The mob also surrounded Aurobindo Bhavan, the university’s administrative building, trapping students inside.
The violence was captured by CCTV cameras installed across the university campus. Students and journalists also recorded several videos of the incident. Alt News accessed multiple such recordings and analysed them to establish the identities of those involved in the ruckus.
What happened at JU: A Blow-by-Blow Account
Around 9:30–10:30 pm on August 19, the DSF-run Faculty of Engineering & Technology Students’ Union (FETSU) held a general body meeting on the campus. The meeting had been announced through the union’s social media account.
ABVP and the allied Right-wing student outfit, Nationalist Students’ Front (NSF), opposed the meeting, citing a Calcutta high court ruling that no activities could be undertaken from student union offices until fresh student union elections were held. According to students present, ABVP and NSF members were outnumbered and were forced to leave the spot. A few DSF members were also injured in the ensuing scuffle.
Ayantik Pal, a third-year B Tech student who attended the meeting, said the GB meeting had been convened to elect signatories for the union’s email ID, Facebook account and bank account. Since the last FETSU election was held in 2020, he said, the meeting was intended to allow the union to continue its functioning.
According to Pal, ABVP activists at the meeting repeatedly objected that it was illegal. He said they nevertheless participated when names for the signatories were being proposed, before becoming agitated as the meeting progressed. They allegedly abused some students, calling them “Naxals” and “Maoists”, following which a scuffle broke out.
Accounts diverge over what happened immediately afterwards.
According to students, Nikhil Das, an ABVP research scholar and president of the organisation’s JU unit, attempted to enter the undergraduate and postgraduate students’ GB meeting and allegedly tried to provoke a confrontation. Students said they intervened to stop him, escalating the situation. They alleged that three DSF workers were injured in the assault by ABVP activists and that one was taken away towards the Sulekha Crossing. ABVP denied these allegations.
ABVP, meanwhile, claimed that Das was assaulted during the GB meeting and subsequently had to be hospitalised at KPC Medical College and Hospital. BJP MLA from Jadavpur Sarbari Mukherjee visited him at the hospital. Students alleged that during the visit, she threatened that ABVP and BJP workers would retaliate if those accused in the assault did not surrender. She later repeated this on camera.
Around midnight, a crowd of approximately 50–60 people gathered outside Gate 4 of the university, which is the only entrance that remains open at night. By around 12:30 am, the group entered the campus.
Pramita Basu, an undergraduate Philosophy student, said that after 7 pm, everyone entering the campus is required to show an ID card, including hostel residents. However, according to her, the crowd entered without being stopped by the guards stationed at the gate.
The group moved from Gate 4 towards the Science-Arts crossing, where some wall graffiti was allegedly damaged, before turning towards Aurobindo Bhavan, the university’s administrative building. Videos from the night accessed by Alt News show some members of the group carrying saffron flags.
Meanwhile, students who had remained on campus after the earlier confrontation gathered inside Aurobindo Bhavan. According to them, they had decided to stay back until morning because they had heard that ABVP activists were looking for them outside the university.
Pal said an all-faculty GB meeting was also convened that night, with students from the arts, science and engineering faculties discussing what to do next. Around 12:30 am, he said, a university staff member alerted them that a mob had entered the campus and advised them to protect themselves.
“Within minutes, we saw a stream of mobile flashlights coming towards Aurobindo Bhavan from the side of the green zone. A few students present at the green zone were thrashed by this mob,” Pal said.
The students then woke the guards at Aurobindo Bhavan, obtained the keys and locked themselves inside, according to Pal.
The crowd that reached the building tried to break through its collapsible gates but failed. It then tore down red flags, festoons and posters belonging to student organisations and set them on fire outside the administrative building. Students trapped inside alleged that members of the crowd abused them verbally, threw stones and eggs at the building, and attempted to throw burning flags inside. Footage of the episode was broadcast live on television and recorded by students and journalists.
The violence continued until around 2 am. Around the same time, another group gathered outside Jadavpur police station and allegedly attempted to breach the entrance to the university’s main hostel, located next to the police station.
At the protest, ABVP West Bengal leaders were reportedly heard telling the media that the organisation was “putting the last nail in the coffin” of the “Dimagi Naxals” and would carry out “surgical strikes” at Jadavpur University to suppress them.
By around 2:30 am, the crowd had dispersed. The students who had taken shelter inside Aurobindo Bhavan began leaving the campus at around 5 am.
Alt News procured a third CCTV footage from University sources, where several persons of interest can be spotted as present on the campus on the night of August 20.
The confrontation did not end with the dispersal of the mob.
Around noon the following day, the Student Federation of India (SFI) and other Left student organisations held a protest near the Lenin statue at Jadavpur 8B bus stand. Kolkata Police barricaded the area and stopped the protesters from proceeding towards the university. Around 2 pm, an ABVP rally that began from Golpark reached Gate 4 of the university. Students inside the campus also gathered in response. As Gate 4 was kept locked to prevent outsiders from entering, a face-off between the two groups on either side of the gate ensued.
During the confrontation, members of the ABVP crowd were seen standing on the historic university emblem designed by artist Nandalal Bose as they attempted to cross the closed gate and enter the campus.
Visuals of Rajyeshwar Sinha, a professor of Bengali at JU, holding the partially damaged University emblem went viral.
We Accessed Additional Footage
Alt news procured footage from a CCTV camera installed near the science-arts crossing. It can be viewed here:
Besides, we collected video footage from a local media outlet whose representatives were present on the campus on that night. It can be viewed here:
ABVP Denial
Directly denying any role of ABVP, the outfit’s central working committee (CWC) member Subhabrata Adhikary said on a talk show on ABP Ananda, that ABVP had no connection with the rampage at Jadavpur University on August 20. When pointed out by the anchor that people in the mob were holding ABVP flags, Adhikary said, “It doesn’t prove anything. SFI workers have done the vandalism while holding ABVP flags”. When asked if ABVP was condemning the night-long violence, he again said, “It is clear that ABVP has no connection with the incident.”
Talking to The Times of India, south Bengal ABVP secretary Neelkantha Bhattacharya, too, denied his presence during the campus violence. However, he then said, some of ABVP boys entered the campus “out of over-enthusiasm. The gate was open. We just pushed inside. I went at most 10 steps inside the university to get them out”.
Adhikary, on the other hand, contradicted his own statement on ABP Ananda, and told TOI, “I was standing right by the gate. I have no connection with the mob. After hearing about the situation, I went there to ensure that no untoward incident happened. ABVP has no involvement in any vandalism.”
CCTV and Video Footage Disprove ABVP Claims
Alt News examined CCTV footage from the intervening night of August 19-20 and identified several prominent ABVP faces and BJP-linked political figures on the campus.
1. Subhabarta Adhikary
Visible in JU CCTV footage-1 (Captured by a camera fixed on the external wall of PG Arts building)
As the gate opens at 12.38.17 am, Adhikary is one of the first persons to enter the campus, followed by a crowd. When the group nears a large white SFI banner, he is seen saying something in an animated manner. Within seconds, others in the crowd tear down the banner. It is not clear whether he instructs them to do it or tries to dissuade them.
2. Neelkantha Bhattacharya
Visible in JU CCTV footage-2 (Captured by a camera installed on a pole at the science-arts crossing).
Around 12:40 am, Neelkantha Bhattacharya is seen carrying a rod or a stick while instructing a group. In the same footage, at the 12:39:22 am mark, Subhabrata Adhikary is seen next to him. They are in front of the PG science building. At 12:40:28, the two once again can be seen together. This time Bhattacharya is carrying sticks in both hands.
It is worth noting that Bhattacharyya first told TOI that he was not present on the campus. Then, he claimed, he had barely taken 10 steps inside the gate. The distance from Gate 4 to PG Science building, according to Google Maps, is over 360 feet, i.e., about 110 meters.
3. Somsurya Banerjee
Visible in JU CCTV footage-3 (Captured by a camera on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4)
Banerjee, an NSF activist, is spotted on the campus around 1.14 am on August 20. Banerjee had earlier courted controversy by claiming that cows were slaughtered within the University during Iftar.
4. Aditya Mondal
Visible in footage captured by Mrittika TV, a local media outlet.
The portal captured the exact moment when the crowd entered the campus, in a livestream. Although the video was later deleted from the page, Alt News accessed the footage. In that video, (embedded in the story above) Aditya Mondal, the ABVP candidate for the recently held election to internal complaint committee (ICC) of the Arts Faculty, was spotted near the PG science building. The wall had an SFI graffiti, where a person was seen urinating on the Nazi Hakenkreuz. The writing next to it said, ‘Break Fascism with Red’. Mondal was seen with a group that tried to rub the symbol off. Mondal can be heard saying, “The left-naxals had insulted the symbol of India, Swastik. We are correcting it.”
5. Partha Chakraborty
Visible in the footage captured by students stuck inside Aurobindo Bhavan, during the rampage.
Partha Chakraborty, a Bharatiya Janata Yuva Morcha (BJYM) worker from the Dhakuria area, was also present at the scene. In videos captured by the students stranded inside Aurobindo Bhavan, he was seen burning flags of SFI and other Left organizations in front of the collapsible gate of the building, and throwing the burning flags inside. Three days later, on August 23, he was seen with BJP’s losing candidate from Kasba assembly Sandeep Banerjee and South Kolkata Yuva Morcha leader Shatadru Ghoshal.
6. Abhijeet Roy (Raja)
Visible in JU CCTV footage-3 (Captured by a camera on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4)
Another prominent face identified in the footage from that night is Abhijeet Roy alias Raja, the election agent of Jadavpur MLA Sarbari Mukherjee. In a video posted on social media, Roy was seen standing with a group outside Gate-4, with one member holding an ABVP flag. ABVP leader Neelkantha Bhattacharya is part of the group. Roy’s entry into the campus was also captured on CCTV footage. He is seen interacting with a group of men with former VC Buddhadeb Sau standing at an arm’s length.
7. Buddhadeb Sau
Visible in JU CCTV footage-1 and JU CCTV footage-3.
The most talked about entry on that eventful night was perhaps that of Buddhadeb Sau, professor of mathematics and ex-VC of the university. Sau’s presence raised eyebrows not only for the fact that it is unusual for an academic of his stature to be on the campus past midnight, but also because of his Sangh connections. He is associated with the RSS-backed Akhil Bhartiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh (ABRSM), and represented the organisation at a joint press meet held by Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh JU unit, ABVP JU unit and ABRSM JU unit, held after the campus violence.
Sau can be spotted in JU CCTV footage-1 and JU CCTV footage-3. In the JU CCTV footage-1 feed, he is seen entering the campus through a side gate at 12:39:44 am, and exiting through the same gate at 12:44:35 am. For the entire duration, he stood in front of the security guards’ room, occasionally speaking to others. From 12:44:09 till his exit 26 seconds later, he is seen watching others tearing down what appears to be political flags put up on Gate-4.
Sau is seen once again in JU CCTV footage-3. This time he was captured by the camera installed on the outer wall of security guards’ room at Gate-4, at 1:06:33 am. This time also, he is seen standing in front of guards’ room.
Asked about his presence during the rampage, Sau told TOI, “I went to the spot as soon as I received news of the disturbance. No one from the authorities was present there. I was concerned. I told the police to get additional cops to manage any potential flare-up. Once the group retreated and the situation was brought under I returned to my quarters. I went and tried to protect the students; is that my crime?”

An egg retrieval is the culmination of several weeks of ovarian stimulation, as multiple follicles develop under the influence of fertility medicines, with the ovaries undergoing significant changes in response to hormonal stimulation.
The quality and number of eggs ultimately retrieved are influenced by several factors, including age, ovarian reserve, genetics and the underlying cause of infertility. A woman’s diet cannot alter these fundamentals, nor can any particular food guarantee better eggs or a successful IVF outcome. Nutrition can, however, influence the metabolic and physiological environment in which the body responds to treatment. For this reason, what a woman eats in the weeks preceding egg retrieval should be viewed as part of overall preparation rather than as a means of ‘boosting’ fertility.
Biology behind the preparation
Egg development is a prolonged process. Although the final stages of follicular growth occur during the IVF stimulation cycle, the oocytes have been undergoing maturation over a much longer period. This means that nutrition in the weeks before retrieval is unlikely to produce a dramatic change in egg quality on its own, but maintaining good nutritional status can support general metabolic health during a demanding treatment cycle.
During ovarian stimulation, the body is also adapting to changing hormone levels, increased follicular activity and, in some women, symptoms such as bloating, constipation, fatigue or changes in appetite. A balanced diet can help maintain energy levels and provide the protein, fibre, vitamins, minerals and healthy fats required for normal physiological function.
Among dietary patterns studied in relation to IVF outcomes, the Mediterranean-style diet has received some of the most consistent attention. A 2023 evidence-based review published in Frontiers in Nutrition, covering multiple IVF nutritional interventions, concluded that a Mediterranean-style dietary approach is the most consistently supported pattern for women undergoing ovarian stimulation. This diet is rich in vegetables, fruits, legumes, whole grains, healthy fats, and lean protein, with limited processed foods and refined carbohydrates.
What to eat more of
Protein is the macronutrient that most women underestimate in the lead-up to retrieval. Both animal and plant sources such as eggs, fish, lentils, chickpeas and dairy support follicle development and give the body the building blocks it needs during stimulation. Aim to include a source of protein in every meal.
Healthy fats, particularly omega-3 fatty acids, carry documented benefits for IVF outcomes. A review published in Reproductive BioMedicine Online found that supplementation with omega-3 free fatty acids may lead to improvements in both clinical and embryological IVF outcomes. Practical sources in an Indian context include fish such as salmon, sardines, and mackerel, as well as walnuts, flaxseeds, and chia seeds.
Folate belongs in this conversation for two reasons: it supports healthy cell division, and many women undergoing IVF are not getting enough of it through food alone. Dark leafy vegetables such as spinach, methi and palak are among the richest dietary sources. Iron from leafy greens, lentils, and lean meat supports the blood supply that developing follicles depend on.
Antioxidants such as vitamins C and E, selenium, zinc help protect developing eggs from oxidative stress, which increases during stimulation as the ovaries work at higher capacity. Berries, bell peppers, nuts, and seeds are practical sources worth building into daily meals.
Hydration matters more during stimulation than at other times. As follicles grow, the risk of bloating and fluid retention increases. Consistent water intake of at least two to three litres a day supports the body through this phase and helps manage stimulation-related discomfort.
What to limit
There is no single food that will undo an IVF cycle, but some patterns are worth avoiding in the weeks before retrieval. Highly processed foods, refined carbohydrates, and excessive added sugar affect blood sugar stability and create an inflammatory environment that does not serve follicle development. Alcohol should be avoided during stimulation. Excess caffeine, more than one to two cups of coffee a day, is worth reducing, as higher intakes have been associated with poorer IVF outcomes in some studies.
What patients should know
There is no fertility diet that guarantees better egg quality or a successful cycle, and any approach that promises otherwise is worth approaching with scepticism. What a balanced, nutrient-dense diet does is support your body through a physically demanding process the same way good nutrition supports any period of heightened physical demand.
The specifics of what your body needs during your particular stimulation protocol are best discussed with your fertility specialist, who can account for your individual clinical picture, any nutrient deficiencies identified through blood work, and whether supplementation is appropriate in your case.
(Dr. Shivika Gupta is a fertility specialist at Birla Fertility and IVF, Gurgaon Sec- 51. shivika.gupta@birlafertility.com)

The Clean Label Credibility Test India’s clean-label boom is facing its toughest test yet. FSSAI’s recent crackdown on health and purity claims is threatening the marketing language that helped many D2C brands grow. Can “healthy” food startups survive when every claim must stand up to evidence? The Label Under Fire: FSSAI’s recent notices to 20 legacy and D2C brands has brought claims such as “100% natural” and “healthy” under scrutiny. Brands built on “ingredient transparency” were caught using date powders and fructose while advertising zero added sugar. Rather than challenging the FSSAI's notices, several brands quietly opted to scrub these absolute claims and overhauled their packaging. But the situation took a sharp turn after the SC began questioning what a front-of-pack warning label should look like. SC Weighs In: The apex court accepted FSSAI’s proposed red hexagon warning for packaged foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat. At the same time, it also sought more clarity on scientific thresholds, label size and possible confusion with existing food markers. The next hearing in the matter could establish a clearer path for how health warnings must appear, potentially reshaping packaging and product listings across India’s food market. Trust Needs Proof: Experts believe that the crackdown can potentially create a better opportunity for brands to demonstrate better ingredients, transparent formulations and verifiable nutritional claims. However, it will raise the cost of entering the category and will require the brands to rethink product formulations. So, will new-age food brands adapt or will this regulatory reckoning shatter consumer trust in "clean-label" promises? The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has issued an alert on the use of unauthorised cosmetic products manufactured in Pakistan, which are on sale in India.
A public notice dated September 8, 2026, stated that cosmetic products named ‘Goree Beauty Cream’ and ‘Chandni Whitening Cream’ are unauthorised for sale and no trade registration certificate was issued to the manufacturers.

India and Pakistan summon diplomats after ships collide in international waters
- Published
India and Pakistan have summoned each other's top diplomats in Delhi and Islamabad after two of their naval vessels collided in the Arabian Sea.
Both sides blamed each other for the collision, which happened on Tuesday. They also accused each other of violating a 1991 bilateral agreement that requires either side to give advance notice of military exercises.
While India said the incident did not cause any major damage, the statement released by Pakistan did not make clear whether its vessel was damaged in any way.
The incident comes more than a year after the South Asian neighbours conducted military strikes against each other before agreeing on a ceasefire.
In its statement, India said it had lodged a strong protest with the Charge d'Affaires of the Pakistani High Commission in Delhi over what it called "unacceptable and unprofessional conduct" of the naval unit.
"The Charge d'Affaires of Pakistan was advised to convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents," India's external affairs ministry said.
On the same day, Pakistan also summoned India's Charge d'Affaires in Islamabad, lodging its complaint against what it called a "highly provocative and unacceptable" action by India's naval vessel.
In its statement, Pakistan's foreign affairs ministry said that its navy was conducting its biennial exercise, SEASPARK-26, in its exclusive economic zone when the Indian vessel "carried out aggressive manoeuvres in dangerously close proximity" of its ship.
Pakistan also urged the international community to call upon India to "refrain from irresponsible actions that could further destabilise South Asia", saying that the region could not afford to be held "hostage to India's reckless pursuit of conflict and instability".
The Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements - which both sides accuse the other of violating - was signed in 1991, external to prevent "any crisis situation arising due to misreading of the other side's intentions".
India specifically accused Pakistan of violating Article 10 of the agreement, which says that the two countries' naval vessels and submarines must not be closer than three nautical miles from each other so as to avoid accidents while operating in international waters.

Amid the ongoing debate over the introduction of MDR on select UPI transactions, the finance ministry’s Department of Financial Services (DFS) has said the move was not driven by “external pressure”. The clarification came after allegations linked the reintroduction of MDR on UPI to the US Trade Representative’s (USTR) 2026 National Trade Estimate Report, which flagged India’s digital payment policies as a barrier for foreign payment service providers. In a statement, the DFS highlighted two concerns raised in the USTR report — the inability of US payment service providers to participate in the UPI ecosystem, including credit card transactions, on a level playing field with RuPay, and NPCI’s proposed 30% market share cap for third-party application providers (TPAPs). Responding to the first concern, the DFS pointed to NPCI’s Tuesday’s (September 15) circular, saying credit card transactions on UPI continue to be permitted only through RuPay credit cards. According to the ministry, this is part of a deliberate policy to make RuPay the preferred credit card network among Indian users. On the TPAP market share cap, the DFS said NPCI introduced the 30% limit in November 2020, but it could not be enforced because smaller payment apps lacked a self-sustaining revenue model needed to compete with market leaders. The government said introducing MDR on select high-value UPI transactions would provide these players with a revenue stream and enable more domestic companies to expand their operations. It added that the move was aimed at protecting India’s sovereignty in the electronic payments ecosystem. The DFS also linked the policy to the government’s efforts to promote RuPay credit and debit cards as domestic alternatives to global card networks. RuPay debit-card payments will continue to remain outside the MDR framework. “The allegation that MDR has been introduced under any external influence is patently false and misleading,” the ministry said. The MDR Uproar Beyond the "external pressure" allegations, the new UPI MDR framework has drawn opposition from retailer and fuel dealer associations, capital-market platforms, and consumers over its potential cost impact. Retailer groups have raised concerns over the additional cost and its potential impact on UPI acceptance. “Small merchants will now think twice about whether to accept cash or UPI. During the festive season, a larger share of transactions cross the ₹2,000 mark, and the moment a fee attaches itself to digital payment, cash becomes the path of least resistance,” Retailers Association of India CEO Kumar Rajagopalan said. The framework provides concessional rates for certain sectors. Fuel, insurance, railways, telecom, and utility payments above ₹2,000 will attract a flat MDR of ₹5 instead of the standard 0.4% charge. However, the All India Petroleum Dealers Association (AIPDA) has sought the finance minister’s intervention over the payment processing costs arising from the framework. The association subsequently held discussions with senior officials at the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. Meanwhile, UPI transactions above ₹2,000 involving mutual funds, securities, and stockbrokers will attract an MDR of 0.02%, capped at ₹300. Zerodha and INDmoney have flagged the potential cost impact of the measure. Warning that brokers could incur charges on fund transfers without necessarily generating corresponding trading revenue, Zerodha cofounder and CEO Nithin Kamath called for the MDR on broking transactions to be capped at ₹5 or ₹10. A petition was also filed in the Supreme Court yesterday challenging the Centre’s framework. It contended that merchants could pass on the additional cost to consumers indirectly by raising prices. The government has repeatedly said consumers will not be charged a separate UPI fee and that merchants cannot levy a direct surcharge on customers. It expects the MDR revenue to support UPI infrastructure, cybersecurity, innovation, and customer service, along with a proposed fund for payment infrastructure and merchant onboarding in smaller centres. New Revenue Stream For Fintechs While merchant bodies and investment platforms have raised concerns, banks, payment companies, and TPAPs have largely welcomed the return of MDR, which has been a longstanding industry demand. Under the standard 0.4% MDR structure, the merchant will pay the acquiring bank, which will transfer 0.28% to the issuing bank as an interchange. The issuing bank will pay 0.12% to the payer-side payment service provider, which, in turn, will pay 0.08% to the UPI app provider. The framework will open a new revenue stream for companies operating in the UPI ecosystem. Following the MDR notification, PhonePe is looking to revive its IPO plans. The Walmart-backed fintech startup is eyeing a listing in February-March 2027, Inc42 reported yesterday. Edited by Vinaykumar Rai

Expensive flash drives: When and why it's worth paying more
Faster transfers are only part of the story when you're deciding whether a premium flash drive is worth it.
Flash drives aren't the first device you think about when considering the current sky-high cost of RAM and storage, but they've certainly been affected. Thanks to AI and data center demand, NAND flash prices have risen significantly. USB drives haven't absorbed those increases dollar for dollar, but cheap flash memory can no longer be taken for granted either.
That makes the price difference between various flash drives more interesting. While two drives of the same capacity may cost vastly different amounts, usually the extra cost brings something you'll notice: faster transfers, stronger security or hardware better suited to life outside a desk drawer.
Still, expensive doesn't automatically mean better. The trick is figuring out what you're actually paying for.
Faster transfers are a clear benefit of spending more
USB 3.0 was the first major successor to USB 2.0. It bumped the maximum theoretical transfer speed to 5 Gbps, compared to the earlier standard's 480 Mbps. From there, USB naming got complicated. The two following standards were initially called USB 3.1 and USB 3.2, but everything was retroactively changed to use "Gen" names.
The group behind USB now recommends using the max transfer rate for clarity, instead of "USB 3.2" followed by the generation — these cap out at 5 Gbps, 10 Gbps or 20 Gbps. Thus, if you see "USB 3.2" on a box, it doesn't necessarily indicate how fast that drive will be. You'll need to check the transfer rate elsewhere in the specs.
USB-C doesn't fix this problem either. USB-C is a connector type, not a performance promise, so USB-C devices can run at USB 2.0 speeds. What USB-C can give you is convenience. Having both USB-A and USB-C connectors on a single drive makes it easier to switch between older PCs and newer laptops, tablets or phones without having to carry an adapter around.
It's the actual read and write speeds that count. For example, Kingston rates its DataTraveler Max at up to 1,000 MB/s reads and 900 MB/s writes. In a 10GB transfer test, Tom's Hardware measured Samsung's cheaper Fit Plus at 319.7 MB/s reads and just 58.4 MB/s writes. That gap won't matter much when copying a PDF, but a folder full of 4K video is a different matter.
A USB driver's controller handles tasks such as error correction and write management, while the flash memory itself also influences performance. Unfortunately, flash drive manufacturers don't always disclose enough about those components to make them easy to compare. Actual speeds can also drop during long transfers, so anyone regularly moving hundreds of gigabytes should pay special attention to sustained write performance rather than assuming the largest number on the package is what you'll always get.
Sometimes you're paying for factors other than speed
A premium flash drive doesn't need to top a benchmark to warrant its cost. The Kingston IronKey Keypad 200, which focuses on security instead of speed, is a good example. It has a physical keypad, XTS-AES 256-bit hardware encryption, brute-force protections and FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validation. These are advanced features not found in basic flash drives that protect the device from physical tampering and technical attacks. Yet its fastest variants are rated at 280 MB/s reads and 200 MB/s writes. The idea isn't to make the progress bar disappear faster, but to make the files much more difficult to access if the drive goes missing from your pocket.
Capacity can push up the price too. While you can find 2TB flash drives, packing more storage onto your keyring doesn't guarantee strong performance. In the same 10GB test mentioned earlier, Tom's Hardware measured the tiny 1TB SanDisk Extreme Fit at 318.3 MB/s reads and just 82.52 MB/s writes. It also came close to blocking the adjacent USB-C port on the reviewer's laptop.
Ruggedness is another reason to consider spending more. Samsung rates its BAR Plus for protection against water, shock, extreme temperatures, magnets and X-rays. It also has a five-year limited warranty. That matters if your flash drive lives on a keychain, in a camera bag or anywhere else less hospitable than your desk.
None of those features makes an expensive flash drive a substitute for a proper backup, though. If you're looking for a USB drive for occasional documents, installers or file transfers, then a good, inexpensive USB 3.x drive might be enough. But if you're willing to spend big bucks for capacity and sustained speed, compare the price with top portable SSDs. External SSDs are often the better choice for regularly moving large amounts of data, or for extra storage that sits permanently attached to your computer.

The iPhone Duo hides several firsts and oddities: horizontal rear cameras, vertical UI elements, top-mounted volume buttons, Apple Pencil support, titanium construction, Smart Take, a circular status bar, unusual USB-C placement, and no Action button or Pro camera controls.
Apple launched many devices at its recent Surprise and Shine event, but there was no doubting the star of the show. It was the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, and the device that many are expecting to do for foldables what the iPhone did for smartphones almost two decades ago. Small wonder then that the past few days have seen everyone and their grandmother discussing the iPhone Duo.
Debates have been raging over its animations, its crease, its cameras, its apps, and of course, its price. Some are hailing it as the coolest thing since sliced bread, while others insist it is a spawn of Satan in smartphone shape. But in all this debate and discussion, some important aspects and features of the Duo have either escaped attention or have not been adequately covered.
Here are ten things you might have missed about Apple’s first foldable.
Table of Contents
The first iPhone with horizontally arranged cameras on the back…selfie cameras on the corners
iPhones have been coming with multiple cameras (two or three) on their backs for a while now. However, they have always been arranged vertically, one below the other, or in the case of some Pro devices, with two cameras one below the other and the third one placed between them but slightly to the side, forming a triangle of sorts. The iPhone Duo thus becomes the first iPhone to have cameras placed next to each other horizontally, in what some would term a very Pixel-like style. The selfie cameras also get new locations – moving to the right corner of the external display and close to the right corner of the internal display (when opened), where it actually lies under the display. Regular iPhone users are sure to notice a change in perspective.
The dock, navigation, and even the Dynamic Island just got radically right, and utterly vertical
The cameras on the iPhone Duo might have gone horizontal, but some elements of the UI have gone vertical! While everyone has been focusing on the crease in the middle of the iPhone Duo and its visibility (it’s not easy to spot, by all accounts). Apple moved many iOS elements to the right side and gave them a vertical orientation. Lock screen controls, navigation buttons, the home screen dock, and even the Dynamic Island are on the right side of the iPhone Duo, and what’s more, are arranged vertically.
The Dynamic Island even slides open vertically to show information and updates. Evidently, this was done because of the width of the iPhone Duo (it is also the widest iPhone ever), which would have made it difficult to reach these elements. They have therefore been placed on the same side as the display unlock/power button, which is also a fingerprint scanner. This is pretty right-wing in UI terms, literally.
Volume buttons on the top
The iPhone Duo comes with a rather different volume button placement from other foldables. While it is conventional for most foldables and indeed, most ‘normal’ phones, to have volume buttons on the right or left side, the iPhone Duo actually has volume buttons on the top, aligned slightly towards the right. This is a volume button placement we have seen on the newer iPad minis but not on any other iPhones or iPads. It is a rather odd location in our opinion, and if opened and rotated clockwise, it would place the buttons on the lower part of the right side, and on the top of the left side if rotated anti-clockwise.
Camera Control? Present! Action button? Er…
While the iPhone Duo comes with a Camera Control button like other recent iPhones, it, rather surprisingly, does not have an Action button, which is generally seen on the left side of most iPhones and can be customized to carry out a number of tasks. It used to toggle Silent mode on and off, before being changed to an action button. Clearly, it was either not good enough to make the cut for the Duo or perhaps there simply was not enough space for it.
Apple Pencil support exists, but only for the Type-C one
The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone to come with Apple Pencil support. What’s more, it supports the Apple Pencil on both its internal as well as external display. But there is a catch – it only supports the basic Apple Pencil (USB-C). This means that while one can scribble and sketch easily, there’s no pressure sensitivity and no support for double taps. One will also need a Type-C cable to charge it, as it cannot charge magnetically. Given the price and potential of the device, it would have been good to have Apple Pencil Pro support on it.
Only new iPhone with Titanium
Remember how Titanium was the coolest thing in premium phones a few years ago. Well, while it still remains a very premium material, it has largely disappeared from the smartphone scene, with even Apple seemingly moving on to other materials, with only the iPhone Air using Titanium last year. This time around, it is the iPhone Duo that carries the Titanium legacy forward. While the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max use “forged aluminum” and ceramic glass, the iPhone Duo comes with a main chassis made with grade 5 Titanium, and 3D-printed titanium is also used for the hinge cover.
The only iPhone camera with Smart Take
Although its cameras might not seem as formidable as those on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the iPhone Duo has a slice of camera magic up its sleeve that no other iPhone has. This is Smart Take, which, with some AI magic, automatically works out when you are perfectly placed for a photograph and takes it without you needing to hit a capture button or prompt the device in any manner. It is supposed to work very well with individual and group selfies, and uses the rear cameras while showing you a preview on the cover display. While the feature is designed mainly for the fold form factor, it would be great to see it on “normal” iPhones too, although one might not be able to see previews!
A Type-C port placed under the cover display
In another case of rather unusual placement, the Type-C port of the iPhone Duo is actually placed on the base of the cover display or the upper panel. In many foldables, the charging port is placed on the lower panel, so that the phone can be opened without moving the charging cable. That is clearly not going to be possible on the iPhone Duo.
The status bar is closed…and is now a circle
The move to a foldable form factor has led to a redesign of some UI elements on the iPhone Duo. Perhaps the most surprising of these is the status bar. Until now seen in the top right corner, and displaying signal strength, Wi-Fi, and battery, it has now been changed to a circle, with the battery life and signal strength being on the circumference and Wi-Fi being at the center. It is not really as intuitive as its predecessor, but we guess users will get the hang of it.
No Pro controls in the camera
The iPhone Duo comes with two 48-megapixel cameras on the back – a new Fusion Main camera, and the same ultrawide that is on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. But while these pack in a lot of features such as three photographic styles, smart focus tracking, next-generation portraits, macro photography and more, the iPhone Duo’s camera app does not come with the Pro Controls seen on the 18 Pro and Pro Max, which let users play around with shutter speed, white balance, and aperture. This l is a bit of a pity, especially given the vast viewfinder the open Duo can serve up. But well, to be fair, this was never meant to be a camera phone.

The Vesuvius Challenge is an ongoing project that combines “digital unwrapping” with crowdsourced machine learning to decipher the so-called Herculaneum scrolls, badly charred 2,000-year-old papyri too fragile to be physically unrolled. The effort just got an additional boost. A team of researchers created their own contemporary model papyrus scrolls—charring them just like the originals—to validate a screening method to determine which of the Herculaneum scrolls were written in lead-based ink and hence are the most promising candidates for further analysis. They described the process in a new paper published in the journal PLoS ONE.
As previously reported, the ancient Roman resort town of Pompeii wasn’t the only city destroyed in the catastrophic 79 AD eruption of Mount Vesuvius. Several other cities in the area, including the wealthy enclave of Herculaneum, were fried by clouds of hot gas, called pyroclastic pulses and flows. But still, some remnants of Roman wealth survived. One palatial residence in Herculaneum—believed to have once belonged to a man named Piso—contained hundreds of priceless written scrolls made from papyrus, singed into carbon by volcanic gas.
The scrolls stayed buried under volcanic mud until they were excavated in the 1700s from a single room that archaeologists believe held the personal working library of an Epicurean philosopher named Philodemus. The few opened fragments helped scholars identify various Greek philosophical texts, including On Nature by Epicurus and several by Philodemus himself, as well as a handful of Latin works. But the more than 600 rolled-up scrolls were so fragile that it was long believed they would never be readable, since even touching them could cause them to crumble.
Brent Searles’ lab at the University of Kentucky has been working on deciphering the Herculaneum scrolls for many years. He employs a different method of “virtually unrolling” damaged scrolls, which he used in 2016 to “open” a scroll found on the western shore of the Dead Sea, revealing the first few verses from the book of Leviticus. The so-called En Gedi scroll was recovered from the ark of an ancient synagogue destroyed by fire around 600 CE. To the naked eye, it resembled a small lump of charcoal, so fragile that there was no safe way to analyze the contents.

Carrick 'not bothered' by pressure - but should he be after this latest mess?

Sir Alex Ferguson was St Mirren manager the last time Manchester United lost at Old Trafford having taken a 2-0 lead.
That is the context to the shocking Carabao Cup third-round exit his old club suffered against Brighton on Wednesday.
It is a period of time that encompasses the legendary Scot's dynasties at Aberdeen as well as United. The Class of '92 were in nappies when John Pratt scored the winner for Tottenham on 4 September 1976.
After holding protests inside and outside the ground before Sunday's loss to 10-man Manchester City, United supporters made their feelings known about their latest embarrassment in three ways.
- Most fans simply left as the players embarked on their post-match lap of appreciation.
- Some of those who remained booed, as they had done when their side fell behind 21 minutes from time.
- By the time they approached the tunnel, close to United's 'singing section', supporters were asking Michael Carrick and his players 'what was that?'. Their wording was somewhat more colourful.
It is not certain where 15-year-old JJ Gabriel was while all this was taking place, but nothing happened that would make him think he had got it wrong by turning his back on the club.
Indeed, it is quite possible, probable indeed, that the promised senior debut would have been scrapped given the game situation - and the fact skipper Bruno Fernandes was among the experienced players introduced in the frantic final stages.
"Of course we can turn it around, we have got some really good players," said Carrick. "It feels bad because we haven't had a great week or two, or three weeks."

Carrick's side have won twice this season, against newly promoted Ipswich at home after falling behind, and Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in the Champions League. They have now lost on three occasions, more defeats than he experienced in 17 matches after replacing Ruben Amorim in January.
He has been around Manchester United long enough to know the pressure losing runs can build.
"I don't feel under pressure," he said. "Either way, that doesn't bother me one bit.
"I understand what goes on outside and how the world works, but it doesn't bother me. What bothers me is winning games, having a good feeling around the place and a good feeling around the group to know we're moving in a good direction."
The problem is it doesn't feel as though they are moving in a good direction. There were certainly not many positives to take from this mess.
The obvious one was Shea Lacey, who marked his first senior start with a well-taken eighth-minute goal. It meant he became the first teenager to score on his first United start since Marcus Rashford in February 2016.
Lacey was one of eight changes made by Carrick. Defensively, those changes were not a success.
Diogo Dalot was one of the three players to keep their place. His form has deserted him. Noussair Mazraoui is the back-up left-back, which only heightens the debate over the wisdom not to buy one before the transfer window closed. Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven looked like the inexperienced defenders they are. In midfield Manchester United were overrun.
Yet again, Rashford threatened without managing a goal or an assist. He came closest to levelling when he sped beyond the Brighton defence, but his shot was saved by Jason Steele.
"The longer the game went, the more we had control," was the concise assessment of Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler. "I thought we deserved to win."
Carrick didn't dispute the assessment.
'Being here toughens you up'
His greatest sadness was for Lacey, who should have had his name in lights but instead was part of a team scuttling off the pitch to the sound of boos and harsher criticism.
"It's a shame that Shea's moment, such a great moment for him, for his family, his friends and the whole academy; to have an academy player come in and have a moment like that, gets a bit lost, unfortunately," said Carrick.
"It won't for him when things settle down but, as we sit here now, it feels that it was a long time ago."
Carrick also addressed the JJ Gabriel situation.
"He's a young boy, he's 15, and for me, definitely, and from a club point of view, looking after our younger players, their welfare, their wellbeing, their exposure, we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation," he explained.
But ultimately, for any manager, the assessment of their work comes through results.
"Being here toughens you up over a period of time," he said. "It depends how you deal with it. You've got to deal with it in a way where you can cope with it and you can bring out the best in yourself. However you do that, with your motivation and the confidence deep within yourself to know we can win football matches.
"We've gone out of the cup tonight, and the feeling around the place feels bigger than that. I'm honest enough to say that's how it feels. But it doesn't have to be like that. If we win football matches again, it can go in a different direction."
Manchester United have one more game before the international break, at Fulham on Sunday.
For the general wellbeing of the club, Carrick's team really need to win.
Speaking on Sky Sports, former England midfielder Jamie Redknapp said he wasn't sure they will.
"Right now, they're miles off it," he said. "It doesn't matter how good the manager is, if you don't have the right players it makes it really difficult.
"There's a reason why the other managers have struggled. Sooner or later the pressure's always going to come on.
"This weekend becomes a huge game. He doesn't need another poor result, otherwise all of a sudden you're going into the international break and everyone's talking about you. The winners tonight are the players who didn't play."

Georgia district hopes to install license-plate capturing cameras to fine drivers passing school buses
Officials estimate that drivers in the state illegally pass school buses over 9,000 times a day
A Georgia school district is looking to install stop-arm cameras on school buses to dissuade drivers from illegally passing — a move that warrants a $1,000 fine in the state.
DeKalb County Schools is looking to find a vendor to add cameras to over 1,000 school buses in the district. The buses already have cameras inside, but the stop-arm cameras would show what’s happening outside, CBS Atlanta reported.
“The goal of DeKalb County School District is to ensure we’re protecting 100 percent of our students 100 percent of the time by providing safe and reliable consistent transportation to and from school each and every day,” Director of Student Transportation Bernando Brown said.
The district, which transports about 45,000 students, says it plans to get cameras with multi-angle video, license plate recognition, GPS tagging and automatic activation. Data collected with the cameras would automatically be sent to law enforcement.
“The camera will actually be mounted right on the side of our bus,” Brown said. “Directly up under our stop arm. As long as no one passes the bus, there’s nothing to worry about.”
However, cars that pass buses will be tracked by the camera the entire time, Brown said.
A survey from the Governor’s Highway Safety Association found that 46 percent of children riding the school bus have had a close call with a dangerous driver.
The data also found that 53 percent of parents believe dangerous driving continues because motorists think they won’t get caught.
Georgia officials estimate that drivers in the state illegally pass school buses over 9,000 times a day.
“It’s pretty frequent,” Brown told the outlet. “We have certain areas in DeKalb County where it’s almost every time a bus stops, you’re going to see it.”
In Georgia, the fine for passing a school bus starts at $1,000.
The district says it hopes to install the cameras no later than January.

In September 2026, with the midterm elections only two months away, Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson appealed to voters that the GOP-led Congress gets things done.
For example, while speaking at the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas on Sept. 10, Johnson claimed (archived) the 119th Congress — which is ongoing as of this writing and scheduled to end on Jan. 3, 2027 — has been "the most productive Congress in 80 years":
The media won't tell you this, but this has been one of the most productive congresses in the history of the institution since 1789. In the House, we passed over 900 pieces of legislation, and that includes the Save America Act four times. It's been the most productive Congress in 80 years, and we're not done yet.
Social media users who shared the clip (archived, archived) focused on Johnson's "most productive Congress in 80 years" remark. Other videos of him making similar claims were shared on YouTube (archived).
Snopes contacted Johnson's staff to ask what metric he used when calling the 119th Congress the most productive in 80 years. We had not received a reply prior to publication but will update this article if we hear back.
In the absence of a response, we used multiple potential metrics to compare the productivity of the 119th Congress, which has a Republican-led House and Senate, to that of the 118th Congress (Republican-led House, Democrat-led Senate through caucusing) and the 117th Congress (Democrat-led House and Senate, the latter through caucusing and the vice president's tie-breaking votes).
Based on the metrics we used, the 119th Congress was not as productive as either of its two predecessors. Therefore, we've rated this claim false.
According to Congress.gov, the House of Representatives has passed or agreed upon 922 pieces of legislation as of Sept. 14, 2026 (though the 119th Congress is not complete until Jan. 3, 2027). During the 118th Congress, the House passed or agreed upon 995 pieces of Legislation. During the 117th Congress, the House passed or agreed upon 1,127.
It is possible the 119th Congress could surpass the 118th and 117th Congresses by its end. Even so, it would likely fall short of beating prior Congresses from the past 80 years, as measured by the number of bills passed or agreed upon by the House of Representatives. For example, there were 1,663 such bills in the 93rd Congress, which served between 1973 and 1974.
To measure Congress' productivity as a whole, we can compare what each Congress has passed or agreed upon in both the House and Senate, as well as how many laws they were able to pass. A piece of legislation needs to pass in both chambers of Congress and then be signed by the president to become law.
Both chambers of the 119th Congress have passed or agreed upon 139 pieces of legislation as of this writing. That's compared to 315 pieces of legislation from the 118th Congress and 397 pieces of legislation from the 117th Congress.
The 119th Congress has produced 110 new laws, whereas the 118th Congress made 274 and the 117th made 365.
GovTrack, which compiles statistics on legislative action in Congress, also measures total enacted legislation when including bills that ultimately passed by being included in another bill (via incorporation). This might include acts that were ultimately passed as part of an annual budget bill, for example. Even when including such legislation, the 119th Congress has so far enacted 429 pieces of legislation, according to GovTrack, as opposed to 619 pieces of legislation in the 118th Congress and 1,236 in the 117th Congress.
GovTrack also compiles a "Total" figure that includes: enacted legislation, enacted legislation (including via incorporation), passed resolutions, bills and resolutions that had a significant vote but weren't passed or enacted, failed legislation, vetoed bills, and bills and resolutions that were introduced or reported but saw no further action. The 119th Congress' total of 18,670 is bigger than the 117th's of 17,817, but is smaller than the 118th's of 19,315 and several of those in the 1970s, that ranged between 22,313 and 26,222.
In sum, based on every relevant metric Snopes could find, it is incorrect to call this Congress the most productive in the past 80 years — at least to date.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

What weapon could the US have put into space?
- Published
The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena.
Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.
So what could this weapon be, and what is wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry?
Advanced militaries already deploy satellites in space for range of purposes, from supplying secure communications to reconnaissance, and providing precise location information for targeted strikes and detecting missile launches.
As warfare become more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase.
Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US.
"I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless."
Bowen also would not rule out some sort of more disruptive and riskier weaponry, which could create a lot of debris and destruction.
"Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile of some sort that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said.
"Possibly some sort of close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well."
But while the weapon placed in orbit appears to be a first, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time.
In fact in the last 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites.
"Theoretically, these RPO sats can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC.
Bowen adds that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit."
This, he says, can be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites.
Thornton says that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability.
"The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike sats in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he says.
"From the Russian point of view they see Nato as having much better and more sats than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat."
Thornton adds a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EPM blast would 'fry' any unhardened sats over a wide expanse."
He says that, having so few satellites, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, which would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring sats designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers".

There's a battle brewing at Costco, and it's not over parking spaces.
The warehouse retailer will offer delivery across the US through DoorDash. The companies already worked together in Puerto Rico and some international markets, DoorDash said on Thursday.
One day earlier, Costco expanded its partnership with Uber Eats to 47 states, up from 17.
That's bad news for Instacart, which has worked with Costco since 2017.
DoorDash and Uber Eats both started out delivering restaurant orders. The more expansive partnerships with Costco are their latest move to expand into the grocery business — and, potentially, eat Instacart's lunch.
Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi called grocery and other retail sales "another trillion-dollar opportunity" on an earnings call in February. And DoorDash CEO Tony Xu has said that the service's growing number of partnerships with grocers gives it an edge over Amazon, which has been expanding its own grocery delivery facilities.
Amazon is building its own network of warehouses and getting its own delivery workers to bring groceries to customers' doors in as little as 30 minutes.
DoorDash, Instacart, and Uber Eats, meanwhile, largely compete by filling orders from traditional retailers' shelves with their own armies of gig workers.
Costco represents a special addition to the delivery services' offerings.
Costco's in-store visits from shoppers were up 18% over the last seven years, Business Insider previously reported. Visits to Walmart and Target were roughly flat over the same period.
The chain "ranked among the most-searched retailers not yet available on DoorDash," the delivery service said on Thursday.
Uber President and COO Andrew Macdonald recalled shopping at Costco on Saturdays with his father growing up in a Wednesday post on X. "I've already started carrying on the tradition with my own daughters," he wrote.
Instacart has a head start. Last year, for example, the delivery service started offering a credit on some orders to Costco executive members, who pay a higher annual membership fee at the retailer and receive more benefits.
The benefit is "continuing to deepen the relationship with Costco, but also with folks that are looking for that additional value," Instacart CFO Emily Reuter said on the service's earnings call in August.

Europe's EU Kids Act would ban social media access for children under 13
Fifteen would be the minimum age for minors to open their own account.
The European Commission has introduced the EU Kids Act, the most sweeping proposal yet to limit minors from accessing social media platforms. If adopted, the law would ban social media for kids under 13 and require parental supervision for 13- and 14-year-olds. Only when a child turns 15 would they be able to create their own social media accounts.
"Today, there is a robust body of evidence on the harm that social media does to a developing brain and personality, and too well parents see the effects of this," said EU Commission president Ursula Von der Leyen in a statement. "To be very clear, an age limit does not mean letting tech companies off the hook for the content of the platform. Platforms have been playing fast and loose with our children's mental health. Now we are reversing the burden of proof."
Children under 13 would not be able to access social media, but would be able to use "specially designed child-friendly video-sharing services through accounts managed by their guardian," the proposal states. Services on those "mini accounts" must be designed with safeguards like limited screen time up to one hour per day and offer adults an easy way to control what their kids see.
For kids aged 13 and 14, the proposal would allow parents to set up sub-accounts that would give their kids supervised access to "age-appropriate social media and video-sharing platforms," the act states. Services available on these sub-accounts would also be designed with safeguards, like limited social contact and one hour per day of screen time.
For platforms, the EU Kids Act would be among the first to force platforms to remove addictive features. Those would include recommendation algorithms that "drag minors into 'rabbit holes' of harmful contact," the Commission wrote. It would also block infinite scroll, nighttime push notifications and unsolicited contact from strangers. AI chatbots would have to be turned off by default and not be allowed to create emotional dependency.
Age verification is another key pillar, but has proved challenging to implement, as exemplified by territories like Australia. The EU would require platforms to perform such checks when someone opens a new account, and employ "reasonable proxies" like credit card details to estimate the age of current users. Apps must use age assurance tools that don't retain identity documents or biometric data, like the new EU age verification app.
Platforms would be obliged to submit compliance plans, with enforcement based on structures already in place under the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA). The Commission didn't specify sanction amounts, but under the DSA, penalties can reach six percent of a company's global annual turnover. It would also include a fast-track 90-day enforcement procedure.
"Considering the clear demand for urgent and comprehensive action at Union level, it is essential that the act is adopted swiftly," the EU wrote. Its passage isn't a given, though. France's top court blocked a similar proposal, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression.
The EU has a population of around 450 million people, so the EU Kids Act would affect more users than any other social media age restriction laws, if implemented. The ban of addictive feature like recommendation algorithms would also be a new twist. Meta and other tech platforms have yet to comment, but criticism so far is mainly around the problems of age verification and duplicative legislation. "Age verification remains a technical challenge, and parallel regulation to existing laws like the Digital Services Act is problematic and unnecessary," said Bernhard Rohleder, CEO of Germany's IT industry association BITKOM.

On Modi's birthday, CM Omar Abdullah wishes PM would grant J&K statehood
Omar Abdullah also advised the Ladakh leadership to not rely on Centre's verbal assurances regarding their struggle for constitutional safeguards.
Wishing Prime Minister Narendra Modi on his birthday, Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah on Thursday reiterated his demand to restore statehood, saying all they have received so far on the matter were verbal assurances.
PM Modi celebrated his 76th birthday on Thursday, September 17.
"What can I say as to what he (Modi) does… If nothing else, let him grant us statehood; what else could we want?" Abdullah said, when asked about what announcement he expected today, news agency PTI reported.
The J&K CM was in Amritsar for the inauguration of renovated heritage building of the Jammu & Kashmir House on Court Road.
“You all know what happened with us. We were told that statehood would be restored after the (J&K) elections. But nothing was given in writing; only verbal assurances were given,” he was quoted as saying, as he also advised the leadership of Ladakh not to rely on the Centre's verbal assurances regarding their struggle for constitutional safeguards with regard to land and jobs.
"Hence, I suggest to people and friends in Ladakh not to trust the Centre's words… Rather, have them in writing. We did not get anything in writing, and we are at the same place today. J&K has been a victim of the Centre's verbal assurances," Abdullah said.
Abdullah said that the Centre had outlined a three-step process – delimitation, Assembly elections and the restoration of statehood.
"Even in Parliament and in the Supreme Court, this assurance was given. While we saw delimitation and elections in J&K, in which people participated, statehood has not been restored even till now," he said.
The Centre on August 5, 2019, scrapped Article 370 of the Constitution that granted special status to the erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir and bifurcated it into two Union territories – J&K and Ladakh.
In December 2023, the Supreme Court upheld the Centre's decision to revoke the special status and create the two UTs but told the government to restore J&K's statehood as soon as possible.
In July, when Abdullah announced a fresh phase of its campaign for the restoration of statehood, he had said the the National Conference had exhausted its patience and would now intensify its movement by taking the demand directly to the national capital, news agency PTI reported.

"Enough is enough! There will be no more waiting!" Abdullah had declared before a large gathering of party workers.
Later that month, Abdullah said that statehood was an imperative or basic need for restoring Jammu and Kashmir’s special status, stressing that Article 370 restoration is meaningless without statehood.
“We are seeking the base i.e statehood from this government. And Article 370 ( restoration) is meaningless without statehood,” Omar said at a press conference after he and party leaders’ returned from Delhi following a protest seeking restoration of J&K’s statehood.

Archibald V. Hill and Otto Meyerhof studied how muscles use chemical energy to contract and recover. Hill measured the heat produced by working muscles, while Meyerhof traced the relationship between oxygen consumption and lactic acid metabolism. Their work earned them the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
The prize was divided equally. Hill was recognised “for his discovery relating to the production of heat in the muscle”, while Meyerhof was recognised “for his discovery of the fixed relationship between the consumption of oxygen and the metabolism of lactic acid in the muscle”. The prize was awarded for 1922 but presented in 1923 because the Nobel Committee had initially decided that no 1922 nomination met the required criteria.
Measuring muscle heat
Hill approached muscle physiology as a problem in physics as well as biology. Working largely with frog muscles, he developed precise methods for measuring the very small amounts of heat generated during contraction.
The changes were tiny. In one experiment described in his Nobel lecture, a single contraction of a frog’s sartorius muscle at 20°C raised its temperature by no more than about 0.003°C. Hill used sensitive instruments and carefully controlled contractions to separate heat produced during activity from heat generated during recovery.
His measurements showed that heat production did not end when the muscle stopped contracting. A second phase, which Hill called recovery heat, continued after contraction and depended on oxygen. When oxygen was removed, this recovery heat was abolished.
This was important because it showed that the energy changes associated with muscle contraction and recovery occurred in distinct phases rather than as one continuous process.
Meyerhof traces the chemistry
Meyerhof investigated the chemical side of the same problem. In experiments on frog muscle, he measured heat production and oxygen consumption and followed the conversion of carbohydrates into lactic acid.
He showed that during muscle activity, lactic acid was formed from carbohydrate. During recovery, some of the lactic acid was oxidised while the remainder was converted back into carbohydrate. These observations helped establish the relationship between oxygen use and lactic acid metabolism for which he received the Nobel Prize.
Meyerhof’s work went further. Between 1918 and 1922, he provided evidence that glycogen was converted into lactic acid when oxygen was absent. He also found that only a fraction of the lactic acid produced during anaerobic muscle activity was subsequently oxidised in the presence of oxygen, with much of the remainder being reconverted to glycogen.
Two sides of muscle metabolism
Hill and Meyerhof were investigating different aspects of the same physiological problem. Hill measured the physical consequences of muscle activity -- heat, work and energy expenditure. Meyerhof examined the associated chemical reactions.
Their findings connected the physical and chemical sides of muscle metabolism. Hill’s measurements of recovery heat could be explained by Meyerhof’s observations on lactic acid and oxygen consumption. Hill himself acknowledged that Meyerhof’s biochemical work helped complete the picture that physical measurements alone could not provide.
A link to modern metabolism
Meyerhof’s research contributed to the emerging understanding of glycolysis, the pathway through which cells break down glucose and other sugars to obtain energy.
His observations also led to what became known as the Pasteur-Meyerhof effect: respiration can suppress the breakdown of carbohydrates through glycolysis. His work provided early evidence that energy transformations in living cells could involve cyclical processes, an idea that became important in the development of modern intermediary metabolism.
The terminology and biochemical models have since changed substantially. Muscle metabolism is now understood to involve multiple pathways and energy carriers, including ATP, rather than being explained simply through lactic acid.
An interesting part of Meyerhof’s scientific career is that he did not remain committed to every interpretation that emerged from his early work.
The discovery of creatine phosphate in 1926 led him to question the idea that lactic acid itself was directly responsible for supplying the energy required for muscle contraction. He subsequently revised aspects of the model that had become associated with his work.
The Nobel recognition
Hill and Meyerhof delivered their Nobel lectures on December 12, 1923. Hill’s lecture was titled The Mechanism of Muscular Contraction, while Meyerhof’s was titled Energy Conversions in Muscle.
Their work established quantitative approaches to studying muscle metabolism, bringing together measurements of heat, mechanical work, oxygen consumption and chemical changes.
More than a century later, the details of muscle energy metabolism are understood in far greater molecular detail. But Hill’s measurements of heat and energy and Meyerhof’s work on oxygen, glycogen and lactic acid were important steps in establishing muscle as a system whose mechanical activity could be linked to measurable chemical and thermodynamic processes.

England squad: Will Cole Palmer, Phil Foden and Trent Alexander-Arnold be left out again after World Cup snubs?
Thomas Tuchel is set to name his first England squad since the World Cup on Friday; having stated publicly that England's DNA does not allow for ball-retaining passers, can he continue to leave the likes of Cole Palmer, Phil Foden and Trent Alexander-Arnold out?
Thursday 17 September 2026 16:43, UK
Cole Palmer's outstanding form this season has put him in a strong position for an England recall, with the Chelsea man the most likely to be included from all the big names left out of the World Cup squad.
Palmer, along with Phil Foden and Trent Alexander-Arnold, was a headline omission from Thomas Tuchel's tournament squad in May, but he is one of the most startlingly in-form players in the Premier League right now, and the smart money is on him winning his international place back.
In the hugely oversubscribed No 10 role, the England boss went with Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers and Eberechi Eze in May, but Palmer is now fully fit after groin problems limited him to just 26 appearances last season, and his form has flourished.
Two goals and two assists show that. Only his team-mate Joao Pedro has more in the Premier League so far this season and only Bruno Fernandes has created more chances and had more shots combined (25) than Palmer (24).
