- England news and analysis | Follow our England blog
It also feels like a space may have opened up for Palmer, with Eze's indifferent form for Arsenal. While starting in Europe and the Carabao Cup, Eze has yet to start in the Premier League so far this season.
Morgan Gibbs-White is in with a shout, after an impressive start to the campaign. But Tuchel constantly talks about "connections" between players as the key to England's success, and right now it is hard to argue there is a better attacking connection in the Premier League than Palmer and his close friend Rogers. There certainly is not an all-English one.
Will Tuchel try to change England 'DNA'?
This squad selection will be the first staging post in Tuchel's brave new post-World Cup era. Having stated publicly that England's DNA does not allow for ball-retaining passers, can he continue to leave Palmer, Foden and Alexander-Arnold in exile - three generational talents in terms of their passing and attacking prowess?
The issue here is that Tuchel is not a man to admit he was wrong. Like many, if not all, of the very best coaches in the world, there is an in-built self-belief - an arrogance, some would say - which is very hard to shake. It is partly what gives him his aura.
And if Tuchel does recall one of those big three, does that show the mask is slipping? Plenty in the media will pounce and take it as proof that the England boss got it wrong on the biggest stage when he named his World Cup squad three months ago. But he will also be criticised if he leaves those superstars out again. It is a lose-lose.
Despite his sending off in the Manchester derby last weekend, Foden has started the season in fine form. He leads the Premier League in assists after a ball carry (2), alongside Cody Gakpo and Julio Enciso. And of all the English players at Tuchel's disposal, he is probably the most technically adept with the ball at his feet. It remains to be seen whether Foden fits into the England plans right now.
Issues in defence
Alexander-Arnold may struggle to force his way back in, despite the glaring right-back issues Tuchel faced at the World Cup. Reece James and Tino Livramento both suffered injuries, leaving many to lament the Real Madrid star's absence, especially when centre-back Trevoh Chalobah was called up as a late replacement for Livramento instead.
But Tuchel has been adamant that the former Liverpool full-back's profile does not suit how he wants his England side to play, and it would be a big shift in the manager's philosophy if he went back on that now.
Alexander-Arnold has started only two LaLiga games this season, yet he has managed more successful crosses than all but two defenders in the league (6).
Tuchel knows top-quality delivery comes standard with Alexander-Arnold, but the manager has always thought defensive prowess matters more.
Tuchel does have something of a defensive crisis. The absences of John Stones, Dan Burn, Djed Spence and Ben White due to injury mean there are plenty of opportunities at the back. James has also missed Chelsea training this week, but has not been ruled out.
Despite those doubts, it still feels unlikely that Harry Maguire will get the nod for an international recall. Speaking out in frustration about his World Cup omission - the day before Tuchel publicly named the squad - was not well received by the England hierarchy.
The 33-year-old has been ever-present and impressive in Manchester United's four league games so far this season. He is currently ranked third in the Premier League for ball-carrying.
Newcastle left-back Lewis Hall - another controversial omission from the World Cup squad - is expected to get the chance this time in the Nations League. His consistency is clear and he has been excellent again this season - the best in the Premier League for winning possession in the defensive third (19 times) and fifth for successful blocks (5).
Whether Maguire's United team-mate Kobbie Mainoo is included in this Nations League squad remains to be seen. He did not play a minute of football at the World Cup, and was thoroughly disillusioned by the end.
Sky Sports News expected him to be selected for the third-place play-off match, but back pain developed in the final training session before the game, ruling him out. Nevertheless, his form for Manchester United so far has made him a strong England candidate.
Who will support Kane up front?
Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin is pushing hard for a recall after an explosive start to the season. His double against Newcastle on Monday means it is four goals in six games so far.
It is form Tuchel cannot ignore, especially since Calvert-Lewin's main rival Ollie Watkins is now playing in the Saudi Pro League. Watkins' move to Al Hilal has seen him start in sparkling form, however, with three goals and two assists in four appearances.
Ivan Toney, who was the surprise inclusion at the World Cup, is unlikely to be considered for selection this time. He is due to be in court in Westminster in the middle of the international break to answer charges of assault causing actual bodily harm. His lawyer says he is looking forward to the opportunity to clear his name.
Despite the excitement around Max Dowman's performances for Arsenal and his two goals in the Carabao Cup win over Ipswich, no one expects an early call-up to the senior squad. The 16-year-old has not yet played for England's U21s, which is a more likely route as the FA, similarly to Mikel Arteta, carefully manage his minutes and his progression.
Dean Henderson has a foot injury, meaning there is space for a third goalkeeper to be called up alongside the guaranteed Jordan Pickford and James Trafford.

Russian attack on Ukraine's capital injures at least 16
Authorities say at least 16 people were injured in Russian attacks on Ukraine's capital
KYIV, Ukraine -- A Russian barrage of missiles and drones targeting Ukraine's capital injured at least 16 people overnight and into Thursday morning, local authorities said.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said the attacks were recorded at more than 10 locations. A 10-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy were among the injured, the administration said in a statement on Telegram.
Ukraine’s Air Force said it destroyed or suppressed 131 Russian aerial targets in the overnight attack. The main areas targeted were Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions, it said. Strikes were recorded at 36 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell on five locations. The attack involved ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and 157 drones and decoys, it said.
In the Dniprovsky district, a warehouse, an office building, residential buildings and cars were damaged, the statement said. A warehouse was damaged in the Solomyansky district, while a warehouse and cars were damaged in Darnitsky district.
In the Podilsky district, the roof of a non-residential building was damaged, authorities said.

Congress members fleeing DC all say the same thing about filling their gas tanks
Trump insists rising fuel prices are ‘a very inexpensive price to pay,’ for his war in Iran. Eric Garcia asks Republicans and Democrats on Capitol Hill about the last time they stopped for gas
President Donald Trump has said that rising gas prices are a small price to pay for the war in Iran. But members of Congress in both parties are warning that this could become a crisis for Republicans in the midterm election.
The Independent spoke with members of Congress this week as Speaker Mike Johnson sent the House of Representatives home early to campaign for the midterm elections after only three days in session.
“It’s a lot lately,” Rep. Aaron Bean (R-Fla.) said. The average cost for a gallon of gas as of Thursday in Florida is $4.30, according to AAA, slightly lower than the national average of just over $4.40.
And gas prices don’t discriminate by vehicle. Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) uses a Jeep Wagoneer SUV and said she feels the pinch.
“It was $100, close to $100, which is expensive,” she told The Independent. In South Carolina, the average cost of gas is $4.11. Mace will not return to Congress next year after a failed bid for governor. But she had a word of caution for her colleagues.
“The No. 1 issue, everybody knows, is cost of living, and neither party has addressed it,” she said. “I mean, they're full of s**t. They're bullsh**ing people. They're lying to the electorate about what they can do.”
She also panned Trump’s promise to give every American adult citizen a $5,000 check if Republicans hold the majority.
On the other end of the spectrum, Democratic Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said she pays significantly more than she did in the beginning of the year.
“I think it was about $45 and I’ve got a [gas-electric hybrid] Prius,” Dexter told The Independent.
The price of gas has spiked ever since Trump began the war in Iran in late February. In response, the Iranian regime closed off the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world’s oil supply passes. Fighting between Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen against Saudi Arabia also caused the price of fuel to spike.
Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) said that it cost him $69 to fill up his tank last time.
"We got a war going, I don't blame the president for that,” he told The Independent. “He does need to explain to the American people."
Norman attempted to run for the Republican nomination for governor like Mace, but lost. He then tried to challenge Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) for the Republican nominate to replace her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, in the Senate but lost.
Some Republicans dodged the question. Rep. Nick LaLota of Long Island dodged when asked, as did Rep. Andrew Clyde of Georgia, a member of the hardline House Freedom Caucus.
President Donald Trump has been more blunt in his assessment.

Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories on Tuesday said it is foraying into the biosimilar immuno-oncology therapy segment in India with the launch of Nivorz, a biosimilar of Bristol Myers Squibb’s Opdivo (nivolumab).
The biosimilar has been developed and manufactured entirely in-house at its biologics facility in Bachupally, Hyderabad. The launch reflects the company’s end-to-end capabilities across the biosimilar value chain, from development through commercialisation, Dr. Reddy’s said.
In 2025, the immuno-oncology market in India was estimated to be around ₹3,900 crore and predominantly driven by checkpoint inhibitors such as nivolumab, pembrolizumab and toripalimab, it said.

Ramana said.
The company said Nivorz was evaluated through a multi-country clinical development programme involving 288 patients, including 252 from India and 36 from Russia, and demonstrated comparable efficacy, safety, pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity to the reference nivolumab. Global Head of Biologics at Dr. Reddy’s Sridevi Khambhampaty said “the launch of Nivorz marks an important milestone for the company’s biologics business. It reinforces our commitment to expanding patient access to high-quality and reflects our continued focus on developing complex biosimilars.”

Fiji declares national crisis as HIV infects one in every 60 adults
Pacific nation reported 27 per cent surge in new diagnoses last year
Fiji declared HIV a national crisis following a 27 per cent surge in new diagnoses last year, raising fears that an outbreak previously concentrated among people injecting drugs was spreading broader across the Pacific nation.
In a statement published on Facebook, the government revealed that 2,016 individuals were diagnosed with HIV in 2025, estimating that one in every 60 adults was now living with the infection.
The announcement noted that 59 infants were born with HIV last year, with 18 dying before reaching their first birthday.
Officials stated that increased testing capabilities had exposed previously undetected cases, allowing patients to access earlier care.
In response, authorities intend to expand free, voluntary, and confidential testing, along with preventative medications, harm-reduction initiatives for intravenous drug users and medical treatment.
According to UNAIDS, the nation of 900,000 people is facing one of the steepest global increases in new HIV infections. The agency estimated that 9,100 Fijians were living with the virus last year, yet only 39 per cent were aware of their status and merely 22 per cent were undergoing antiretroviral therapy.
"Fiji has recognised the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response," UNAIDS executive director Winnie Byanyima said. "It is also a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over."
For cases where the mode of transmission was identified, UNAIDS noted that sexual contact accounted for over half, while injecting drugs represented more than 42 per cent.
The agency praised official plans to launch a needle-and-syringe programme and broaden availability of pre-exposure prophylaxis, a medication used to lower the risk of contracting HIV.
The government recently established a five-minister cabinet subcommittee to remove barriers to action, while officials reiterated that discriminating against anybody with HIV was illegal and care remained accessible nationwide.
Although severe, Fiji's rate of one in 60 adults living with HIV remains lower than some regions of Africa, where close to one in 35 adults carries the virus, according to WHO data.

Srinagar, Sep 17: Jammu and Kashmir Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Thursday said the Government of India has planned a month-long programme to mark Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday, with various events scheduled across the country.
Speaking at a programme organized with sick children at Government Medical College, Bemina, Sinha highlighted what he described as the achievements of the Modi government in economic growth, infrastructure development and welfare schemes.
“Across the country, the Prime Minister’s birthday is being celebrated from today. The government has issued a detailed month-long programme,” Sinha said, adding that a programme had also been organized at Bemina with sick children to mark the occasion.
He said India had moved from being known as a “fragile five economy” to a “top five economy” over the past 12 years.
“It is a matter of pride for the country that a country which was once known as a fragile five economy has, over the past 12 years, through the efforts of the Prime Minister, become a top five economy,” Sinha said.
“If we look at the economic growth rate, broadly speaking, our current economic growth rate is 7.8%, which is the best in the world,” he said.
Sinha credited Modi with the country’s progress across sectors, particularly infrastructure and welfare.
“The progress the country has made in every sector over the past 12 years certainly deserves credit to the Honorable Prime Minister,” he said.
Referring specifically to Jammu and Kashmir, Sinha said the Union Territory had witnessed major changes in infrastructure and social security schemes.
“If I talk about Jammu and Kashmir, whether it is infrastructure here or social security schemes, or ending the discriminatory system, Jammu and Kashmir has witnessed quite revolutionary changes in six years,” he said.
Sinha said more than ₹1.5 lakh crore worth of work was underway in Jammu and Kashmir in road infrastructure and tunnels.
“If we talk about road infrastructure and tunnels, roughly more than ₹1.5 lakh crore worth of work is underway here,” he said.
He also referred to the completion of the railway connection to Kashmir, describing it as the fulfillment of a long-standing dream.
“There had been a long-standing dream of connecting Kashmir by railway, and that dream has been fulfilled,” Sinha said.
Highlighting welfare measures, he said 25 crore people had moved out of poverty, while 80 crore people were being provided free rations.
“Broadly speaking, today 25 crore people have been able to come out of poverty in six years. The Government of India is providing free rations to 80 crore people. “I would certainly appeal to the people of Jammu and Kashmir to participate enthusiastically in the month-long programme,” he said.

“I would appeal to the citizens of Jammu and Kashmir to increase their participation in the programmes being held throughout the month and to celebrate them with enthusiasm,” he said.

There is reason to be cautiously optimistic about the trajectory of the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the director-general of the World Health Organization said Wednesday.
In a news conference in Geneva, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said disease transmission rates are declining in most of the affected provinces, though he warned there are months of work remaining to get the outbreak under control.
“The epidemic continues to grow and continues to kill,” Tedros said. He noted that while there has been a reduction in cases in Ituri province — the epicenter of the epidemic — that decline is based on a high level of cases to begin with.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, is the second-largest on record. As of Sunday, there had been 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths occurring across seven provinces in northeastern DRC.
That’s a quarter of the size of the West African Ebola outbreak, but that earlier outbreak ran for about two years. In this case, the outbreak was only discovered to be underway in mid-May, though investigations suggest it may have started early this year.
Complicating efforts to contain the spread of the deadly virus is the fact that this part of the DRC has been wracked by violence for decades, leaving huge numbers of people displaced and struggling to feed their families.
Early in the outbreak, Tedros talked about having visited the outbreak zone and being struck by the fact that many people seemed to view Ebola as a lesser of evils. In their view, he said, more people in the region die from malaria or hunger, or in political violence.
He said people he spoke to suggested that outsiders only turn up to help in response to Ebola outbreaks they fear could spread to their own countries.
The rise in Ebola deaths as the outbreak has grown has moderated that view to a degree, Tedros noted.
“There is improvement. There is better cooperation. They’ve started to realize that this thing is serious,” he said.
In related news, the WHO said it expects a Phase 3 randomized clinical trial of Ebola vaccines to begin in the next couple of weeks, with the first vaccine to be put into the field being Merck’s Ervebo, which targets the Zaire Ebola virus. There is some evidence it may also provide cross-protection against Bundibugyo. When vaccines that specifically target Bundibugyo complete Phase 1 safety and dosing trials, they will be added to that trial, said Meg Doherty, director of the agency’s department of science for health.
Independent of that trial, frontline workers in hot spots are going to be offered the vaccine as part of an observational trial that should start later this week or early next week, she said. That study, being conducted by DRC and Doctors Without Borders, will give participants a shot of Ervebo, followed a month later by a shot of an experimental vaccine designed to protect against the Sudan version of the Ebola virus. The approach will compare cases among people who were vaccinated versus people who were not.

The Australian athlete who caused a storm by winning a Hyrox event in China despite soiling herself during the race has apologised to the “people of China” and rival athletes in a statement online.
Posting on Instagram, Joanna Wietrzyk, said she offered a “sincere apology” to the “people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing”.
Footage of Wietrzyk, a world record holder, went viral after it showed her competing in – and winning – Saturday’s event with demanding exercises and using communal equipment, despite having faecal matter running down her legs.
But she admitted in her post on Thursday night that she should have “stepped off the track” and that there is “more to life than racing”.
“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness,” Wietrzyk wrote.
“Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused.”
Furhtermore, she said, she would forfeit the points from winning the event.
 ”I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected. I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away. On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned.”
Hyrox, an increasingly popular fitness competition launched in Germany in 2017, is now held in locations across the world. It debuted in mainland China in late 2024.
In each race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at shared high-intensity stations – including a rowing machine, sled pushes, burpee jumps, medicine ball throws and lunges while carrying a sandbag.
Ending her statement, Wietrzyk said: “Thank you to those standing by me, both as an athlete and as a person, during this time, and to everyone who has reached out with kindness and support. It means more to me than I can properly express right now. I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise.”

What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
- Published
The UN has just called for the predominant world map to be replaced with one that more accurately reflects the true size of continents like Africa.
The "Correct the Map" resolution adopted by the General Assembly aims to fix the discrepancy on the Mercator map, in which the African continent is shown as being of similar size to Greenland - even though it is in reality about 14 times larger.
It adopted a new map, the Equal Earth projection, which better represents the true sizes of landmasses - but comes with problems of its own.
There have been many prominent attempts over the years to solve the problem of accurately representing the surface of a sphere on a flat rectangle, each with its own benefits and drawbacks.
Mercator map
The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.
Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University London College explained.
"He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."
To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.
His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.
The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.
More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.
But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.
For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities.
"Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.
Equal Earth map
The Equal Earth map aims to address this problem with the Mercator projection.
It was developed by a team of cartographers in 2018 to present the size and shape of landmasses more accurately.
As a result, the Equal Earth map was initially adopted by 54 members of the African Union, before being adopted by the UN.
But to do this, it sacrifices the straight lines that made the Mercator projection perfect for navigating with - and it cannot be used for measuring the true distance between different places.
"You can preserve area, or you can preserve shape, or you can preserve distance and direction, but not everything at once perfectly, because otherwise you'd be back to a sphere," Cheshire said.
Peters map
The Peters world map was designed by German historian Arno Peters in the early 1970s. The rectangular map is based on the projection first described by Scottish cartographer James Gall in 1855.
The projection sacrifices accuracy of shape in favour of accuracy of scale. So, polar regions are squished, while the bits near the equator are stretched.
This fixes the Greenland-Africa size issue, allowing those who use it to get a sense of the comparative size of different landmasses, all while preserving straight lines of longitude and latitude.
However, the map severely distorts the shapes of Earth's landmasses, making them all look slightly off.
The straight lines on the Peters map do not represent true constant compass bearings and so are useless for navigation.

Every day, a newsletter from the prediction market Polymarket hits my inbox with a subject line that could easily come from any number of politics-focused newspapers or magazines. Recent entries include “Houthis Reveal New Precision Strike Capabilities,” “BREAKING: Trump Unveils Green Energy Beam,” and “World War I, 2.0?”
These dispatches are roundups with breathless summaries of the day’s top stories, linking out to corresponding Polymarket markets—yes, this thing will happen; no, it won’t. As far as business news analysis goes, the newsletter is not exactly Bloomberg’s Money Stuff, or even Emily Sundberg’s Feed Me—but it’s recognizably a commercial editorial product, and one that plays an important role in the prediction market ecosystem.
The industry is currently embroiled in a series of legal battles over whether prediction markets are financial services (the view held by the markets and the federal government) or gambling platforms (the position of many state authorities and regulators). The fight over what kind of companies these are could end up in the Supreme Court, but in the meantime, both Polymarket and its even-more-popular archrival, Kalshi, have successfully positioned themselves as new media organizations too. For two companies associated with risk, it’s a notably old-school hedge.
All kinds of tech startups have launched editorial projects—did you know the alternative dating app Feeld has a surprisingly good magazine?—but the leading prediction markets are entrenching themselves into the mainstream media apparatus in a particularly aggressive way. A recent report noted that they’re integrated into a quarter of the top 20 companies listed in the S&P 500’s Communications Services sector. Polymarket has partnerships with Dow Jones and Substack, while Kalshi has deals with CNN, CNBC, and Fox Corp.
None of the agreements facilitate trading. Instead, they’re mainly about data sharing; news outlets want to know what people are putting their money on, and prediction markets are happy to oblige. The deals showcase prediction markets as information channels—places to go to find out about what’s happening. They’ve given Polymarket and Kalshi much-needed boosts in credibility and offered a straightforward introduction to the wider public. Prediction market boosters hype these products as “truth machines,” revealing public sentiment more accurately than polling or traditional reporting; when media outlets decide the odds themselves are newsworthy, they reinforce that message.
“Given the forecasting success of the markets, it's clear there is informational value,” says Kalshi spokesperson Jack Such. “And three out of four users don't trade, which suggests the informational use case is popular enough to be taken very seriously.” (Polymarket declined to comment.)
Providing data is only a small part of how these companies function as new media entities. On social media, their official accounts post like news outlets, adopting a vernacular that mashes up PopCrave’s frenzied sensibility with Bloomberg’s coverage areas. (The efforts haven’t been wholly reliable: A New York Times analysis earlier this year found that Polymarket’s newsy social accounts have published “false and misleading information.”)
Chief executive and founder Shayne Coplan has referred to the company’s partnership with X as “News 2.0.” In 2024, the company hinted at even more expansive ambitions, recruiting for an editor in chief role to lead “content and data journalism” efforts. It never made that hire, although political analyst and media founder Nate Silver came on later that year as an adviser. But on its careers page, the company beckons prospective employees by playing this angle up: “Become the new front page of the internet.”
Kalshi is less inclined to describe itself this way. When asked if it considered itself a media company, Such, the spokesperson, tells WIRED that it does not, though the markets themselves have “quasi-media” attributes because they follow the news. “We see ourselves as a financial exchange,” he says.
Sure. But why not both? Financial services companies have jumped into the media sector before, most obviously Bloomberg, which initially focused on providing market data and financial analytics before expanding to include journalism products. More recently, the online trading hub Robinhood—now also a Polymarket competitor with its own prediction market offerings—ran a media subsidiary called Sherwood before winding it down earlier this summer. Then there’s Hunterbook, which operates both an investigative outlet called Hunterbook News and a hedge fund that executes trades based on its outlet’s investigations.
Polymarket doesn’t have a dedicated subsidiary or editorial arm. But it has launched a weekly podcast called What Are the Odds? in partnership with the podcast network Dear Media. It stars a rotating cast of hosts known for celebrity news content, including podcasters and cocktail entrepreneurs Claudia and Jackie Oshry, the daughters of a prominent anti-Muslim activist.
It has also partnered with a prediction-markets-focused media startup called Eventual, which raised money from venture capital firms like Lightshed Capital as well as serial media entrepreneur and Bustle Digital Group owner Bryan Goldberg, who was also an early investor in Polymarket itself. “Polymarket's role in shaping media narratives was always a big piece of the puzzle,” Goldberg, who is best known for operating 2010s media brands like Bustle and Elite Daily, tells WIRED.
Much like those two digital media companies once did, Polymarket has put its own spin on engagement via rage-baiting. What’s the 2026 version of an ill-advised xoJane personal essay riling up Twitter? It looks an awful lot like the podcaster Amanda Hirsch getting eviscerated on TikTok for creating paid content for Polymarket promoting how people could wager on the outcome of the Lindsay Clancy trial. The backlash was severe enough that Hirsch, who is another one of the What Are the Odds? hosts, apologized.
There are obvious advantages to these companies going all-in on media strategy. For starters, it turbocharges brand awareness, doubling as marketing. For companies that like to talk about how they might be used to protect investments, creating a potential revenue generator separate from trading fees is itself a way to diversify risk. It also helps the markets shape their own narratives.
In a January 2026 announcement about its decision to partner with Polymarket, Wall Street Journal publisher and Dow Jones CEO Almar Latour described the prediction market as a “rapidly growing source of real-time insight into collective beliefs about future events.” It did not mention that the company’s flagship product remains banned in the US. (Polymarket now has an app that is federally regulated in the United States called Polymarket US, though it offers a narrower range of markets than its original decentralized product.)
Not every media outlet is embracing these markets as a potential partner or peer. The New York Times recently scuttled a potential partnership between Kalshi and its sports-focused subsidiary, The Athletic, after pushback from its union.
Still, things aren’t slowing down. Earlier this month, Polymarket launched a group-chat feature called Squads, with the idea that people wagering on its platforms want to socialize and strategize together. The recognition goes both ways. As NPR first reported, Meta considered buying Kalshi and later discussed launching its own internal prediction market. The social media juggernaut sniffing around the prediction market space isn’t an indication that the company is hungry to get into trading or gambling—it’s more evidence that this is part of the future of media. Meta, despite its best efforts, remains a digital media company, and it’s savvy enough to see that these markets are increasingly part of how people use the internet.
As these companies keep expanding their reach, their media maneuvers will only grow more important. There may well be other efforts to refine editorial products in the near future, even a renewed attempt to hire journalists.

They also serve science, who are not scientists. One of science’s most egregious instances of epistemic dominance, where a powerful institution overrode and exploited a marginalised individual - was Henrietta Lacks – donor of the famous, immortal HeLa cell line. Cells extracted from her, without permission, transformed medical research, but her story was ignored, erased and obscured for decades. The scientific world that generously used this unique cell line for successful research into virology, vaccines, genetics and even cancer care, but the erasure of the donor of those cells was historic in its completeness.
Lacks, an African American tobacco farmer from southern United States, sought treatment at the ‘coloured ward’ in Johns Hopkins Centre for cervical cancer, way back in 1951. While it was common for medical professionals, in those days, to take samples and cells without the express permission of the patient, particularly if it was an African American woman, these cells were different. Johns Hopkins used the cells from her tumour to culture a line of cells that was extraordinarily durable outside the body. Usually human cells die outside of the body. Anonymised by a laboratory acronymn, Lacks’ cells (HeLa) turned out to be the first human cells to successfully grow, divide, and survive indefinitely outside the human body.
HeLa was a miracle that scientists had chanced upon. With HeLa, they could mass produce human cells in a standard format that could be used for biomedical research, and would underpin several breakthrough discoveries, that would revolutionise medical care. No one knew, however, of the immense exploitation behind this miracle cell line, and the profound lack of consent in procuring the samples.
Lacks, who died at merely 31 years, and was buried in an unmarked grave, remained invisible, not even a footnote, completely uncredited and her family entirely in the dark about her contribution to the world of science. Henrietta Lacks’ family first learned about her cells in nearly quarter of a century later, when scientists reached out to them, requesting blood samples once they suspected that the HeLa cell line had contaminated other research samples. This came as a bolt on the family, who could not fathom how cells from their mother had survived this long outside of her, and how this strange situation had come to be. While the academic world and several sections of the corporate world benefited richly from the HeLa cell line, Lacks’ own family had remained entrenched in poverty and struggling to make ends meet. The struggle of the family to come to terms with this exploitation, and the battles they had to fight with the system and science itself is well curated by Rebecca Sloot in her best selling book The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks.
In the 1950s, bioethical norms, particularly around informed consent were either non existent, or, at best, weak. But, in this particular case, Lacks was a black farmer from a rural unit, being treated in a segregated section in a large hospital. Consequently, an entrenched rascism, still alive in the southern United States in the 50s, and class bias contributed in good measure to the shabby treatment of this very valuable patient. Unhesitatingly and boldly, Sloot dragged this out into the open, through the book, knocking on the consciousness of the world and science, biomedical research, urging a discussion, a debate and at the end of it, a nod to what happened. It took years before these units would shamefully acknowledge the great injustice meted out to Lacks’ and her family.
The book, published in 2010, drew attention to the larger debate of patient rights and bodily autonomy. Sloot also underlined the fact that donors need to be acknowledged, heralding a new woke world of bio ethics, laboratory practices and the responsibilities of researchers. No longer could a moral failure be allowed to take patients for a ride, rules and regulations should replace the conscience and a situation like this would hopefully never happen again.
But this story does not end this way. After nearly 75 years of fighting this battle, the Lacks’ family finally found some closure. Reparation was finally achieved with the family settling with Johns Hopkins and other associated institutions in a landmark agreement that firstly acknowledged harm had been done, and also included measures to compensate the family and honour Lacks’ role in science. This included significant financial recompense, and involving the family into research using HeLa cells.
This agreement did reinforce the supremacy of informed consent practices, thus refining research ethics policy, but it also expanded the involvement of the patient and the community in research work. The Lacks’ family success is a milestone of sorts in biomedical research, with calls now being made to improve how institutions and labs credit how their biological materials, and also look at reparative action for families historically exploited by science.
Lacks’ story is a cautionary tale for science. It’s a reckoning with what has historically gone wrong, to set some wrongs right , and make sure the violations of the past are not repeated, but do inform the future, so that scientific progress can proceed without losing respect for human dignity. For this stupendous achievement, we have Henrietta Lacks to thank. From being denied even the footnote in history, she has created a brave new world in science.

Locked offices and millions in donations: Inside India's little-known political parties
- Published
There was little to suggest that the locked flat in Anand, in the western Indian state of Gujarat, was the headquarters of a political party.
There was no signboard, campaign poster or obvious trace of political activity. But on paper, the Satyawadi Rakshak Party had recently received an extraordinary amount of money.
In the financial year ending in March 2024, official records show the Gujarat-based party received more than 3.3bn rupees (approx $35m; £25m) in donations. A few months later, when India held the world's largest general election, it fielded a single candidate, who lost his deposit.
Its accounts say that 84.8m rupees went towards election campaigning, while more than 3.16bn rupees were listed as spending on "public welfare".
"We have spent the money on charity but have not maintained records," said Swati Ben Patel, the party's president, who lives in the same residential complex as its registered office.
The party is one of more than 2,800 Registered Unrecognised Political Parties, or RUPPs - a vast but little-known tier of Indian politics. These parties are legally registered but have not won enough votes or seats to be recognised at the state or national level.
Some contest elections only sporadically or field a handful of candidates. Yet, like larger parties, they can receive donations and claim tax exemptions. Donors can also reduce their taxable income through eligible contributions.
The rules are intended to support political activity, but tax officials say they can be misused.
A months-long BBC investigation examined six RUPPs that reported some of the largest donations in 2023-24. Together, they received about 17bn rupees, despite fielding just 15 candidates in the 2024 election. None came close to winning.
The gap between the money some parties receive and their limited electoral presence has drawn increasing scrutiny from India's tax authorities.
An internal Income Tax department document reviewed by the BBC shows that officials have been investigating suspected misuse of RUPPs since at least 2022.
It identifies 55.91bn rupees in suspected bogus political donations made by taxpayers seeking tax benefits, as well as 6.65bn rupees in foreign transactions. It also notes possible violations of tax, foreign-funding and election laws.
None of the six parties examined by the BBC has been publicly named in these wider inquiries. The BBC has not established that any of them committed financial wrongdoing.
But in several cases, it found a striking gap between the way the organisations were described in their records and what reporters encountered on the ground.
Some registered offices were closed or appeared inactive. Party officials sometimes said they did not control their organisations' finances or could not explain how large sums had been spent.
The BBC found signs that the political presence of some of these parties was limited. Although their websites sometimes carried photographs of door-to-door canvassing, one candidate, Indradevi Hiralal of the Garib Kalyan Party, said she had not visited her constituency to campaign in 2024. She showed a single poster printed for the election.
There were also signs of scrutiny from the authorities. Three parties said they or their officials had faced action by the Income Tax department. At a fourth, a relative of a party official said the family home had been searched. The other two denied facing such action.
Tax authorities in Bihar, Gujarat and Delhi, as well as the Central Board of Direct Taxes, did not respond to questions about whether any of the six parties had been investigated or subjected to searches.
Of the six parties, Aam Janmat Party reported receiving the most money.
Founded in Patna in 2020, it reported no individual donations above 20,000 rupees - the threshold at which donors must be identified to the Election Commission - during its first two years.
Then its finances changed dramatically.
Aam Janmat Party reported 2.16bn rupees in donations in 2022-23. The following year, the figure nearly tripled to more than 6.2bn rupees - more than twice the roughly 2.8bn rupees received by the Indian National Congress, the country's main opposition party.
Aam Janmat Party officials could not explain the sudden rise.
Aam Janmat Party party fielded just one candidate in the 2024 general election. He received a tiny share of the vote and lost his deposit.
The BBC traced its founding president, Anamika Paswan, to Patna city in Bihar state. Paswan, now a vice-president of the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the state, said she had resigned from Aam Janmat in 2022.
When reporters later sought documents relating to her departure, Paswan was not present. Her husband produced what he said was her resignation letter and another document stating that the party had moved hundreds of miles west to Ahmedabad in Gujarat state with Gaurav Mishra as its president.
But the office at its registered address there was shut.
Its treasurer, Dharmendra Vaishnav, said by telephone that Aam Janmat had "shut operations". He said he knew nothing about its finances and directed questions to Mishra, who did not respond to repeated calls and messages.
The party's listed bank account, however, could still receive money. The BBC transferred a small donation and the payment went through.
The registered office of the Garib Kalyan Party was also closed.
It reported receiving 1.38bn rupees in donations in 2023-24, but fielded just three candidates in the general election.
At the home of its president Neeraj Kumar Kshatriya, his mother said she knew little about the party. But she recalled Income Tax department officials searching the family home, although she did not know why.
Researchers who track political finance say the pattern raises questions about what these parties do with the money they receive.
"These parties are not electorally active, yet they are getting such huge funds and they are spending the money as well," said Shelly Mahajan, a researcher at the Association for Democratic Reforms, an election watchdog.
But tracing such transactions can be difficult. Tax officials told the BBC that money can pass through a web of taxpayers, political parties and intermediaries, obscuring where it came from and where it ultimately went.
The BBC could not establish that any donations to the six parties had been returned in this way.
It did, however, trace two people listed as donors to the New India United Party who said they had claimed tax benefits on their contributions.
One Ahmedabad resident confirmed donating 500,000 rupees. The other said he had donated on a friend's advice. "I did it as a way to save tax, and have declared the same," he said, adding that the authorities had not contacted him.
Three tax officials in Ahmedabad, Delhi and Patna, speaking on condition of anonymity, said chartered accountants and other middlemen can connect taxpayers seeking deductions with parties willing to receive donations.
In some cases, they said, intermediaries can also exercise considerable control over party finances.
Surender Tiwari said that was what happened at his Swatantrata Abhivyakti Party, which reported receiving 2.19bn rupees in donations in 2023-24.
Although he was its president, Tiwari said he did not control the party's money. Its chartered accountant handled the finances and gave him campaign funds, he said.
"The chartered accountant gave me some money for the election campaign," Tiwari said. "He would then show videos of the campaign to clients who wanted to get tax relief through donations."
Tiwari said the party received a notice from the Income Tax department in July and accused its chartered accountant Mayur Singh of keeping him "in the dark".
Singh denied wrongdoing. He said his role was limited to preparing audit reports that parties must submit to the Election Commission, although he acknowledged working for several examined by the BBC.
"Try to understand, it's the same people behind these parties," he said, without elaborating.
Concerns surrounding India's little-known parties extend beyond their finances. The Election Commission has also been trying to remove inactive parties from its official list.
Last year, it delisted more than 800 RUPPs that had not fielded a candidate in six years. But it cannot cancel a party's legal registration, limiting the effect of such action.
The BBC asked the commission whether tax authorities had shared information about suspected financial irregularities involving RUPPs, including the six examined. It did not respond.
As scrutiny grows, the challenge for authorities will be to establish who controls these parties, where their money comes from and how it is ultimately spent.

Toronto cop charged in Project South allegedly didn't care if selling information harmed people
Investigators believe inmate connected to 4 charged in probe ordered alleged hit on corrections official: ITO
Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt knew the information he sold to a civilian from police database searches could help facilitate "serious violence and explicitly stated that he did not care if individuals were harmed," according to an Information to Obtain (ITO) application supporting more than 50 warrants in the Project South investigation.
The sweeping corruption probe began in June 2025, when York Regional Police thwarted an alleged plot to kill a senior corrections official from Toronto South Detention Centre (TSDC).
Investigators subsequently discovered Barnhardt allegedly ran an unauthorized search on the official's licence plate less than a month before the attempted hit, and he is accused of then sharing confidential information about that official with civilian Brian Da Costa. The identity of the senior corrections official is covered by a publication ban for their safety.
Both Barnhardt and Da Costa are in custody facing several charges in the probe, which have not been tested in court. Their lawyers declined to comment for this story.
The unauthorized query on the jail official was one of 17 times Barnhardt allegedly accessed the Ministry of Transportation server to do searches while off-duty in the first six months of last year, according to the ITO. Police-intercepted communications revealed to investigators that Barnhardt "routinely sold confidential database information to known criminal associate Da Costa, often at Da Costa's direction."
A publication ban was lifted on those revelations, and many others, from the Project South ITO on Wednesday in a ruling from Ontario Superior Court Justice Laura Bird.
Other new details include why investigators believed TSDC inmate Gurpreet Singh ordered the hit on the senior jail official, along with his alleged connections to a corrections officer and four men charged in Project South, including Da Costa.
Neither Singh nor the corrections officer have been charged in this investigation.
CBC News was part of a group of media organizations fighting to lift a publication ban on the ITO in court. Bird previously lifted the ban on some details earlier this summer. In her decision this week, Bird lifted the ban on the majority of the rest of the court record.
"Permitting the media to publish the vast majority of the ITO while maintaining a temporary publication ban over limited portions of it strikes an appropriate balance between the court openness principle and the fair trial rights of the criminal defendants," wrote Bird.
An ITO is a legal document from a police officer laying out the evidence they have of a criminal offence in order to request judicial authorization for a warrant or production order from a judge or justice of the peace. The allegations in the ITO have not been tested in court.
The search warrants were executed as investigators arrested and charged seven Toronto police officers, one retired cop and 19 civilians in Project South. The charge against one of those civilians has since been stayed, and one of the officers retired and pleaded guilty to two charges in July.
The charges against the others accused in Project South have not yet been tested in court.
Police believed Singh behind attempted hit: ITO
Elsewhere in the ITO, police say Singh had motive to harm the senior corrections official who was targeted, and that he was named by that official as one of a handful of inmates who'd expressed hostility toward them. The official told police that Singh and his former cellmate were angry after the official seized cellphones and steroids from their cell and then separated the pair.
CBC News previously reported that Singh and correctional officer Nishwant Dosanjh were investigated for potential involvement in the alleged conspiracy.
The ITO also states Dosanjh was Singh's former romantic partner and she allegedly took the photo of the senior corrections official's licence plate in the employee area of the jail. The photo was allegedly later provided to Da Costa and then shared with Barnhardt, who's accused of using the image to search a police database on May 27, 2025.
The results of that query were allegedly provided to Da Costa, then shared with a gun-for-hire group accused of conspiring to kill the senior corrections official the following month.
The allegations in the ITO concerning Dosanjh and Singh have not led to charges, nor have they been tested in court.
In a statement, Dosanjh’s lawyer, Kim Schofield, told CBC News her client has co-operated with police, maintains her innocence and had no part in the attempt on the senior corrections official's life.
Schofield says she hired an independent digital forensics expert to review the "data dump" she received of Dosanjh's seized cell phone. The lawyer says the expert found no photos or chat discussions relating to the attempted hit.
"There is absolutely nothing to connect her to that incident," wrote Schofield.
CBC News contacted Singh's lawyer for comment, but did not receive a response before publication. In an emailed statement in June, Singh's lawyer, Brian Greenspan, said his client had not been charged with any offence in Canada, months after the execution of the February warrants.
Singh has been held at the Toronto jail since his October 2024 arrest amid allegations he acted as an accomplice in a drug-smuggling organization allegedly involving killings and led by accused cocaine kingpin Ryan Wedding.
Singh is fighting extradition to California.
Inmate connected to 4 men charged in Project South: ITO
Investigators also connected Singh with others charged in Project South. According to the ITO, Singh was associated with four of the civilians charged in the corruption probe, including Elwyn Satanowsky, Da Costa and Dequon Lemonious.
Satanowsky is accused of arranging several shootings connected with the probe. He deposited money into Singh's inmate trust account and he spoke to Singh on the phone more than 300 times between the beginning of January and mid-September 2025, according to the ITO.
Police intercepted communications between Da Costa and Singh through TSDC's inmate telephone system.
Lemonious is charged with conspiracy to murder the senior corrections official. The ITO identifies him as someone "who plans and structures violent criminal activity" within a gunmen-for-hire group.
In an intercepted phone call, Keajean Doman, an alleged enforcer in the group also charged in the conspiracy, blames Lemonious for "plays" that resulted in his incarceration. Doman was arrested last September after allegedly carrying out a shooting related to Project South in Vaughan, Ont.
Other intercepts connect Singh and Lemonious by way of them both speaking to, or about, a former cellmate of Singh's who's in custody on a different range at TSDC, according to the ITO.
CBC News contacted lawyers for Satanowsky and Lemonious for this story but neither provided a comment before publication.

Forklift incident sparks fears Trump could demolish Kennedy Center after closure
Congresswoman leading legal battle against Trump’s takeover demands emergency court hearing
One day after Donald Trump announced the immediate closure of the Kennedy Center, construction crews erected metal fencing around the building and barred workers from entering without hard hats.
A member of the legal team fighting Trump’s attempts to rename the property after himself wrote in court filings that she saw a forklift “run into and hit the pillars on the building several times.”
The Democratic congresswoman leading the legal battle has called for an emergency court hearing to get to the bottom of the closure, which a federal judge had previously blocked without an explicit court order. The Trump-dominated Kennedy Center may be “violating the ‘clear and unambiguous order of the Court,’” lawyers for Rep. Joyce Beatty wrote Wednesday.
“Given the unexplained and unlawful closure, it is possible Defendants intend to undertake immediate steps in order to make public access practically impossible for the foreseeable future, including by demolishing public avenues of access to the building, and thereby evade the court’s order,” lawyers wrote.
The venue’s abrupt closure and installation of orange barricades have drawn fears that the president is not merely closing the building for planned renovations but potentially demolishing it altogether, an idea first floated by the Department of Justice in court filings this summer.
Laura Bligh, who attended protests with the advocacy group Hands Off the Arts, told the Associated Press that she feared some or all of the building could be torn down before the legal battle has ended.
“The worst case scenario is a wrecking ball,” she said, adding that the Trump administration can’t be trusted because “look what they did to the East Wing.”
Trump demolished the East Wing of the White House, of course, to make way for a gold-filled, bullet-proof ballroom sandwiched between a “military complex” that includes a sprawling underground bunker with a “drone port” roof.
Hours after Beatty’s request, Judge Christopher R. Cooper ordered the Kennedy Center to respond by 10 a.m. Thursday. “The Court will schedule a prompt hearing if necessary after reviewing the response,” he wrote.
An all-staff email told Kennedy Center employees that the main building is closed “effective immediately” for the next seven days “due to safety concerns.”
“The need to extend this temporary closure will be evaluated on a weekly basis,” the message says.
Kennedy Center spokesperson Roma Daravi also confirmed the venue’s closure on Wednesday morning.
“Compounding systemic infrastructure failures from decades of neglect have left a crumbling building and safety concerns require an immediate closure of [the Kennedy Center] main building,” she wrote on X.
Trump “continues to support this great American institution while legal battles halt the progress to save it,” she added.
Asked why he needs to add his name to the building, Trump told reporters on Wednesday night that “it's a very simple question to answer, because it's a mess.”
“For the Trump administration, for me, to get involved, to take that on long-term, and to carry it, or to raise money to carry it, I think the Trump administration should certainly have recognition,” he said. “Frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down. It’s in very bad shape.”
Closing the venue without Judge Cooper’s approval “appears to directly violate his order,” according to Beatty’s counsel Norm Eisen.
“This is an assault on the rule of law,” he said in a statement shared with The Independent. “The board cannot simply ignore Judge Cooper’s rulings whenever it suits them. In this country, no one — including the president — is above the law.”
Maria Shriver, John F. Kennedy’s niece and former first lady of California, called Trump’s takeover “a sad state of affairs” and a “tragedy.”
She said in a post on X that it appears Trump “will not rest until his name is permanently connected to the name of a great president, whose memory this building was dedicated to.”
“Imagine spending your days focused on this, while a war rages under your leadership,” she wrote.
“Closing the Kennedy Center is an affront to President Kennedy's memory, an attack on Congressional power and an outrageous assault on the livelihoods of the artists and workers who operate and perform in our cultural center,” Rep. Jamie Raskin said Wednesday.
“We're demanding it remain open and free from the President’s graffiti, vandalism and desecration,” he said.
On Friday, Hands Off the Arts will attempt to create a human chain around the main building to send a “crystal clear” message that “the Kennedy Center belongs to the American people, not one man.”

Noida traders threaten to switch to cash over new UPI payment levy
Several traders said they may either have to absorb the cost themselves or find ways to recover it from customers, despite the government's direction that MDR should not be passed on to buyers.
Amid growing calls for the rollback of the latest government move concerning charges on some UPI payments, Noida traders have expressed strong concern over the new Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) framework, warning that the additional cost could squeeze already-thin profit margins and push some businesses towards cash transactions.
Several traders said they may either have to absorb the cost themselves or find ways to recover it from customers, despite the government’s direction that MDR should not be passed on to buyers.
Under the revised framework, effective October 15, merchants will pay an MDR of 0.4% on specified person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, subject to a maximum charge of Rs 300 per transaction.
Payments between individuals will remain free, while transactions up to Rs 2,000 and those covered under the zero-MDR framework for eligible small merchants will continue without the charge.
The government has clarified that MDR is a merchant-side fee and is not a tax collected by the government.
TRADERS MAY REFUSE UPI PAYMENTS
Speaking to an India Today team in Noida, traders said the move could create difficulties for businesses that rely heavily on digital payments.
Vikas Jain, who deals in hardware and building materials, said business was already under pressure because of competition from online shopping and declining market footfall.
"Margins are already very low. If an additional cost is imposed on UPI payments, the question is whether the trader should bear it or recover it from the customer," Jain said.
He added that some shops had begun putting up notices encouraging cash payments and warning customers about a possible surcharge.
Another trader, Karan Grover, said UPI accounts for around 50-70% of his business payments. "When the margin itself is around five per cent, even a small additional cost matters. If traders have to bear MDR along with taxes and other expenses, it will put further pressure on the business," he said.
Grover said traders could increasingly encourage customers to pay in cash. However, if buyers refuse to bear any additional cost, merchants may ultimately have to absorb the expense.
Arif, who runs an interior-design business, said the dependence on online payments was even higher in his case, with around 90-95% of transactions taking place digitally.
"Very few customers pay in cash now. If digital payments become more expensive for merchants, it will directly affect us," he said, adding that the timing was particularly concerning with the festive season approaching.
The government, meanwhile, has said consumers will continue to use UPI without a transaction fee and that banks have been advised to ensure merchants do not recover MDR directly from customers.
Officials have also said the framework is aimed at creating a sustainable funding model for the digital-payments ecosystem.
The move has also triggered criticism from Opposition parties, which have called for its rollback, while the Centre has rejected allegations that the decision was taken under foreign pressure.
For traders in Noida, however, the immediate concern remains the impact on business costs.
With the October 15 implementation date approaching, merchants are watching how the MDR is enforced and whether the added expense changes customer payment preferences or business pricing.

Swedish PM Kristersson resigns after election loss
- Published
Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has resigned after his ruling right-wing bloc was narrowly defeated by the centre-left opposition in the country's general election.
He made the announcement in a post on X on Thursday afternoon, after preliminary votes from Sunday's election showed about 50,000 votes separated the two blocs in the country of about 10 million people.
Opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats look set to win 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, Sweden's parliament.
Kristersson, a conservative, had been supported in government by the anti-immigration hard-right Sweden Democrats (SD), and had promised them cabinet jobs if he won the election.
His right-wing bloc looks set to win 173 seats in the Riksdag, according to data from the Swedish Election Authority.
The results will be subject to formal certification in the coming days and are expected to finalised this weekend.
In Sweden, there are two major political blocs - with four parties on the right and four on the left, so Swedes are used to coalition and minority governments.
After a prime minister resigns, the Speaker of the Riksdag holds talks with all parties to proposes a candidate for the next leader, which is then voted on by MPs.
"Now it is the speaker who will lead the next stage of the way to a new government. I am herewith requesting that I be relieved of the office of prime minister to allow that work to start immediately," Kristersson's statement read.
In a speech posted on Instagram, Andersson said: "The Swedish people have voted for a new direction for our country".
The Social Democrats have regularly led Swedish governments since World War Two and have been the country's dominant political force for much of the last century.
Its leader, Andersson, is expected to return to power after four years in opposition, and has initiated talks with the other opposition parties - The Left Party, The Centre Party and The Green Party - about forming a government.
But discussions could drag on due to major differences between the parties on issues such as taxes.
After the 2022 election in Sweden, it took 37 days to form a government, while in 2018 it took 134 days.
In his resignation, Kristersson said the opposition faced "complicated" conditions for forming the next government, "because the parties' various statements before election day could pose obstacles".
The right-wing bloc is formed of Kristersson's Moderates, as well as the SD, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals.
The SD were founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s and were shunned for decades by the mainstream.
But the party has rebranded itself since the mid-2000s, culminating in a watershed moment in 2022 when it became Sweden's second-largest party on a campaign focused on issues around immigration and violent crime.
They had offered outside support to the current centre-right coalition, which had overseen a dramatic tightening of migration policy. Kristersson had promised to bring them into government if he remained at the helm.
But in a surprise upset for the party, it lost support for the first time since entering parliament in 2010 - down three percentage points on 2022.
A preliminary vote count started after voting closed on Sunday evening and continued into this week.
On Wednesday, election committees began counting early votes that were submitted late, as well as votes from abroad that did not arrive before election day.

Man who was duct-taped on American Airlines flight after alleged violent outburst breaks his silence
Layne Lundeen told a judge in Annapolis, Maryland that he cannot remember anything that happened on the flight
Layne Lundeen, the man who made headlines after he had to be duct-taped to his American Airlines seat following an alleged violent outburst, has spoken publicly for the first time about the incident.
Flight attendants and passengers on an American Airlines flight between Dallas and New Jersey on September 3 duct-taped Lundeen to his seat after he allegedly began shouting racial slurs at the flight crew and choking his seatmate. The flight was diverted to Baltimore-Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport, where he was arrested.
The following day, Lundeen, 67, appeared in an Annapolis court to face second-degree assault and disorderly conduct charges, according to the Baltimore Banner.
During his hearing, he said that all he remembers was talking to a man in the seat next to him, Jonathan Cahn, who is a Messianic rabbi and author.
The Baltimore Banner obtained the court transcripts of the hearing.
“I don’t remember any of what happened,” Lundeen said.
District Court Commissioner George Haag told Lundeen his charges, noting that he allegedly assaulted a police officer.
“I assaulted a police officer? Is that what it says?” Lundeen asked, noting that he couldn't read his charges because he did not have his glasses.
After having the charges read to him, Lundeen said, "Oh my God, what a mess," before insisting that he did not remember anything.
Cahn — whom The New York Times called "an entrepreneurial doomsday prophet" in 2019 and who holds up President Donald Trump as a Biblical figure — spoke to the Baltimore Banner in a phone interview about the incident.
According to Cahn, he and Lundeen spoke on the plane for about two hours, but the conversation took a turn when the topic turned to religion. He claims Lundeen began shouting profanities and blasphemy in response to him.
“He was slurring everything and everybody,” Cahn told the paper, noting that some of the remarks were allegedly anti-semitic.
When the plane landed, police took Lundeen into custody and he allegedly struck an officer in the chest.
Following the incident, Lundeen, Long Realty, which worked with Lundeen, said it severed ties with the man.
“The conduct described in the reports is wholly inconsistent with the professionalism, integrity, compassion, and respect for others that Long Realty expects from those affiliated with the company,” the company said in a statement. “We expect those associated with our company to uphold those values, and we have no tolerance for conduct that so clearly falls short of those expectations.”
Haag ultimately released Lundeen on his own recognizance and ordered that he not use alcohol or drugs except for medicine he's been prescribed.
His next court date is scheduled for October 19.

Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
- Published
Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS.
The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings.
The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.
One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public.
"We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face."
The White House referred the BBC to US Central Command. Centcom did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran.
One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal.
While the photo is undated, BBC Verify previously confirmed a similar photo, apparently of the same radar aircraft in March.
The Boeing E-3 Awacs are used to detect and track potential targets at long ranges to provide an early warning of possible threats.
At the time, a US official told Reuters that 12 US personnel had been wounded, two of them seriously, in an Iranian attack on the air base.
A pair of undated images reportedly from Camp Beuhring, Kuwait, show crumpled trailers, and a large tent-like structure that had been reduced to shreds as smoke billowed from the site.
Another image shows a four-storey building damaged by an Iranian strike at Camp Arifjan, in Kuwait.
Damage to the site was reported in March, including on satellite communications hardware, though it is not clear whether this image is from the same attack.
The images were published on the heels of a report from the Pentagon's watchdog, which found Iranian strikes had "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict".
It also noted that equipment losses have totalled $3.7bn (£2.8bn). Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war up to 29 June, the report said.
In the months after the war began, "dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged", the report continues.
The document lists several of the aircraft damaged, including five refuelling aircraft which were "damaged or destroyed on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian munitions".
A separate report , externalfrom the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) notes that the E-3 aircraft is no longer in production and would have to be replaced with a more modern equivalent, the E-7.
The CBO noted that the E-3 aircraft alone costs $500m (£371m), and the estimated total cost of equipment lost in battle - including planes, drones and a terminal high altitude area defence system - amounts to $1.9b (£1.4b).
CBO said that its review was subject to "uncertainty" because the defence department did not respond to its requests for information, requiring the agency to rely on government databases and public reports.
Additionally, the extent of repairs and rebuilding that the US military plans to do remains unclear, according to the report.
Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.
Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.
On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval.
The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what could be the final House vote on the matter ahead of the US midterm elections in November.
It faces an uncertain path to passage - the US Senate has not indicated if it will take up the matter.
The same day, outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie announced an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as new details emerged about the Iran war's price tag for the US.
The Trump administration backed Hegseth, with US attorney general Todd Blanche telling reporters he was "doing a phenomenal job".
