The key talking points from Pocognoli's bold Scotland squad
- Published
Six new call-ups, seven uncapped players, a refreshed defence, a more-of-the-same midfield and an exciting, new-look attack.
The Sebastien Pocognoli Scotland era is already creating serious intrigue - and the Belgian's squad are yet to assemble for a training-ground rondo, never mind play a game.
The 39-year-old's first taste of competitive action starts with a Nations League opener in Slovenia on 26 September - live on the BBC - beginning an extended four-game international period.
In the meantime, let's dissect the talking points from a bold 28-man selection.
- McBurnie & seven uncapped players in Scotland squad 
  - Published6 hours ago
- Scotland fans allowed to buy alcohol at upcoming games 
  - Published6 hours ago
- Is Sevilla's 'all-round striker' Ure ready to lead Scotland's attack? 
  - Published23 August
Gunn to continue behind refreshed backline?
There have been no new call-ups in the goalkeeping department. Angus Gunn, now playing with San Jose Earthquakes in the MLS, has 25 caps and will be the favourite to continue between the sticks.
Pocognoli's first selection has shown that a surprise is not beyond him, though. The Belgian stressed the importance of his style in relation to his squad picks, and Falkirk's Scott Bain is a goalkeeper who can deal with the ball at his feet.
Jon McCracken is also playing regularly for Bradford City in England's League One, but Liam Kelly very much remains second choice at Rangers.
As for the backline, the new Scotland boss has predominantly played with a back three throughout his coaching career at both Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco.
He insists on his teams being aggressive in and out of possession, so will want defenders capable of picking brave passes but also with the pace to cover big distances when playing a high line.
Scott McKenna, Jack Hendry and Kieran Tierney all have experience of playing in a back three under Steve Clarke, albeit the approach will differ under Pocognoli. Captain Andy Robertson also clocked up a lot of minutes at left wing-back.
Aaron Hickey, Nathan Patterson and young Colby Donovan, who has impressed Pocognoli "but needs to improve on things like every young lad", are options for the opposite flank.
Uncapped trio Luis Binks, Stephen Welsh and Luke Graham add more depth at centre-back.
Brondby captain Binks, who qualifies for Scotland through a grandparent, has had an interesting career. "The feeling and the timing about him was right," Pocognoli said of the former Bologna and Como man.
At the age of 25, the left-footed centre-back has already played in the MLS, Serie A, English Championship and now Denmark's top tier.
Meanwhile, Stoke's Graham - also left-footed - enjoyed a breakthrough spell at Dundee last season and continues to excel in England's second division, along with Swansea's Welsh, who proved he could thrive in a possession-based Motherwell side last term.
McPake included in familiar midfield
It is much of the same in midfield, although Scott McTominay is absent following a successful heart procedure and Udinese's Lennon Miller is back after being left out of Clarke's World Cup squad.
There is a welcome return for McTominay's Napoli team-mate Billy Gilmour, who suffered a crushing injury just before the start of the finals.
Arguably Scotland's most composed midfielder and best progressive passer, many expect the 25-year-old to thrive in Pocognoli's system. Miller, 20, could also fall into that category.
Experienced campaigners John McGinn, Ryan Christie, Kenny McLean and Lewis Ferguson - the Scots' standout performer earlier this summer - are all included in a seven-man midfield selection, which also features thriving Hearts player Josh McPake.
Signed this summer from St Johnstone, it has been a remarkable rise for the 24-year-old, who has been listed as a midfielder in the squad despite featuring on the left wing for the Tynecastle side. He was a Stirling Albion player just two years ago.
How excited should fans be by new-look attack?
While Ben Gannon-Doak, Findlay Curtis and McPake offer options in attacking wide areas, there is a centre-forward spot up for grabs in the absence of injured pair Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland, plus the omission of Lyndon Dykes.
A free-scoring spell in Sweden earned Robbie Ure the number nine shirt at Sevilla, Oli McBurnie and his Hull team have made an impressive return to the Premier League and Sassuolo's Kieron Bowie scored in a win against Juventus on Sunday.
"Players who are performing well are in the new pathway," Pocognoli said when asked about Rangers academy product Ure, who is yet to score since his switch to La Liga.
"Robbie is adapting well to La Liga. He's put in some good performances, but he maybe needs to adapt to the intensity. Being selected gives him an opportunity."
On the return of McBurnie, who has received his first Scotland call-up in five years, he added: "It's regarding style of play, playing time and performance. I have to start on a new journey, a new book and it's a new opportunity for some players."
The head coach also spoke of his desire to mix youth with the "DNA and heritage" of his squad, evidenced by the inclusion of teenage James Wilson, who is showing signs of fulfilling his serious potential at Hearts.
By the end of the first week in October the Tartan Army, many of whom have been calling for what Pocognoli is preaching to deliver, will have a clearer idea of what that formula is going to look like on the grass, with a fascinating four-match window approaching.

Athletic Club forward Williams retires from Ghana duty
- Published
Athletic Club forward Inaki Williams has announced his retirement from international duty with Ghana.
The 32-year-old scored two goals in 28 caps for the Black Stars after making his debut in September 2022.
He featured for the West Africans at the 2022 and 2026 Fifa World Cups and the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon).
Williams appeared twice at this year's World Cup as Ghana were knocked out in the last 32 by Colombia.
"I feel the time has come to bring my journey with the Ghana national team to an end," he said in a post on social media.
"I leave happy, proud and with the peace of mind of knowing that I gave everything every time I wore this shirt."
Williams, who was born in Bilbao to Ghanaian parents, chose to represent the Black Stars after previously playing for Spain at youth level and in a 2016 friendly at senior level.
His younger brother Nico, who also plays for Athletic Club in Bilbao, chose to represent Spain and has gone on to become a World Cup and European Championship winner with La Roja.
Inaki Williams' announcement comes a week after it was confirmed that Carlos Queiroz would return as Ghana coach in the build-up to the 2027 Afcon in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.
He said his time with Ghana had given him "much more than football".
"It has allowed me to come back home, feel even closer to my roots and experience the enormous pride of representing my country and wearing this flag on my chest," he added.
"Thank you from the bottom of my heart to everyone who has been part of this journey and for all the love you have always shown me.
"Ghana will always be a part of me. I will continue supporting the Black Stars as one of you, wherever I am."

McConnell voted against a range of sick leave measures in all four years, albeit with a clarification. On March 18, 2020, McConnell voted in favor of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act, an emergency response bill passed at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. That legislation, providing temporary relief, mandated employers provide employees with paid sick time through the end of the year. Earlier the same day, he voted against an amendment that purportedly would have strengthened the bill's offerings, including extending the benefits an additional year through 2021. As Senate majority leader, he later reportedly blocked efforts to extend the bill's paid sick leave mandate past Dec. 31, 2020.
On Sept. 14, 2026, U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell returned to the Senate floor after a monthslong health-related absence. He previously attributed the time away to recovering and rehabilitating from a fall he had, reportedly on June 14. Upon his return to Congress, and in the preceding weeks, people shared a claim that in 1993, 2015, 2020 and 2022 he voted against or blocked measures mandating employees receive sick leave.
The rumor spread on Bluesky, Facebook and X, among other social media platforms. For example, one Bluesky post from August read: "Mitch McConnell is currently on paid sick leave for 2+ months. Fun Fact: U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell voted against or blocked measures mandating employees receive sick leave in 1993, 2015, 2020 and 2022."
(SarahBCalif via Bluesky)
In sum, research showed this rumor about McConnell's voting record is mostly true, albeit in need of a few clarifications on the specifics. In the four years mentioned, he did vote against measures focused on providing legislation for paid and unpaid sick leave.
- In 1993, McConnell voted against the Family and Medical Leave Act. The bill provides 12 weeks of unpaid leave, not paid leave as users claimed.
- In 2015, he voted against a paid sick leave amendment attached to a budget resolution for fiscal year 2016.
- On March 18, 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, he voted in favor of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act, which included emergency paid sick leave, although earlier the same day, he voted against an amendment aimed at strengthening that legislation and extending its benefits an extra year (through the end of 2021). Later, in December 2020, he reportedly blocked Congress from extending the paid leave mandate, resulting in its expiration on Dec. 31.
- In 2022, McConnell voted in favor of a bill to prevent a rail worker strike. Earlier the same day, he voted against a resolution providing those same rail workers seven days of annual paid sick leave.
Snopes emailed a McConnell representative to request comment on his sick leave votes and will update this article if we receive further information.
Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993
On Feb. 5, 1993, President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, signed the Family and Medical Leave Act into law. The signing, which took place in the White House Rose Garden two weeks after his inauguration, was the new administration's first major social legislation achievement.
The bill provides parents who work for companies with 50 or more employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave — not paid leave, as users claimed — to care for a new child or sick relative.
In a roll call vote in the Senate, McConnell voted against the FMLA. A C-SPAN video shows McConnell's vote (beginning at 10:22:25).
In searches of C-SPAN for congressional video archives and of Newspapers.com for newspaper articles from the time period, we found no record of McConnell explaining his nay vote. McConnell's written statement marking the beginning of the 103rd Congress didn't mention the bill, either.
Paid sick leave amendment, March 2015
On March 26, 2015, senators passed, by a vote of 61-39, an amendment submitted by Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., in an effort to provide more Americans with paid sick time. The amendment's passage did not enact law but instead established funding for a paid sick leave provision in the Senate's budget resolution for fiscal year 2016.
In a roll call vote, McConnell voted nay on the amendment.
At the time, the Washington state-based Peninsula Daily News reported on the amendment:
SEVEN DAYS' PAID SICK LEAVE: Voting 61 for and 39 against, the Senate on Thursday amended the Republican budget (S Con Res 11, above) so that it would not impede any new law entitling workers to seven days' paid sick leave per year.
At present, the Family and Medical Leave Act allows qualified workers 12 weeks of job-protected unpaid leave per year.
A yes vote was to adopt an amendment in behalf of paid sick leave.
A C-SPAN video shows Murray introducing the amendment (beginning at 4:18:10), saying in part, "Working families should not have to sacrifice a day's pay or sacrifice their job altogether just to take care of themselves or a sick child."
As the only Republican speaking on the floor prior to the vote, Sen. Mike Enzi, R-Wyo., urged others to oppose the amendment, citing the FMLA's 12 weeks of unpaid leave as sufficient.
McConnell's actions during pandemic, 2020
According to social media posts, McConnell either blocked or voted no on paid leave measures pertaining to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
At the onset of the pandemic in the U.S., on March 18, 2020, the Senate passed the Families First Coronavirus Response Act. The legislation served as an emergency response to the quickly escalating situation.
Among several offerings, the act provided employees affected by COVID-19 with up to two weeks of paid sick time, as well as 12 weeks of leave — the latter 10 weeks paid with the requirement that employers pony up at least two-thirds of the worker's normal rate. The bill also amended FMLA to provide leave, as well as some pay, to employees who worked for an employer at least 30 days — as opposed to the standard FMLA law requiring at least 12 months, or 1,250 hours, of employment.
McConnell voted in favor of the temporary legislation, with 90 members voting yea, eight voting no and two not voting. The bill mandated its benefits expire on Dec. 31, 2020.
Earlier the same day, in another roll call vote, McConnell and 50 other senators voted against a paid sick leave amendment that proposed allegedly favorable mandates for employers and employees through 2021 (Murray also introduced that amendment).
The amendment, with the short title of "Providing Americans Insured Days of Leave Act of 2020," sought to expand the "Families First" act to offer private sector workers affected by COVID-19 with 14 days of paid sick leave. Employers were to receive immediate government reimbursements conditional upon providing documentation to the Labor Department. The amendment also sought to expand FMLA to offer at least 10 out of 12 weeks of paid leave — as opposed to FMLA's standard of unpaid leave — for private sector workers during emergencies, as well as to propose a standard of seven days of accrued paid sick leave.
In remarks on the Senate floor on March 18, Murray said, "But for those who may not be ready just yet to agree we need paid sick days and paid leave going forward permanently, the amended version of this bill that we are introducing today and asking for a vote on shortly would only provide this support through December 2021." A C-SPAN video features Murray's full remarks (beginning at 3:43:45).
Some social media posts said McConnell, then the Senate majority leader, also blocked COVID-19 relief. In December 2020, BuzzFeed News reported he "was pushing to block the paid leave mandate from being extended," as well as that "the extension was left out of the aid bill as a concession to McConnell." Ultimately, the Senate did not extend the paid leave mandate beyond Dec. 31, 2020.
Rail workers sick leave measure, 2022
On Dec. 1, 2022, the Senate passed a measure to prevent an impending U.S. rail workers strike. Reuters reported such a strike "would have devastated the American economy."
A separate House-passed measure the same day sought to provide seven days of paid sick leave for railroad employees.
That effort failed in the Senate, with McConnell and 42 others voting against the resolution, which required 60 votes to pass.
A C-SPAN video features McConnell speaking without mentioning the paid sick leave resolution.
Speaking in favor of the measure prior to the vote, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., condemned "corporate greed" and billions in profits for the rail industry, saying in part, "Workers who do difficult and dangerous work have zero paid sick days. Zero. You get sick, you've got a mark against you. A couple of marks, you get fired. This cannot and must not happen in America in 2022."
At the time, PolitiFact fact-checked Sanders' remarks as mostly true, noting, "The vast majority of workers at the largest railroads have none, but a small percentage do."
In 2024, a Transportation Department letter reported that "90 percent of Class I freight employees have paid sick days, up from approximately 5 percent at the end of 2022."
For further reading, we previously reported the facts about whether a purported time-lapse video shows McConnell sitting in the Senate chamber and barely moving for 20 hours straight.

Gunman ambushes cops on ninth floor after killing two in apartment rampage
Dramatic video shows the moment two Minneapolis officers were shot after racing to an upper floor of an apartment building in pursuit of a shooter
Dramatic video released Wednesday shows the moment two Minneapolis police officers were shot after racing to the ninth floor of an apartment building where a gunman had killed two people and wounded three others.
Footage released by the City of Minneapolis shows officers moving through the building earlier this month as they attempted to secure it with residents still trapped inside.
Officers are seen approaching a victim lying in a hallway when gunman Carlton Johnson suddenly emerges from around a corner and draws a handgun.
Officer Joseph Michnowski is struck and runs back down the hallway as more shots ring out.
“Shooter’s on the ninth floor. I took some rounds,” Michnowski says over his radio before raising a visibly shaking left hand.
Other officers, separated from Michnowski, shout from a stairwell: “Joe, are you OK?”
Moments later, Officer Yahye Mahmed Ahmed is seen standing on the stairwell landing with his gun pointed toward the hallway when another burst of gunfire erupts.
Smoke fills the doorway and officers scramble back down the stairs.
“Oh, I got hit,” Ahmed yells.
Johnson was later shot and killed by police.
The violence began outside the apartment building during a planned child custody handoff, according to Drew Evans, superintendent of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension.
Johnson allegedly shot and wounded a woman believed to be the mother of his child. The child was not injured.
Authorities said Johnson then shot and wounded two building employees before taking an elevator to the ninth floor, where he fatally shot two residents.
Police subsequently encountered Johnson and killed him. Investigators have said it remains unclear whether the two residents were deliberately targeted or happened to encounter Johnson in the hallway.
The building’s owners had been attempting to evict Johnson, who had previously threatened neighbors and warned that he planned to shoot people, according to residents, court documents and law enforcement officials.
At least one person had sought a restraining order against him.
Police also investigated Johnson in June over allegations that he displayed a weapon, but the county attorney’s office declined to file charges.

The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) has notified the Passports (Amendment) Rules, 2026, introducing changes to passport validity for children and bringing fee provisions in line with revised rates. The rules came into effect immediately after being published in the Official Gazette on September 15.
The amendments come after the MEA revised passport service fees from July 1.
Here is what applicants need to know.
What has changed for children’s passports?
Under the amended rules, a 36-page ordinary passport issued to a child below 15 years of age will be valid for five years from the date of issue or until the child turns 18, whichever comes first.
This provision replaces the earlier Rule 12(1A).
For example, if a passport is issued to a 10-year-old child, it will be valid for five years. However, if it is issued when the child is 14, it will remain valid only until the child turns 18, even though five years have not elapsed.
The change specifically applies to 36-page ordinary passports for children below 15.
What do the amended rules say about fees?
The amendment to Rule 8(1) states that fees for different passport applications must follow the rates specified in the updated Schedule IV of the Passports Rules, 1980.
The change provides regulatory clarity following the MEA's revision of passport-related charges, which took effect from July 1.
The revised fees cover several services, including fresh passports, reissue, Tatkaal applications, replacement of lost or damaged passports and Police Clearance Certificates (PCCs).
How much does an adult passport cost now?
Under the revised fee structure, a fresh or renewal application for a 36-page ordinary passport for an adult costs  ₹2,500, compared with  ₹1,500 earlier.
For a 60-page passport, the fee has increased to  ₹3,500 from  ₹2,000.
Tatkaal applicants also face higher charges. A 36-page adult passport under Tatkaal costs  ₹5,000, compared with  ₹3,500 earlier. A 60-page Tatkaal passport costs  ₹6,000, up from  ₹4,000.
For replacement of a 60-page passport under Tatkaal, the fee is now  ₹8,500, compared with  ₹5,500 previously.
What are the charges for minors?
For minors, a 36-page fresh or reissue passport under the normal category costs  ₹1,750, up from  ₹1,000.
A 36-page Tatkaal passport for a minor costs  ₹3,000.
The MEA has also retained a 10% discount on fresh passport applications for children below eight years and senior citizens above 60 years. However, the concession does not apply to reissue applications.

 leadership crisis has deepened with

N Chandra: 5th-longest serving chairman
Tata Sons said in a statement that "Chandra acceded to the Board's request to reconsider his decision". The board subsequently "resolved by a majority vote to re-appoint him as Executive Chairman for a further term of five years upon the expiry of his current tenure".
Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts, voted against the proposal. The Trusts, along with affiliated trusts, control about 66% of Tata Sons. Despite his opposition, the resolution passed with a majority.
"The Board also resolved to initiate steps to comply with the applicable RBI Guidelines and will seek guidance from RBI, Tata Trusts and other stakeholders on applicable compliance requirements," Tata Sons said.
Tata Trusts, however, disputed the validity of the decision.
What is the structure of the Tata group companies? What is Tata Sons and Tata Trusts? Let’s take a look:
What is the Tata Group?
Founded nearly 160 years ago by Jamsetji Tata, the Tata Group is India’s oldest conglomerate. Its businesses cover a wide range of industries, including automobiles, steel, software, airlines and hotels.
The group has 32 companies, 26 of which are publicly listed. Together, they generated around $170 billion in revenue in the 12 months ended March 2026, according to a Bloomberg report.
Tata's Sprawling Empire Explained
Tata Group is also expanding into high-tech manufacturing. Along with plans to increase production of Apple Inc. iPhones, the group is investing in semiconductor manufacturing.
Tata Group has a presence across a wide range of industries. In aviation, Air India and Air India Express, in the auto sector Tata Motors has businesses spanning commercial vehicles, passenger cars and electric vehicles, with Jaguar Land Rover and the proposed acquisition of Iveco adding to its international presence.
Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) in the IT sector is an important source of dividends for Tata Sons, while Tata Steel has operations in India and Europe. Tata Power’s portfolio covers power generation, transmission and distribution, along with renewables, solar manufacturing and EV charging.
The group’s consumer businesses include Titan, Trent, Tata Consumer Products and Voltas, with brands such as Tanishq, Westside, Zudio, Croma, BigBasket and Tetley. Its joint venture with Starbucks has more than 500 outlets across 80 cities.
Tata Electronics is developing semiconductor facilities in Gujarat and Assam. In financial services, Tata Capital, Tata AIA and Tata AIG operate across lending, wealth management, investment banking and insurance. Tata Communications has operations in more than 190 countries, while Tata Play offers pay-TV and streaming services.
What are Tata Sons and Tata Trusts?
Tata Sons is the holding company for the group’s businesses, including Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, which owns Jaguar Land Rover. It also serves as a platform for newer ventures such as Air India, battery manufacturer Agratas, Tata Electronics and Tata Digital, which operates online grocery service Big Basket.
Tata Trusts, a group of 13 charities, controls around 66% of Tata Sons, while Tata Group companies own about 13%.
The Trusts are headed by Noel Tata, who assumed the role in October 2024 following the death of his half-brother Ratan Tata, the group’s patriarch and one of India’s most prominent business executives.
Tata Sons recorded revenue of Rs 42,367 crore ($4.46 billion) for the year ended March 2026.
The Trusts That Own Tata Sons
Who owns Tata Group, and who runs it?
No individual member of the Tata family owns the group outright. Its ownership is largely held through charitable trusts established by different generations of the Tata family.
These philanthropic trusts collectively own about two-thirds of Tata Sons, which is the main investment holding company and promoter of Tata companies.
Two trusts account for the largest share of this ownership: the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and the Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT). Together, they hold 51.54% of Tata Sons, giving them an outright majority.
Noel Tata is chairman of Tata Trusts, the umbrella body under which the main Tata charitable trusts operate. However, he does not personally own the Tata Sons shares held by the trusts. Those assets belong to the charitable trusts and are managed through their respective boards of trustees.
Tata Sons sits at the centre of the commercial structure as the group’s principal investment holding company and promoter, while individual Tata companies are governed by their own boards.
Tata Group Turbulence After Ratan Tata
Tata.com describes the arrangement this way: “Tata Sons is principal investment holding company and promoter of Tata companies. 66% of share capital of Tata Sons is held by philanthropic trusts, which support education, health, livelihood generation, and art and culture. Each Tata company or enterprise operates independently under the guidance and supervision of its own board of directors.”
SDTT and SRTT together own 51.54% of Tata Sons. When the holdings of the other shareholder trusts are included, the charitable trusts’ combined ownership comes to roughly two-thirds, or about 66%.
Separately, M K Tata Trust owns 2,421 Tata Sons shares, according to a 2024 Income Tax Appellate Tribunal judgment. Those shares were transferred to the trust as corpus when it was established in 1959.
Tata’s public description of its ownership structure therefore rounds the combined holding of the philanthropic trusts in Tata Sons to 66%.
Tata Sons Listing
Tata Sons voted to follow the required steps for listing of Tata Sons. The board agreed to proceed with the listing of Tata Sons, the holding company of the group’s salts-to-software-and-cars businesses.
"The Board also resolved to initiate steps to comply with the applicable RBI Guidelines and will seek guidance from RBI, Tata Trusts and other stakeholders on applicable compliance requirements," Tata Sons said in a statement.
The move comes days after RBI rejected Tata Sons’ request to surrender its Certificate of Registration to operate as a shadow bank. It directed the company to follow the regulatory framework governing top non-bank finance companies, under which a public listing is required.
Natarajan Chandrasekaran’s move to step down in August
Natarajan Chandrasekaran, widely known as Chandra, became the first person from outside the Tata family to head Tata Sons. Ratan Tata selected him for the role after Chandra had spent three decades at Tata Consultancy Services, including eight years as its chief executive. He turned the IT company into India’s most valuable enterprise and established a reputation as a technocrat and a reliable pair of hands.
When Chandra took charge at Bombay House in February 2017, the group’s companies had a combined market capitalisation of Rs 8.4 lakh crore. That figure has since climbed to more than Rs 27 lakh crore.
Tata group: The men behind the legacy
The chairman nevertheless faced increasing pressure over the past year as the group dealt with several challenges. These included a deadly Air India crash, a cyberattack on Jaguar Land Rover that was severe enough to affect the UK’s gross domestic product, and the growing impact of AI on Tata Consultancy Services. Chandra was also tasked with delivering on a major technology ambition, developing India’s first homegrown semiconductor chips.
Chandra announced on August 12 that he would leave as Tata Sons chairman when his current tenure ends in February. The announcement came after months of deadlock over his reappointment.
Now, with the Tata Sons voting to reappoint Chandra and Tata Trusts calling the move illegal, the battle seems to be getting lengthier.
Tata Group m-cap under various chiefs
Tata Trusts opposes reappointment decision
The Trusts said Chandrasekaran’s August 12 decision "has been duly accepted and has attained finality". It pointed out that it had already asked Tata Sons to constitute a selection committee to find his successor in accordance with the company’s Articles of Association.
According to the Trusts, Thursday’s vote "was a legal nullity". It argued that the Articles require both directors nominated by the Trusts to support a resolution concerning the chairmanship. Since Noel Tata voted against the proposal, the Trusts said "it was rendered legally void and without any basis".
The Trusts also said Noel Tata had provided the board with a legal opinion from former Chief Justice of India DY Chandrachud backing its interpretation, but that the opinion "was not taken note of by the Board".
Noel Tata raised another objection in a detailed communication to the board. He argued that the reappointment issue itself was premature because his position as a director remained unresolved after a general meeting "was not able to proceed for want of quorum".
Any decision taken in those circumstances, he warned, "would be open to serious legal challenge by any shareholder who chose to bring it".
Noel Tata also cautioned the board against linking Chandrasekaran’s reappointment dispute to the separate issue of Tata Sons’ pending listing status with the RBI.
"It would not serve this company for a regulatory development to determine the outcome of a succession process," he said, arguing that "the page has turned" on Chandrasekaran’s earlier decision to leave.

Hackers ripped down a Flock camera above a roadway, made a near-complete copy of the data stored inside it, and shared the files with 404 Media and WIRED, revealing in new detail how exactly Flock Safety’s cameras track the movements of both vehicles and people. The hackers say they are also publishing details on how they managed to obtain the software, in the hopes that other people may copy them.
The breach provides an unprecedented look inside a system that Flock has described as protected by on-device encryption. The hackers were able to copy the camera’s storage and recover an encryption key stored on the device, which unlocked videos of thousands of vehicle detections. The hackers shared the material with 404 Media and the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets, which shared the data with WIRED. 404 Media and WIRED then analyzed those files as part of a joint investigation.
While much of the automatic license plate reader’s most sensitive storage remained encrypted and inaccessible, the joint analysis of the recovered data shows that software running on the device explicitly detects people as well as vehicles, license plates, and bicycles. The camera can produce dozens of images of a single passing vehicle and, according to several weeks of recovered logs, generated more than a million images. Its computer-vision software also sometimes isolated bumper stickers and other graphics, including, in one case, an American flag patch on a motorcyclist’s saddlebag.
The act of removing the camera and dumping its software shows that some people are not content with just destroying or removing the cameras. Across the country, multiple people have been arrested for allegedly tampering with or otherwise sabotaging Flock’s cameras. In response, some towns have announced that they are going to stop using Flock’s cameras altogether, and in one case, a police department even made a fake, 3D-printed Flock camera case in order to bait potential vandals.
“Why just destroy them when we can reverse engineer them and find the secrets of those spying on us?” one of the hackers, from a collective calling itself stegan0gram, said in an interview. “We liberated hardware in the field, disarmed them, and proceeded with reverse engineering of the cameras and associated solar equipment.”
Flock’s cameras photograph passing vehicles and send the images and other data to the company’s servers. There, Flock’s system presumably reads the license plate and can identify characteristics such as the vehicle’s color, make, and model. Flock then makes these time-stamped records searchable by whichever local agency owns or has access to the cameras. But in many cases, Flock’s system also allows other police departments from all over the country to search those cameras too, as part of the company’s national network. In Alpharetta, Georgia, for example, WIRED found that records from the city’s Flock cameras were accessible to more than 2,000 agencies, including police departments, colleges, airports, and, inexplicably, the Office of Inspector General for the federal General Services Administration.
This national network has been a selling point for Flock but also a deep source of controversy. 404 Media revealed that local cops were performing lookups in the national network on behalf of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including in areas that banned working with immigration authorities or transferring license plate data out of state. 404 Media also revealed that a cop in Texas searched Flock cameras nationwide for a woman who self-administered an abortion. Those stories, among others, triggered a national conversation about whether people want Flock cameras, or automatic license plate readers more generally, in their communities.
And in the case of stegan0gram, the answer is clearly no.
The hackers said they were able to access the Android system on the camera and found two partitions—sections of its hard drive, essentially. A few of these were unencrypted, the hackers said, including one called “vendor” and another called “media.” The latter contained an encryption key that unlocked another part, which contained much of the media—the videos and stills—the camera took.
In early 2025, security researcher Jon “GainSec” Gaines reverse engineered a Flock license-plate reader and documented flaws that could be used to gain root-level access. After Gaines disclosed his findings, the company acknowledged the findings but downplayed their severity, writing that the flaws required physical access to the device and that even someone who gained access to a camera “would still not be able to gain access to footage,” because images remained on the device only briefly after being transmitted to the cloud.
404 Media and WIRED analyzed the camera’s contents. The device’s processor is similar to those used in midrange smartphones, and it runs about 20 Flock-built apps that handle everything from detecting motion and taking pictures to classifying objects, uploading data, and receiving remote updates.
According to the code, when something moves into view, the camera takes a rapid series of photos. A typical passing vehicle generated about 28 images, though some produced more than 100. The camera uses different exposures to capture both the license plate and the wider scene, then scans the images, selects and crops useful frames, and sends them with other data to Flock over the cellular network. The camera itself does not appear to read the plate or identify the vehicle’s make, model, and color. That appears to happen on Flock’s servers.
According to our analysis, the camera’s logs recorded about 21 days of activity across several periods. During those windows, the device photographed roughly 50,200 vehicles and generated about 1.6 million images. On a typical day, it logged around 3,300 vehicles, with a high of 4,454. Those figures would vary considerably depending on where a camera is installed and how much traffic passes in front of it. The camera was almost certainly operating outside those periods, but older logs had been overwritten or were no longer recoverable from the device.
The software running on the camera explicitly detects people, something which is typically overlooked in discussions around Flock cameras. When it spots a person, it records where they appear in the image and how confident it is in the detection.
To test what the software could actually see, WIRED extracted the models from the camera’s files and ran them against test images and footage recovered from the device. The models readily detected people, including a selfie of a reporter. WIRED then ran them across 27,321 short videoclips stored on the camera. The clips were MP4 files, each about one to two seconds long, recorded at 1,024 by 768 pixels without audio. They were separate from the rapid bursts of higher-resolution still images the camera also takes as vehicles pass. The models detected people in 11 of the clips, all of them riding motorcycles. The small number is likely due to the camera’s position above a roadway, pointed down at passing traffic where pedestrians were unlikely to appear.
The tests also showed how broadly the camera’s license plate detector could interpret what it saw. In some cases it mistook bumper stickers, dealership frames, and other graphics for license plates and cropped them out as if they were plates. In one video of a passing motorcycle, the detector cropped an American flag patch on the rider’s saddlebag as if it were a plate.
Flock insists its cameras do not perform face recognition. WIRED and 404 Media found no evidence of any face-recognition capabilities in the camera’s software beyond ones included by default in the Android operating system. Those capabilities did not appear to be enabled or in active use.
In August, WIRED obtained frontend code for Flock’s police software, now called OS Investigate and previously known as Nightshift, and reconstructed portions of the tool. That software showed how Flock can use the records generated by its cameras, along with police files and commercial data, to identify drivers, surface vehicles that repeatedly travel together, and search for people based on patterns of movement. The data provides a view of the other end of a system.
A Flock spokesperson said in a statement: “The unauthorized removal and tampering of a Flock camera is illegal.” When asked specifically about the encryption key stored on the camera, the company added, “Flock takes security seriously and maintains a public Vulnerability Disclosure Policy for security researchers to report potential vulnerabilities directly to us. We received no report through that process, and based on the limited information provided, we do not have enough detail to assess the claims being made. If the individuals identified legitimate vulnerabilities, we encourage them to submit their technical findings through our vulnerability reporting process so our security team can review them and take any appropriate action.”
One of the hackers said, “Being investigated is a legit concern and something we are trying to avoid. I'm sure our actions have attracted some attention as it is, but we are careful and try to keep a low profile.”
Noel Pichardo, a former Pawtucket, Rhode Island, police officer who became an outspoken critic of Flock after challenging his department’s use of the cameras, says he understands the activists’ frustration but worries that sabotaging devices could ultimately strengthen the case for them. “I think that type of vigilantism will only crystallize the police and the state at large in their belief that this tool is necessary,” Pichardo says. “The longer the state continues to ignore the groanings of their constituents who are against this type of surveillance, the more this will happen.”
The camera’s logs also show the camera struggling with storage. Its logs recorded more than 27,000 “no space left on device” errors while trying to save full-resolution images, along with tens of thousands of related errors, crashes, and reboots. At the same time, about every two minutes, code checked that the camera was still running and logged the message, “Who’s a good boy?!” More than 12,000 of those messages appear in the recovered logs.
When the camera did restart, another service left a final message in the logs: “A reboot was requested! ¡Adiós, Amigos!”
