Australia needs to slow down its artificial intelligence use and create better security laws, the companies creating the technology have told the federal government.
In a submission to an ongoing inquiry, OpenAI said national leaders had a responsibility to work with other countries to stop global security threats:
Many of the most consequential risks will not stop at national borders, making international co-ordination increasingly important.
It said Australia was in a narrow “defender’s window” during which it could use the technology to find and fix cybersecurity threats, rather than create them.
Tech giant Atlassian, which runs AI system Rovo, used its submission to urge the government to bolster its laws. International standards and work already undertaken overseas should be used to protect Australian consumers, it said.
“We need to embrace governance and regulation as a force multiplier for trust,” Atlassian’s head of regulation Anna Jaffe wrote, arguing that tighter privacy crackdowns would also benefit the tech sector as clients would be more likely to engage with them.

For years, researchers have known that, among people diagnosed with lung cancer, the prevalence of nonsmokers has been increasing. But they have been trying to determine what factors — whether genetic, environmental, or something else — might put these “never-smokers” at heightened risk.
Now, researchers have identified a very rare genetic variant that is associated with 25-fold higher odds of lung cancer, they reported in the journal Science on Thursday. In the U.S., the variant is far more common among people in Southern Appalachia than in other regions.
Experts said that the variant likely only plays a role in a small portion of never-smoker lung cancer cases. But the research provides further evidence that these types of tumors can be tied to distinct risk factors, which may in turn require thinking differently about screening programs and treatment strategies. More broadly, the new study highlights the types of narrow but crucial discoveries that can be made by turning to large datasets replete with health information from millions of people. In this case, the investigators relied on genetic data from 23andMe.

Kennedy Center claims it’s only closing for seven days after Trump says it could be ‘ripped down’
DOJ says the institution will close ‘temporarily’ for repairs while the president publicly mentions its potential demolition
The Department of Justice insists that the Kennedy Center is only “temporarily” closing for seven days to address “advanced deterioration” after the institution’s Donald Trump-dominated board voted to shutter the building for repairs, fueling speculation that the president could try to demolish it altogether.
The board’s executive director and chief operating officer decided to temporarily close the Kennedy Center due to “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration” of the building, according to government lawyers.
That decision from Matt Floca was “separate from any Board decision related to closure for ongoing renovations,” lawyers with the Justice Department wrote in court filings Thursday.
The venue’s closure may be “extended” after workers “assess existing safety risks in those portions of the main building exhibiting severe structural deterioration,” according to the Justice Department.
Thursday’s filing follows an extraordinary 24 hours for the living memorial to the assassinated former president, as workers installed fencing and orange barricades around the property while Trump publicly mulled whether to demolish the building entirely after courts blocked his attempts to rename it after himself.
Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, a Kennedy Center board member who is leading the legal battle against Trump’s efforts, has requested an emergency court hearing on the building’s closure, which her legal team says violates an injunction that was issued earlier this year.
She alerted Washington, D.C. Judge Christopher R. Cooper to Trump’s remarks on Wednesday night, telling reporters that the building “will end up being ripped down” unless the president is given “recognition” for his takeover of the memorial.
He later appeared to be reviewing a placard reading “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED” while sitting on Air Force One — images that Beatty’s legal team have now included in court filings.
“Given the emergency nature of this matter and Defendants’ 10 a.m. filing deadline for their response to Plaintiff’s motion, Plaintiff wanted to make sure the Court and Defendants are aware of this new information,” lawyers wrote.
Bill Pulte, Trump’s director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency and former Acting Director of National Intelligence, was aboard Air Force One when AFP photojournalist Brendan Smialowski captured images of the president reviewing the placard.
Pulte did not respond to a text message from The Independent asking for more information about the poster.
Judge Cooper is mulling whether to hold an emergency hearing on the institution’s closure, which will likely raise more questions about the president’s alleged plans to “demolish” the campus to make way for his own memorial.
Floca said in a sworn declaration to Judge Cooper that he independently decided to close the building over “acute risks to public safety” and claimed that a message over the Kennedy Center’s speakers telling people to leave stemmed from an improperly triggered alarm.
“I did not authorize that alarm, nor am I aware of a legitimate reason why that alarm may have been triggered,” he wrote in court filings.
In May, the judge blocked the president from renaming the venue after himself, writing that Congress made it “crystal clear” that the building is only to be named after former President John F. Kennedy, “and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial” based on a “unilateral say-so” from a Trump-appointed board.
Last week, Cooper blocked the board from trying to rename the venue after Trump, again, after board members proposed adding “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump” to the facade.
“Closing the Kennedy Center without Judge Cooper’s approval appears to directly violate his order. This is an assault on the rule of law,” Beatty’s counsel Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group said in a statement Wednesday.
“The board cannot simply ignore Judge Cooper’s rulings whenever it suits them. In this country, no one — including the president — is above the law,” they said.
Eisen has also argued that Cooper’s existing injunction blocks demolition of the property.
Last month, after government lawyers repeatedly argued that the performing arts venue is falling into “financial ruin” and rapidly deteriorating in a state of “terminal decline” without Trump at the helm, the Justice Department suggested that it could fall into such extreme disrepair that will require it “to be taken down.
Trump, with his “unrivaled expertise and experience in real estate and construction” and “prominence” as president to raise money for the venue, must be memorialized on the building’s marble facade — or the Kennedy Center will “deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down,” according to the Justice Department.
The Independent has requested further comment from Beatty’s legal team.
Andrew Feinberg contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.

Justice delayed: Acknowledging women pioneers in science
The debate in the scientific world has often been about glory. Who deserves the glory for a discovery, for an invention, for defining a procedure, a drug, a vaccine? Does credit ever attach to the patients who were experimented upon, the participants of a clinical trial, people who gave of their time and body in order that science may advance, in order that people who come after them do not suffer. Codes of ethics are mutable, they keep changing, and the grant of credit in science also operates on this arc. This story is a page from such an omission, a blunder. Nearly 150 years later, some form of reparation was attempted.
For the world, for the longest time, perhaps even till today, J. Marion Sims was the ‘Father of Modern Gynaecology.’ Sims reportedly earned the title for his ‘groundbreaking surgical innovations, notably the development of a cure for vesicovaginal fistula.” For his achievements, Sims not only received the soubriquet, but also statues and memorials and hospitals and wards named after him. The number of girls on whom he perfected his techniques were not even a footnote in the glorious history he covered himself with.
Among them was Anarcha Westcott, a teenage mother, a patient who developed a terrible vesicovaginal fistula, tears or holes that develop between the bladder and vagina, sustained after three days of labour. The tears made it impossible to control her bowel or bladder and the condition caused her immense pain and suffering. That is how she came under the ‘care’ of Sims, if care could be used to describe what he went on to do.
Anarcha was a young African American woman wrested down in slavery. Sims reportedly believed that African American women do not feel pain, so he experimented on her repeatedly (we know of two others -- Betsey, and Lucy), operating without anaesthesia (though it was available). Sims himself records that he had performed nearly 30 procedures on her, consent was a casualty of the times, before he perfected his technique using silver to suture the fistula, that prevented infection.Before this, a vesicovaginal fistula was considered untreatable, and women would continue to suffer the rest of their life.
Anarcha did not disappear after this though. J. C. Hallman, in his 2023 book Say Anarcha- A Young Woman, a Devious Surgeon, and the Harrowing Birth of Modern Women’s Health, did extensive research to uncover that far from disappearing after the Sims experiments, she went on to serve in Sims hospital, as a midwife, nurse, and ‘doctor woman’ to her own people, women who were also slaves. Many decades after Anarcha died, a groundswell of support arose for her from women who objected to the way she was quietly erased from history, and instead calling for her to be celebrated as the “mother of gynaecology.”
Say Anarcha excavates history, deconstructing the biographical smoke screen of a surgeon who has falsely been enshrined as a medical pioneer and bringing forth a heroic Black woman to her rightful place at the center of the creation story of modern women’s health care. She was more than a medical ‘specimen’, she worked at Sims’ slave hospital near Montgomery, Alabama. She trained and served as a surgical nurse and went on to help other women, also being experimented upon at the hospital.
More recently, efforts have been made to honour her contribution to gynaecology. The American college of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists have dedicated two days – February 28 and March 1—to Anarcha, Lucy and Betsey. Recognition also saw expression in art: At Harvard’s Hutchins Center exhibition in 2023, a prominent exhibit was artist Jules Arthur’s paintings of Anarcha, Luch and Betsey through her work titled “Call and Response: A Narrative of Reverence to Our Foremothers in Gynaecology“.
Artist Michelle Browder created a 15-foot public monument honouring them as “the mothers of gynaecology“ in downtown Montgomery. Tangentially, it was also seen as a victory that Sims’ statue was removed from Central Park in April 2018 and relocated. Hallman’s book was preceded by a documentary Remembering Anarcha.
Unfortunately, Anarcha’s story is not merely a historical wrong. It serves to remind health practitioners and policy makers that several inequities still govern access and affordability of high quality care; that for women, it could be tougher than it might be for men. For that, we will have to keep saying her name, so it will be a reminder. Say her name, say Anarcha.

Tariffs, tariffs, and more tariffs - the Donald Trump administration’s favourite economic weapon is back in focus again with the US passing a new bill that allows its president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that are buying Russian crude oil in a big way. That means India is on the list, and so is China.
The US House of Representatives on Wednesday approved the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026". This legislation will now go to President Donald Trump for his signature.
So, will Donald Trump impose 100% tariffs on India for its Russian crude oil buys? What will that mean for India’s exports to the US and its energy security situation amid the Middle East conflict?
How important is Russian crude oil to India and will it stop buying it if faced with fresh tariffs from the US?
What the Russia Sanctions Bill is about
Initially introduced over a year-and-half ago, the bill had proposed up to 500% tariffs on major buyers of Russian crude oil. But, that was later brought down to 100%.
The House approved the bill by 262 votes to 159. The main aim of the bill is to target Russia's energy and defence sectors along with its "shadow fleet" of tankers that are used to circumvent existing sanctions. The objective is to restrict Russia’s access to funds that the US claims help support Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
Russia Sanctions Bill: What It Means For India
This new legislation gives the US President powers to impose up to 100% tariffs on countries like China and India which are major buyers of Russian crude. 
At present the list of top five importers of Russian energy likely includes China, India, Slovakia, Hungary and Azerbaijan. It also expands sanctions on Iran.
The Graham Act had passed the Senate last month with an 86-11 vote, receiving strong backing from both parties.
So what does the bill mean for India? Let’s first understand India’s dependence on Russian crude:
How Much Oil Does India Get From Russia?
Back in 2022, Russian oil was a negligible part of India’s crude oil imports. But with the Russia-Ukraine war leading Europe to impose sanctions on crude from Moscow, the oil became available at deep discounts.
Since then, Russia’s share in India’s crude imports has steadily climbed up. Russia is the biggest supplier of crude oil for India.
Till the end of 2025, Russia accounted for over 30% of India’s crude oil supplies. The Middle East war has deepened this dependence further.
According to Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), Russia accounted for 30.3 per cent of India's crude oil imports in FY2026, with supplies worth $40.8 billion out of India's total crude imports of $134.7 billion.
In July 2026, Russian supplies accounted for more than half of India's imported oil. This is largely due to continued supply disruptions from the Middle East due to the US-Iran conflict.
As GTRI notes, other suppliers were far behind. The UAE accounted for 10.8% of India’s July imports, Saudi Arabia 9.6%, Venezuela 6.3%, Brazil 5.5%, Oman 5.3% and the US 2.9%. Russia alone supplied more crude than these six countries combined.
In fact, experts see Russian crude oil as a central part of India’s crude oil and energy security strategy. But will that change if the Trump administration imposes 100% tariffs?
Is 100% Tariff Imminent? What It Would Mean For Trade
The important thing to understand is that the bill gives the US President power to impose tariffs of up to 100%. The decision on whether to impose tariffs, and in what quantity, lies with Trump.
Experts believe that the Trump administration may choose not to needle delicate ties with China, which is the largest buying of Russian crude. In the case of India however, there is a precedent from last year, when Trump imposed 25% penal tariffs on Indian exports for the country’s continued purchases of Russian oil.
GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava sees high stakes for India with the passage of this bill
“The bill is a blunt and dangerous attempt to pressurize India to sign BTA on one sided terms. India buys Russian oil to secure affordable energy for 1.4 billion people, not to finance war, and these purchases have helped stabilise global supplies and prices,” says Ajay Srivastava.
He believes that if tariffs of up to 100% are indeed imposed by the Trump administration, they would not only end up punishing Indian exporters and American consumers, but also disrupt trade and give the US president excessive power over major partners.
“Washington should pursue diplomacy and stable energy markets, not threaten a strategic partner for protecting its legitimate economic interests,” he says.
"The actual impact of new tariffs on Indian exports can be assessed only after the US announces the tariff rates, product coverage and implementation timetable," he adds.
India has already faced 50% US tariffs for several months since last year, till the rate was brought down to 18% earlier this year, and now stands at 10% following US Supreme Court’s decision to strike down reciprocal tariffs.
And, while India’s exports basket has been diversified, with several free trade agreements opening up new markets, the US remains an important trading partner and any export hit would have an impact on India.
Ajay Srivastava also points to another nuance: China buys more Russian crude than India, but Washington will put greater pressure on New Delhi as it may fear retaliation by China.
“The new US Act turns sanctions into a trade weapon against India. Washington will now threaten tariffs of up to 100% and then offer a lower rate if New Delhi cuts Russian oil purchases and accepts concessions under a deeply unequal bilateral trade agreement. India should not trade away its energy security for temporary tariff relief. Neither signing a trade agreement nor stopping Russian oil purchases can protect it from future US action under Section 301, sectoral measures or other trade laws. India should continue buying Russian oil as long as it remains commercially competitive and negotiate firmly with Washington without granting unilateral trade concessions,” GTRI’s Srivastava says.
Will India stop buying Russian Crude?
The problem is further exacerbated by the fact that India’s other big oil suppliers are currently hit due to the Middle East conflict. The Strait of Hormuz continues to be blocked and now with the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia’s key pipeline, alternative oil supplies have also been hit.
India’s crude oil procurement is diversified with over 40 countries in it. However, Russia and Middle East countries continue to be the mainstay in the oil security picture.
Experts don’t see Russian crude oil disappearing from India’s crude oil supplies anytime soon. Multiple reasons support this view: India did not stop buying Russian crude oil when faced with penal tariffs last year.
It was only when the Trump administration imposed sanctions on Lukoil and Rosneft - two of the major Russian oil firms - did Indian refiners scale back on purchases.
The logic was simple: tariffs worked as a less effective economic weapon for the US than sanctions since the latter makes trading economically unviable.
In the first two months of 2026, India’s Russian crude oil purchases saw a significant dip. Announcing reduced 18% tariffs on India, Trump claimed that India would stop buying Russian oil. But in March the US-Iran war began and the global oil markets went into a spin.
Faced with Middle East supply disruptions, India aggressively stepped up Russian crude oil purchases. The US even waived sanctions on Russian crude to stabilise global oil prices. But despite that waiver lapsing, India has continued to procure oil from Russia. In fact, Russian crude oil purchases hit an all-time high in July.
The message is clear: energy security at any cost assumes priority for India at the current juncture.
Reacting to the bill India has said that it would take “necessary steps” to protect its economic interests and ensure energy security.
“As stated on several earlier occasions, India remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people,” the Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement.
“It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics," it said.
The statement added that the issue has been "discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors”.
"Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side," it said.
The bill gives the US President additional authority to sanction top 5 foreign nations which are seen as facilitating the evasion of Russian oil and gas sanctions.
“This creates an additional lens that India will have to consider when evaluating its supply options for crude oil. Ultimately, India is likely to take a pragmatic view, weighing all available supply options against considerations of energy security, refinery operations, affordability, supply stability, and the wider economic impact. Any decision on its crude sourcing mix will be guided by what best serves the country's long-term energy and economic interests,” Praveen Rai, Director, Grant Thornton Bharat tells TOI.
Sumit Ritolia, Lead analyst, Modelling and Refining at Kpler told TOI earlier that Russian crude is India’s best hedge against global supply disruptions. “Beyond attractive economics, it has provided reliable supply security despite fluctuations in discounts,” Ritolia told TOI earlier.
Hence, he believes Indian refiners are unlikely to immediately walk away from Russian supplies unless sanctions create significant problems for shipping, insurance or payment arrangements.
But once supply bottlenecks from the Middle East ease, it would be easier for India to reduce its dependence on Russian crude oil.
Until then, experts say, tariffs or no tariffs, Russian oil is unlikely to disappear from India’s crude mix soon.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed making CCTV surveillance mandatory at licensed premises selling prescription drugs, as part of proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945.
The draft notification, G.S.R. 791(E), issued on September 8, proposes inserting a new provision in Rule 65 requiring the supply of drugs on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner, other than through wholesale dealing, to take place under a CCTV surveillance system installed and maintained at the licensed premises. The recordings would have to be preserved for at least three months.
The proposal follows deliberations by the Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) and subsequent consideration by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB). The DCC had earlier recommended that CCTV cameras be made mandatory at medical stores and that they be positioned so that drug sales could be verified.
The move is aimed at strengthening oversight of the sale of prescription medicines and providing a mechanism to verify transactions in cases of suspected unauthorised sale. Under the existing Drugs Rules, medicines covered by Schedules H, H1 and X cannot be sold at retail without a prescription from a registered medical practitioner, with additional record-keeping requirements for certain drugs.
The draft, however, is not yet a final rule. The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from affected persons and other stakeholders for 30 days from the date the Gazette was made available. The proposed rules will be considered after the expiry of this period.
The Ministry has said submissions may be sent to the Under Secretary (Drugs), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, U-6, Work Hall-C Wing, First Floor, Kartavya Bhawan-1, New Delhi, or emailed to drugsdiv-mohfw@gov.in.
“The draft does not merely propose CCTV for Schedule H, H1 and X medicines by name. Its wording is broader — it covers any drug supplied on a registered medical practitioner’s prescription, except wholesale transactions,” said a senior health official.

Alan Curr remembers V.V.S. Laxman’s 281.
He was at university in the UK when Laxman produced one of the all-time great Test innings against Australia at Eden Gardens in Kolkata in 2001. International cricket was not nearly as accessible then as it is today, but Curr remembers following the scores, particularly as it came against England’s arch-rival.
Twenty-five years later, Curr found himself speaking to Laxman. Only this time, the Indian on the other end of the phone was asking him about cricket.
Laxman, coach of the Indian men’s cricket team travelling to the Asian Games, wanted to know what to expect in Japan. What were the facilities like? What was the square like? What was the weather doing?
“Basically he wanted to know what India could expect at the Asian Games,” Curr tells Sportstar.
For Curr, the Chief Operating Officer of the Japan Cricket Association, it was a slightly surreal moment. “Certainly in the two or three minutes leading up to the call, you’re like, wow, I saw this guy play a lot of cricket,” Curr says.
When Curr joined the Japanese Cricket Association (JCA) in 2014, he wasn’t a stranger to unusual encounters. He had previously conducted a cricket match at Everest base camp. But even he admits the idea that a cricketing legend would call him for tips ahead of a match against an Indian team might have seemed ludicrous.
“Even three weeks ago, if you’d mentioned to people in the Japan cricket community that India women’s team – the current ODI World Champions are going to come and play a game here, they wouldn’t have believed it,” Curr says.
But it’s not fantasy anymore. On September 18 at the Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin in Japan’s Aichi prefecture, India’s women’s cricket team will begin its Asian Games campaign against Japan.
It’s beyond obvious just how much of a gulf there is between the two teams. India is a heavyweight in every possible sense. Its players earn in the hundreds of thousands of dollars in contracts and endorsements. In Japan, the women’s game remains largely amateur. It didn’t even qualify for the women’s cricket tournament at the 2022 Asian Games. Yet when the Japanese players step onto the same field as some of the most recognisable professional cricketers in the world, there’s no nervousness, just anticipation.
“It is incredibly exciting. I have waited a decade to play in the Asian Games, so finally being able to compete on home soil is something truly special,” captain Mai Yanagida tells Sportstar.
Tickets please?
It’s a blockbuster encounter by Japanese standards, and it brings with it its own challenge, not just for reasons you’d expect. The JCA isn’t directly hosting the Indian team in Nagoya. That’s the Olympic Council of Asia’s responsibility, but the association is playing a supporting role. “For years, our biggest problem was finding players to come and play matches. Normally we’re desperately trying to encourage people to come to our ground. Whereas when you’ve got India coming, then the tickets sold out in about — it felt like about 20 minutes,” Curr says.
The interest has forced the tiny 20-member organisation to think beyond what happens inside the boundary: security, media zones, spectators and all the infrastructure surrounding a major sporting occasion. “We’re pretty good at organising cricket. But organising all the other stuff around it suddenly is sharply coming into focus. And we’re having to learn pretty quickly. It’s a big ask to try and turn something to a standard that people will probably expect for a Full Member nation,” he says.
But try, they will. Playing India at the Asian Games has a significance all its own. For the wider Japanese public, a Cricket World Cup qualifier may mean relatively little, explains Curr. Japan has hosted one before. The Asian Games, though, are immediately understandable. “The Asian Games is like the Olympics. It happens every four years. Everybody watches it; it’s one of those things that people really do get behind,” Curr says.
He saw that in Hangzhou three years ago, where Japan’s men made their Asian Games debut and beat Cambodia in their opening match. “That suddenly became national news. We had highlights shown on the major television channels! It’s like at the Olympics, when everyone starts following random sports, especially if there’s someone from your nation doing well in it,” he says.
Thirty-nine-year-old medium-pace bowler Kurumi Ota sees the home Games in much the same way. “I hope this will be an opportunity to raise awareness of cricket and inspire people watching the matches in person to dream of aiming for the Japanese national team in the future,” she tells Sportstar. “Hosting an event on the scale of the Asian Games in Japan is a rare and precious opportunity that may not come again anytime soon. I want to turn the energy and support that can only be felt at a home tournament into strength,” she says.
It’s a big opportunity, but to say the Japanese women’s team has it hard is probably an understatement the size of Mount Fuji.
There are just 14 clubs across the country. All of Japan’s women’s players have lives outside cricket. There are university students, office workers and teachers. Some players are based overseas. “Unfortunately, we are not full-time professional cricketers. Most of us balance cricket with a full-time job or school. It can be challenging to take leave for international tournaments and to find enough training time to catch up with higher-ranked nations whose players train full-time. It definitely requires a lot of personal sacrifices,” says captain Yanagida.
Ota knows that balancing act particularly well.
She works full-time as a systems engineer at Hitachi. Her employer allows her roughly two weeks off twice a year, which is when she can compete internationally. But even then, there have been times when Ota has had to choose. She stepped away from the sport for seven years between 2017 and 2023. The reason wasn’t injury or loss of form but work.
Ota had joined one of Japan’s largest core-system modernisation projects, a 10-year undertaking valued at several billion dollars. The scale of the project demanded her complete attention.
Cricket took a step back. Only after the system was successfully released was Ota able to return to the sport.
Despite knowing what they are up against, neither Ota nor Yanagida nor the rest of the Japanese team are approaching September 18 simply as a photo opportunity. “They go out, and they enjoy themselves. They play with a smile on their face. They play respectful cricket. But they take a lot of pride in wearing that Japan jersey,” Curr says.
Drawing India in the first match of the Asian Games competition was a bonus.
“All of them!” the 33-year-old Yanagida says when asked which Indian player she most wants to face. “I watch them on stream all the time. They are world-class players and a world-class team. As a batter, I’m really excited about facing Shafali Verma and Smriti Mandhana. I also hoped to play against Jemimah Rodrigues, but unfortunately she’s not playing. Hopefully our paths will cross another time,” says the off-spin bowling all-rounder who has scored three T20I fifties over the course of her career.
For Ota, one Indian player in particular she hopes to go up against.
Harmanpreet Kaur.
The two belong to the same generation, but their cricket careers have unfolded in almost completely different worlds. “She is of the same generation, has a long career, and plays at the world-class level, so I am really looking forward to actually playing against her,” Ota says.
Harmanpreet might have a mountain of experience that Ota doesn’t, but the Japanese player has accomplishments she’s proud of. The right-arm medium pacer has 26 international wickets in T20Is, holding at one point the record for most by a Japanese woman.
She also has something more tangible. Sixteen years ago, Ota was part of the Japanese women’s team that won bronze at Guangzhou in 2010, the first Asian Games at which cricket was contested.
Ota says she’s kept the medal safely on a shelf at her home, rarely bringing it out for others to see. In the build-up to Nagoya, though, members of the current Japan setup have started asking about it again. “The assistant coach and our social media manager have told me they’d like to see the bronze medal, which makes me really happy,” she says.
International competitions for Japan were extraordinarily rare then. Ota remembers them coming only once every four years, meaning years of practice could culminate in a single opportunity. “The practice we built up day by day finally paid off, and winning the bronze medal together with my teammates is my fondest memory. Including the time we spent working hard and sharing both the hardships and joys with my teammates, it remains a very precious memory to this day,” she says.
Perhaps nothing illustrates the change in Japanese cricket better than Ota’s memories of how she once trained. “When I first started playing cricket, we would sometimes practise under overpasses because there was nowhere else to play. Getting to a proper practice ground meant a six-hour round trip. Today there are international-standard grounds and grass outfields where we players can dive and slide without worrying about gravel,” she says.
Cricket communities have developed in Tokyo and elsewhere. Children can now encounter the sport in elementary school, and some have progressed to international competition. “Compared to when I began, I feel that not only the playing environment but also the starting age for players and the depth of talent capable of aiming for the global stage have expanded greatly,” Ota says.
Ota herself came to cricket almost accidentally. She had played basketball through junior high and high school before arriving at university wanting to try something new. She went to look at the cricket club.
What she saw stuck with her.
“There was this senior student who was practising her bowling alone at night, illuminated only by the faint light from a building. I thought that looked so cool,” Ota remembers.
She later discovered that the bowler was a member of the Japanese national team. Ota had never bowled before. The unfamiliarity became part of the attraction. “I wanted to learn to take a run-up and send the ball towards the wicket the way I had seen that senior player do. That’s how I fell in love with the game,” she says.
Yanagida’s introduction was similarly rooted in another sport. She joined the cricket club while studying at university in Tokyo after previously playing softball. “I got into cricket very quickly because the feeling of hitting the ball was even better than in softball,” she says.
The crossover is not unusual. It’s also what gives Curr reason to believe cricket can grow in Japan.
“Almost everyone coming through the Japanese school system has some familiarity with baseball. Softball provides a similar sporting foundation for many women. You can see a lot of that background visible in our teams fielding and throwing,” he says.
Even the venue where Japan will take on India is a refurbished baseball ground.
But while cricket isn’t entirely unfamiliar, the challenge for Japanese cricket has always been giving people the first opportunity to encounter the game.
‘We have a cricket team?’
Many Japanese people still don’t know their country has a cricket team. “Although awareness is growing, most people are still genuinely surprised to hear that Japan has a national cricket team. Once I explain how it’s not that different from baseball, though, people are very curious,” Yanagida says.
Ota has experienced something similar.
People are initially surprised when she tells them she plays international cricket. Then they begin asking when the next tournament is and wishing her luck.
“Sparked by these conversations, some people actually came all the way to the venue to support us when there was a match in Japan. I am so happy to spark interest in people who didn’t know about cricket and gain their support,” she says.
It is precisely the process Japan Cricket hopes the Asian Games can accelerate.
There is a distinctly Japanese quality to the way Curr talks about the association’s development: the emphasis on long-term planning. Japan Cricket works through five-year strategies that sit inside a broader 20-year plan. The current five-year strategy is called Kaika, which Curr describes as a moment of blossoming or flourishing, like the arrival of the country’s cherry blossoms.
Its objectives extend well beyond results.
The association wants cricket to become recognised as a flourishing sport in Japan, attracting new fans, participants and partners, competing internationally, creating social value and providing professional opportunities. “This means better facilities, role models, digital marketing and school engagement. It means developing not only players but coaches, commentators, curators and others who can create a functioning cricket ecosystem. You need to remember what you want the future to look like, and then everything you do can direct you that way,” Curr says.
The growth is particularly visible in the men’s team. The Under-19 side qualified twice for the U-19 World Cup, in 2019 and last year. A growing number of players of Japanese heritage living overseas, particularly in Australia and England, also began contacting the JCA. Curr says he gets a call every week or so from an interested player. Several are part of the men’s team which will be competing at the Asian Games.
The JCA itself has grown. While a 20-staff federation might seem tiny in comparison to India, Curr reckons the association had seven full-time staff at one point. Japan Cricket has gone from an organisation with a recognisable season and off-season to one that operates throughout the year. “There aren’t really quiet periods any more,” Curr says.
On September 18, when Mai Yanagida walks out to the toss alongside Harmanpreet Kaur, it’s going to be the loudest it’s ever been.
And there are the less tangible bonuses, of course. “I mean, how often do you get to say you had V.V.S Laxman talk to you about cricket?” says Curr.

Reading for pleasure is linked to better mental health, greater empathy and a lower risk of dementia, Cambridge University scientists said on Tuesday.
As part of a National Year of Reading tie-up with the Queen's Reading Room, a charity founded by Queen Camilla to highlight the benefits of reading for pleasure at any age, the scientists argue that it doesn't matter what or how we read.
In a review published in 'Psychological Medicine', Professor Barbara Sahakian and Christelle Langley said reading for enjoyment can bring huge benefits and reading with others, whether it's as part of a book club or a parent reading with their children, can bring even greater rewards.
"Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop important cognitive skills and boost our wellbeing. It's something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it's never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age,” said Sahakian.
Some of the strongest evidence of the benefits of reading for pleasure comes from a study by Sahakian, Langley and colleagues of more than 10,000 young people, which found that children who began reading for pleasure in life showed benefits including: better attention, memory, and executive functioning, greater academic achievement, fewer mental health problems, and healthier lifestyles, including more sleep and less screen time. Langley said: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading.
"The important thing is to find something they really enjoy – it might be a TV programme or a game – and use this as a way in. Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels.”
In ‘Reading and associations with brain health, cognition, well-being, and mental health’ published this week, the experts draw on subjective surveys and objective studies using longitudinal, neuroimaging, and behavioural methods to highlight converging findings that link reading engagement with improved brain and mental health, better cognitive performance, and reduced risk of cognitive decline.
"Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction. They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia,” said Sahakian.
“While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they're perfect for older people who may be not so mobile – they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy,” she added.

Bose refreshes its Ultra Open Earbuds and adds a new sport model to the lineup
Both new open-ear products go on sale next month.
Bose has added two new products to its lineup of open-ear earbuds, with the Bose Sport Open Earbuds and the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) arriving on October 1.
The second-generation Ultra Open Earbuds are a direct follow-up to 2024's earbuds of the same name, which Bose regards as its "flagship open-ear experience," with improvements made to sound, battery life and design. They retain their predecessor's unique (and according to our reviewer at the time, divisive) cuff-clip silhouette, which might look a bit weird, but the first time around proved to be very comfortable. Look closely and you'll spot the new beveled finish on the metallic caps. A redesigned case now supports wireless charging and can stand upright.
A new driver promises better bass and increased volume than the first-generation earbuds, and the updated Ultra Open Earbuds get Cinema Mode, Bose's spatial audio experience for your movies, TV shows and video podcasts. Given the open design, don't expect any noise-canceling features, but you do get a three-band EQ via the Bose app, as well as an automatic volume control setting.
The Ultra Open Earbuds support multipoint connectivity with two devices over Bluetooth 5.4, and on launch day Bose will add support for Google Find Hub and Alexa+ in a firmware update. A new Apple Music shortcut also lets you jump straight into your pre-selected playlists.
Maximum battery life has been boosted to up to nine hours, (up from 7.5 hours on the Gen 1 model), with just under 20 extra hours stored in the wireless charging case. If you plan to use the Immersive Audio and Cinema Mode settings a lot, expect battery life to take a considerable hit.
The other new Bose earbuds are being positioned by the company as completely new, even if they adopt the same name as a discontinued product from 2021. The new Bose Sport Open Earbuds leverage the same OpenAudio tech as the Ultra model, which allows you to listen to your tunes without tuning out the world around you.
They also have a cuff-clip design, but given they're designed for fitness and outdoor sport, Bose has gone for a soft silicone finish and lightweight build. The company says the C-arm cuff attaches gently to your ear, but is secure enough to stay on during head shakes and other fast movements. They're apparently even cartwheel-proof, if you're the acrobatic type. Physical controls should also make adjusting volume or taking calls easier mid-workout.
The Sport Open Earbuds employ custom-designed drivers and also support Auto Volume and multipoint. Battery life is up to seven hours (there are no spatial audio modes to chomp away at the battery here), with 22 hours in the wireless charging case. IP54 dust and water protection means you don't need to worry about getting sweaty on a run, but don't take them for a swim.
The Bose Sport Open Earbuds will be available in two colors, Black and White Smoke, and cost $199. The second-generation Ultra Open Earbuds can be picked up in either Nue Black or White Smoke, and cost $299.

Social media giant Meta may no longer enjoy intermediary status in India, under which Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp can seek “safe harbour” protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 for content posted by their users. As per a report by PTI, Meta may no longer be considered a “simple intermediary” when its algorithms amplify content and influence what users interact with. Government sources cited by the agency said that the company may have to take greater responsibilities as a service provider. Inc42 has reached out to Meta on the development, the story will be updated upon receiving a response. The comments come amid growing regularity scrutiny of Meta’s handling of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), deepfakes and other harmful content on Facebook and Instagram in India. The Centre has also questioned the role of recommendation algorithms in determining the visibility and reach of such content. “Service providers have many responsibilities... Once Meta has agreed to be responsible for what they have on the platform, then as the next steps, they have to start taking many more responsibilities,” the sources said, PTI reported. The development comes a day after Meta said it would report child safety matters directly to the cybercrime portal managed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C). The company has previously reported such cases to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC). “Protecting children on our platforms is a priority for us and we’re committed to working with the government to ensure that the perpetrators of these crimes are held responsible,” a Meta spokesperson reportedly said. The company said the new reporting mechanism would strengthen coordination with Indian law enforcement agencies. Meta’s Widened Scrutiny Over Instagram Ads Meta is also facing a formal inquiry by the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) over alleged ads hosted by its platforms linked to CSAM. The NCPCR issued a notice to Meta on July 3 after taking suo motu cognisance of a BBC report on the alleged advertisements. Meta submitted its response a week later, following which the commission decided to initiate a formal inquiry. Meta India executives, including India head Arun Srinivas, appeared before the NCPCR on Wednesday for the second time in a week in connection with the investigation. The Centre has separately summoned Meta executives and held several rounds of discussions with the company’s global leadership, seeking stronger guardrails against such content. Beyond this, the scrutiny has also extended to Meta’s recommendation systems. The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has also sought reports from government agencies and the Delhi Police over the allegations involving CSAM-related advertisements, including whether mandatory reporting requirements under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act were followed. Meta has also been seeing such concerns raised internationally in recent times. In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 Bn over a decade to settle claims brought by US states alleging that Facebook and Instagram harmed children and teenagers. The agreement includes measures such as limits on teenage usage, overnight restrictions and stronger parental controls. Meta did not admit wrongdoing as part of the settlement. In India, the government is separately pushing social media platforms to strengthen safeguards for children and improve systems for identifying, removing and reporting illegal content. The latest focus on Meta’s algorithms marks a broader shift in the regulatory debate, from how platforms respond to user-generated content to the role their own systems play in amplifying and distributing it.

Six-hitting is a skill that Abhishek Sharma has honed to perfection. He can make it appear ridiculously easy, as though he is playing around with a joystick in a video game, but make no mistake: few can do what the 26-year-old does time and again in the T20 version. A sublime example came in the third T20I against Afghanistan at the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Thursday as Abhishek hammered a record-breaking 34-ball 108, studded with nine fours and 11 sixes, to take India to 221 for seven.
With Afghanistan capitulating for 94 in response, Shreyas Iyer & Co. completed a resounding 127-run win for a 3-0 sweep. Nitish Kumar struck thrice in an over while Ravi Bishnoi also provided three breakthroughs.
AS IT HAPPENED: AFG 94 all out; Abhishek century helps India by 127 runs
Abhishek’s century took merely 30 balls, the fastest against a Test-playing nation and the third-quickest in all in this format. Sanju Samson chipped in with 50 off 35 balls, forging a sensational opening stand of 142 in 9.5 overs. The surface appeared to be a shirtfront when Abhishek and Samson were on song, but the others didn’t find it as easy.
Abhishek imposed himself straightaway. In the second over, Azmatullah Omarzai felt the pinch. The first of the opener’s maximums came when he swivelled and pulled effortlessly beyond deep square-leg. Omarzai persisted with the shorter length and paid the price. Off the fourth ball, he pulled out a forehand slap past mid-on for four. Two balls later, he made room and slashed a back-of-a-length delivery over cover for another six.
Having quickly sized up the Afghan attack, the southpaw’s carnage found a higher gear. The next over, bowled by Fazalhaq Farooqi, went for 23 runs as the Punjab lad stitched together a sequence that read 6, 6, 4, 4.
Afghanistan turned to spin early in the hope of disturbing India’s rhythm. Instead, Samson, who had scored three off his first seven balls, joined the six-hitting party. In the fourth over, he deposited Mujeeb Ur Rahman over long-on.
What followed was a 29-run over by experienced off-spinner Mohammad Nabi as the openers took turns to flex their firepower. By the time ace leggie Rashid Khan conceded 15 runs in the final over of the PowerPlay, India had raced to 100 for none.
In the ninth over, Abhishek entered the record books by reaching the three-figure mark. Ironically, his celebration was unlike the action that had transpired till then: he took off his helmet, sat down and soaked in the moment with a meditative pose.

Greetings from Beijing, where baozi are worth the wait in line
To get the best food in China, I'm told you have to stand in line.
That's true for baozi — a fluffy steamed bun with filling. My go-to in Shanghai is dried tofu and veg.
I don't eat it often because I hate waiting.
But when I was assigned a story about Chinese breakfasts, I dutifully queued at a bun shop outside a Beijing park. I snagged baozi stuffed with their bestseller — soy sauce pork — also an eggplant and green pepper, plus one with pickled veg.
Juice from the fillings stained the buns. That's an indicator of a good bun, Beijing resident Samantha Zhao told me as she took part in a baozi-making workshop at a trendy shop called Bao Er Jiu. She was making the Beijing classic, juicy fennel pork baozi.
Bao Er Jiu also serves eye-catching pineapple-shaped buns, though the signature flavor is chocolate red bean — tasty and not too sweet.
If I pass this shop again — and if the line moves fast — maybe I will wait for baozi.

TOI Correspondent From Washington:
 The US Congress on Wednesday handed President Trump a surgical instrument to punish, at his discretion, not only Moscow but also countries that buy Russian energy, with India and China squarely in the crosshairs.
The House of Representatives passed the “Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026” by a 262-159 margin, voted through by an unusually bipartisan coalition given the deep divisions in Washington: 203 Republicans, 58 Democrats and one Independent voted yes, while 152 Democrats and seven Republicans voted no. The Senate had already approved the measure 86-11 on August 7, meaning the legislation now goes directly to Trump's desk for his signature.
Named for the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July after championing the legislation for more than a year, the measure is designed primarily to squeeze Moscow's revenues from its energy trade and increase pressure on President Putin to negotiate an end to the Ukraine war. It targets Russian energy and defence sectors, financial institutions, officials and the so-called "shadow fleet" of tankers accused of evading sanctions.
 It also extends the Iran Sanctions Act for five years.
But its most consequential provision for India is the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil or gas. The Senate language refers to the five largest purchasers; House debate and amendments have specifically brought India and China into focus. A House amendment identified ten countries potentially eligible for the secondary tariffs: China, India, Turkiye, Azerbaijan, Hungary, Slovakia, the UAE, Singapore, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.
New Delhi is one of the world's largest importers of Russian crude, which became increasingly important after Western sanctions redirected Russian oil toward Asian buyers. India says its priority is affordable and reliable energy for 1.4 billion people. China, meanwhile, has rejected the premise of the US imposing sanctions beyond its own borders, saying the move lacks a basis in international law or authorization from the UN Security Council.
Economically, the stakes are substantial for India since any disruption to Russian crude supplies could significantly increase the country's import bill and put pressure on the rupee and current-account balance. The MEA said on Thursday that India would take "all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests," warning that the bill could affect bilateral ties and international energy markets.
Indeed, even some prominent US analysts blasted the move, taking into account the large US-India ties, with former administration official Evan Feigenbaum saying it amounts to “blunt coercion, gross interference in Indian foreign policy, impractical given India’s economic needs… and a cynical effort to blame India for the West’s (and Trump’s) collective failure to get Moscow to stop its war on Ukraine.”
“In strategic terms, if you value US.-India relations, this is not going to be a winning message. Broadly speaking, the last year-and-a-half has tanked 25 years of bipartisan work to build the US.-India relationship, including in Trump's own first term," Feigenbaum said.
Critics also point to familiar American double-standards in the matter. The US itself continues to import Russian commodities, including nuclear fuel. Moscow has historically supplied 20–25% of US. enriched uranium, while Congress's 2024 prohibition on Russian low-enriched uranium contains national-interest and supply-shortage waivers. The US also continues to buy Russian palladium, fertilizers and chemicals.
The hypocrisy is compounded by the bill's extraordinary delegation of tariff power, with some House Democrats arguing that Trump already possesses extensive sanctions authority. “We cannot grant more tariff power that we know he will abuse,” New York Congressman Gregory Meeks said, warning that the legislation could raise prices for Americans while giving the President excessive discretion.
Supporters see precisely that discretion as leverage. Atlantic Council sanctions expert Daniel Fried, a former State Department sanctions coordinator, says the bill could allow Washington to negotiate gradual reductions in Russian oil purchases rather than demand an immediate cutoff, making presidential waivers a surgical instrument. The administration explicitly backed the legislation partly because it gives Trump "full Presidential discretion on waivers" and allows sanctions to be terminated after a peace agreement. The law therefore creates a threat rather than an automatic 100% tariff on India or China.
For New Delhi, the practical battle now shifts from Capitol Hill to the Oval Office -- and potentially to the rather interminable US.-India trade negotiations. Trump can sign the bill, designate countries, adjust tariffs as countries reduce Russian-energy purchases and use waivers as bargaining leverage. The question for India is therefore not simply whether Washington has fired the tariff gun, but how often and when Trump, fully armed, chooses to pull the trigger.

Malaysia seizes 3 Israeli-bound containers as Anwar pledges to stop shipments for Gaza war
The seizures follow an initial detainment of a container for Israeli defence technology firm Elbit Systems, suspected of containing weapons
Three containers bound for Ashdod Port south of Tel Aviv were detained at Malaysia’s Tanjung Pelepas port in mid-August and to date had not been released as authorities investigate their contents, the people familiar with the matter said, asking not to be identified because they were not authorised to speak publicly.
The seizures follow an initial detainment of another container on August 7 that originally came from the Philippines and that was suspected by the Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency of containing weapons because it was headed to Elbit Systems, an Israeli defence technology firm, according to a statement from the agency at the time. Tracking data from Hapag-Lloyd, the container line carrying the cargo, show the shipment still at Tanjung Pelepas.
The other three seizures happened on August 19, the people said. Those containers housed electric bike parts that were being shipped from a Chinese manufacturer, Chongqing Mobimax Technology, according to manifests. Tracking data from the liner carrying those cargoes, A.P. Moller-Maersk, also show them still at the busy transshipment port almost a month later.

It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah.
But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own.
From point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record.
The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famous wildebeest and zebra migration across the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012.
Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published their findings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become.
“Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.”
The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings.
Two months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. Related dogs do not form new family packs, and typically have to travel long distances through the landscape to find prospective mates.
Only 6,600 or so adults remain of 39 distinct populations of African wild dogs, and the species is classified as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. Habitat loss, declining numbers of natural prey, bushmeat hunters’ snares and human conflict are among the biggest threats to their survival.
But researchers say the three brothers’ epic journey shows the wild dogs can still survive in a human-dominated landscape despite the enormous challenges they face. Alongside African savannah elephants, whose ancient migration routes are increasingly being blocked by human development, African wild dogs need to be able to make long journeys to find new homes.
“These long-term studies provide key evidence that connectivity between large landscapes is still there,” says Dr Nyambe Nyambe, director of the Kavango-Zambezi transfrontier area secretariat, a key conservation region that spans five countries, including Zambia, where governments are trying to keep space for wildlife to move through the landscape.
“If we conserve and continue to improve these connections – spanning the range of national parks, community areas, nations and regions – a lot of species like wild dogs can make the rest happen,” Nyambe says.

Pressure on global chokepoints drives Asia's increased use of Arctic Trade Routes
SEOUL - Chaos in the Middle East is adding incentive and urgency for some trading nations to navigate both ice floes and geopolitical competition at the top of the world.
The first South Korean container ship to reach Europe via the Arctic arrived in Felixstowe, England over the weekend, a day after Houthi rebels seized control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea, putting pressure on yet another global trade chokepoint.
Asian nations, especially China and South Korea, both of which depend heavily on maritime trade routes, including the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea, began pilot voyages more than a decade ago to find routes to Europe and the Middle East which were faster and less vulnerable to chokepoints. The ongoing U.S. war on Iran has added impetus to those efforts.
India says it is planning its first cargo ship voyage via the Northern Sea Route (NSR), an east-west shipping corridor along Russia's Arctic coastline, next year. Japan's Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology is building its first Arctic research icebreaker and preparing to send it to explore polar waters as early as next year.
The contest distantly echoes early modern history, such as 15th-16th century Europe, when Spain and Portugal and later England and the Netherlands vied for control of sea lanes, ports and access to resources to gain the upper hand against rival states.
In a social media post, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung congratulated the captain and crew of the Panstar Acro ship for opening a historic route. The ship took advantage of late summer temperatures when ice is scarcest to make the 45-day round trip voyage, starting in Busan, via the NSR, and stopping in Rotterdam, the Netherlands and Gdansk, Poland.
Climate change breaks the ice
Due to global warming in Arctic waters, "we're seeing the surface area covered by the ice in September, much lower than it used to be. We're losing an average of about 10 to 15% per decade," says Walt Meier, a senior research scientist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center in Boulder, CO.
With pack ice covering most of its waters, Meier adds, much of the Arctic was previously unnavigable without icebreakers — ships with reinforced bows to cut through ice. But now, "we are seeing a lot more people going up there and it's small sailboats and cruise ships as well as commercial vehicles. So it's becoming a busier place."
But it's no trade superhighway yet. Insurance costs for Arctic shipping are high, and the window of opportunity when ice is at its minimum is short, from late summer to early fall.
"I think what's significant," says geographic studies professor Frédéric Lassere at Laval University in Quebec, Canada, "is that for the first time, there are shipping companies that are trying to implement regular container services across the Arctic," and betting that it could eventually be profitable.
For now, Lassere says, most shipping companies are reacting to Middle East risks by taking the longer but more predictable route around southern Africa.
Geopolitical competition intensifies
Meanwhile, geopolitics and Russia's war with Ukraine have constrained South Korea's Arctic ambitions.
Russia views the North Sea Route as part of its domestic waters. It requires ships to get a permit to transit them and reserves the right to require the use of its state-owned nuclear-powered icebreakers. Those icebreakers are under Western sanctions due to Russia's war with Ukraine.
Seo Hyun-kyo, principal research specialist at the Korea Polar Research Institute, argues that South Korea is managing to balance between Russia and the West.
"Our security allies are the U.S. and the EU," he says. "I understand that we are proceeding while strictly adhering to prior consultations with them" about shipping through the Arctic.
China has declared a "no limits" strategic partnership with Russia, and opposes Western sanctions against it.
"Unlike the current situation," Seo adds, "where China cooperates with Russia without broad international consensus, we intend to pursue a different path."
But Choi Subeom, Secretary-General of the Korea Arctic Shipping Association, is critical of the fact that, although the Panstar Acro ship was sailing through Russian waters, South Korea's government "put far more effort into ensuing no issues arose with the U.S." than with Russia, whose waters the vessel transited.
"Experts like us were quite dissatisfied with that approach," Choi says, because "it was seen as diplomatic behavior that was overly subservient to the U.S."
Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the work of the Arctic Council, which includes Russia, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Canada, ground to a halt, as did international environmental and climate cooperation.
Meanwhile, NATO officials say that Russia and NATO have stepped up Arctic military exercises and restored military bases that became obsolete with the end of the Cold War. According to them, the Arctic remains important as the shortest route for missiles and bombers to travel between Russia and America, while its ice caps still shield submarines from detection.
And the Trump administration has floated, then disavowed, the possibility of acquiring Greenland by force.
For roughly three decades since the end of the Cold War, the idea of the Arctic as an "exceptional zone" of international cooperation persisted. 
Despite the prospect of growing trade along Arctic maritime routes, that exceptionalism appears to some analysts to be increasingly unrealistic.
NPR's Se Eun Gong contributed to this report in Seoul.

Sachin Bansal-led Navi continued to gain ground in the UPI market in August, with its share of transaction volumes rising to 4.4% from 4% in July. The fintech platform’s market share has risen steadily over the past few months, from 3.7% in June to 4% in July and 4.4% in August, according to Inc42’s calculations based on NPCI data. Navi processed around 1.08 Bn UPI transactions worth ₹52,512.85 Cr during the month, compared with approximately 947 Mn transactions worth ₹48,318 Cr in July. Meanwhile, market leaders PhonePe and Google Pay saw their shares decline marginally, with their combined market share falling to 78.3% from 78.6% in July. PhonePe processed around 11.25 Bn transactions worth ₹14.26 Lakh Cr in August, while its volume market share slipped to 45.9% from 46.1% in July. Google Pay’s market share declined to 32.4% from 32.5%. The platform processed around 7.9 Bn UPI transactions during the month under review. Paytm retained its position as the third-largest UPI app, with its transaction volume market share rising marginally to 8.1% from 8% in July. The fintech major processed around 1.98 Bn transactions worth ₹2.04 Lakh Cr during the month. Meanwhile, Flipkart-backed super.money saw its market share decline to 1.7% from 1.9%. It processed around 421.87 Mn transactions worth ₹20,363.26 Cr in August. BHIM’s share increased marginally to 1.04%, translating into around 253 Mn transactions. FamApp by Trio retained a 0.9% share, processing approximately 223 Mn transactions. Overall, UPI platforms collectively processed a record 24.51 Bn transactions in August, up 3.6% from 23.66 Bn in July. The latest data comes ahead of the implementation of the new merchant discount rate (MDR) framework for certain UPI transactions. Starting October 15, merchants receiving eligible UPI payments above ₹2,000 will be charged an MDR of 0.4%, capped at ₹300 for transactions exceeding ₹75,000. Person-to-person payments will continue to remain free. Payments exceeding ₹2,000 in sectors such as railways, fuel, telecom, insurance, and certain utilities will attract a flat charge of ₹5. Capital market-related payments will carry a lower MDR of 0.02%, capped at ₹300. The MDR framework will open up a direct revenue stream for third-party application providers, which have so far been unable to monetise UPI transactions directly and have largely relied on payments data to cross-sell other financial services to users.

Fall is here, and the autumnal turn marks a season of returns. Back to school, back to work—and when it comes to the best films on streaming services, back to some of the best films of yesteryear.
September finds John Carpenter’s brilliant 1982 remake of The Thing crawling its way onto Prime Video, Luc Besson’s mind-bending and eye-popping The Fifth Element on Netflix, and an unexpected blast from the past coming to Hulu in the form of The X-Files: I Want to Believe—Vrach Frankenshteyn, an R-rated director’s cut of 2008’s second cinematic case for Mulder and Scully, now closer to creator Chris Carter’s original vision.
Even the new arrivals have a vintage flair this month though. Star Wars spinoff The Mandalorian and Grogu brings the big-screen bounty hunters back to Disney+ for a retro-tinged adventure, Netflix’s Mobile Suit Gundam: Hathaway expands on the world of the classic 1970s anime series, and Edge of Tomorrow on Paramount+ shows the past can be hard to escape at the best of times.
Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.
The Mandalorian & Grogu
Sure, The Mandalorian and Grogu has the dubious distinction of being the lowest-grossing live-action Star Wars movie ever (only 2008’s animated Clone Wars performed worse). And yes, for fans of the Disney+ space western series, a full fourth season might have been more welcome (and the three seasons of homework beforehand may have put off wider audiences anyway). Yet this spinoff is, in its own way, the “purest” Star Wars movie in years, capturing the feel of the classic serials that originally inspired George Lucas all those decades ago.
This stand-alone adventure finds Mandalorian bounty hunter Din Djarin (Pedro Pascal) and his apprentice-slash-adopted-son Grogu (aka Baby Yoda) running jobs for the New Republic but, after being sent on the trail of an Imperial officer turned warlord, getting swept up in a battle against twin Hutt crimelords, battling hordes of alien monsters, and shooting their way through a factory’s worth of droids. Best of all, though, is that while there are plenty of nods for hardcore Star Wars fans, this isn’t trying to establish a new “saga” or a pivotally important entry in the wider lore. It’s just two hours of solidly enjoyable swashbuckling adventure. Star Wars could do with more like this.
The Wild Robot
Dreamworks Animation has had a solid streak recently, but The Wild Robot stands as one of the studio’s best films ever. A gorgeously animated ode to the power and importance of the natural world, it follows Universal Robots ROZZUM Unit 7134—soon shortened to “Roz” (Lupita Nyong’o)—who becomes the stand-in mother for baby gosling Brightbill (Kit Connor) after being stranded on an isolated island. Guided by the fox Fink (Pedro Pascal, again) and the opossum Pinktail (Catherine O’Hara), Roz struggles to raise the infant, desperately trying to teach him to fly in time for migration season—and before her manufacturers track her down.
A blend of Studio Ghibli’s reverence for nature and The Iron Giant’s emotional heart, The Wild Robot earned a near-total clean sweep at the 2025 Annie Awards—animation’s Oscars. Once you’ve finished sobbing from watching this, you’ll understand why.
Obsession
“Be careful what you wish for” is such a beautifully simple concept for horror, but it’s rarely as well executed as in Obsession. When lovelorn Bear (Michael Johnston) makes a wish on the “One Wish Willow” for his friend and coworker Nikki (Inde Navarrette) to love him, he thinks it’s just a dumb toy. It works though, better than he dared hope. Or rather, worse—Nikki goes from besotted to bunny boiler faster than you can blink, stalking Bear’s every movement, reacting with increased hostility to anyone who comes near him, and going to brutal lengths to keep the man she “loves,” whether he likes it or not. Balancing some shockingly gory scenes with darkly comedic moments, Obsession was the breakout hit of the summer.
Mobile Suit Gundam Hathaway: The Sorcery of Nymph Circe
Yes, the title is a mouthful, and no, it has nothing to do with sorcery or nymphs. Instead, this second in a planned trilogy of movies returns to the core “Universal Century” timeline of the Gundam franchise for blistering battles between military mecha, with a side of complex planetary politics to keep things cerebral.
The eponymous Hathaway Noa (Kenshō Ono in Japanese; Caleb Yen in English) is secretly Mafty, leader of a rebel group of fighters dedicated to overthrowing the corrupt Earth Federation Government. One man’s rebel is another’s terrorist, though, and Federation loyalist Kenneth Sleg (Junichi Suwabe; Aaron Philips) is finally on Mafty’s trail, having uncovered his true identity. Yet as the two head toward a clash over the skies of Adelaide, the visions of precognitive Gigi Andalucia (Reina Ueda; Megan Shipman) could change everyone’s fates. You’ll definitely want to catch the first Hathaway film (on Netflix, too) before jumping in here, but this captivating anime epic packs in plenty of emotional depth alongside the giant robot smackdowns. Fingers crossed the finale isn’t too far off.
The Thing
John Carpenter’s remake of the 1951 classic The Thing From Another World was intended to be a more accurate adaptation of the original source material, author John W. Campbell Jr.’s 1938 novella Who Goes There? What he ended up creating was one of the most influential and enduringly brilliant pieces of sci-fi horror ever committed to celluloid.
In the sheer isolation of an Antarctic research station, a crew of scientists—a powerhouse cast including Kurt Russell and Keith David—find themselves facing a shapeshifting menace from the stars, with the paranoia mounting as they turn on each other, unsure of who among them is really human. It’s a masterclass in tension, all brought gruesomely to life with pioneering effects work. Almost paradoxically, it bombed on release, but audiences have seen the error of their ways in the decades since. Learn the same lesson now, if you’ve not seen it yet.
The X-Files: I Want to Believe—Vrach Frankenshteyn
Originally released in 2008, this second feature length X-Files thriller was never anyone’s favorite chapter for the long-running sci-fi conspiracy franchise. It abandoned much of the mythology of the core series and instead charged returning leads Mulder (David Duchovny) and Scully (Gillian Anderson) with investigating a missing FBI agent, a rash of murders, and grisly organ harvesting. It all felt like an odd fit.
In hindsight, that might be down to the film being in development hell for years, then subject to studio interference, its release ultimately neutering creator-director Chris Carter’s vision. This Vrach Frankenshteyn edit corrects that, reinserting cut scenes and restoring the almost “folk horror meets body horror” approach that the original was aiming for, while trimming some other scenes for a tighter, better-paced experience. Longtime fans of The X-Files will appreciate this more authentic take on the film, while newcomers will find it a solid stand-alone horror—and perhaps a perfect introduction to the vibe of the series ahead of Ryan Coogler’s upcoming TV reboot.
The Fifth Element
Set in the 23rd century, but with a mythology spanning millennia, this wildly ambitious sci-fi adventure sees humble cab driver Korben Dallas (Bruce Willis) drawn into a battle to save Earth from impending doom when runaway Leeloo (Milla Jovovich) crashes into his life—literally, falling onto his flying taxi while escaping from the forces of the exquisitely evilly-named Jean-Baptiste Emanuel Zorg (Gary Oldman). Cut to: a race to find ancient elements, a cosmic opera diva, warring alien races, and a scene-stealing turn from Chris Tucker as the phenomenally flamboyant media mogul Ruby Rhod.
Director Luc Besson’s gloriously weird, experimental outing was something of a sleeper hit in the US when it was released in 1997, but with its phenomenal practical effects, mind-bending world designs, and bizarre fashions dreamed up by Jean Paul Gaultier, it has more than earned its status as a bona fide cult classic. If you’ve never experienced it, prepare for sensory overload as you take in this vibrant vision of the future.
Edge of Tomorrow
It’s rare for a film’s tagline to outshine its actual name, but Edge of Tomorrow’s striking “Live. Die. Repeat.” so perfectly encapsulates this time-loop action epic that it has supplanted the title for many. Then again, you might also know it as All You Need Is Kill, the original Japanese light novel by Hiroshi Sakurazaka and Yoshitoshi Abe that it’s based on.
Director Doug Liman’s live-action take reframes humanity’s battle against seemingly unstoppable alien “Mimics” to grand cinematic scale, with Tom Cruise as Major William Cage, a cowardly public affairs officer in the United Defense Force, killed almost as soon as he’s forced onto the battlefield—only to wake right up and have to go through it all again and again. His only hope is to learn from Sergeant Rita Vrataski (Emily Blunt), a legendary soldier who’s been caught in her own cycle of violent death and rebirth. An explosive take on Groundhog Day, the film packs in a surprising amount of heart alongside the thrilling clashes against alien monsters.
