“Can you check my child for PDA?” the mother asked me on the telephone about two years ago. Though I had been a behavioral/developmental pediatrician for more than four decades, the only PDA acronym I could recall came from my days as a general pediatrician: patent ductus arteriosus (a persistence of embryonic circulation around the heart).
“Gee, I’m not sure,” I said. “What does PDA stand for?”
“Pathological demand avoidance,” she explained. “My son won’t do anything I ask.”
PDA represents the latest and perhaps most extreme shift in how parents and professionals view children’s noncompliance. I came to realize that this wasn’t simply a new diagnosis, but rather part of a much larger change — and as these new explanations for children’s noncompliance multiplied, an older diagnosis was quietly disappearing. Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) — once one of the most common behavioral diagnoses in child psychiatry — was becoming increasingly absent from clinical practice. That tells us something important about how our culture now understands children.
Children have no doubt been noncompliant since before recorded time. Aristotle complained about the younger generation in the fourth century BCE. What’s changed over the millennia, but particularly in the past 25 years, is how we understand and respond to children who don’t “listen.”
My Bay Area private practice has given me a front-row seat for these changes. Over the last 46 years, I’ve witnessed and participated in the explosion of diagnoses such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in younger children and similar rises of anxiety and depression in older children and teenagers.
It’s easier to catch an uptick than an absence. But I had noticed in my examination of children’s neuropsychiatric evaluation reports — replete with details of ADHD, ASD, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, depression, and sensory-motor disabilities — a conspicuous absence of the ODD diagnosis over the last 10 years. I was aware that it had become “unpopular” (I’ll explain more in a moment), but I hadn’t thought of its decline beyond my own office. Then, I read a 2024 study in the Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry.
Between 2013 and 2021, Ramin Mojtabai and Mark Olfson, two highly respected pediatric psychiatric epidemiologists, surveyed the mental health diagnoses of children ages 4 to 17, examining more 13 million records. Not surprisingly, they found that rates of anxiety, depression, and PTSD in children had markedly increased while the rate of some diagnoses declined.
In particular, the authors noted the largest was an eight-fold decline in the diagnosis of bipolar disorder in children. In the previous 20 years bipolar rates for children had climbed 40-fold. The bipolar diagnosis had been strongly promoted as an explanation for acting out behavior by the leading child psychiatrist at the time in the United States and by his colleagues at Harvard. He believed the diagnosis could be made in children as young as 2 years old.
Reactions to this interpretation, with its implications of a lifelong disorder, most often treated by psychiatric medications with serious side effects, grew in the first decade of the 2000s, culminating in the American Psychiatric Association’s (APA) decision to add a new diagnosis, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD) to their newest version of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual in 2013. DMDD was offered as an alternative to bipolar disorder, with many of the same criteria that had been utilized to justify the bipolar diagnosis. But DMDD didn’t carry the same lifelong stigma attached to bipolar. DMDD treatments also promoted nondrug intervention strategies to address the behavioral issues.
The 2024 study further found the prevalence of two other disruptive behaviors — conduct disorder (essentially a more severe form of ODD in children, now teenagers), and ODD — had also significantly declined (by one-third) in the period studied and went relatively unnoticed.
Mojtabai and Olfsen noted the decline but didn’t comment on this decrease. But their study confirmed that a decline in the ODD diagnosis went beyond my local experience. The reasons for this decline are subtle and also relevant to our current views of children’s behavior problems and how to address them.
I’d like to believe that children are behaving better for their parents, but I doubt that’s the case. Indeed, there is little evidence that oppositional behavior itself has become less common.
Instead, clinicians seem to have gradually stopped asking, “What is happening between this child and the adults around him?” and instead ask, “What neurological or psychological deficit prevents this child from complying?” This change tells us a lot about how we now see children in general, and how we raise them.
ODD first appeared as a psychiatric diagnosis in the landmark third edition of the DSM published in 1980. Children who met ODD criteria were described as persistently negativistic, argumentative, disobedient, and hostile to adults. Subsequent editions of the DSM have retained these criteria.
However, over the years, many child psychiatrists, either reflecting or leading the general culture, began shifting their conception of children’s noncompliance. Instead of a relational problem, it became an inherent developmental incapacity calling for alternative diagnoses.
Rather than deliberate opposition, ADHD meant she had a problem with executive functioning and self-regulation. Autism meant he became anxious and overwhelmed with the demands of interaction. PTSD and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) were also invoked as explanations for noncompliance, albeit less frequently.
This shift toward interpreting childhood behavioral conflicts as reflections of dysregulation, neurodivergence, anxiety, and trauma has had a profound effect on treatment.
ADHD diagnoses began expanding greatly beginning in the mid-1990s, while ASD has multiplied several-fold over the past 20 years. For a time, ADHD was often diagnosed in combination with ODD. These children — impulsive, hyperactive, and angry — were considered the most vulnerable and most likely to develop conduct disorder, and to be most at risk of becoming enmeshed in the juvenile justice system.
It is also likely that the decline of the ODD diagnosis was driven not only by changing clinical theories but also by changing social values. Increasing evidence that disproportionately high numbers of Black children were being diagnosed with ODD and conduct disorder led many clinicians to question it. Did the diagnosis sometimes reflect cultural misunderstanding or implicit bias rather than psychopathology? As concerns about the school-to-prison pipeline gained prominence, a diagnosis that could be interpreted as branding children as bad rather than distressed became increasingly difficult to defend.
As a result, many clinicians began avoiding the ODD diagnosis altogether. It not only sounded pejorative, it was perceived as blaming the child. Parents disliked hearing the term and schools disliked seeing it in reports. Increasingly, ODD sounded like a moral judgment disguised as psychiatry.
I, too, long had a problem with the ODD diagnosis. Not for these reasons, but because, in the general sense, psychiatry focuses on the individual. I’ve always viewed individual children as contributing to the problem-behavior cycle, but within interactions between their parents, family, school, and peers. My primary issue was that ODD leaves out the child’s opposition to whom and defiance of what. Nonetheless, it does strongly imply the existence of a relational problem that should be addressed.
An ODD diagnosis (or no psychiatric diagnosis at all) has an element of choice: The child simply won’t comply. That framing implies some moral responsibility, not just the child’s, but even more, the parents’ and the school’s — i.e., those who have failed to provide the proper environment.
In contrast, alternative diagnoses are often interpreted as suggesting that the child has an inherent incapacity or deficit. If a child’s behavior meets the criteria for ADHD or ASD, for example, it is assumed that the child is unable to comply. The problems are the result of genetic, biochemical, or brain problems.
These diagnoses reduce or eliminate the child’s agency, responsibility, or accountability and offer similar relief to the parents and school. If the child simply can’t do something, it’s no one’s fault. It would be like blaming a child with a congenitally shortened leg for coming in last in a race. Punishing that child for a slow speed would be considered both ineffective and cruel.
The dichotomy between won’t and can’t is simplistic, rigid, and false. A child’s biology and personality contribute to a pattern that may make it harder to comply, but not impossible. Given the right environment, one that employs combinations of positive and adverse responses, love, and discipline, children with ODD, ADHD, or ASD all can improve.
Behavioral treatment options for ODD start from the point of view that children possess constrained but meaningful agency that can be shaped through relationships and contingencies. Perhaps surprising to some, these treatments have demonstrated significant success; one, psychologist Gerald Patterson’s Parent Management Training (PMT), became a model for many behavioral programs. Subsequently, Yale psychologist Alan Kazdin conducted numerous randomized clinical trials demonstrating that PMT significantly reduced oppositional, aggressive, and antisocial behavior.
Regardless, as ascendant neurodevelopmental models of noncompliance have emphasized impairments in capacity, responses have shifted. This has had a profound effect on treatment strategies. Now, the focus is on making the environment more accommodating and adding special services to support the child’s assumed inherent weaknesses and decrease anxiety and stress associated with the demand to comply or perform (as in school). Parents are encouraged to “understand” their children’s noncompliance as involuntary. That may take some of the personal sting out of a voluntary refusal, which implies the child doesn’t care for or love the parent enough to comply.
This shift from asking the child to adapt to the environment to shaping the environment to adapt to the child is all well and good in the short term and can certainly reduce conflict.
But how then do children learn to get along with others in the wider world? Accommodations and specialized environments may work during childhood’s early years when parents and school systems can certainly adjust. But as children move into late elementary and middle schools, their peers are very unlikely to be as understanding.
How, then, does a child respond when asked to do things he or she does not want to do? That question remains important regardless of whether the child has ADHD, autism, anxiety, trauma, or sensory sensitivities. Indeed, functioning in society depends heavily on the individual’s capacity to tolerate frustration, delay gratification, accept limits, and comply with reasonable expectations. Those capacities remain relevant even when the reasons for struggling are understood more compassionately.
Limits are not fashionable in child rearing today. In an effort to avoid negative emotional experiences, conflict avoidance has become paramount. Some experts even believe that timeouts can be harmful. Certainly, no adverse consequence should be repeated if it isn’t changing the maladaptive behavior. But parents too often equate consequence with punishment and shame. Even when they have ADHD, autism, anxiety, or ODD, children learn from consequences. Behavioral learning doesn’t disappear because a child has a neurodevelopmental diagnosis.
Learning theory has shown that consequences are simply information. Some increase future behavior; some decrease future behavior. If avoiding an adverse consequence (like a timeout) improves behavior in the long-term, the benefits for child, parent, and family far outweigh the short-term risk of the child temporarily feeling alone and unhappy.
To return to the metaphor of the child with the shortened leg, she could be fitted with a proper prosthesis, timed in the race, and rewarded for trying and achieving within her capability. She can be held accountable, however, if she doesn’t try. Consequence in the form of a limit (e.g., not getting her favorite beverage after the race) is reasonable if she doesn’t make an effort. Entirely avoiding an adverse consequence or limit precludes potentially effective motivators and behavior shapers.
We should not go back to blaming children (or parents, for that matter) for not obeying, but we can understand a child’s difficulties compassionately without abandoning the expectation that the child needs to develop adaptive capacities. Many contemporary clinicians would agree with the first half of that statement but become uneasy with the second half. Words like “expectations,” “limits,” and “consequences” are often heard as code for punitive approaches.
The disappearance of the ODD diagnosis tells the story of a broader shift in child psychiatry and parenting culture. We have become more sophisticated and compassionate in understanding why children struggle with compliance, frustration, and authority. We are also more attentive to trauma, anxiety, neurodevelopmental differences, and sensory sensitivities. We’ve abandoned a diagnosis that seemed blaming.
But we’ve also become much less comfortable in addressing the necessity for children to adapt, tolerate frustration, and learn self-control. We don’t have to choose between compassion and accountability. We must endeavor to preserve both.
Lawrence Diller, M.D., practices behavioral/developmental pediatrics and family therapy in Walnut Creek, Calif., and is also on the clinical faculty of the University of California, San Francisco. He is the author of four books and numerous articles on children and medication.

Some of the most widely used private torrent trackers for pirating movies suspect that a banned user may have posed as a filmmaker protecting copyrights in a failed attempt to seek revenge.
TorrentFreak has been tracking this story closely, reporting last September that an alleged independent filmmaker named Matthew Schneider sued six private trackers for infringing copyrights on some films that he supposedly made. Trackers targeted include PassThePopcorn, BroadcasTheNet, and HDBits. For months, the filmmaker sought to get Cloudflare to unmask operators of the trackers through a copyright fight, which went on until trackers alerted the court last month that Schneider appeared to be an impostor.
In a sworn declaration, the actual filmmaker behind the movies cited in the complaint wrote that he had no association to the plaintiff in the case. “I am not involved in, nor have I ever appeared in, this case,” Schneider wrote.
To keep the copyright fight alive, the plaintiff swore, “I’m a different Matthew Schneider.” He then claimed to have coincidentally made three films with the same exact titles as the other filmmaker’s movies, Split: A Film Anthology, Do Us Part, and Orlando Gloom, Always the Same.
For the judge, Andrea R. Wood, this unusual turn in what could have been a major case was unexpected. TorrentFreak noted that this was the first copyright case to target “multiple prominent private torrent trackers,” and the judge warned that the plaintiff could face sanctions if the private trackers’ allegations were true and he filed a frivolous claim with intent to deceive the court.
As pressure mounted on the plaintiff to clarify his complaint, he abruptly decided to voluntarily dismiss the claims, TorrentFreak reported Tuesday. But that last-minute move might not save him from being sanctioned.

Sydney Sweeney on a billboard in Times Square in her birthday suit and a tradwife milking a cow in a prairie-style dress have more in common than you might think.
They both use a tactic we'll call "outrage then deny."
First, they perform (very different) stereotypes of the ideal woman for lucrative attention: Sweeney the hot "pick me" girl, and tradwives like Ballerina Farm's Hannah Neeleman and Nara Smith, the pious mother and wife. Then, when it comes to responding to the inevitable backlash, they plead ignorance.
Sweeney and tradwives "are two sides of the same publicity coin," Lawrence Rosenberg, a communications strategist and media trainer for business leaders and companies, told Business Insider. "Plausible deniability keeps the conversation going and allows them to maintain their brand," he said.
Sweeney means business
After Sweeney's nearly-nude ad for the sports betting app Novig sparked outrage, she said the concept was "simple: cut through the noise and put the focus entirely on sports. The campaign brings that idea to life with confidence, humor, and a playful edge."
In the ad, Sweeney, who is a strategic partner with and has equity in Novig, poses naked bar the minimal coverage provided by a basketball or tennis racket, and says: "No betting on wars or deaths and no politics. Just you, your takes, and sports."
As the backlash grew, on September 14 she posted an Instagram story featuring athletes, including Serena Williams, posing nude for ESPN's "The Body Issue." The post seemed to suggest her ad and their photoshoots were the same, after female athletes said they found the Novig campaign reductive. On September 16, Novig's CEO, Jacob Fortinsky, said Sweeney drove the messaging and visuals of the ad.
"Sweeney is extremely savvy, and that's the part getting lost in the noise," Lauren Beeching, a celebrity crisis PR, told Business Insider. In an interview she gave as a rising star in 2024, Sweeney shared how she convinced her parents to let her pursue acting by giving a Powerpoint presentation outlining her five-year business plan. Sweeney likely did the math on the Novig ad and "worked out that the disapproval costs her far less than the attention earns her," Beeching said.
She added: "If she had a hand in writing it, she had a hand in her own defense, because a brand that's declared itself interested only in sport can dismiss any criticism as somebody else introducing politics. The answer was ready before the ad was."
Sweeney already used the "outrage then deny" tactic after critics labeled her 2025 American Eagle ad a white supremacist dog whistle. After staying quiet for five months, she told GQ last November that she loves jeans and simply "did a jeans ad."
Being a tradwife sells
On the other side of the coin, trad wives like Neeleman and Smith have both rejected the "tradwife" label, a stance they have doubled down on in recent press interviews as they've tried to enter the mainstream.
Critics say their content promotes a regressive form of womanhood that they themselves are not living. They film themselves in spotless kitchens, cooking time-consuming meals for their husband and kids with a smile, when in reality they are building successful businesses.
Smith spent close to her entire 1.5-hour-long episode of "Call Her Daddy" arguing that while she was made the "posterchild" for the tradwife movement, she said she doesn't "prioritize being a homemaker. I'm a working mom." In the same episode, she said her online presence took off when she took on the passive, cooking-for-her-family-in-the-kitchen format she has become synonymous with, so she leaned in.
In a June 2026 interview with New York Magazine, Neeleman said, "When the term tradwife comes up, or I'm seeing things about 'Yesteryear,' I don't lean into them." "Yesteryear" is a buzzy novel about a tradwife influencer who gets a rude awakening when she is transported back in time to the 1800s.
But her signature homesteading content is what got her the November 2024 cover of Evie Magazine, which calls itself the "conservative Cosmopolitan" and publishes articles with titles like "The male gaze is not a hate crime."
The word "tradwife" now carries a political association that brands who influencers want to work with take into account, Beeching said. It's therefore wise to separate themselves from the label, while carrying on making the same content that helped them build their followings.
Neither Sweeney nor the trad wives have changed what she's selling, Beeching said, adding: "They've changed the label on the tin."
"Images are incredibly powerful messengers of information that would be less savory or compelling if stated aloud," Katie Gatti Tassin, a cultural critic who co-hosts the podcast "Diabolical Lies" with the "Yesteryear" author Caro Claire Burke, told Business Insider.
Sweeney, Neeleman, and Smith's representatives didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.
So far, this strategy has proven effective. Sweeney's Instagram post of the Novig ad has garnered 1.2 million likes and 54,800 comments in just over a week. Smith has a cookbook coming out with HarperCollins in October, and Neeleman has queues out the door of her Utah farm shop.
But with Sweeney losing 200,000 followers in recent days, Tassin, wonders how many more times the "naked outrage chesspiece" will work for her.
"Attention and sales aren't the same thing," Beeching said.

England crush Sri Lanka to seal T20 series win
- Published
Second Vitality T20, Cardiff
Sri Lanka 145-9 (20 overs): Nissanka 37 (21); Dawson 3-32
England 146-4 (12.1 overs): Banton 52* (24); Rathnayake 1-25
England won by six wickets; lead series 2-0
England's impressive T20 form continued as they thrashed Sri Lanka by six wickets in Cardiff to seal the series with a match to spare.
Tom Banton's unbeaten 52 ensured England made light work of chasing a below-par 146, reaching the target in just 12.1 overs.
Jos Buttler and Aneurin Donald raced to an opening stand of 51 in 4.3 overs before they both fell in the space of four balls for 30 and 21 respectively, but England's middle order followed suit in their aggression.
Captain Harry Brook needed to score 49 to break Tilak Varma's record of 336 T20 international runs without being dismissed, and he looked on course, whacking three sixes in his 23 off just eight balls, before he was brilliantly caught by a diving Eshan Malinga.
Banton then took on the charge, clubbing four sixes in his 24-ball knock as England remain unbeaten in the shortest format this summer.
Brendon McCullum's side have now won 22 of their past 25 completed T20s since the start of last summer - a win percentage of 88%, with India (73%) the next best among full-member nations.
England's fluency juxtaposed Sri Lanka's innings as the tourist batters struggled again, limping to 145-9 after being bowled out for just 135 in the opener on Tuesday.
There will be added frustration from this innings, though, as their openers started so brightly by reaching 55-0 from the first five overs.
But Liam Dawson took two wickets in the final over of the powerplay to halt their momentum and the middle order failed to recover, losing 9-90 thereafter and adding just 12 from a dire final four overs.
Dawson finished with 3-32 and Jamie Overton 2-23, while Sonny Baker impressed again with his pace and control in a miserly spell of 1-15, including a wicket maiden in the 19th over.
The series concludes at Old Trafford on Saturday and is followed by three one-day internationals.
Dawson and Banton lead England dominance
Though it is proving to be a mismatched series so far, England are building a well-balanced line-up under Brook's leadership and have barely broken sweat in notching a 2-0 lead.
Sri Lanka's explosive start, led by Pathum Nissanka, who top-scored with 37, was the only time England have been on the back foot, but it was the ever-reliable Dawson who dragged it back, having become a mainstay in Brook's T20 line-up.
The two soft dismissals highlighted Sri Lanka's woes - Lahiru Udara was caught at mid-on and Kamil Mishara chipped one straight back to the slow left-arm spinner.
What followed was a series of soft dismissals, most caught trying to find the boundary, as Overton and Baker hammered away at a good length before Archer, who had started expensively, claimed two wickets at the death to revive his own figures.
Sri Lanka managed just two sixes in their innings compared to England's 10, with it being only the seventh time their top five have all hit at least one in T20 internationals.
Newcomer Donald started the carnage, ramping Dushmantha Chameera's first ball over the ropes, before Buttler joined the party and Brook then launched three of his own into the stands.
England's intent was clear from the fact Donald's strike-rate of 161.54 was the lowest of the top five. Spinner Wanindu Hasaranga took most of the damage as he conceded 42 off just three overs, with a couple disappearing out of the ground.
Banton, one of few batters to miss out in England's 254-4 on Tuesday, made the most of his opportunity to produce a fine finish by sweeping and striking firmly down the ground.
England have set themselves up nicely to finish unbeaten in T20s this summer after thrashing India 4-0 earlier in the year.

Gurugram-based test-prep major Aakash Educational Services Ltd (AESL) managed to narrow its net loss for the financial year FY26 by 15.5% to ₹186.5 Cr from ₹220.8 Cr loss incurred in the previous fiscal. The improvement in the bottom line came despite flat top line performance in the fiscal. Operating revenue rose marginally by 0.4% to ₹2,040.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,032.1 Cr in the previous year. While coaching revenue — the core business — inched up 0.3% YoY to ₹1,956.2 Cr, franchisee revenue grew 4% to ₹84.4 Cr. The real swing factor came with revenue registered from non-operating income, with other income more than doubled to ₹113.7 Cr. This was driven largely by a ₹76.1 Cr write-back of provisions or liabilities alongside a ₹19.7 Cr gain from remeasurement of lease liabilities. Including other income, total income rose 3.3% to ₹2,154.3 Cr in the year under review from ₹2,085.1 Cr in FY25. Aakash is one of India's largest test-prep brands for engineering and medical entrance exams and has been operating under the ownership of BYJU’S parent Think & Learn since its 2021 acquisition — a deal that has since been entangled in the broader financial and legal troubles at the BYJU’S group. As of September, Byju Raveendran proposed relinquishing his claimed beneficial interest in 17.89 Mn shares of Aakash Educational Services to settle Qatar Holding’s arbitration claim of more than $235 Mn against him. The latest proposal further places Aakash at the centre of overlapping disputes over ownership, creditor recoveries, and the future of BYJU’S, which once commanded a valuation of $22 Bn. Creditors have been separately exploring a broader settlement centred around Aakash as it remains the most valuable surviving asset within the collapsing edtech. Global TLB lenders, represented by GLAS Trust, are said to be in advanced talks to acquire a 30% stake in Aakash Educational Services, valuing the coaching chain at around $2 Bn. Zooming Into Aakash's FY26 Expenses Total expenses were largely flat, up almost 1% to ₹2,397.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,378 Cr in the previous year. As a result, loss before exceptional items and tax narrowed nearly 17% YoY to ₹243.5 Cr from ₹292.9 Cr. However, a ₹23.3 Cr exceptional charge widened this to a pre-tax loss of ₹266.8 Cr — still 8.9% narrower than FY25's ₹292.9 Cr. A deferred tax credit gain of ₹80.3 Cr brought the final loss after tax down to ₹186.5 Cr. Here is a more closer look at where AESL spent the most in the reported year: Employee Benefits Expense: Aakash’s single largest expense declined 2.4% to ₹1,299.6 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹1,331.5 Cr in FY25. Depreciation And Amortisation Expense: Spending under this head declined 4.4% to ₹234.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹245.6 Cr a year ago. Advertisement And Publicity: The company’s promotional expenses fell 6.9% to ₹145.7 Cr in the year under review from ₹156.5 Cr in FY25.

Delhi HC declines Centre’s appeal over ₹20 lakh release to CHRI, seeks fresh plea
The Delhi HC asked the Centre to seek vacation of the interim order directing release of ₹20 lakh from the reserved funds of CHRI, whose FCRA registration was cancelled.
The Delhi high court on Thursday declined to entertain the Centre’s appeal against an order directing it to release ₹20 lakh from the reserved funds of NGO Commonwealth Human Rights Initiative (CHRI), whose registration under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA) was cancelled, and asked the government to seek vacation of the order through an application within a week.
The Union home ministry had cancelled the NGO’s certificate of registration on September 12, 2024, citing utilisation of foreign contributions abroad, the depositing of purported fees into the FCRA account, and mismatches in opening balances for the periods 2013-14 and 2018-19. The development bars CHRI from receiving foreign funding.
A bench of chief justice DK Upadhyaya and justice Tejas Karia instead asked the Centre to file an application seeking vacation of the single judge’s May 19 order within a week.
“Having considered the submission of the counsel of the parties, we need not go into the merits for the reason that the order passed by the single judge is an interim order, vacation of which can be sought by the appellant. We permit the appellant to file an application within a week from today. Pleadings in this matter are complete and written submissions have been filed. In case it is not possible to hear the matter on 30.9, an endeavour shall be made to hear the application filed,” the court said in its order.
In its appeal, the Centre, represented by additional solicitor General Chetan Sharma, contended that although the single judge had permitted it to present oral arguments, it was not allowed to file written submissions.
CHRI’s counsel submitted that following the order, the Centre had filed an application seeking its recall, which was heard on July 10. However, the Centre subsequently withdrew the recall application, with liberty to file an application seeking vacation of the order. Despite this, the Centre later chose to challenge the order by way of an appeal.

Later today, Max Verstappen will strap on his helmet and take to the track at the Silverstone circuit in England for a rather unusual race. The four-time Formula 1 world champion is recognized as the leading talent of his generation, but unlike some of the legends that have preceded him, Verstappen’s passion for motorsport extends beyond just the rarified world of F1. With apologies to Midweek Motorsport, but if it has wheels and they keep score, odds are good Verstappen’s down to race it. So at noon Eastern Time (5 pm BST) today, September 16, Verstappen will slip into something a little more basic: a kart.
It’s one of 101 identical karts that have been sourced from Eastern Europe for the event—the other 100 will be driven by a mix of content creators and Red Bull athletes, all of whom fancy their chances at beating one of the world’s greatest drivers at his own game. They get a bit of an advantage, all starting ahead of Verstappen. Once he passes another karter, they’re out of the race, and Verstappen has 30 laps of a purpose-designed layout at Silverstone to get through them all and win.
Other F1 drivers have attempted slightly similar challenges in the past—Alex Albon raced 25 kids last year, and last month Oliver Bearman raced 50 amateurs. But neither is as high-profile as Verstappen, and neither is facing as much competition.
It might have been many years since Verstappen traded his kart for things larger and faster, but that’s no reason to doubt his abilities.
“Max is pretty unique in comparison to the other Grand Prix drivers in that he’s already done the Nürburgring 24 hours in his GT3. He’s out testing those cars often. I saw his quote saying that it’s been a while since he did karting; do we honestly think that he hasn’t gone and done a little test? It’s Max Verstappen! He’s a serial winner, and therefore he’s not turning up here to shine a spotlight on some other individual. He’s going to go for it, and he’s going to try and achieve this target,” said David Coulthard, a Grand Prix winner and one of Red Bull Racing’s first factory drivers.

Trump specifically called 40 Wall Street the tallest building on downtown Manhattan, not all of Manhattan or New York City. Whether Trump's comments amounted to bragging, as some people online claimed, is open to interpretation.
Around the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, a claim (archived) circulated online that U.S. President Donald Trump, then a New York City real estate developer, said after the attacks that he now owned the tallest building in downtown Manhattan or New York City.
For example, one X user posted a clip from an alleged TV news interview with Trump captioned, "Here is Trump on 9/11 bragging that Trump Tower is now the tallest building in Manhattan."
Here is Trump on 9/11 bragging that Trump Tower is now the tallest building in Manhattan pic.twitter.com/Fy5ZW85tZc
— FactPost (@factpostnews) September 11, 2026
Similar claims that Trump had said his building was the tallest in Manhattan or even New York City after the Twin Towers fell circulated on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers also contacted us to ask about the claim.
Trump did tell (time code 2:05, archived) a reporter soon after the 9/11 attacks that 40 Wall Street, which the Trump Organization still owns, was "the tallest" building in downtown Manhattan (not Manhattan as a whole or New York City). As such, we've rated this quote as correctly attributed to Trump.
Whether Trump's comments amounted to bragging, as some people online claimed, is open to interpretation.
Fox 5 New York posted a video of Trump's phone interview with WWOR-TV reporter Alan Marcus on YouTube in 2016. Trump made the claim about owning the tallest building in downtown Manhattan after Marcus asked if 40 Wall Street had sustained any damage during the attacks. The exchange went as follows (at 1:43 — emphasis ours):
MARCUS: Donald, you have one of the landmark buildings down in the financial district, 40 Wall Street, did you have any damage or did you know what's happened down there?
TRUMP: Well, it was an amazing phone call I made. 40 Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan. And it was, actually before the World Trade Center, was the tallest. And then when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second-tallest. And now it's the tallest.
During the 2001 interview, Marcus also asked Trump how he would have handled 9/11 if he were president given that he had considered running for the office the year before (at 4:14). Trump said he would have taken a "very, very tough line" against "the group of people that did this."
In an interview with Politico in 2016, Marcus reportedly said that Trump's remark about 40 Wall Street was "Donald being Donald." Marcus added, "He is the brand manager of Trump, and he is going to tout that brand, and he does it reflexively."
Trump's claim that 40 Wall Street was the tallest building in downtown Manhattan following the attacks was incorrect. The nearby 952-foot tall 70 Pine Street skyscraper, which was also part of the Manhattan skyline in 2001, is 26 feet taller than 40 Wall Street.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Trump attacked the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York for telling him he would not be allowed to speak at its 25th-anniversary commemoration.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

The Union Health Ministry has asked States and Union Territories to ensure that stem cell therapy is offered as standard clinical care only for disease conditions and indications approved by the Ministry, with its use for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) restricted to duly approved clinical trials.
In an advisory issued on September 16, the Ministry reiterated the existing regulatory framework governing stem cell research and therapy. The advisory was issued to States and Union Territories that have adopted the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, following a January 30, 2026, judgment of the Supreme Court in Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
For ASD, the Ministry said therapeutic use of any type of stem cell must remain confined to duly approved clinical trials in accordance with the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, issued by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) and the Department of Biotechnology.
Stem cell interventions that have not been approved for routine clinical use, including those offered for autism, should not be provided as routine, standard or commercial clinical services, the advisory said.
The move comes against the backdrop of the continuing use of stem-cell interventions for autism despite the lack of established evidence supporting them as a standard treatment. An ICMR review has said that available evidence does not support stem cell therapy over behavioural and supportive therapies for ASD and recommended that such therapy be restricted to approved clinical trials.
The Ministry has asked States and Union Territories to disseminate the Supreme Court’s directions to State and district regulatory authorities as well as government and private clinical establishments involved in stem cell research, treatment, promotion or administration.
The advisory also draws attention to the consequences of non-compliance. The Supreme Court, in its January judgment, said violations of the statutory framework could attract consequences including professional misconduct under Regulation 7.22 of the erstwhile Indian Medical Council Regulations, 2002, as well as action under Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments Act, including cancellation of registration and penalties.
The National Medical Commission (NMC), in an advisory issued on September 5, has separately reiterated that stem cell therapy may be offered as standard clinical care only for approved indications. It said unauthorised administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement of stem cell therapy beyond approved indications would constitute professional misconduct.
The NMC has asked State Medical Councils to examine allegations of violations and, where professional misconduct by a registered medical practitioner is established after due process, take disciplinary action under the applicable provisions.

The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.
The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.
The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.
“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.
“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”
Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.
Schools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.
A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could be classified as potential harassment.
The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.
Courts in England and Wales in the UK and New York state in the US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedly classified them as body-worn cameras and barred them from the “federal workspace”.
A local council in Sydney on Tuesday became the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.
In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.
The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.
Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisions and said she would consult businesses on their approach.
“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.
“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”
Vision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.
Gallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.
“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.
Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.
The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.
Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.
Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.
“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.
Additional reporting from Caitlin Cassidy

Argentine judge orders halt to Falklands oil project as tensions with Britain rise
An Argentine judge has ordered British and Israeli companies to stop developing an oilfield off the British-controlled Falkland Islands
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- An Argentine federal judge on Wednesday ordered British and Israeli companies to stop developing an oilfield off the Falkland Islands, opening a new legal front in the decades-old sovereignty dispute between Argentina and Britain that Argentine President Javier Milei has revived in recent weeks.
The injunction by Judge Mariel Borruto, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press, targets the Sea Lion oil project 220 kilometers (140 miles) north of the British-controlled archipelago in the South Atlantic, barring drilling, offshore installations and port construction until Argentine authorities can conduct an environmental review and issue a decision.
But in practice, Wednesday's order is unlikely to halt progress on the project. Judge Borruto acknowledged that enforcement “depends on international cooperation and the conduct” of the two companies, Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration, which have already vowed to press ahead with the project despite Milei's threats of tougher sanctions against them and other companies operating around the islands.
Rockhopper declined to comment, and Navitas did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the injunction.
With its commercial oil production expected to start in 2028, Sea Lion has raised the stakes of a territorial dispute that led Britain and Argentina to a short and bloody war in 1982.
For the territory’s roughly 3,500 residents, the oilfield promises to transform an economy long dependent on fishing. For Argentina, which calls the islands the Malvinas, the project would allow foreign companies to extract oil riches it regards as its own. Its claim to the archipelago, roughly 480 kilometers (300 miles) off its coast, is enshrined in the constitution and woven into national identity, drawing support across the country’s political divisions.
U.S. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Argentina's radical libertarian leader, has brought new uncertainty to the dispute in recent weeks. Citing Britain’s lack of support for his war against Iran, he has suggested that Washington could change its historically neutral stance on the islands’ sovereignty.
Speaking to reporters in Dublin on Saturday, Trump again expressed skepticism that Britain would be able to retake the Falklands as it did after Argentina's military dictatorship invaded in 1982, saying, “I don’t know if they’re going to be willing to travel that far."
Milei seized on what he called “winds of change” following Trump’s comments earlier this month, using a Sept. 3 national address to announce measures against companies developing oilfields around the islands. He warned that the projects posed a “clear and urgent danger” to Argentina’s sovereignty claim and pledged to use all “diplomatic, economic, judicial and legal tools” to defend it.
His administration is now preparing legislation to broaden sanctions against companies involved in oil projects around the islands and filed three criminal complaints against Tel Aviv-listed Navitas and nine other companies and their executives, accusing them of violating Argentine law by pursuing oil operations without the country's authorization. It's unclear what impact the charges have on the project.
Britain has responded to the Argentine government’s legal campaign with defiance. It argues that the people who live in the Falklands should determine its status, citing the results of a 2013 referendum in which islanders overwhelmingly voted to remain a British territory.
“Argentine domestic law does not apply within the Islands,” the British government said Tuesday in guidance aimed at reassuring businesses operating there.
Wednesday's ruling issued by the federal court in Argentina's southernmost province of Tierra del Fuego stems from a separate civil lawsuit brought by environmental lawyers and veterans of the 1982 war seeking to prevent environmental damage from the project. The complaint cites ecological threats ranging from chemical pollution and underwater noise to ship traffic and potential oil spills.
Borruto warned that allowing drilling and construction to proceed could alter the marine ecosystem in ways that would be difficult to reverse.
“The risk is neither hypothetical nor remote,” she wrote, noting that work on the project’s infrastructure had already begun.

New Delhi, December 1975. It was love at first sight when a Swedish hippy called Lotta von Schedvin sat down to be sketched by an Indian street artist, Pradyumna Kumar Mahanandia, known to everyone as PK. In the 10 minutes it took PK to complete her portrait, everything clicked into place for the pair. They were swept headlong in a whirlwind romance, and PK took Lotta to his village in the east of India to meet his family. But soon after, the time came for Lotta to pack up her VW campervan and head back home with her friends.
Heart-stricken PK promised to follow, but a plane ticket to Sweden was an impossible dream. Determined not to lose the love of his life, PK bought a secondhand Raleigh bike, and with $80 sewn into the waistband of his trousers, set off to cycle 6,000 miles to Lotta. He knew the sun set in the west, so that was the direction he took. His plan was to follow the hippy trail, cycling through India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, crossing Europe, finally arriving in Sweden.
Actually, he was heading to Switzerland until a fellow backpacker pointed out that Switzerland and Sweden were two different countries. In a new Netflix documentary, The Cycle of Love, PK jokes that his strength was his fuzzy grasp of European geography. Watching the film, you wonder if his superpower might have been his smile – warm and joyous, it lights the room. Either way, he made it to Sweden. The journey took 123 days, and ended up involving a flight or two, and a couple of trains. In May 1977, PK knocked on Lotta’s door in Borås, Sweden. They have been together ever since.
Documentary-maker Orlando von Einsiedel first heard about the story when he gave a talk in Sweden. “At the end, two young people came up and handed me a book,” he says. “They said: ‘This is about our parents’ story. We know your work. Would you be interested in this as a film?’” The book was The Amazing Story of the Man Who Cycled from India to Europe for Love by Swedish journalist Per J Andersson.
The two young people were PK and Lotta’s grownup kids Emilie and Karl. Von Einsiedel politely took the book but didn’t think too much about it. “Normally in my experience, when somebody approaches you and says ‘I’ve got a brilliant story’, it doesn’t work out.”
A couple of months later, Von Einsiedel picked up the book as a holiday read, opening it on the flight out of London. “The moment I started I thought, ‘Oh my God, you idiot Orlando! This is extraordinary.’” It wasn’t just the against-all-odds, 6,000-mile cycle ride, PK’s story was a tale of fate and destiny. When he was born, the astrologer in his village made four predictions about his future wife: she would be a Taurus, born outside India, musical and own a jungle. So naturally the first question he asked Lotta was: “Are you a Taurus?” Her answer was yes. She was also a gifted musician, and – most bonkers of all – her family owned land with a forest in Sweden.
“When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true,” says Von Einsiedel, cheerful and chatty on a video call from New York. The previous night he attended the US premiere of The Cycle of Love with PK and Lotta, who have been happily married for nearly 50 years. The pair have been getting the celebrity treatment wherever they go. “Everybody in the cinema stands up for them, people are weeping when they come on stage.” What do the couple make of the film? He grins. “I know they like it, because whenever they go to a festival, they watch every single screening from beginning to end.” How many times have they seen it? “A lot.”
The film tells their story with enormous warmth. It includes a dramatisation of the epic ride, with PK played by the British-based Indian actor Chirag Lobo, and Mina Dale as Lotta. Everybody else is non-professional, explains Von Einsiedel. “Our producers would go out and street-cast people on the morning of filming.”
What about the script, I ask? There are gorgeous, heartwarming scenes as PK shares his story with people he meets on the road, who in return tell him about their life and loves. How were those scenes scripted? “No script. Everything is improvised. When PK interacts with everyday people he meets along the way, those are just normal conversations about love and hopes and dreams.”
Wasn’t that a bit risky – getting a plane to India with two actors, no script and trusting that deep and meaningful conversations would materialise from conversations with ordinary people? “Massively risky, except I tested if it might work in Lewisham town centre,” Von Einsiedel says, grinning. “I have a friend who’s an actor. We went to Lewisham with a bike.” Armed with a notepad, his friend told people that he was cycling from London to Cape Town for love. “He pretended to draw portraits. What was extraordinary is the first person he sat down to draw turned around and said: ‘I love your story. I’ll buy you a plane ticket immediately.’”
It’s the kindness of strangers that makes the documentary so uplifting. When PK cycles out of Kabul, he stops to help an Austrian backpacker, Linea, who crashed her car, knocking out most of her teeth. He stays with her for several days at hospital, even though it means his visa expiring and further delay. Later, when he arrives in Istanbul and checks his post, there is a train ticket to Vienna – a thank you from Linea for his kindness.
What struck Von Einsiedel when he met the real-life PK was that his story about love went beyond boy-meets-girl. “For me, it’s not just about romantic love. It’s about self-love and love for all the people that we share this planet with.” PK was born into a dalit family, the marginalised group in India formerly known as “untouchables”. At school, he was made to sit outside during lessons and not allowed to play with the other children. Even after he won a scholarship to study fine art in Delhi, he experienced periods of homelessness and isolation.
“From the moment I started talking to PK it became clear what a difficult and traumatic childhood he’d had,” Von Einsiedel says. “He spoke so movingly about being on the journey and how it was the first time that strangers would touch him and hug him. That it was key to him starting to believe in himself and love himself. He said: ‘How can you love anybody if you can’t love yourself?’ I get emotional just saying that.”
PK explained how he felt accepted on the journey, hanging out with hippies and locals in the villages and towns he passed through. People with very little offered him hospitality, a meal or a roof for the night. In the documentary, this warm feeling of togetherness thuds to the ground when PK arrives in Europe, grilled by hostile and overtly racist German border officers. “That was his first experience,” says Von Einsiedel. “He travelled through all these countries, Afghanistan and Iran, and everybody treated him with respect. Then as soon as he got to Europe he immediately experienced racism.”
Von Einsiedel grew up in south London. At university he studied social anthropology and in his 20s was a professional snowboarder. “I learned the craft of film-making making snowboard films,” he says. “When I knew how to do that, I segued into making films about social issues I believed in.” He started working with Al Jazeera, travelling to conflict zones.
In 2015, he was nominated for an Oscar for his first full-length documentary, Virunga, about the battle to save a national park in eastern Congo, home to some of the world’s last mountain gorillas. His documentary short, White Helmets, following Syrian volunteers rescuing civilians, won an Oscar. Next he made Evelyn, an incredibly moving film in which Von Einsiedel turned the camera on his own family. His brother Evelyn took his own life aged 22 over a decade earlier. In the film, Von Einsiedel and his two surviving siblings hiked the routes their brother loved to walk with friends and family. “I was very emotionally closed for a long time after my brother died,” he says. “I used to think being emotionally open was a sign of weakness. I was terrified of my own emotions. I see the opposite now. I think being emotionally open is a sign of strength.”
When it comes to picking a subject for a new documentary, he says he is attracted to people who inspire him. “I’m drawn to stories that show the better side of human beings. That’s a thread that runs through the work I like to make.” The Cycle of Love is by far the sunniest film he has made to date. What’s that all about, I ask? “I wanted to make an optimistic film that’s about joy and human connection. The world is difficult. Love is one of those things that all of us can agree on. This story just felt so important to tell.”

For over a month and a half, residents of Chitpur Jyotinagar Colony in Cossipore, North Kolkata, have been without regular water supply after five public taps serving the colony ran dry following pipeline work in the area. Home to around 5,000 people, the 200-metre-long stretch is largely inhabited by people belonging to the Muslim community, and from lower-income backgrounds.
Residents, whose daily lives and livelihoods have been disrupted, alleged that water supply has been deliberately cut off by the state’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government to target them on the basis of their identities and force them out of the slum.
It is worth noting days after the election results were declared, local BJP MLA Ritesh Tiwari had pledged not to do anything for Muslims in his constituency. “Today, in front of Baba Bholenath, I swear, I will not do one job for them (Muslims) in the next five years. Will not issue any certificate for them. I am saying this live. I do not care about what anyone else says or thinks,” he had said.
Residents of Jyotinagar this colony, around 95% of them Muslims, depend on informal jobs for their sustenance. While women manage household chores in the morning before working at nearby factories in the afternoon, where they clean glass bottles and break glass panels into shards, most men work as daily wage labourers, masons, drivers, rickshaw pullers, or at factories.
How Did Water Supply Stop?
Alt News visited the water-deprived area, located a few meters from the over 200-years-old Cossipore Gun and Shell factory. The colony has five taps, which used to supply water from 5 am to 11 pm daily. Since July 29, after water supply was cut off, all five taps have been dry, locals said.
Locals said that water supply was perfectly normal and no complaints from the neighbourhood was made to the local civic body or any authorities, and yet, pipeline work was carried out in the area by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) from July 26-28.
“Pipeline work was happening, they had dug two pits, one at the beginning of the slum and another at the end, marking the slum. On July 28, the water supply stopped around 11 pm. The next morning, we were waiting for the water supply to return. It has not been restored since,” said a resident, Mohinudeen Sheikh.
Sheikh, along with other residents, alleged that the pipelines were shut during the night while the roads were being repaired. “They used the cover of midnight to close the pipelines and mend the streets. We had no water from the early morning onwards,” he claimed.
‘They Also Took Away Electricity’
Residents said the water crisis was accompanied by a disruption in electricity supply as well. “They took away both water and electricity,” one youth said.
“They thought we were drawing electricity illegally from the main line, so they stopped the supply,” said a resident, Pinki Bibi. “All our houses have separate electricity connections and we receive separate bills. Then how can they say we are drawing electricity illegally?”
Residents claimed that electricity was restored after more than a week, following an incident during the Kanwar Yatra when poor visibility allegedly led some Kanwariyas to fall into the pothole-ridden lane. Alamgir Biswas, secretary of the Jyotinagar Colony, said that the supply was restored 10-15 days after the Basti Unnayan Samiti protested against the disruption.
Locals alleged that Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation (CESC) said the main-road connection had been shut to verify whether allegations of illegal electricity tapping were true. However, electricity supply remained available in the lanes branching off the main road. After seven days, CESC was able to verify that no illegal tapping was taking place and restored the connection, they added.
‘They are Trying to Evict Us’
Residents alleged that the disruption of these essential services was a part of a concerted attempt to evict the slum dwellers. Alamgir alleged: “The plan was to cut off the basic needs of water and electricity so that we leave the area. In this area, there is absolute communal harmony. Hindus and Muslims live harmoniously together. However, this government is trying to create a rift between us.”
Morjina Begum, who works at the glass factory, also alleged, “They are trying to evict us from this colony and therefore employing these tricks of cutting off the water supply. We are not new to this place. I was born here. My grandfather had settled here years ago,” while asserting, “We are not going to leave this place so easily. We will fight.”
Begum said residents had also approached the local councillor, Suman Singh, but has received no meaningful assistance as of yet. Alt News tried to speak to Singh, but he did not answer our calls till press time.
Saraswati Biswas, a 60-year-old Hindu resident, alleged that Tiwari, the newly elected MLA, had referred to the residents as “Bangladeshis and encroachers”. “He is calling us Bangladeshis and encroachers. How am I a Bangladeshi? My forefathers used to live here. I have proper documents proving that I am an Indian. I voted this year,” she said.
Legal Entanglement With Kolkata Port
While investigating the possible reason behind the elongated water supply disruption, Alt News found an intricate legal entanglement between the residents of the colony and the authorities of the Kolkata port.
As per legal records, the entire colony is built on a parcel of land measuring approximately 3478 square metres officially belonging to the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata. On February 23, the estate officer of the port issued an eviction order for the colony.
Alt News accessed the order, and found that it was issued based on the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. The notice terms the residents of Jyotinagar Colony as ‘unauthorised occupants and/or trespasser to the port property’. The estate officer ordered the residents to vacate the land within 15 days of date of publication of this notice. Before the eviction order was passed, a hearing took place, wherein, port authorities submitted that ‘there is potential threat to communal unrest’ due to the existence of the colony.
According to legal documents accessed by Alt News, the residents of the colony came to know about the existence of this eviction order on June 9. The residents alleged that after the change of government in West Bengal, local BJP supporters started to campaign for the demolition of the slum. The locals claimed that they began deeming the colony as “a den of illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators”.
In order to seek legal protection from the eviction drive, residents appealed before the chief judge of the city civil court, Calcutta, however, on August 18, the court declined to grant any immunity from eviction to them.
The Port authorities in their submission before the city civil court had mentioned that ‘unlawful activities’ were ongoing in the colony. They described the premises as congested and unsafe for human habitation, citing the presence of inflammable materials and several uninsulated electrical wires that could potentially cause a fire. They also lodged two police complaints at the North Port police station on September 9, 2020 and July 25, 2022.
On August 19, the residents appeared before the Calcutta high court, seeking protection from eviction. The court granted an interim stay order on the eviction process till September 18. In the meantime, the water and electricity disruptions happened, which residents believe was done to purposely disrupt their lives to expedite the eviction.
Nine residents of the colony: Alamgir Biswas, Pinki Bibi, Mafajel Gazi, Sk Mainuddin, Rahima Bibi, Saraswati Biswas, Anita Prasad, Lima Bibi and Bonani Bibi appeared as petitioners before the high court. In their appeal, the residents had informed the HC that although the proceedings recorded before the estate officer of Kolkata Port mentioned two persons: Hafizul and Tarcina Bibi as respondents from the colony, the order does not record that any notice for eviction, under section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, was issued publicly.
It was also submitted before the HC that the order issued by the Kolkata Port does not record that the petitioners were called upon to show cause against the proposed eviction, were afforded an opportunity to produce evidence or were given an opportunity of personal hearing.
According to Section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, all concerned persons, that is all persons who are in occupation of the public premises, have to be given the opportunity to show cause why they wouldn’t be evicted.
Section 4(3) of the Act clearly mentions: The estate officer shall cause the notice to be served by having it affixed on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the public premises, and in such other manner as may be prescribed, whereupon the notice shall be deemed to have been duly given to all persons concerned. However, the order issued by the estate officer makes no mention of any such notice being issued or served. This issue was also raised in the petition before the high court.
A team of lawyers including Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya, Samim Ahammed, Md Nasirul Hoque and Ivi Banerjee represented the residents legally. Speaking to Alt News, Ahammed said, “The Port authorities are claiming that the land in question is their property. But in reality, it is public property. Therefore, a government body like the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, must ensure the fundamental rights of the public, in this case, their right to shelter.”
The State has the power to regulate and make sure people follow the law and cannot occupy public property illegally. They are exercising this power through the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. But while doing this, the State cannot treat people unfairly or take away someone’s home and leave them without shelter. Having a place to live and being able to live with dignity are part of a person’s inalienable rights protected by the Constitution, he explained.
Simultaneously with the HC appeal, another appeal was submitted by the residents before the chief judge of the city civil court seeking the restoration of water connection. This prayer, however, is still pending.
According to the port authorities, the total damage incurred due to the existence of the colony, starting from 1990, has reached approximately over Rs 61 crore. As per the legal records, the estimated monthly damage amount is calculated to be more than Rs 19 lakh rupees, and the port is losing more than Rs 2 crore annually in terms of revenue due to the colony.
Questions Of ‘Communal Targeting’
The geographical location of the water disruption has become a point of contention for residents, who have alleged that this is a form of communal targeting.
When one walks along Khagendra Chatterjee Lane towards the Ganges, with the Gun and Shell Factory on the right, the road turns left towards the river after two temples, and becomes Chitpur Strand Road. The Cossipore Jetty is on the right, followed by Jyotinagar Colony.
Residents showed Alt News the two points where pipeline work had been carried out. They said the entire stretch between the two points had remained without water. They also alleged that the points where the road was dug up correspond to the boundaries of Jyotinagar Colony, which has a predominantly Muslim population. According to the residents, taps immediately before and after this stretch, located in predominantly Hindu residential areas, continue to receive water.
Alt News checked the taps inside the colony and found them dry. Taps located immediately before and after the stretch where the pipeline work had been carried out, however, had water supply. We found that the tap directly opposite a temple, just before the first point where the road had allegedly been dug up, had water supply. The tap at the other end, near the second point where digging had taken place, also had water. In between, however, an approximately 150-metre stretch, had no water supply.
‘A Basic Need’
For residents, the suspension of water has led to tremendous daily struggle. “Water is a basic need. There are so many people in our colony, and there is no water. People have to stand in queues to fetch water from the taps that are present in the nearby areas. Though people are sharing their taps, they prioritise their own needs. This affects our work,” a resident said.
A woman in her mid-twenties, while cleaning utensils, showed buckets filled with water fetched from the river. “Look at the condition of the water we are using to clean. It is so muddy and filthy. At this point, all we can hope is we don’t fall ill,” she said.
The monsoon season has made it more difficult. “The water level is very high in Ganga now, so it becomes dangerous to bathe in the river or fetch water. The river water is muddy and unfit for consumption. But we are left with no option,” an elderly woman said. “We are scared that our children will develop skin infections. There are already a few cases,” said a woman in her thirties, while standing in queue to bathe her children.
Residents have to walk some distance from their colony to a functioning tap to fill water, which they then transport back on vans.
Locals Allege Administrative Apathy
Alamgir elaborated that after water and electricity supply was cut off on July 29, the following day, locals reached the corporation office and complained. “They took my number and told us that they would look into the matter. But nothing happened. On the following day, we submitted a written complaint at the main corporation office in Hatibagan. They also told us they would try to look into it. However, as everyone can see, nothing has changed as of yet,” he said.
Several residents had approached the local police station, the councillor, and MLA Tiwari, seeking their intervention, but no official visited the colony to inspect the reality so far, they lamented. Residents also said that when a group of women approached Tiwari, he dismissed them stating he was not responsible for the disruption of water supply and refused to restore it.
Further, Pinki Bibi alleged that Tiwari had used communal slurs and threatened the locals with eviction. “While talking to the people, he threatened them, ‘If I want, I could demolish the mosque that was built in the colony. And evict the entire colony with it,’” she said.
Morjina Begum told Alt News that residents believe they are being purposely treated this way because of their Muslim identities. Asked why they felt this was the case, she referred to speeches by chief minister Suvendu Adhikari and the local MLA following their election victories, in which they said they would not work for Muslims because Muslims had not voted for them. “Where are we supposed to go? There are so many of us?” she asked.
Also Read: I swear I won’t do anything for Muslims, says Bengal BJP MLA Ritesh Tiwari
Burdened by the uncertainties of their future in the colony, an elderly woman in her 70s, sitting on the threshold of her house, said, “I pray that in my next life I am not born as a Muslim in this country.”
On September 9, Minakshi Mukherjee, CPI(M)’s central committee member, visited the locality along with other workers and leaders, and expressed her solidarity with the residents and protested against the eviction drive. At the initiative of the party, a water tanker visits the colony every two to three days to provide residents with an alternative source of water.
MLA Ritesh Tiwari Responds
When Alt News asked Tiwari about the predicament of people in his constituency, he distanced himself from the issue, saying, “The plot belongs to the Port. The people have a feud with the Port. The Port had ordered them to vacate. Later, the high court ordered them to refrain from taking temporary coercive action. The water supply is provided by the KMC. So, what role do I play here? What can I say here? The matter is sub judice, and it is better for political leaders to refrain from making any comments.”
When asked whether he could stand by the people of his constituency and help restore their water supply, he said, “This is not my job…they [residents] have sought the assistance of established political leaders… so they should keep faith in the people they have called. Should they lose that faith so quickly?”
Upon being further prodded on why he was not helping people in his own constituency, the MLA replied (in Bengali), “Why don’t you do my part of the job!” (“Amar bhaag er kaaj ta apni kore deben”)
