Jammu, Sep 17: Two Pakistan-based proscribed outfit Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM) militants were killed, and an alleged over-ground worker was detained in a remote high-altitude area in Jammu and Kashmir's Udhampur district, officials said on Thursday.
The joint operation by the Army, police and CRPF was conducted in the dense Brattal Sohan and Khubban forests of Majalta bordering Kathua district amid heavy rain, they said.
Army confirmed the killing of two militants in the operation.
“In a joint intelligence-based operation during the intervening night of September 16-17, confirmed inputs indicated the presence of terrorists in the general area of Brattal, Udhampur.
“Despite hostile weather, difficult terrain and poor visibility, troops of White Knight Corps, Police and CRPF launched a targeted counter-terrorism operation, resulting in the neutralisation of two terrorists.
“The operation is still in progress, with search and surveillance continuing in the area. Security forces remain deployed to track and neutralise any remaining threat,” the Jammu-based White Knight Corps said in a post on X.
The officials said police and security forces were looking for a terrorist group after its movement was noticed in the forested area last week.
The security forces cordoned off a particular area around 9 pm on Wednesday following fresh inputs, leading to the initial contact.
A few rounds of firing and blasts were heard shortly after the operation began, the officials said, adding that the area, however, remained largely quiet through the night before the lull ended on Thursday morning, when the terrorists opened heavy fire in an attempt to break the cordon.
Reinforcements were rushed to the area, and the search operation was continuing when the last reports were received, they said.
Meanwhile Jammu and Kashmir Police identified the two killed militants as Saddam and Mustafa.
In a post on X, J&K Police wrote, "You Can Run But You Can't Hide! Op Soan: the two neutralised Pakistani Jaish-e-Mohammed terrorists have been identified as Saddam and Mustafa."
Police said that arms and ammunition including an AK Assault Rifle with 4 magazines, an M4 Carbine with 3 magazines, a Glock Pistol with 2 magazines and 4 grenades were recovered from their possession.
A local youth, believed to be an over-ground worker (OGW), has been detained for questioning, they said.
It was the second major encounter in Udhampur district this year. In February, two Pakistani terrorists, including a self-styled commander – Rubani alias Abu Mavia, who was active in the area for the past several years – were killed in the Ramnagar forests.
Over the past several years, the difficult mountain terrain of the Kathua-Udhampur-Doda belt was used by JeM terrorists to establish hideouts and evade security forces after infiltrating from across the border.
However, security forces have dismantled these networks to deny terrorists safe passage and shelter in the upper reaches, the officials said.
They said the relentless operations have resulted in the elimination of a large number of active terrorists operating in the region, many of them identified as Pakistani nationals.
Security agencies are also maintaining heightened surveillance and launching searches in remote forest areas based on intelligence inputs and assessments of possible terrorist movement.
In Doda, four terrorists and five security personnel were killed in separate encounters in 2025, while five people, comprising four terrorists and one security personnel, were killed in adjoining Kishtwar district this year, compared to four deaths in 2025, including three terrorists and one security person.
In 2024, the district recorded five deaths – three security personnel and two civilians.
In Udhampur, four people were killed in 2024, including two terrorists, one security person and one civilian, while 2025 saw four deaths – one terrorist and three security personnel.
Kathua recorded the highest casualties among the four districts in 2024 with nine deaths, including two terrorists and seven security personnel.
The following year, seven people were killed – three terrorists and four security personnel – while 2026 has so far witnessed the death of one terrorist.

Opening summary: race to rescue tunnel workers
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the aftermath of the deadly flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Rescuers in Nepal and China are still trying to locate thousands of people who are missing days after a wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region.
The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to at least 750 dead and more than 3,000 people missing after China’s latest update on Sunday. Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, while Nepali officials confirmed 734 dead and 2,498 people missing. There were reports of some dead swept downstream as far away as India.
China said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were missing on the Tibetan side of a border crossing with Nepal: the highest number was from Nepal at 104, while 49 Indian, 33 Latvian, 18 American and 15 British citizens were also unaccounted for.
In a breakthrough late on Saturday, the Nepali army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site where workers are believed to be trapped.
“We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside,” said the home minister, Sudan Gurungd. More than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside such tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.
Here’s the other main developments:
- 
  Four days after the disaster, authorities said some bodies being recovered had decomposed beyond recognition. They would be buried after legal formalities because of health risks and a fear of disease outbreaks. “DNA samples will be collected, and the bodies will be buried in an open space,” the Chitwan district administration said in a notice.
- 
  The foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said Nepal required specialist assistance to rescue people trapped in tunnels; restore transport and communication lines where bridges had been destroyed; identify bodies; conduct DNA testing; and store bodies for longer periods.
- 
  A team of Indian tunnel experts arrived in Nepal on Saturday, Khanal said. China’s Xinhua news agency reported Beijing had dispatched five tunnel experts to support rescue efforts, with four more due to join them.
- 
  The US will provide $3.6m in humanitarian aid to Nepal, “including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households,” the state department said in a post on X.

Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
- Published
When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.
Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.
Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.
Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny".
"This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."
The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.
Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves.
"It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."
The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.
In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.
"We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service.
"Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."
One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.
They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.
Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.
Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.
Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing.
"Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."
Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.
Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state.
"The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.
Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.
But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.
Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment.
"Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said.
"If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."
Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums.
"Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.
Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.
All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.
Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps.
"The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng.
"Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."
An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".
France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment.
"[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall.
"There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."
Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.
The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa.
"It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said.
"It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."
But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.
This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.
Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency.
"These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said.
"I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."
Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

Investment firm leader gets 11 years for Ponzi scheme that bilked dozens, including Travis Kelce
The creator of a Texas-based investment company has been sentenced to 11 years in federal prison for running a Ponzi scheme that prosecutors say bilked dozens of people, including Kansas City football star Travis Kelce
The creator of a Texas-based investment company has been sentenced to 11 years in federal prison for his role in a Ponzi scheme that prosecutors say bilked 64 victims, including Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce.
U.S. District Judge Zachary Bluestone sentenced Siddharth Jawahar, 38, on Tuesday and ordered him to pay $31.35 million in restitution to victims. Jawahar's attorney did not immediately respond to a voicemail requesting comment.
The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Missouri said between July 2016 and December 2023, Jawahar took in more than $35 million from investors in his company, Swiftarc Capital LLC, but only invested about $10 million of that amount.
Instead, prosecutors said, he used money from new investors to repay older investors and to fund an extravagant lifestyle including luxury apartments in New York City and Austin, Texas, private jet travel and expensive outings.
St. Louis news station KMOV-TV reported that prosecutors said in court that Kelce was among the victims, but they did not elaborate. A 2021 Forbes article said Kelce invested in a fund established by Jawahar’s company Swiftarc.
Robert Patrick, a spokesperson with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Missouri, said there were 64 victims total, but declined to answer questions about Kelce's connection to the case. Kelce's spokespeople did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment.
Jawahar was indicted by a grand jury in 2023 and pleaded guilty in January to three counts of wire fraud.
Jawahar is from India and was living in the U.S. without legal status since 2005, according to court documents. Prosecutors say that after his indictment, Jawahar tried to coach a victim into giving a favorable statement to the FBI, that he lied about his immigration status and tried to get a relative to remotely wipe his iPhone in order to hide evidence.

Romanian border residents fear fallout as frequency of drone alerts rises
Romanian residents near the Ukraine border are living in fear due to Russian drone strikes
ISACCEA, Romania -- The text alerts blare first, then the blasts arrive.
For 48-year-old Robert Marian, who lives in Isaccea, a small Romanian border town in eastern Tulcea County along the Danube River with a crossing into Ukraine, the proximity of Russian drone strikes — just hundreds of meters across the river — has become a source of constant fear.
“There are alerts warning us that something is coming,” he told The Associated Press. “It happened two weeks ago, maybe three. I was asleep at midnight … One was quieter, but another was really loud. I got scared and ran out of the house.”
As Russia’s war in Ukraine grinds on, drone incursions into Romania’s airspace have increased significantly. The blasts just across the Danube are a reminder of how close war is to NATO territory — at a time many fear Russian President Vladimir Putin might want to test the alliance’s resolve.
A Ukrainian border crossing with Romania was “deliberately damaged ... as well as export infrastructure,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sept. 1. Romanian customs announced the same day that activity at the Isaccea-Orlivka crossing had been temporarily suspended.
Alina Mihail, another Isaccea resident, says she feels sick when she hears the drone alerts and blasts ringing out across the border.
“I have so many nights where I don’t sleep anymore," she said. "I live in terror, me and my husband.”
Data from Romania’s Ministry of National Defense indicate a threefold increase in drone incursions so far this year compared with the whole of 2025 — 27 compared with 9 — and more than double the number of drones and drone debris found on the NATO member's territory, at 37 compared with 16.
Already this year, there have been 73 attacks near the border on Ukrainian territory, and some 56 military aircraft have been scrambled to “monitor and manage the situation.” Last year, there were 28 attacks near the border and 21 aircraft were raised. In the first year of the war, there was only one attack near the border.
In May, a drone injured a mother and child after crashing into an apartment block in the eastern town of Galati along the Danube River. A drone that entered Romania from neighboring Moldova was tracked through several counties last week before it reentered Moldova and crashed in a sunflower field.
Moscow has denied sending combat drones to Romanian territory.
The growing menace of drones crossing into Romania’s skies, many of which officials have blamed on Russia, prompted the NATO member to shoot down four drones this year, the first time since the war next door started.
NATO countries across Europe have accused Moscow of being behind a string of “hybrid war” actions against their countries, including drone incursions, sabotage, an attempted attack at a German airport and a Danish helicopter that was fired on with flares in the Baltic Sea.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on Sept. 2 that “Russia has grown increasingly reckless” as Moscow continues its war.
“We have seen more drones and missiles crossing into our airspace, along our eastern flank, creating increased risk,” he said. “The dangers Russia poses are clear."
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also warned that he had received information from CIA Director Jim Ratcliffe indicating Europe should be prepared for intensified Russian provocations, including on the European Union’s eastern flank.
Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta told The Associated Press that Russia is considered a “primary, significant threat” to the eastern flank and to Romania in both the National Defense Strategy and NATO assessments.
“We are engaged in discussions regarding the capabilities needed to counter this common threat — facing the same risks as Poland and the Baltic states — and we are coordinating to ensure these capabilities are distributed in a way that allows for interconnection," he said.
In the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, NATO bolstered its presence on Europe’s eastern flank by sending additional multinational battle groups to Romania, Hungary, Bulgaria and Slovakia.
But last year, the U.S. reduced troop deployments to Eastern Europe, including Romania, after Washington shifted its military posture, which officials denied was a sign of lessened commitment to NATO.
Miruta said there are over 1,000 U.S. troops in Romania, which he said is higher than it was after the U.S. troop rotation last year. "We have a solid relationship,” he said. "The security dynamics along the eastern flank are highly fluid.”
Miruta said that discussions regarding NATO’s Article 5 — that an attack on any member can be met with a collective response — “can take various directions,” but said Romania currently has no information suggesting a ground invasion is imminent or likely.
“From this perspective, we can rest easy,” he said. He added that the ongoing threat posed to Romania is unique because of Russia’s frequent attacks on Ukraine’s Danube River ports, a short distance across the natural river border.
“Once the border is crossed, the distance involved is merely tens of meters, leaving very little reaction time,” he said. “In contrast, in the Nordic countries, targets are tens of kilometers away, providing a sufficiently comfortable window for various forms of intervention.”
Live fire across the border is visible and audible in some areas and has long put Romanian residents on edge.
“We see the drones coming, we see them heading toward those ports,” Miruta added. “Most stop there, bombarding port infrastructure, but we cannot know if any might cross over to the other side … If one does cross over, our communities … would be at risk.”
In response to the growing array of security threats, Romania and Poland acquired the MEROPS system, which fires short counter-drones to take down incoming stray drones. The defense ministry also announced last month that it had received its first 2.5 billion euros from the EU’s Security Action for Europe program, from the total amount of 16.6 billion allocated.
In June, the defense ministry also announced it had signed a $2 billion contract with an Israeli firm to acquire short and very-short-range air defense systems, “designed to protect against aerial threats, including drones and cruise missiles.”
Romanian President Nicusor Dan said at the Ankara summit that defense spending would reach up to 3.7% of GDP this year. He added that Romania joined NATO’s Drone Edge project, which aims to invest over $40 billion in “counter-drone capabilities” over the next five years.
Back in Isaccea, Mihail says she and her husband stay in the house when the text alerts warn of potential airspace breaches.
“We have no support, no one to help us," she said.
—
McGrath reported from Leamington Spa, England.

There will always be a use case for owning both a laptop and a tablet as stand-alone products. But the 2-in-1 laptop is the utopian dream of combining these two into a single device.
Of all the models I've tested, no 2-in-1 laptop is equally good at being both a tablet and a laptop. They always lean toward one or the other. But that doesn't mean you shouldn't buy one, especially since the convenience of having both in one device makes it an easier pill to swallow, price-wise.
The products below should meet most people’s needs. But if none are a fit for you, check out WIRED's other computer buying guides, including the Best Laptops, Best Surface Devices, Best Cheap Laptops, the Best Tablets, and the Best iPad.
Updated September 2026: I've made the Surface Pro 12 my new top pick and rearranged many of the other recommendations on my list.
The Best Detachable 2-in-1 Tablets
You can't talk about 2-in-1 laptops without talking about Microsoft's Surface devices. These tablets have removable keyboards that attach magnetically, not unlike an iPad. This form factor lets you switch between tablet and laptop modes. It's just as functional as a tablet as it is as a laptop. As I said, the Surface Pro is the epitome of this design, pioneering the idea of a tablet with a built-in kickstand that runs a full version of Windows.
The best model to buy right now is the Surface Pro 12 (6/10, WIRED Reviewed). The smaller screen and compact design befit a 2-in-1 tablet that's meant to be held in one hand (at least occasionally). This wasn't my favorite when it came out, largely because it was overpriced at the time. But with all the configuration changes and price increases in the Surface Pro lineup, this model has become my go-to recommendation.
This is the most successful small tablet Microsoft has ever made, and a big reason is that it doesn't cheap out on quality or shrink down the size too much. With a 12-inch screen, it still allows the keyboard to be large enough to type on comfortably. It doesn't have the option for an OLED screen, but the device still feels surprisingly premium, and it is even more portable than its older sibling.
Not only is the Surface Pro 12 cheaper overall, but it's also the only 256-GB storage model on offer, which gives you a more affordable starting configuration. Regardless, you get the Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus, which gives the Surface Pro 12 excellent battery life and solid performance. And because Surface devices run a full version of Windows, they are the best 2-in-1 options to use as full laptop replacements. But be careful: Microsoft sells a $750 starting configuration with only 8 GB of RAM, which may limit multitasking and heavier applications.
An even better laptop replacement, however, is the Surface Pro 13.8 (7/10, WIRED Recommends). The larger screen gives you more visual real estate, and the larger touchpad on the keyboard cover is more comfortable to use. The keyboard cover also comes with fabric-like textured palm rests and a built-in spot to hold the Surface Slim Pen 2. I also like the option to upgrade to an OLED screen, which makes it a more capable iPad Pro competitor. The only problem is that price increases have made this larger Surface Pro feel overpriced. The 2026 Snapdragon X2 Elite or X2 Plus models have largely replaced the 2024 model I tested, priced at $1,600. For me, that's too expensive for something meant to be more of a compact travel device. That's especially true since you still have to buy the keyboard cover. That's why I'd recommend this older Snapdragon X Elite model, which gets you the OLED display with a 120-Hz refresh rate and also bundles in the keyboard and stylus. On top of that, it even includes a terabyte of storage. That's well worth it.
While the hardware makes for a good tablet, Windows still isn't a very touch-friendly operating system and lacks a touch-first app ecosystem to support it. That's where iPads come into play. The iPad Air and iPad Pro are the best tablets you can buy, largely thanks to the breadth of touch-first apps available in the App Store. In many ways, that's what makes an iPad such an ideal 2-in-1 laptop, especially if you actually want to use it as a tablet. They are also easier to hold in one hand because they are lighter than Surface devices. These days, iPads are increasingly becoming legitimate laptop replacements too. With the Magic Keyboard attachment, you can add an additional USB-C port and a full-size keyboard and trackpad. I also like that this design doesn't rely on a kickstand, which makes it easier to use on your lap than the Surface.
While iPadOS isn't perfect, the introduction of windowing and improved cursor support over the years have made iPads work more like laptops than ever. But which iPad should you buy? The latest model I tested, the M4 iPad Air, is immensely powerful, and with the Magic Keyboard attached, it's a solid 2-in-1 laptop that costs less than the Surface Pro with the keyboard included. It's plenty of performance for just about anything you'd want to do with an iPad, especially if you opt for the larger 13-inch model. My only real complaint is that the palm rests on the Magic Keyboard are quite small.
Lastly, I have to point to the Asus ROG Flow Z13, one of the most interesting detachable 2-in-1s. I don't know anyone who has asked for a gaming-based 2-in-1, but Asus went out and made one anyway that actually works. Although you likely won't use the ROG Flow Z13 much as a tablet, the form factor keeps heat away from your hands. Unlike almost every other portable gaming device you can buy, your hands on the keyboard stay cool and sweat-free. This 2025 model is still a good buy, since only a more expensive, special-edition version came out in 2026.
The Best Convertible 2-in-1 Laptops
A different breed of 2-in-1 is commonly called a convertible laptop. These look like traditional laptops, but they have two unique features: a 360-degree hinge that allows the screen to flip to the back of the device, and a touchscreen. Most often, people enjoy tilting the screen back and laying the keyboard upside down on the table to watch movies and videos. You can go into tablet mode by folding the screen all the way back against the bottom screen, but the thickness and weight of these devices make it fairly uncomfortable to use that way.
I'll admit these aren't my favorite laptop designs. While I appreciate a touchscreen, I rarely use the 360-degree hinge in these other poses, not to mention downsides like a wobbly screen, an unattractive hinge, and extra cost. Lenovo, however, has made a name for itself in this category with its Yoga line, creating the very best of this look (though even Lenovo has begun launching “Yoga Slim” models that ditch the 2-in-1 aspect). That aside, I really enjoyed the Lenovo Yoga 9i that I reviewed in 2025.
The 2026 version, the Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition, is largely the same laptop, except with a newer Intel Core Ultra 7 355 processor. Bar none, this is one of the most premium laptops you can buy, sporting a classy design, a very sharp OLED screen, and a thin chassis. One interesting aspect of this design is that Lenovo added an extra benefit to the 360-hinge by building a loudspeaker into it that delivers higher-quality audio, regardless of the mode you're using it in.
The other convertible 2-in-1 I'd point you to is the Framework Laptop 12 (7/10, WIRED Recommends). I'm a big fan of Framework devices because of their great repairability, which lets you replace or upgrade nearly every internal component. You can even upgrade the processor and motherboard, which Framework sells separately. In theory, that means more years of use and less e-waste. Admittedly, it has a fairly thick chassis. But it's affordable, and the 2-in-1 hinge makes it a great, versatile family or student computer. To save money, you can opt for the DIY Edition, which requires assembling the laptop from its components. Framework's elegant, well-documented system makes the building process much more enjoyable than you might think. It would also make for a fun education project for a kid.
I've also tested many convertible Chromebooks over the years, but my favorite is the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514. Not only is this the best 2-in-1 Chromebook, it's also the best 2-in-1 you can buy for under $600. It uses a powerful (and efficient) chip from MediaTek that gives it competitive battery life, something Chromebooks have lacked for years now. It even comes with a higher-resolution screen and 12 GB of RAM; it's pretty stacked for a Chromebook. Googlebooks are coming soon to take the baton from Chromebooks, but for now, the selection of 2-in-1 Chromebooks is dwindling. Hopefully, we'll see a surge of interest in Googlebooks that brings more 2-in-1 laptops to market.
Other 2-in-1 Laptops to Consider
Lenovo Chromebook Duet Gen 9 for $259: The Lenovo Chromebook Duet Gen 9 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) was one of my favorite pieces of tech when it came out for one reason: its size. This diminutive detachable laptop is only 11 inches, which sounds painful at first. But this isn’t a productivity machine. Rather, it’s better viewed as a companion you can take anywhere for light web browsing, writing, and watching videos.
Lenovo Flex 5i Chromebook Plus for $630: We’ve long been fans of the Lenovo Flex 5i Chromebook Plus (8/10, WIRED Recommends), though it's beginning to show its age next to newer models. This one used to sell for as low as $500, which made it a solid budget alternative to the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 mentioned above, but these days the prices are on par. The Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 is better on every front, though, so depending on the current discount, I’d recommend that one over the older Flex 5i.
Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1 for $750: You might think a 16-inch 2-in-1 laptop sounds silly. It's not portable enough to use as a tablet, that's for sure. But if you need a large touchscreen on your laptop, there's reason to pick up something like the Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1 (6/10, WIRED Review). The flexibility of having a 360-degree hinge is useful in all sorts of scenarios. This 16-inch 2-in-1 balances price, portability, and performance with just enough finesse to be worth it—but only consider it when on sale.
Asus ProArt PZ13 for $1,250: Another detachable, the Asus ProArt PZ13 (6/10, WIRED Recommends) takes inspiration from Microsoft’s Surface Pro 13 design at a much more affordable price. For $1,250, you get a detachable 2-in-1 that can go up to around 19 hours on a single charge—and importantly, the keyboard comes bundled. Unfortunately, the performance leaves much to be desired, and its three-piece design is confounding. Still, it’s a nice alternative to the 13-inch Surface Pro if you’re dead set on the style.
What Is a 2-in-1 Laptop?
A 2-in-1 is a laptop that can go from a standard clamshell laptop configuration to a tablet setup. Two main designs fall into this category: detachable tablets and convertible laptops.
Detachable tablets are Windows tablets meant to be used with magnetic keyboards, not unlike an iPad Pro. These let you completely separate the screen from the keyboard, using a kickstand on the back of the display to keep it upright. Microsoft’s Surface lineup popularized this design, and it's still going strong more than a decade after its introduction. We’re even starting to see dual-screen laptops arrive, adding even more flexibility (if you have the cash to spare). The main benefit of the detachable 2-in-1 is the portability. While they aren't as good to use on your lap, they are thinner and lighter, making them better stand-alone tablets and travel devices.
Laptops with convertible displays, on the other hand, use a 360-degree hinge that can position the screen flat, in “tent” mode, or flush against the laptop's underside. Think of this as a touchscreen clamshell laptop with a fancy rotating hinge. This flexibility makes them great for everything from signing documents to streaming TV shows and movies—and you can switch back to a standard laptop orientation when it’s time to work.
Should You Buy a 2-in-1 Laptop?
The big draw of 2-in-1 laptops is that they can be used as both a laptop and a tablet. While in laptop mode, they’re generally comparable to any other clamshell laptop you’ll find. However, Windows and ChromeOS aren’t exactly the best touch-oriented operating systems out there, so you may find the touchscreen experience lacking when using it as a pure tablet.
If you already use a recent iPad or Android tablet regularly, you may not get as much out of a 2-in-1. But if you don't, these 2-in-1 laptops can give you the functionality of both devices in one—hence the name. Beyond that, convertible laptops use 360-degree hinges to offer even more capabilities, such as flipping the laptop upside down in various modes.
The only real downside to choosing a convertible 2-in-1 over a clamshell is the design tweaks needed to incorporate the hinge. Sometimes the weight balance can feel off, and the heftier hinge can look ugly and sometimes require a larger bottom bezel under the display. They're often more expensive too.
Why Not Just Buy an iPad?
It's a good question. All in all, it remains difficult to beat the iPad or iPad Pro for pure tablet use. From a software and third-party app perspective, iPadOS is far more robust without a keyboard, though that may change with Apple's multitasking improvements in iPadOS 26.
Windows tablets are the opposite, benefiting from the full Windows 11 experience. That means you can get all your work done, in theory, on one device, while still having something highly mobile. Some people can even do all their work on an iPad Pro, for example, but others prefer (or require) a desktop computing environment such as macOS or Windows.
I still wish Microsoft would improve Windows' touch experience, though, which would make 2-in-1 laptops much more enticing than iPads.
How I Test
I test 2-in-1s much like how I test clamshell laptops. Before you add in the 2-in-1 element, laptops are already incredibly complex devices, and I test every possible aspect of them. That means I measure display quality, benchmark CPU speed, run it until the battery dies, and type on the keyboard—a lot.
With 2-in-1 laptops, though, there's more of a physical element that needs testing. If it's a detachable, I extend the kickstand and use it in a variety of scenarios. How does it balance on your lap? What's the adjustability of the angle of the kickstand? If it's a convertible 2-in-1, does the touchscreen feel responsive? Does the screen wobble like crazy when you tap it? These are questions only hands-on time with the 2-in-1 laptop can answer.
All the products I recommend were provided by the manufacturers. However, our opinions and test results are completely independent. I don't guarantee positive coverage (or coverage at all) when I agree to accept a review unit from a company. I often send units back once I'm done testing unless I need to do long-term testing.

In September 2026, people shared an image purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump leaving a brown stain on a chair during his trip to Ireland that month.
One X post (archived) featuring the alleged photo had amassed roughly 4 million views as of this writing.
(@StillADog via X)
Trump visited the country on the weekend of Sept. 12-13, during which he met with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin. The U.S. president sparked controversy following that meeting after calling for Irish unification, an act that would merge the United Kingdom's Northern Ireland with the Republic of Ireland. Trump also met with Ireland President Catherine Connolly and attended the Irish Open at his golf course in Doonbeg.
Several Snopes readers asked if the image of Trump leaving the stain — which also spread on Bluesky, Facebook, Threads, TikTok and YouTube — is authentic.
One Threads user claimed artificial intelligence was not used to create the alleged photo, though it was not clear whether or not this was said sincerely.
(@becca_reptile_and_human_momma via Threads)
Some users commenting under the posts seemed genuinely unsure whether the image was real, while other remarks of bewilderment were possibly written in jest.
In sum, the image is fake and originated from an AI-generated video. That AI-generated clip originated from a prompt seemingly using an authentic photo that did not display a stain.
Creator Tom Adelsbach first posted the content as a fake video on Facebook, Instagram and X on Sept. 12, as confirmed by a reverse image search. His posts' captions read, "BREAKING: Donald Trump causes an international incident during his meeting with Ireland President Catherine Connolly."
Snopes emailed Adelsbach to ask for the exact text prompt he submitted to the AI tool to create the fake video. We also emailed the White House to request comment and will update this article if we receive additional details.
Adelsbach's 22-second, AI-generated video features a fake depiction of Trump sitting next to Connolly. The U.S. president appears to sigh, stand up and shake Connolly's hand. The sound of photographers taking pictures can also be heard. As the inauthentic clip continues, Trump exits left, revealing the brown stain on his chair. The stain then grows in size and drips on the floor, leaving Connolly's AI depiction audibly reacting in horror.
Adelsbach previously labeled similar content with disclaimers about comedy, parody and satire. His posts featuring the fake chair stain do not show the same disclaimer. However, Meta's "AI content" label does appear on Facebook and Instagram.
The original photo
Another reverse image search revealed that the Northern Irish Belfast Telegraph newspaper published an authentic photo that Adelsbach appeared to use when creating the AI-generated video. The newspaper credited the picture of Trump and Connolly to photographer Tony Maxwell. The caption says the pair were seated inside Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president's residence. The full caption reads, "President Catherine Connolly and President Donald Trump at Aras an Uachtarain (Tony Maxwell/Maxwells/PA)."
President Connolly's social media accounts also feature a similar photo of her sitting next to Trump.
For background, here is why we alert readers to rumors created by sources calling their output humorous or satirical.

China’s porcelain city carries centuries-old heritage to a new generation
China’s Jingdezhen porcelain sites were inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2026
JINGDEZHEN, China -- Chinese porcelain artist Chen Qing has a vivid memory of her grandfather. It was the only time he wrote down the formula for her family’s distinctive red pigment.
He asked her mother to memorize it and burned the paper minutes later. The secret has since been passed down orally from one generation to the next.
“My mother did not reveal the formula to me until I was over 30,” Chen said.
Her family has practiced the craft since around 1860 in Jingdezhen, known as China’s “Porcelain Capital.” It is located in Jiangxi province, about 1,180 kilometers (735 miles) southeast of Beijing.
Jingdezhen’s pottery-making history spans more than 2,000 years. It began during the Han Dynasty and its porcelain sites were inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2026.
Jingdezhen’s craftsmen have kept alive techniques once used to produce porcelain for the imperial court. That knowledge later spread to private artisans.
Chen’s ancestors adopted some of those traditions after the fall of the Qing Dynasty in 1912.
“The craft is very difficult for an outsider to master,” Chen said. “A family might spend nearly a century developing a single technique.”
Two tables in her studio are covered with brushes, unfinished pieces and pigments. She works in silence, a lamp lighting her strokes.
Chen’s fingers never touch the porcelain’s surface. She steadies her hand against its outer edge, holding the brush firmly as she paints delicate, precise strokes.
Painting a porcelain teacup can take days to complete. A single particle of dust or sweat could ruin the piece and require her to start from scratch.
Landscapes are the most difficult scenes to paint because their boundaries are not clear. A mountain summit might be emerald green, gradually shifting to brown and other warmer colors farther down the slope.
“Mastering a craft is a lifelong process,” Chen said. “Few people are willing to spend more than 10 years learning such a painstaking craft.”
Artists like Chen work alongside archaeological sites and museums to preserve China’s porcelain heritage.
Jingdezhen’s Imperial Kiln Institute researches and restores ceramics excavated from an adjacent complex, where pieces for emperors were crafted in kilns whose remains are still visible today.
The institute is incorporating new technologies into its work, including artificial intelligence, to help match and reconstruct ancient porcelain fragments.
“By the establishment of our ceramic gene bank, we can collect all kinds of information,” said the institute’s president, Weng Yanjun. “We hope that we can retrieve ancient technology with modern science.”
That research can also shed light on the culture and beliefs that surrounded porcelain-making centuries ago.
Among the tiles made at Jingdezhen’s imperial kilns were those used in the Bao’en Pagoda.
It was part of a Buddhist temple complex that was destroyed during a 19th-century rebellion in the city of Nanjing. Its exterior walls were covered with porcelain tiles, each bearing an image of the Buddha.
Traces of other religious traditions can also be found in porcelain studied by the institute, Weng said.
“Islam, Buddhism, Taoism and, later on, European Catholic Christianity harmoniously blend into the porcelain decorations,” he added.
Within Jingdezhen’s imperial kiln complex stands a shrine commemorating Tong Bin, the protective spirit of ceramics.
Known as the “Immortal Master of Wind and Fire” or “Kiln God,” Tong was revered during the Qing dynasty for sacrificing himself in protest against the abuse of kiln workers, according to local tradition.
The shrine remains open today, with a statue honoring Tong inside alongside figures representing other traditional roles in porcelain-making.
“In ancient times, the technology was not as advanced as it is today, so, in many cases, people had to rely on their beliefs — their gods — to help bring good luck and better results,” Weng said.
Some Jingdezhen craftsmen say they hold no particular beliefs associated with porcelain-making. Others display figures of Budai — or the laughing Buddha — in their workshops as symbols of good fortune and prosperity.
For artisans like master Sun Lixin, however, the work retains a spiritual dimension. He is a fourth-generation practitioner who learned the trade from his father at age 13.
“Some traditional rituals have faded considerably,” Sun said. “Yet in the hearts of craftspeople, that reverence remains.”
Every time he paints or fires a piece, Sun is mindful of the hundreds of millions of years of geological history the white clay has undergone before reaching his hands.
He does not visit Jingdezhen’s shrine, but has a practice of his own. Sun instinctively bows to the Kiln God before a firing, wishing for it to be successful and for fine porcelain to emerge.
“If we do not care for it, paint it with devotion and treasure it, how could we possibly do it justice?” Sun said.
While Jingdezhen’s pottery-making continues to be passed down within families, universities and residency programs host new generations of Chinese and international practitioners.
Paola Masi is an Italian ceramic artist in a residency program through October.
She said Song dynasty porcelain shaped her early training. So coming to Jingdezhen feels like going back to the roots of her own path as an artist.
Chinese artist Huang Qi graduated from Jingdezhen Ceramic University in 2015 and left the city to work elsewhere. She eventually decided to come back and is also now an artist-in-residence.
“Jingdezhen is where my dream began,” Huang said. “More and more people are coming and the city is attracting growing attention.”
Encountering fellow craftspeople has allowed her to learn new techniques, while Jingdezhen’s inscription on UNESCO’s World Heritage List makes her optimistic about the future.
“It gives us confidence,” Huang said. “Things will continue to get better.”

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

Trump says ‘major progress’ made towards US base in Poland
The news comes despite fears among allies that the US military could cut back its forces in European nations
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that there had been “major progress” towards establishing an American military base in Poland, after Warsaw said it was holding talks with Washington on the issue.
“Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a U.S. Army base in Poland,” Trump said on social media.
“If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance.”
Trump’s announcement comes despite his administration launching a formal review of its military presence in Europe, raising fears among allies that it could cut back its forces in European nations.

Fintech startup Lendingkart’s NBFC arm Lendingkart Finance has managed to trim its loss by 62% to ₹32.4 Cr for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 (Q1 FY27) from the ₹84.8 Cr loss incurred in the year-ago quarter. The loss also shrank dramatically on a sequential basis, down 73% from ₹121.9 Cr in Q4 FY26, signalling that the sharp deterioration seen through FY26 may be bottoming out. However, the topline also continued to shrink. Operating revenue fell 55% to ₹52.7 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹116.9 Cr in Q1 FY26. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, operating revenue rose about 15% from ₹45.9 Cr. Interest income declined 20% YoY to ₹38.9 Cr, while fees and commission income drag fell 78% to ₹15.3 Cr. Including other income of ₹1.8 Cr, total income for the quarter stood at ₹54.5 Cr, down 54.5% from ₹119.8 Cr a year earlier. The company also booked a net loss of ₹70 Lakh on fair value changes and a ₹80 Lakh loss on assignment of loans during the quarter. During the quarter, the NBFC transferred stressed loans worth ₹94.7 Cr in aggregate principal to an asset reconstruction company for a consideration of ₹2 Cr. Lendingkart Finance, founded in 2014 by Harshvardhan Lunia and Mukul Sachan, is a wholly owned subsidiary of Lendingkart Technologies and serves as the licensed lending vehicle for the group's MSME-focussed digital lending business. The company slipped into loss in FY25. Its net loss widened further through FY26, alongside a sharp pullback in disbursals and a leadership overhaul following Fullerton Financial Holdings' takeover — with former DBS Bank executive Prashant Prakash Joshi now serving as managing director and CEO. The company also remains party to a pending case before the NCLT Ahmedabad, filed by certain minority shareholders of Lendingkart Technologies alleging oppression and mismanagement. Zooming Into Lendingkart Finance's Q1 FY27 Expenses Total expenses for the quarter fell 58% to ₹97.5 Cr in the first quarter from ₹230.2 Cr in Q1 FY26, driven primarily by the narrower loss. Here is a breakdown of where the startup spent the most in the reported quarter: Impairment Of Financial Instruments: This fell the sharpest among expense heads, dropping 83%to ₹13.2 Cr from ₹78.5 Cr in Q1 FY26. Finance Costs: Spending under this head nearly halved, falling 53% to ₹26.3 Cr from ₹55.8 Cr. Employee Benefit Expenses: Expenses towards paying salaries, wages, gratuity fund and provident fund, came down 18% to ₹25.4 Cr from ₹30.8 Cr.

Can an AI chatbot save lives by answering texts about pregnancy?
It started with an accident.
A network of clinics for pregnant women in Kenya set up an automated text messaging service to send out appointment reminders. But when the moms received the texts, they started to write back.
Some asked if it's safe to eat avocados during pregnancy (you can!). Others asked if certain symptoms they were experiencing, like swelling or headaches, are normal during pregnancy.
"At the time I joined I think we were getting less than 100 questions a day," recalls Jay Patel, director of technology for Jacaranda Health. "Now it's 15,000."
At first, Jacaranda hired nurses to answer questions one by one. But over the years since 2020, developers have created a program that uses artificial intelligence to understand patient's questions, prioritize them and flag when a user may need immediate medical care. It's called PROMPTS — and is used by patients visiting public clinics in 24 Kenyan counties.
For women without a smartphone, cell reception, or easy access to the internet, a text to PROMPTS may be the fastest way to get a question answered. Other times, it's a reliable way to determine if a long trip to a hospital is necessary.
"If a mom in a rural part of Kenya starts bleeding at 2 a.m., she can't just Google it," Patel says. "But this service runs completely over SMS. It's completely free to the user, and it's accessible to anyone who has a basic phone."
About 7% of messages are flagged by the system as potentially urgent. These are routed directly to a nurse.
"It bypasses all AI functionality and gets straight to the help desk, into a special queue," Patel says. "They can pick it up immediately, look at the mom's question history and call her."
That kind of quick response is critical in Kenya, where about 6,000 women die each year from childbirth or pregnancy-related causes. That's 16 women a day. Almost a third of those deaths are believed to be related to delays in seeking care.
Lisa Mushega, a policy expert for HENNET, a Kenyan coalition of health care providers, says PROMPTS helps prevent these delays by giving women a direct line to a health professional. (Jacaranda Health is a member of the coalition).
"It's a referral," Mushega says. "[PROMPTS] is data driven and can improve the quality of care — informed by the voices of mothers themselves."
Mushega says she has met women who used PROMPTS to correctly identify signs of pre-eclampsia, a life-threatening condition that can start with swollen legs. Another new mother used the system when her newborn seemed sick, and she wasn't sure how to calm him.
"She was told to go to the nearest health facility, because her baby was actually having jaundice," Mushega says. "It really comes in handy."
At a time when the use of artificial intelligence is drawing existential concerns and calls for regulation, a program like PROMPTS demonstrates its potential value, says Smisha Agarwal, director of global digital health at Johns Hopkins University.
The AI Edge
Historically, most public health messaging is one-sided: Public service advertisements, billboards or automated messages written by health authorities and disseminated to the public.
"That conversation is really bounded by what a health system decides a mother should know," Agarwal says. Artificial intelligence sets a different course: "What the LLM really changes is the direction of conversation. Because now we can center it on what the mother actually wants to know, and in a private space on her own phone. There is a fundamental change in power."
In Kenya, PROMPTS understands messages in English, Swahili and Sheng — a popular dialect in Nairobi that is a mix of the two languages. Jacaranda has also expanded to parts of Ghana, Nigeria and Tanzania, building versions for speakers of Twi and Hausa.
"There's local context," Patel says. "If there's a question about nutrition in Kenya, and you give the same answer from a question about nutrition in Nigeria, you're going to get laughed out of the room."
Jacaranda Health is also using PROMPTS to help doctors identify areas of need, based on anonymous feedback from some of the estimated 700,000 users each year.
"Lots of mothers are reporting that they're getting blood pressure checks, but very few report getting breast exams," says spokesperson Laura Down. "It gives mums more agency in the health system — as well as a better understanding of their pregnancy history."
In other cases, Down says the questions mothers are asking can help doctors understand what's happening in their own community.
"So for example, we're starting to see correlations between a spike in extreme heat and a spike in mothers reporting issues like headaches or swelling or dehydration," Down says.
Any potential drawbacks?
But there are limits. These interventions work best in places that already have functional healthcare systems, Agarwal says. There's very little margin for error when human medical needs are processed by a machine. The way the system is trained to do a rapid handoff to a human nurse in an emergency becomes a key factor.
"The first thing I want to know is, what happens when the system gets a message wrong?" says Javaid Iqbal Sofi, a researcher focusing on AI policy and governance at Virginian Tech University. "Suppose a woman describes something urgent, but the system treats it as routine. Would someone catch that? How quickly?"
Patient privacy issues and missed opportunities for care are common concerns, as AI platforms are adopted in medical contexts worldwide. Last month, the use of platforms developed by Palantir to automate staff schedules in hospitals in the United States drew protests by a national nursing union. The use of AI by insurance companies to process and deny medical claims — even without a human reviewing them — has led to outrage and calls for regulation.
In contrast, PROMPTS operates as a limited-use program, trained on a relatively narrow set of issues and concerns. Its developers say the human element of the system is the most important part. A team of 18 nurses are employed to monitor, audit, and respond to PROMPTS questions around the clock.
"Humans are responsible for ensuring the quality of messages going out, and we audit the quality of the answers," says Javan Waita, Jacaranda Health's director of programs in Kenya.
Maintaining a significant human component of the program improves accuracy but raises the cost. Right now, it costs about $2 per user to maintain PROMPTS, which is absorbed by the nonprofit. That gets a mom through pregnancy, and stays with her for a year after birth.
Waita says this is an important backstop, especially when mothers might not have an alternative.
"The sooner a mother is able to access care, the sooner doctors will be able to understand the problem," Waita says. "If PROMPTS isn't there, it means more complications for mothers, more complications for newborns."

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)
