There’s not much to dislike about the Diverge 4 Pro. The Quarq DUB-PWR meter estimates total wattage from the left leg alone; I’d prefer a spider-based meter that measures total power at the crank spider rather than extrapolating from one side. The cranks on the 56 cm Diverge are 172.5 mm, which is out of step with an industry trend toward shorter cranks. After my second right knee replacement, I swapped out the 172.5 mm cranks on my road bike for 165 mm. Getting into an aero posture is easier and more comfortable with shorter cranks, and since my knees don’t go as high at the 12 o’clock position, there’s less hip impingement, and I experience less discomfort overall. I’m also not a fan of the mountain bike-style S-Works Carbon Zee bottle cage with the openings on the side. I ride with one-liter bottles on hot days, and my leg would occasionally bump the bottle lid on the open side of the cage.
But those are truly minor quibbles. Ultimately, the Diverge 4 Pro is a fantastic gravel bike that is ideal for those who love rough gravel, long rides, or bikepacking through the wilderness. But let’s be frank: Not everyone needs to ride around on an $8,000 gravel bike—if you would be happy with a less-expensive aluminum bike or carbon setup with a mechanical groupset, this isn’t the bike for you. (And if your wallet is wide open, Specialized just launched the $12,500 S-Works Diverge 4 this week.) But if you’re more Unbound Gravel than groomed gravel, you can’t go wrong with the Diverge 4 Pro.
Eric Bangeman is the Managing Editor of Ars Technica. He lives in the northwest suburbs of Chicago, where he enjoys road cycling and plays bass in a band.

Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
- Published
Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way.
His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb.
But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta.
And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present.
"If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can."
Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. And it delivers vital food and medicine to people on the margins of society.
As such, it offers a lifeline to millions of poor and elderly Ukrainians living in remote villages where shops are rare and trips to the city are expensive and dangerous. In a vast rural nation wracked by war, Ukrposhta is part of the glue that holds the country together.
That has made the service a target for Russia - which in recent months has stepped up not only its attacks on postmen and women but also sorting offices and logistical hubs. The Kremlin has claimed strikes like this are retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian online retailers like Wildberries.
Speaking in his imposing Soviet-era office building that overlooks Kyiv's famous Maidan square, Smelyansky said: "If we don't go [to a village], we don't have basic supply. We don't have food. We don't have medicine. People will struggle. If we do go, they may delay a decision to evacuate from the areas they probably should have evacuated."
There are many risks. If a post van turns up unannounced, a crowd can form, creating a target for an opportunistic Russian drone operator. But if they call ahead, information could leak.
"Is it a danger?" Smelyansky said. "Absolutely. Because there are Russian sympathisers who can give them the location of the truck that's coming."
By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in
If Smelyansky chooses not to send a van in, he faces criticism. "You get messages from people from those villages: 'You betrayed us. You didn't come...' But if I go, I may risk the life of the driver."
Smelyansky says Russia is deliberately targeting his staff because of the vital role they play shoring up Ukraine's resilience, helping people stay alive in their homes through the fighting and bitter winters.
"It's not an accident, it's deliberate," he said. "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in." Russia denies targeting civilians.
Since 2022, hundreds of Ukrposhta branches and vehicles have been hit, and more than 50 staff have lost their lives, either on the frontline or on their rounds, according to Ukrposhta.
We travelled with Kateryna Marynych, a 38-year-old postmistress, near Zaporizhzhia - a city not too far from the southern frontlines.
She lost her home and her husband during the full-scale invasion, and came to the area to rebuild her life. She ran the post office in the village of Lukasheve for two years until it was destroyed in March by a Russian drone, targeting soldiers working nearby.
After her van drew up, a steady queue of elderly folk formed. She sat in the front passenger seat, window open, handing out cash, taking payments.
One customer, Nadiia, said she was grateful: "It's a long way for us to travel to Zaporizhzhia. Especially now, at a time when there are attacks all around us. The fact that they come here is really nice."
Oleksandrivna, 77, arrived wearing a purple dressing gown, walking with a crutch. When I asked her where she would be without Kateryna, she replied: "We would be stuffed! I am just out of hospital after a stroke. Where could I go for my medicine?"
But Mykola, 64, pointed to another service the post office provides to a largely elderly population. "It is very important," he said. "It's one of the few joys of the month: you come out, have a chat with people, collect your pension, and go home."
For many people in remote communities, Kateryna can be their last link with the Ukrainian state.
She says she hopes her customers are proud of her. "They love me, they need me," she said. "They are waiting for me. Sometimes they call me, especially after attacks on Zaporizhzhia and ask me how I am. We are like a big family. My attitude towards them is like a grandmother or grandfather."
The attacks on Ukrposhta form part of Russia's wider escalation of its war on Ukraine, stepping up fast drone attacks on civilian infrastructure including business infrastructure, energy facilities, transport networks and border posts. Analysts say that as Russia's invasion stagnates on the battlefield in the east, it is looking for other ways of putting pressure on Kyiv.
For safety, Kateryna always travels with her partner, Slava, who drives. While she sorts the cash, he works from the back of the van, taking and receiving parcels, delivering food and water. He also carries a side-arm in a holster, for personal protection; these vans carry a lot of cash.
Both wear body armour when close to the front line. And they have an antenna in the van that shows them the location of the small first-person-view drones that render the frontline so deadly. They have seen drones from the car but luckily have not yet been hit.
She accepted her job was dangerous but would never change it. "It is my work," she said. "If I can't, who will do my job?"
Ukraine's defence comes in many forms - and it's not always delivered at the barrel of a gun.
Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk

It's that time of year: The weather's finally starting to cool off, Halloween decor has taken over most of the stores, and tech companies are dropping their fall launches. Last week was Apple's annual September iPhone event, and last night another tech launch hit the books, though this one's a little more niche. (Though I'd still say folding smartphones are in their early days.)
If you're a fan of e-paper devices that use E Ink, a technology that mimics the appearance of ink on paper, you've probably stumbled across Boox's wide range of E Ink digital notebooks and tablets. One of Boox's most popular models is the smartphone-sized Palma, and the company just announced its third-generation Palma along with two other new products.
Here are all three products released last night and what’s available to shop now (and which one I'm most excited to test as WIRED's resident E Ink device tester).
Boox’s New Generation
Boox launched three new E Ink products: the Boox Note Air6 C ($580), Note Mini C ($580), and the Palma 3 ($340).
The Note Air6 C is a new addition to the Note Air line I've previously tested for my guide to the best digital notebooks. These are essentially E Ink Android tablets that come with a stylus, making them an excellent choice for a powerful digital notebook. That remains true with the Note Air6 C, which will run on Android 16 for an even more tablet-style user interface and apps. The C stands for color, since this model has a color screen with a 10.3-inch Kaleido 3 color display. The Note Air6 C also has new firmware that adds Dual Notes so you can annotate two documents side by side. There are also several AI features, including a meeting and audio insights feature and a document summary. Out of the three devices announced, the Boox Note Air6 C is the only one available right now.
The Boox Note Mini C will cost the same as the larger Note Air6 C, but it has a smaller, 8.52-inch screen. It uses the same Kaleido 3 color display but is designed for more on-the-go work and for holding the device in one hand compared to the larger Air6 C. The Mini C and Air6 have fairly similar specs when it comes to power—both models have an octa-core processor, 6 GB of RAM, and 64 GB of storage. You can expand that storage on both devices up to 2 TB with a microSD card. Overall, it's more about size than it is power if you're choosing between them, but the Note Mini C is not on sale yet. Boox says it's coming soon.
Size also comes into play for Boox's final of the three launches. The Palma 3 is the device I'm most excited to check out, as it's the latest iteration of the beloved Palma line. It's another E Ink screen device with an Android 16 base, but it's shaped like a smartphone—“palm-sized.” Boox promotes this as a low-stimulation second screen, and we've liked it as an e-reader option before. The screen isn't color, but it is 6.13 inches with a dual-tone front light and ambient light sensor to adjust to your surroundings. You'll also get a rear camera (promoted for the Palma 2 as great for document scanning rather than photography), dual microphones, and a customizable smart button like the Palma 2 had before it. The Palma 3 also has an aluminum build, which is a new look after the plastic design of the Palma 2. It's due out simply “soon,” with no formal release date. I'm most interested in how it will compare against smaller models like the Xteink.

Srinagar , Sep 17: In a significant development, the Ministry of Education (MoE) has proposed a comprehensive review of the existing arrangements governing the Teacher Eligibility Test (TET), including the eligibility framework and issues faced by teachers already in service.
The MoE has taken these measures relating to Teacher Eligibility Test (TET) and proposed legislative review in view of emerging issues concerning teachers and teacher eligibility.
In an Office Memorandum, the Department of School Education and Literacy (DSEK) MoE said it had taken note of representations and issues raised by teachers, teacher associations, educational institutions and other stakeholders over implementation of the TET requirement.
The Ministry said it had also taken note of the directions and observations of the Supreme Court concerning the requirement of TET for teachers covered under the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009.
In wake of this, the government has proposed to review the existing TET arrangements with the stated objective of ensuring a “transparent, fair and workable framework” for teacher eligibility.
The proposed review will examine the existing TET eligibility and qualification framework as well as issues concerning teachers already in service who are required to acquire TET qualification.
The MoE has also proposed examining measures to ensure that TET examinations are conducted periodically and at reasonable intervals.
Another component of the proposed exercise will focus on the practical difficulties faced by serving teachers in obtaining TET qualification.
The MoE has further proposed consultations with State Governments, Union Territory Administrations, the National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE), educational experts and other stakeholders as part of the review process.
The memorandum also proposes examining whether amendments to relevant statutory provisions are necessary in the larger public interest.
"The government will examine the practical difficulties faced by serving teachers in obtaining TET qualification and will hold consultation with State Governments, Union Territory Administrations, NCTE, educational experts and other stakeholders besides examining whether appropriate amendments to the relevant statutory provisions are necessary in the larger public interest," the memorandum issued by MoE reads.

FDA still haunted by DOGE cuts
In April 2025, Elon Musk’s U.S. DOGE Service took a chainsaw to the Food and Drug Administration, slashing 3,500 workers and triggering a broader staff exodus. More than a year later, the FDA is trying to add more than 2,000 employees back, but it can’t — thanks to the same DOGE cuts.
DOGE’s push to centralize what were once individual human resources offices has backfired, creating bottlenecks and confusion. Hundreds of prospective new employees are stuck in pre-onboarding limbo and routine administrative tasks, like purchase approvals and travel payments, have fallen by the wayside.
When asked about the paralysis, an agency spokesperson demurred, highlighting the hiring efforts instead. But multiple employees told STAT’s Margaret Manto a different truth. Read more.
Is this a mouse, a human, or something else?
Researchers have created a mouse whose brain is half-human by volume.
In recent decades, scientists have gotten much better at growing “cerebral organoids” — miniature, three-dimensional brain-like structures — from human stem cells as a way to study brain development and disease. Now, a group from Stanford University has advanced their usefulness by growing these globs of cells inside mice missing chunks of their own brain.
Across memory and motor tests, the scientists reported that these neuro-chimeric mice performed about the same as normal mice. But hours of open field observations revealed something totally different.
What a wild item to write and a phenomenal story from STAT’s Megan Molteni. Read on for more about the scientific utilities for and ethical implications of these mousensteins.
Will Chris Klomp stand up to RFK Jr.?
That was the question on senators’ lips as two key committees grilled the senior federal health official nominated to be Kennedy’s second-in-command.
Over two days of hearings, senators fired questions at Klomp about whether he would stand up to the health secretary — especially on Trump and Kennedy’s vaccine policy changes, which have coincided with measles outbreaks across several states and multiple deaths in Pennsylvania.
The “famously thrifty technology entrepreneur” has already been a major player in the Trump administration as Medicare director and then chief counselor to Kennedy. He has negotiated deals with pharmaceutical companies and acted as a liaison between the Department of Health and Human Services and the White House.
What did Klomp say about the measles deaths? Read Chelsea Cirruzzo’s story.
I promise this photo is not AI-generated
This is a real picture of twin girls, Hiyab and Wuhbto, who were born in Ethiopia with conjoined skulls in 2024. They are now recuperating, unconjoined, after surgeons at a St. Louis hospital separated their heads in February.
Twins joined at the head — craniopagus twins — are exceedingly rare. One in every 2.5 million live births! Only 62 separation attempts have ever been made worldwide. Hiyab and Wuhbto shared brain tissue and blood vessels, which made surgery last more than 24 hours and required more than 60 specialists, according to an announcement from SSM Health Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital. Surgeons completed repair of Wuhbto’s skull earlier this year. Hiyab is slated for the same procedure this fall.
Medicine ain’t always perfect, but wow can it do some marvelous things. You can watch the livestream of the announcement here.
Purer fentanyl won’t solve the U.S. overdose death crisis
In January, a paper published in Science analyzed government mortality figures, data on drugs seized by the DEA, and Reddit posts to determine that decreasing fentanyl potency due to Chinese government crackdowns could explain the recent decline in U.S. opioid overdose deaths. But when another research team tried to replicate that study, they didn’t come to the same conclusion.
“A simplistic supply shock is not supported by the evidence,” the authors wrote yesterday in Science Advances.
The researchers noted that as fentanyl purity increased across the country, there was no associated national drop in overdose rates. While there did seem to be a broad association between declining purity and overdoses, it was shared with other, unrelated trends. And importantly, the DEA acknowledged at the time that increasing purity in its drug seizures was likely due to a change in its sampling plan.
It’s also critical not to overlook geographic variability in the drug supply, the replication study authors wrote. As one of them told Lev Facher when the first study was published, many regions had declining overdose rates before potency apparently began to drop. — Theresa Gaffney
Potentially good Ebola news
After 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths, there is reason to be cautiously optimistic about the trajectory of the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Disease transmission rates are declining in most of the affected provinces, though months of work remain to get the outbreak under control, said Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director-general of the World Health Organization, during a news conference yesterday.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, is the second-largest on record. The WHO said it expects a Phase 3 randomized clinical trial of Ebola vaccines to begin in the next couple of weeks. The inimitable Helen Branswell has the full update.

The 20th edition of the Asian Games will take place in Aichi-Nagoya beginning on September 19.
India will be sending a 492-member strong contingent to compete across 36 disciplines as it looks to put up an impressive showing at the continental event.
In the last edition of the Asiad in Hangzhou, India walked away with its best-ever medal tally. It took home 107 medals in total (28 gold, 38 silver, and 41 bronze), including 29 in athletics alone.
That display ensured that India finished fourth in the medal table, its best showing since 1962, behind China, Japan, and South Korea.
In the very first edition of the Asian Games, held in New Delhi in 1952, India finished second in the medal table with 51 medals (15 gold, 16 silver, and 20 bronze). During that edition, Kanti Shah became the first Indian to win an Asian Games medal when he claimed silver in the men’s 100m backstroke swimming, while Sachin Nag won the first Indian gold medal in men’s 100m freestyle swimming.

You can build an Android app with Google Antigravity by designing the UI in Google Stitch, generating the app with Gemini using Expo React Native, previewing it through Expo Go, and creating an APK with Expo EAS. You can also connect Supabase for cloud sync.
Building apps on software is now everyone’s cup of tea, thanks to AI. Even if you have never written a single line of code before, you can just go to any AI tool and build the app you want. However, the real complexity lies in making those apps useful instead of AI slop. To help you out, we have created this series where we help you learn how to build fully functional and reliable apps using AI tools.
To start with beginners, in this guide you will learn how to create an Android app using Google Antigravity.
There are multiple ways to create an app. However, this guide explains how you can create Android apps using Expo, a cross-platform builder that lets you easily build apps and share them between Android and iPhone, and you can also run Expo apps on the web. In the future, you will learn how to create Flutter apps, which offer more flexibility.
Table of Contents
Prerequisites
To create Android apps, you need:
- A Google AI Pro subscription
- Antigravity installed on your Mac or Windows
- An Android phone
- Download the Expo Go app. You can install it for free from the Google Play Store
- An Expo account (which you can sign up here for free)
How to Create Android apps Using AntiGravity
Step 1: Get Google Gemini AI Pro
First, opt for Google Gemini AI Pro. This subscription gives access to the Google Gemini models inside Antigravity. If you are looking for a totally free way with a generous limit to create Android apps, you can view our tutorial on how to create Android apps using Google AI Studio for free.
If you already have a Google One AI Premium subscription, you can directly install the Google Antigravity application and get started.
Although Google isn’t the best at its coding models, it offers very generous free terms compared to other models. Moreover, Google’s recently launched Gemini 3.8 Flash is also reliable for building apps if you guide it in the right way.
Step 2: Create the app UI using Google Stitch
Once you have opted for a Google AI Pro subscription, go to this website: stitch.withgoogle.com to design the UI of the app you are building. It is a free tool, and if you have a Google AI Pro subscription, you get better rate limits.
Stitch is a UI design website similar to Figma, but it relies more on an AI approach, which lets you generate UI for apps and websites just by prompting.
In my experience, Google Stitch, in most cases, produces generic UI designs, but it’s a great start for someone to get started with the app UI.
You can also skip this step if you have reference images. Most AI models are very good at replicating designs and understanding the structure. However, if you want a structured approach and a little customization, you can follow this process: Generate your initial designs using Stitch, then edit and modify them. Finally, use those references in tools like Google Antigravity to generate apps with the best UI, exactly the way you need.
To create a UI design, you can view our full, detailed tutorial on how to create UI designs using Google Stitch.
Step 1: First, open Google Stitch and enter the prompt for the app you want to create.
In this case, let’s create a to-do list app because that is a very good starting point, even for beginners. Remember to select “app” as an option while creating, because Google Stitch supports both app and website designs.
Step 2: Now, enter a prompt to generate the UI of the app. Then tap on Enter
Step 3: Now wait until Google Stitch provides a full UI design of the app.
Step 4: You can tap on any element or use AI to describe the changes you want, or you can just use the built-in basic tools to edit sections, text, and much more.
Step 5: If you dont like the design, you can click on the plus icon and tap on upload files, and then you can upload the reference files.
Step 6: To preview how the app works, you can tap on the prototype option to preview how the full app works
Step 7: And once you have the design, tap on Export, and you can export directly to Google Antigravity or save it as a ZIP file.
I recommend downloading it as a ZIP file because sharing to Google Antigravity doesn’t work in most cases.
Step 3: Open Google Antigravity
Now open Antigravity and set it up as a CLI. You can also use it as an agent for UI; Antigravity supports both, but I prefer the CLI experience. Now tap on Open Folder and create a new app, or you can select an existing folder. For those who are unaware, all app files will be stored in this folder.
Now open the CLI, and on the right, you can see the chat interface. Now, in the chat, you can tap on the model’s name and select Google 3.8 Flash High. For your information, Google 3.8 Flash is better than the Pro series. It is the latest model and very good at AI generation, especially if you have reference images.
Step 4: Add your UI reference images
Now, click on the plus icon and attach the images. You can attach up to five images at a time.
Now enter this prompt to ask Google Antigravity to create an app.
Please build an Expo React Native app in TypeScript based on the attached UI designs.
Requirements:
Replicate the layout, typography, colors, and components from the attached screenshots as closely as possible.
Use standard Expo packages (@expo/vector-icons, @react-native-async-storage/async-storage, expo-linear-gradient, react-native-safe-area-context).
Implement full client-side state with local persistence using AsyncStorage so added tasks and items persist across app reloads.
Keep the code modular with clean components in a src/ folder.
Ensure there are zero TypeScript compile errors.
Step 5: Create the app using Gemini
Once you are done, wait for some time until Google Gemini 3.8 Flash creates an app.
Since it runs on Expo, you can preview the build on your Android phone. Simply enter this prompt, and it will generate your QR code in the terminal. If you want to make any changes, you can ask Google Gemini to do that for you.
Step 6: Preview the app on your Android phone
Now, open your Android phone and install the Expo app. Open the Expo app on your Android phone and tap on “Scan QR code,” and the app will be installed on your device. Now you can preview all the changes that you have made.
If you want to make any changes, you can enter the prompt with the required changes. Maybe also include better UI references to help the Google Gemini model understand better. In my experience, Google models hallucinate a lot. Once everything is finished and you are happy with the output.
Step 7: Create an Expo account
Now, before that, you need to go to Expo.io and create a free account. If you have already created one, you can just sign in. Now, Expo EAS will use your Expo account to create the build.
Now, once the account is created, there are two ways to connect Expo Go with your Google Antigravity. First is using a local authentication session, which is stored in your home folder. You can run login in Terminal at any time to connect.
To do that, open Terminal in Antigravity and then run this command
Command: npx eas-cli login
Now enter the username and password you created for your Expo account. Google Antigravity will remember these credentials for all future builds. So this is a one-time process; you don’t need to do this for every new app build.
If you don’t want to submit your credentials, you can create an Expo access token (perhaps for one-time use, or if you are sharing with a friend). You don’t need this if you are using it personally on your device.
However, if you want to connect your Expo account through an access token:
- Go to expo.dev/settings/access-tokens.
- Create a token, name it “Antigravity”, and generate the new token.
- Open the terminal and run this command:
Commad: export EXPO_TOKEN="your_copied_token_here"
Step 8: Build the Android app
You can simply enter the prompt and wait for some time until Google Antigravity starts an Expo build in the Expo build app. Once it finishes, it will give you a direct download link for the app.
Prompt:
Since you are using a free version, Expo offers some free rate limits, and then later it uses buffer time to build the app, which averages between 1 and 7 hours, depending on the traffic. If you are lucky enough, the app should be ready in less than 5 minutes. Once it’s ready, Google Antigravity will offer a direct download link.
Step 9: Download the app
You can copy the download link and paste it into any app on your Android, tap on it, and install the app. Alternatively, you can just download the app on your PC and share it to your Android.
Once the build process is completed. you can see the app download link. You can directly share the download link to an Android device.
Step 10: Scan the app before installing
Even though the app is built by you, I highly recommend scanning it before installing it on your Android phone. You can use any free online scanners to scan the app and confirm there are no security issues or malware within your app. Once you are done, you can install the app.
Step 11: Install the app on your Android phone
If this is your first time installing a third-party app, Google Chrome will block the app download from unknown sources. When prompted, you can enable unknown sources; once enabled, you can use the package installer to install the app on your Android phone.
Connect your Android app to Supabase (Optional)
Now that the basic Android phone app has been set up and will successfully run on your device, if you want to back up data in the cloud, you can connect it to Supabase.
Supabase is a free database hoster that lets you host small files in the cloud so that your app can use this data, allowing you to use the same app on other devices with sync enabled.
Step 12: Enable Supabase Integration
To connect it to Supabase: Go back to Google Antigravity and enable Supabase MCP. Next, open this URL and create a new account in Supabase. Now, in Supabase, create a new project. Example: my-to-do-app.
Once a project is created, go to your project settings and then API, and copy the following details:
- Project URL – You can go to Project Settings > General
- Publishable key (Go to Supabase project settings > API and find the key here: Publishable key
Step 13: Connect the app to Supabase
And now, once you have connected your Supabase account to Google Antigravity, open Google Antigravity and enter the following prompt: Next, ask Google Antigravity to create a new Supabase database to use for storing the data.
Prompt:
“I want to sync this app’s data with Supabase.
Here are my Supabase project details:
Supabase URL: https://your-project-id.supabase.co
Supabase Anon Key: your-anon-key-here
Please do the following:
Install @supabase/supabase-js.
Create a Supabase client configuration file in src/services/supabase.ts.
Provide the SQL table definition script I need to run in the Supabase SQL Editor for our tasks and projects.
Update our data context so that it fetches from and syncs with Supabase when online, while falling back gracefully to offline local storage.
Now wait for some time until your app is connected to the Supabase free plan. Once done, your application successfully uses and stores data in the cloud, and it fetches it to your app in real time.
Step 14: Test the Expo build again
To confirm again, you can ask Google Antigravity to use this prompt to access the Expo build on your Android device, so that you can check everything. And once you’re done, you need to rebuild the app.
Step 15: Rebuild the app
Enter this prompt, and Google 3.8 Flash will start the build on Expo Application Services (EAS). Wait for some time until it provides a direct app download link. Once it does, you can download it on your PC and share the app directly to your Android, or share the link directly to your Android.
This time, you will see an update prompt instead of an install prompt, since you have already installed the app on your Android phone.
That’s it. On a high level, this is how easily you can create an Expo Android app on your Android phone using Google Gemini. Except for getting access to the Google Gemini models, every other process is free to use.

Gets very loud for its size. Clear, detailed sound. Very durable build. Swappable battery. IP66 dust and waterproof.
TIRED
Expensive. Overkill for many. Single hand-carry grip. Pricey strap sold separately.
How loud is too loud? That's the question I find myself asking as I turn up the volume dial on the Soundboks Rider portable Bluetooth speaker. By myself, outdoors, a five or six on the dial is plenty loud; anything more starts to get uncomfortable. But this speaker can push out a ridiculous 118-decibel sound pressure level (dB SPL). That's basically a rock concert.
If that's your jam, this may be your perfect speaker. It's distinct, stylish, built to last, and, importantly, sounds great. But it's absolutely overkill for most people, who would be better off with a smaller, more affordable speaker from the likes of Sony, JBL, or Marshall, all of which offer plenty of tamer options below the Rider's $600 price tag.
Bring The Party
Soundboks Rider Specs
Dimensions
13.8 x 9.4 x 7.9 (H x W x D) inches
Weight
14.3 pounds
Water and Dust Resistance
IP66
Battery life
Up to 35 hours
Charging
USB-C, swappable LiFePO4 battery
Connectivity
Bluetooth 4.2, 3.5-mm AUX
Drivers
8-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter
The Soundboks Rider looks like no other portable speaker I've tested. It resembles something you'd find on stage at a concert rather than at your next barbecue. Its restrained design is almost the antithesis of the flashy, LED-pulsing party speakers you might find from brands like JBL or Samsung.
The build quality is impressive, confidence-inspiring, and clearly made to last. It's built like a tank, with a steel front grille, silicone rubber ball corners, and a thick plastic cabinet. During a drop test, I was frankly more worried about the speaker breaking my stairs than my stairs breaking the speaker. Another win for longevity is the replaceable battery—it charges via USB-C, and you can swap it in and out in seconds. This feels like a speaker you could have for decades.
While smaller than Soundboks' other speakers, it is still much larger than your average Bluetooth unit, and a bit awkward to carry with its single carry-grip on one corner. I would have loved to see two carry handles, one on each side. That would make the Rider easier and more flexible to carry, similar to the Sony ULT Field 7.
Unlike the larger Soundboks Mix and Soundboks 4, this is meant to be a stand-alone speaker—it does not have Soundboks' wireless multi-speaker connectivity (SKAA TeamUp), a speaker stand mount, or additional inputs (read: XLR).
Soundboks speakers can get loud, and despite the Rider being the smallest in the brand's lineup, its audio output is astonishing. I was frankly scared to turn this speaker up to max volume (11 on the dial, IYKYK).
To spare my New York City neighbors, I took this speaker outdoors and cranked it to 11; even then, I could only manage it for a short while before I worried someone would call 311 to file a noise complaint. Which is to say: the Rider is plenty loud for most parties I can think of.
But the Rider isn't just loud—it's clear. Across all volume ranges, it sounds great. While it can produce big bass, it isn't overpowering in the mix. The sound profile matches the speaker's understated, PA-style aesthetic—clear, strong, and detailed.
The speaker can output up to 118 dB SPL. That's well within painful levels, and similar to a rock concert. I'm honestly not sure when or where I'd need to push out that much audio, but if you ever do, the Rider is game.
Fine Tuning
The app is similarly streamlined and unfussy. You can control basically every speaker function remotely, including volume, sound profiles, EQ modes, and even turning it off.
Connecting, however, was a little finicky. I had to pair, unpair, re-pair, power off, and power on a few times before the app and speaker would actually start talking to each other. That was even more irritating because, after a firmware update, the app told me to forget the speaker and re-pair all over again. I've tested hundreds of wireless audio gadgets—Bluetooth connectivity issues with brand-new products are less surprising than you might think and often get sorted out within a month or two of software updates. Still, it made the whole experience feel decidedly less premium than the Rider's $600 price might suggest.
Is It Overkill?
The Soundboks Rider is an excellent speaker. In terms of loudness, durability, and battery life, it runs circles around most of the competition, including larger party-slash-karaoke speakers like the Sony Tower 5 and JBL PartyBox Club 120.
But as a larger, portable Bluetooth speaker meant to stand all on its own, it's a bit niche, especially for $600. I do think it's overkill for a lot of people—I can't think of many folks in my life who need this combination of loud and bombproof in their speaker. You can also get plenty of portable Bluetooth speakers for less (the aforementioned $500 Sony ULT Field 7 and $330 JBL PartyBox Encore Essential 2 come to mind) that might do the job just fine.
Soundboks says this is a portable party speaker built for spontaneity and outdoor adventure. For my spontaneous adventures, the Rider is overkill. But if your adventures include a lot more people (and a lot more space) than mine, it might be the perfect fit—big enough to bring to any party and durable enough that you never have to worry.

Why cash continues to thrive even as India's digital payments grow
- Published
Every year, more Indians tap, scan and swipe. Every year they also hoard more paper.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) - the country's central bank - now has 176 billion banknotes in circulation. It's printing 28-30 billion fresh ones across six denominations annually and retiring roughly 21 billion. It is a vast logistics operation.
And yet, as Unified Payments Interface (UPI) digital transactions surge towards a billion a day, cash sloshing around the economy keeps climbing at a brisk pace.
"Currency in circulation continues to grow at double-digit rates even as cash's share of individual transactions declines, thanks to growing digital payment adoption. That combination makes future demand harder to predict, which complicates our planning for production and distribution capacity," Shirish Chandra Murmu, RBI deputy governor, said in a speech to central bankers in Jakarta last month.
He called it the "cash paradox". But what exactly do we mean by currency in circulation?
It is the total value of physical banknotes and coins held by the public and businesses, whether spent or simply held. In India, cash reaches them through four main channels: the RBI's 19 regional offices; bank branches; more than 250,000 ATMs and cash dispensers; and millions of "business correspondents", local agents who provide basic banking services in rural areas and smaller towns.
That is a huge stock of cash by any measure. For context, about 56 billion US dollar bills and 30 billion euro banknotes were in circulation at the end of last year, according to Murmu.
The comparison comes with a caveat: the RBI's count is partly driven by a higher share of lower-value notes, meaning more notes are needed to handle the same value of transactions.
The puzzle is not that Indians still use cash - 94% of transactions were cash-based as recently as 2019, according to new research, external by Anirudh Tagat, Mehmet Ozmen and Pushpa Trivedi. It is that cash is growing even as its share of everyday payments shrinks.
"The cash paradox has been examined globally, and India is a unique and novel case study of the same given the scale of both cash and non-cash payments," Tagat, an economist who studies Indian payment behaviour, told the BBC.
He notes that the phenomenon of cash growing alongside digital payments has been especially prominent since the 2007-08 global financial crisis, with Bank for International Settlements research showing a similar pattern worldwide.
In Tagat's framing, currency still serves three purposes - as a means of payment, a store of value and a hedge against calamity. Apps are replacing only the first. That helps explain why digital payments alone cannot tell the whole story of cash demand.
David Humphrey of Florida State University, who has studied cash use across 14 economies with co-author Tanai Khiaonarong, says digital payment adoption is just one of several factors that can influence how much cash people hold.
That raises another question: are households holding more cash outside the banking system - for emergencies, safekeeping or to buy assets such as gold in India?
He also points to a factor that is especially important for major reserve currencies: a lot of the growth comes from notes held or used abroad, rather than in the country that issued them.
The US is a case in point: large-denomination $50 and $100 notes are widely held and used overseas but are "rarely seen in normal domestic legal cash transactions", Humphrey says.
He add that the Federal Reserve regularly receives unfit US currency from abroad, replaces it with fit notes and returns them to the sender. Most of the value of these unfit notes is in $50 and $100 bills.
This helps explain, he says, why the Fed reports that the total value of US currency in circulation continues to rise even as the value of cash withdrawn from domestic ATMs - a proxy for everyday spending, mostly in $20 notes, along with $5 and $10 bills - has recently fallen.
Then there is the less visible side of the cash economy. Humphrey's research identifies the rising value of domestic illegal activity, which often relies on unrecorded cash transactions, as one structural reason currency growth can outpace recorded spending - a factor particularly relevant to India.
Property deals in India routinely involve cash payments, partly because stamp duty and government-set "circle rates" can lag market prices, giving buyers and sellers an incentive to under-declare the transaction and settle the difference in cash.
Demonetisation, which overnight invalidated 86% of the country's cash by value in 2016, attacked the stock of "black" cash but left this flow largely untouched, say economists. That helps explain why decades of estimates of "black money" sunk into real estate have never produced a reliable figure.
Then there is what might be called the psychology of frictionlessness. Tagat points to research, including work published recently in the Journal of Consumer Research, showing digital payments are increasingly engineered to strip out the "pain" of paying - the wince of handing over notes - and replace it with a satisfying beep.
That should, in theory, hollow out cash demand further. That it has not suggests something else is propping currency up: fear - not just the fear of spending, but the fear of what happens when digital systems fail.
Here the Indian story rhymes with Europe's.
The European Central Bank (ECB) has watched euro banknotes in circulation rise from about €1 trillion in 2016 to €1.6 trillion, external this year, even as cash's share of point-of-sale transactions has fallen towards half.
Philip Lane, the ECB's chief economist, told a summer conference in Ireland this year that while the number of notes used in transactions is falling, the stock held by households keeps growing - something identical to what Murmu alluded to in Jakarta.
Olive McCarthy, a professor at University College Cork, traces this to the ECB's own 2021 research, external on what it dubbed the "paradox of banknotes", driven by households hoarding cash as savings and by demand for euros outside the currency zone itself.
Governments in Austria, Finland, external, Germany, external, Sweden, external and the Netherlands, external have responded by formally advising citizens to keep a minimum amount of cash at home, insurance against blackouts, cyberattacks or war. Clearly, cash, in rich democracies as much as in India, is being repositioned as critical infrastructure for bad days rather than good ones.
McCarthy lists who depends on it most bluntly: the elderly, the rural poor, domestic-violence victims hiding transactions from an abuser, and children learning what money is. "Some consumers," she told me, "prefer the privacy and convenience of cash."
For India's RBI, this creates an awkward budgeting problem.
It runs its own paper mills, four currency printing presses and ink plants - an entire supply chain built for self-reliance - while promoting the world's most successful instant-payments network.
Tagat says this creates a difficult choice for the RBI: how much to invest in managing cash and how much in promoting digital payments, especially as trials of 10 and 20 rupee polymer notes - first proposed a decade ago - finally get under way. (Polymer notes are more durable than paper ones, potentially reducing the cost and frequency of replacing worn-out cash.)
Murmu framed reliable cash as part of "monetary sovereignty". Tagat says the rupee's informal use across South Asia gives India another reason to keep its currency machinery running, as a shock-absorber for the whole region.
"The RBI," Tagat says, "has a strong case for keeping cash going despite new digital payments alternatives."
If UPI, as reported, starts attracting transaction charges on smaller payments, cash may claw back share even in the payments column, not just the savings one, he adds.
The lesson for policymakers is clear, and mildly humbling: digital payments have not made cash obsolete. Cash is less a technology being replaced than an insurance policy nobody wants to give up.

'No doubt' that climate change played role in Nepal-Tibet flood, study finds
- Published
A study has found that climate change had contributed to the glacier collapse that unleashed devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border.
More than 1,400 people were killed and thousands are missing following the deluge on 26 August.
There was "absolutely no doubt that human-induced climate change played a role here in the preconditioning of the disaster", said Friederike Otto, a climatologist at Imperial College London and one of the study's authors.
The World Weather Attribution study, published on Thursday, said the disaster was the result of a "compound event" caused by rising temperatures, thinning glaciers, thawing permafrost and pre-existing geological weaknesses.
Massive floods and landslides swept through border towns and villages in Nepal and Tibet, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead or missing.
Scientists had previously said that the floods were caused by the collapse of a glacier slope near the peak of Langtang Lirung, a mountain on Nepal's side of the Himalayas.
The large chunk of glacier hit the bottom of a valley with such force that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, according to United States Geological Survey (USGS) data.
The World Weather Attribution study said climate change was a "destabilising factor acting on a pre-existing geological predisposition", but it was not the only cause of the disaster.
According to the study, July and August temperatures in the area were around 1.5C (34.7F) warmer "due to human influence on the climate".
Meanwhile, glaciers in the region had also been thinning by about half a metre (1.6ft) a year, which could weaken existing fractures and increase instability.
Heavy snowfall last October and November also added to a large amount of meltwater early this year.
This combination of activities "may have interacted to amplify the compound event," the study said.
A magnitude 7.8 earthquake that struck the area in 2015 and triggered a rock-ice avalanche, could have also weakened the underlying rock mass, according to the study.
However, authorities said they could not confirm that earthquake's exact impact on the glacier collapse last month.
Another co-author of the report, Utrecht University mountain hydrologist Walter Immerzeel, told reporters that the area was a "geologically vulnerable slope".
Immerzeel said it was "potentially weakened by the 2015 earthquake" and "destabilised further" by glacier and permafrost retreat.
In the wake of the disaster, Nepali authorities have called for global efforts to tackle climate change, saying the country is one of the lowest contributors to greenhouse emissions yet one of the most vulnerable places to the effects of global warming.
In his first foreign trip as Nepali Prime Minister, Balendra Shah is set to appear at United Nations General Assembly in New York next week to talk about the recent disaster and climate justice.

Assam detains 27 Bangladeshi nationals in joint operation with railway police
Assam Police and GRP detained 27 Bangladeshi nationals in Guwahati and Rangia. Officials have begun the process to send them back to Bangladesh.
Assam Police, in a joint operation with the Government Railway Police (GRP), detained 27 Bangladeshi nationals who had allegedly entered the state illegally, from Guwahati and Rangia on Wednesday, officials said on Thursday.
The process to send them back to Bangladesh has begun, they added.
Police said the Bangladeshi nationals included men, women and minors. Initial investigations suggest they came from several districts of Bangladesh, including Dhaka, Sunamganj, Gopalganj, Bagherhat, Khulna and Mymensingh.
“They are citizens of Bangladesh and were travelling without valid documents, so we detained them. Now we’ll examine how they entered Assam and where they were trying to go,” a senior police officer said.
Deputy commissioner of police (border) for Guwahati Kulendra Nath Deka said on Thursday that 12 of them were detained at the Assam State Transport Corporation (ASTC) campus in Guwahati’s Paltan Bazar area on Wednesday.
He said that during questioning, the 12 detainees told police that another group of 15 people was travelling on the Jammu Tawi Express, and border police immediately alerted the GRP.
“We immediately informed the GRP at Rangia but the train had left the station by that time. The GRP identified and detained them on the moving train and they were handed over to us at Bongaigaon Railway Station,” he said.
The detained individuals told police they had entered India through a secret route in Meghalaya and that a racket had helped them do so in exchange for money, officials said.
Deka said the border department had started the process of sending the detainees back to Bangladesh and had placed a request before the concerned deputy commissioner for an expulsion order.
The Assam government follows the Immigrants (Expulsion from Assam) Act, 1950, to deport suspected illegal migrants.
In September last year, the Assam Cabinet approved an SOP under the 1950 Act, empowering district commissioners (DCs) to issue an expulsion order to any person who, in the view of the DC, is a foreigner.

Deaths of eight women in South Africa spark fears of serial killer – what we know
South African police have discovered the bodies of eight women in the Kempton Park area, east of Johannesburg, over the past two months
The bodies of eight women have been discovered by South African police in the Kempton Park area, east of Johannesburg, in the last two months.
The discoveries have sent shock waves around the country, sparked a high-level investigation and highlighted the scourge of femicide and high levels of violent crime.
Here's what to know about the murders and the police investigation.
Police looking into whether a serial killer was responsible
The Gauteng provincial commissioner Fred Kekana said police are examining whether the cases are linked, but warned against prematurely describing the deaths as the work of one perpetrator or a serial killer.
“Investigators are considering all possibilities, including the possibility of multiple suspects or separate perpetrators,” he said. “Police are comparing the evidence, timelines, locations, victim profiles and circumstances of each case before reaching conclusions.”
However, he pointed out that the similarities and proximity of the locations where they were found was concerning.
Some of the bodies discovered more recently were in Olifantsfontein and Kwa-Thema areas, respectively about 25 kilometers (15 miles) and 34 kilometers (21 miles) from Kempton Park, where the first five bodies were discovered.
“While investigations are still underway and SAPS has not, at this stage, confirmed that the deaths are linked to a serial killer, the similarities are sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning and intensify investigations,” said Kekana.
The victims were all young women
By Wednesday, police said there were a total of eight victims. All were women between the ages of 20 and 38, and all were found either naked or partially clothed with bruises on their bodies, according to the police.
The first body was discovered on 17 July, naked and restrained with cable ties. A suspect believed to have been the victim's boyfriend was arrested and remains in custody, according to the police.
One of the victims was identified as 38-year-old runner Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who went missing last week.
She was reported missing after her 8-year-old daughter alerted family members that she had not returned from her daily afternoon jog, and was found dead several days later.
The body that was recovered in Olifantsfontein on Tuesday was found naked and in an advanced stage of decomposition.
The youngest victim has been identified as a 20-year-old woman.
High rates of femicide and violent crime
The recent deaths have highlighted high rates of femicide and violent crime in the country and sparked an outcry over the safety of women.
Between April and July this year, the country recorded 5,427 murders, which is an average of about 45 murders per day, according to the latest crime statistics.
Femicide rates in South Africa are among the highest in the world, according to the United Nations' agency for gender equality.
A study in 2022 by a South African think tank found that more than 35% of South African adult women had experienced physical or sexual violence at some point.
Police have offered a cash reward for any information to related to the murders.

Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last year, prompting many communities to set up self-defence units, according to the latest annual death toll by the independent watchdog Global Witness.
Organised crime groups or professional killers were implicated in more than a third of the 124 killings of defenders in 2025 as narco-trafficking activities overlapped with intrusions into indigenous territories and environmental crime, such as illegal logging and wildcat gold mining.
This was particularly true in Latin America, which accounted for 85% of last year’s deaths of people trying to protect forests, rivers and other ecosystems.
Colombia had the highest toll with 39 killings, followed by Brazil with 26 and Honduras with 12. In Asia, the most dangerous country for defenders was the Philippines, with 12 killings – many during crackdowns by state security forces.
Since Global Witness began compiling statistics in 2012, the overall global tally is now 2,375 deaths and disappearances – on a par with a small-scale war.
On a more positive note, the headline figure has declined over the last two years, from 196 in 2023 and 142 in 2024, though the report authors say this is likely to be an underestimate because data collection is difficult in war zones and authoritarian regimes.
Many countries and companies are also carrying out nonlethal attacks on defenders, including criminalisation and online smear campaigns.
Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community, partly as a result of cuts by the Trump administration. “The dismantling of USAID, which previously supported initiatives for Indigenous peoples to steward their own land, has had particularly serious implications for defenders,” the report says.
Almost three-quarters of the killings documented in 2025 were of Indigenous people and small-scale farmers targeted for defending their land. With less outside help, an increasing number of these communities are establishing their own territorial defence mechanisms.
The report highlights the example of the Kakataibo Indigenous Guard in the Peruvian Amazon. Six of the community’s leaders have been killed since 2020 amid growing incursions into the forest by criminal groups. Starting in 2022 with a few dozen recruits, the guard now has more than 150 volunteers in its 10 bases.
Segundo Ispón, the commander of the organisation, said the self-defence groups provided a global benefit: “Defending our territory is important to us as a community and as a people, and we’re proud to support the climate that we all depend on. In our culture, the work of defending our resources and territory is taught from an early age. But for this next generation coming up, the work is more dangerous than ever.”
At least a dozen other communities in Peru have organised self-defence units. Similar bodies have existed for some years in Colombia and Brazil. But it is risky. Last year, seven Indigenous guards were murdered. In at least five of these cases, the killings were linked to organised crime.
Many forest communities report the narco-threat is growing closer. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes, apparently in search of assassination targets.
In the Ucayali basin on the other side of the border, Global Witness said there was a 600% increase in coca production between 2019 and 2023. This is pushing gangs to expand smuggling networks, including through the opening of illegal roads and trails through the forest. Corruption further adds to the risks facing forest protectors who stand in their way because many local politicians and police are in the pay of the traffickers.
Forest communities want help from governments to ease these pressures but there are concerns the opposite may be happening. Under US leadership, many rightwing governments are pursuing military crackdowns on coca growers and drug traffickers, which is pushing narco-gangs further into remote regions and indigenous territories.
Ricardo Soberón, a former head of Peru’s anti-narcotics office, said many communities were also affected on the border of Peru and Colombia. “We are in a situation where transnational criminal groups have appropriated the daily life of the Huitoto, Quichua, Bora, Secoya Indigenous people, who live along the Putumayo basin,” he said.
Of particular concern, he added, were the threats against local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists who call for a more effective state presence. He fears the newly elected rightwing governments in affected countries will make matters worse by militarising the conflict in line with the “America shield” priorities of the Trump administration.
Global Witness has urged the authorities to respect and work with nature and land defenders rather than making their role more difficult.
Toby Hill, the lead author of the report, said: “Defenders are the world’s eyes and ears on the ground. It’s thanks to them that we know when ecosystems are being destroyed, where forests are being cleared or rivers polluted. We can’t forget the thousands of defenders around the world who are working every day to protect their territories and cultures under increasing pressure.”

'Built differently' - Hodgkinson reveals hamstring abnormality

Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson says an MRI scan has uncovered an "abnormality" in her hamstring.
Following a suspected tear last year, Hodgkinson had a scan which revealed she has a "split" hamstring, giving her two tendons instead of one.
The 24-year-old is still learning how to manage the anomaly, which allows her to continue running when one of the tendons is torn but may also make her more susceptible to breakdowns.
Following her second-place finish to Swiss Audrey Werro in the 800m final at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest in September, Hodgkinson announced she had sustained another hamstring tear at the European Championships in Birmingham a few weeks earlier.
"My body is quite literally built differently," said Hodgkinson. "Where most people have one tendon, mine is split - I have two - and we're trying to figure out if it's a strength or a weakness.
"So when one of them tore, I still had another one because it's split. In Birmingham, it didn't affect me during the race, but I could feel something wasn't quite right.
"It's a weird one. You can still run on them. I haven't missed any training the last three weeks. But I've just had to alter my approach. I've had to take my foot off the speed [training], because that's when it's most risky."

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”

Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.

The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.

A recommendation from someone with great taste
Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”

Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).
It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.
It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

Trump withdraws Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, as his nominee to lead ICE
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House said Thursday that it was withdrawing its nomination of Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, to lead U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, ensuring that an agency at the forefront of President Donald Trump's domestic agenda will remain without a Senate-confirmed leader for at least a while longer.
Schroyer, who has little experience in immigration, is close to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former U.S. senator from Oklahoma.
The White House offered no comment in a brief statement.
The latest setback comes as the agency remains under withering scrutiny over its handling of enforcement operations. Critics have question how ICE has recruited and trained officers as it raced to hire thousands to carry out Trump's promise of mass deportations. Officers have shot and killed multiple people, including two American citizens in Minneapolis earlier this year.
Sen. Rand Paul, the chairman of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, had refused to hold a hearing on the nominee until DHS provided him with information he had been seeking about civilian deaths during ICE enforcement operations.
"I don't have a concern with who the nominee was. I had asked them to give me an update on the internal investigation into civilian deaths," Paul, R-Ky., told The Associated Press.
"And I'm still waiting."
When Mullin took over DHS in March, he pledged a lower-profile approach to immigration enforcement, pulling back on the aggressive, tumultuous crackdown on the streets of large cities that sparked widespread public condemnation.
Arrests have continued to accelerate, reaching nearly 51,000 in August, the highest single monthly arrest total during the second Trump administration.
Paul said he intended to hold a hearing on Schroyer's nomination but it never came to that. He only heard about the nomination being withdrawn when the White House made it public Thursday.
ICE has not had a Senate-confirmed leader since the Obama administration. David Venturella, a former executive at a private prison operator, returned to the agency as acting director earlier this year after Todd Lyons resigned.
When Trump nominated Schroyer in June, Trump said on his Truth Social platform that his pick was "a PATRIOT with real operational experience" and a "proven leader with DECADES of experience locking up the worst of the worst."
The administration did not indicate when it might announce another pick for the position.
