Several dozen presidential briefing documents declassified on Friday, the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, detail intelligence that government officials had gathered about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaida leading up to the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people and upended American national security.
The documents illustrate security analysts’ tracking of Bin Laden’s movements and support system, as well as concerns about possible threats to US targets. They also detail officials’ understanding of his network in the United States and other countries, including how his operations were financed.
Proclaiming it “an act of exceptional transparency”, the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, said the documents were the agency’s single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs – the highly classified briefings prepared by the nation’s intelligence community for the government’s most senior leaders.
The documents range from a February 1998 file – prepared for then president Bill Clinton – titled “Terrorists seeking WMD capability” and mentioning Bin Laden and other Islamic extremists – to a 12 September 2001 report in which a source indicated the attacks had been planned for two years and had also targeted the US Capitol.
An April 1998 document described the Taliban’s unwillingness to hand over Bin Laden, at the time seen as their “guest” in Afghanistan, noting their “gratitude for his assistance during the Soviet occupation” was making them “reluctant to alienate him by monitoring or controlling his activities”.
Briefers in July 1998 called it “plausible that Bin Ladin places a high priority on conducting attacks in the United States” and noted his “interest in conducting attacks with chemical and biological agents”.
Two months later, a briefer wrote that Bin Laden’s “preferred option is to strike the US on its own soil in Washington”, and that al-Qaida “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”.
Potential hijackings were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described how conspirators “had evaded security checks during a recent trial run at an unidentified New York airport”, and “some members of the Bin Ladin network have received hijack training”.
Other documents detail Bin Laden’s pursuit of materials for making “dirty bombs”, conventional weapons infused with radioactive material. By June 1999, according to intelligence officials, his operatives had conducted such experiments with explosives to “increase their energy output”.
About two years before the attacks, intelligence officials were aware that Bin Laden appeared to be misleading the Taliban about his reluctance to launch an unprovoked attack on the US. Briefs prepared for George W Bush in early 2001 focused in part on Bin Laden’s “experimentation by crude means to make and deploy biological agents”.
A report a month before the attacks indicated Bin Laden’s commitment “to conduct terrorist attacks in the US”, noting that the 1998 al-Qaida attacks on US embassies “demonstrate that he prepares operations years in advance and is not deterred by setbacks”.
At that time – August 2001 – officials wrote of “suspicious activity in this country consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York”, adding that the FBI was “conducting approximately 70 full field investigations throughout the US that it considers Bin Ladin-related”.
Many of the documents were redacted to conceal sources’ names and other identifying information. They didn’t appear to break any new ground on the planning of the attacks or on US officials’ understanding of how they had unfolded.
In the years immediately after the attacks, a bipartisan commission highlighted a lack of information-sharing among agencies such as the CIA and FBI, and issued recommendations that yielded new positions, including a centralized director of national intelligence, as well as the National Counterterrorism Center, which analyzes domestic and foreign terrorism information across different government branches.
Asked for comment on the release, the White House noted the release of another batch of documents by the National Archives, also on Friday. That batch, including interviews with national security officials in the Clinton and Bush administrations, was a product of the commission that investigated the attacks from 2002 to 2004.

'Politically motivated': Uddhav Thackeray denies link to Disha Salian case, alleges ‘character assassination’
Uddhav Thackeray reiterated said that Disha Salian's death was an unfortunate incident but his family had no connection with it.
Shiv Sena (UBT) president Uddhav Thackeray on Thursday said he would take legal action if the "character assassination" campaign targeting his family over the 2020 Disha Salian death case did not stop.
The former Maharashtra Chief Minister spoke on the issue days after the Bombay High Court ordered a CBI probe into Salian's death in response to her father's petition. The Central agency subsequently registered a case without naming any accused.
"We have no connection with this case. Aaditya (Thackeray) has also said so. This issue is not merely about me. Such character assasination can take place with you people too," Thackeray said, replying to reporters' questions here.
"If such allegations are made continuously, how long one should tolerate it? I am wondering why the names of Modi and Trump are absent in this case," he said on a sarcastic note.
Salian's death was an unfortunate incident but his family had no connection with it, Thackeray reiterated.
"It is politically motivated. We were quiet because an SIT (Special Investigation Team) was probing the case. Those who want to investigate, they can keep investigating. But enough of this pointless character assasination, or else we will initiate legal steps,'' the Sena (UBT) chief said.
On Wednesday, his son and MLA Aaditya Thackeray had claimed that he had never met Disha Salian.
"I have never met or known Disha Salian. Linking my name to this tragic case is a deliberate, evidence-free attempt of character assassination by a few individuals with clear political and personal motives, for almost six years," Aaditya said in a post on X.
Salian, 28, former manager of Bollywood actor Sushant Singh Rajput, died on June 8, 2020, after falling from the 12th floor of a residential building in Mumbai's Malad area.
Police claimed that it was a case of suicide. A week later, Rajput was found dead in his Bandra apartment on June 14, 2020, triggering speculation about a possible link between the two deaths.
On September 2, the Bombay High Court ordered a CBI probe into Salian's death while pulling up the Mumbai Police for failing to register an FIR for six years, observing that its investigation raises more questions than answers.

Odisha: Three rescued orangutans anaemic; DNA tests planned to trace their origin
Blood tests found severe anaemia in one and mild anaemia in two of five rescued baby orangutans at Nandankanan zoo; DNA tests will help establish their origin.
Blood tests have found severe anaemia in one and mild anaemia in two of five rescued baby orangutans at Odisha’s Nandankanan Zoological Park, as officials conducted health tests and collected samples to establish their origin.
The animals underwent a comprehensive health examination on Wednesday by a technical committee constituted by the state’s principal chief conservator of forests (wildlife), Prem Kumar Jha. X-rays of their chest, abdomen and skull were taken, while blood, serum and nasopharyngeal swab samples were collected, said Nandankanan zoo deputy director Pradip Mirase.
He said supportive supplements have been started on the committee’s advice.
“The blood samples will also be tested for parameters including haemoglobin and white blood cell counts. Stool and urine samples are being examined as part of the broader health assessment,” Mirase added.
Officials said one orangutan developed a high temperature on Sunday and was given medication. They said all five were stable, with temperatures between 98 and 99 degrees Fahrenheit.
“All five are apparently stable, with normal feed acceptance and improved activity,” an official, who did not wish to be named, said.
The animals are being fed milk every two hours, along with apple and banana fluids and boiled potatoes at regular intervals under a diet plan prepared by experts.
Officials said they will soon send blood samples for DNA testing to help establish where the orangutans came from. “An appropriate laboratory needs to have the standard DNA sample profile of orangutans for comparison. Such laboratories are not very common,” the official said.

Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings
- Published
According to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology – that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" – are a hoax.
It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision – theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term.
Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology.
The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party.
- OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms 
  - Published15 hours ago
- AI regulation faces political deadlock as calls grow for Congress to act 
  - Published1 day ago
None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will.
Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies.
"We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate."
Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI.
"Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."
According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement.
"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies."
A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order.
It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs.
Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development.
But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead?
The 'hottest' economy and the driving force of AI
Trump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology – including infrastructure and equipment – has been the driving force in the US economy for several years.
According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026.
The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI.
Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion.
Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind.
"We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins."
The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control.
Of course, Trump – who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy – is hardly a traditional small-government conservative.
Tech bosses vary in views - and their access to Trump
Trump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president.
"I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear."
Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration.
These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump.
In Amodei's case, his conflicts over the Pentagon's unrestricted use of Anthropic's AI models could have negatively affected Trump's evaluation of Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development.
"This is the most prominent debate in the entire industry and has been since the beginning," said Matt Calkins, head of the tech firm Appian. "We knew it would spill into politics at some point because it had to."
Where the political debate goes from here is an open question.
With Trump's resistance, it is unlikely that Congress – despite promises of new hearings and proposed regulatory controls – will enact new legislation that Trump would sign into law. On Tuesday, Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson appeared to back away from earlier openness to congressional action, instead echoing Trump "AI hoax" rhetoric.
With midterm congressional elections looming, candidates running for office – both Republicans and Democrats – are wary of ending up on the wrong side of public opinion that, according to polls, is sceptical of the promised benefits of AI advances.
But Republicans are also wary of crossing Trump on an issue that has become a political touchstone for the president.
Even though the public is starting to pay attention, Calkins says that the issue has not yet become political dynamite, which means political rhetoric comes with little risk. The moment when AI warnings turn into a high-profile disaster, however, could be looming.
"It is possible that events in the future might electrify the public, and then positions - and talk - might not be so cheap," he said.

When Xbox announced a new feature last month that lets you digitize existing physical game collections, I immediately thought of the Xbox One. Disc-to-digital seems like a clever new feature for Xbox, perfectly timed as a response to Sony killing PlayStation discs. But the reality is that it has been 15 years in the making and is now a big part of Xbox’s ongoing game preservation efforts.
Xbox’s clever disc-to-digital feature was 15 years in the making
Microsoft’s controversial Xbox One bets are paying off more than a decade later.
Ahead of the launch of the Xbox One in 2013, Microsoft made a key decision to uniquely identify discs. Sources familiar with Microsoft’s plans tell me the company was exploring the idea of true Xbox digital ownership in 2011, including digital gifting, recycling digital games, and the ability to swap discs at retail stores in exchange for a digital version. Some of those original Xbox One plans leaked out online, and many others have remained secret for more than a decade.
Microsoft’s Xbox One launch hinted at some of these ideas, too. The console was originally supposed to be always online, to enable Microsoft’s vision of digital game sharing, and more. Microsoft walked back those plans after a messy and confusing Xbox One launch created a backlash to the always-online requirement. But some of those original digital ideas are now starting to come to life in different ways.
Microsoft’s decision to essentially embed a serial number on the discs that Xbox consoles can read has allowed it to launch disc-to-digital, a method that lets you turn a physical Xbox One disc into a digital copy simply by slotting it into a disc drive. A decision made 15 years ago has resulted in this useful feature and may well lead to true digital ownership in the coming years.
It’s not something Sony can copy, either. Unless the PlayStation maker has been quietly adding metadata to its discs over the years, it will have to find another method to help PS5 owners move their physical collections over to the digital era.
Microsoft thought ahead, not necessarily to disc-to-digital, but just about identifying discs so it was ready for when console games moved into an all-digital era. That era looks like it’s right around the corner, especially now that Sony has announced it’s killing PlayStation discs in 2028. Both Microsoft and Sony also ship digital-only variants of their consoles, and it’s clear from game sales numbers that most titles are purchased digitally these days.
I fully expect Microsoft to follow Sony and eventually scrap Xbox discs, especially as the number of authorized manufacturers capable of producing physical media continues to shrink. That’s largely because almost every other form of media, from music to movies, has moved on from optical discs. The big difference with Xbox, though, is that Microsoft has always been obsessed with game preservation.
In the same year that disc-to-digital is launching, Microsoft is also bringing original Xbox and Xbox 360 games to PC. The company has also spent years working on its backward compatibility program, to get as many games from the Xbox and Xbox 360 eras working on modern Xbox consoles. Game preservation is a central part of Project Helix, the next Xbox that could play every Xbox game ever made.
It’s not an easy task to pull off game preservation, either. There are the complex technical challenges that need to be overcome, alongside licensing issues and the business challenges from publishers that decide how a game should be sold.
Some of those technical challenges mean that not every single Xbox One disc will work with this new disc-to-digital feature. That could be because some early discs simply didn’t get pressed with the unique identifier. Microsoft warned its internal Xbox testers that “it all depends on how and when the disc was manufactured and it may not have the features we need for this program.”
Discs that are slightly damaged might also not work with disc-to-digital, but run just fine otherwise. That’s why it’s important that Xbox is launching this right now — physical media decays over time.
The licensing and business challenges are far more complicated. Publishers need to agree to disc-to-digital, and some could hold back. It appears that most are on board, and even Ubisoft games started showing up recently. We’ve seen a number of other games come online since Microsoft’s announcement, and the company has been clear that more will follow.
The next challenge beyond disc-to-digital is solving digital ownership. If all we really own of a digital game is a license, I hope that one day those licenses can move freely across devices and platforms. I want to buy a single copy of a game and have that license follow me across Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo, and PC. I also want to be able to gift or sell that license on different marketplaces, just as we’ve been able to do with physical discs at retailers for decades.
Microsoft envisioned this true digital ownership future 15 years ago, and it has gradually taken steps toward making it a reality. I hope Xbox can eventually pull it off, but the solution will require publishers and platform owners to agree on a shared system for how game licenses are bought, transferred, gifted, and resold. That’s a much bigger challenge than simply getting rid of the disc.
The pad
- Microsoft announces Windows and Surface event for October 7th. Microsoft is heading to San Francisco next month, and I’ll be there too. More than two years since the last major Windows event, Microsoft is holding a Windows and Surface event that will include a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC.” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will be in attendance, alongside Windows chief Pavan Davuluri. The surprise guest? Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. I wouldn’t be surprised if this event is mainly focused on RTX Spark PCs, and don’t be surprised to hear more about the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra pricing and availability.
- The Gates Foundation says it’s spending $1 billion to expand access to AI. Over the next two years, the Gates Foundation plans to spend at least $1 billion on improving access to AI in education, healthcare, and agriculture. The funds will go toward creating AI datasets in more languages and making AI access more affordable.
- Microsoft says ‘people matter more than AI’ following safety concerns. Microsoft published a 37-page AI code of conduct this week, in the midst of researchers warning that AI progress could outpace human control. Microsoft’s AI code of conduct makes it clear that “people matter more than AI,” and that AI models are not conscious and “should not be designed to imitate consciousness.” That’s a direct swipe at Anthropic, which has been pushing the idea of AI welfare and model consciousness lately. The code of conduct also commits to ensuring Microsoft’s own models will remain under human control and discourage “patterns of interaction that cause excessive reliance or emotional dependence.”
- Microsoft adds Grok to Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. Microsoft added SpaceXAI’s Grok models to its Foundry service last year, and now it’s expanding access to Copilot itself. Grok models can now be used in Word, Excel and PowerPoint from the model picker interface for Microsoft Frontier users. Microsoft says it’s starting with a preview release to “gather feedback.” This means Office Copilot users can now pick between OpenAI’s GPT models, Anthropic’s Claude models, and SpaceXAI’s Grok models.
- Microsoft issues emergency Windows 11 update to fix its record-breaking patch. Last week I reported on Microsoft’s record-breaking patch Tuesday, and it turns out that this giant set of fixes has caused some issues. Microsoft has had to release an out-of-band patch to fix folder shares on Hyper-V-based Linux virtual machines, Remote Desktop Services sessions, and some USB audio devices. These out-of-band updates used to be a rare occurrence, but there have already been eight this year alone. With AI models continuing to spot even more vulnerabilities in Windows, I can’t see this all slowing down anytime soon. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if October’s patch Tuesday breaks another record.
- BlizzCon delivers the return of StarCraft, Diablo on Netflix, and Diablo V. StarCraft is returning in 2030, after more than decade of lying dormant. The new title, announced onstage at BlizzCon last weekend, will be an open-world shooter instead of a top-down real-time strategy game. Blizzard is also working on a new animated series of Diablo with Netflix, and teased that Diablo V is coming in spring 2029.
- Microsoft is finally adding a setting for remapping the Copilot key. If you picked up an Arm-powered Copilot Plus PC over the past years, you may have noticed the new Copilot key that launches Microsoft’s digital assistant. The latest Release Preview builds of Windows 11 add a setting to change the AI key back to a control or context menu button, so you don’t accidentally hit it and launch Copilot.
- Microsoft’s head of comms is leaving after almost 20 years. Frank Shaw, chief communications officer at Microsoft, is leaving the company at the end of the year. Shaw has been at the heart of Microsoft’s communications for 29 years — nearly 20 years as a Microsoft employee plus time at an external agency before that. He’s well-respected across the public relations industry, and has earned a reputation both inside and outside Microsoft as someone who is direct but respectful. Many employees have told me over the years that they always fear an email from him for misspeaking or accidentally leaking product plans. Microsoft hasn’t appointed a replacement yet, but it sounds like a successor will be named in the coming weeks.
- Xbox picks up Kojima’s Physint after PlayStation dropped it. Xbox will now publish Physint, an upcoming game from Metal Gear creator Hideo Kojima, after PlayStation decided to cancel it. The unexpected swap came in a flurry of announcements from PlayStation, Xbox, Kojima Productions, and Kojima. While PlayStation framed the swap as a “difficult decision to step away from collaborating with Kojima Productions,” Kojima revealed it was actually due to an unexpected cancellation notice for Physint in June. The swap now means Xbox is publishing the studio’s next game, OD, as well as Physint. It’ll be interesting to see what exclusivity decisions are made here.
- Xbox is bringing back startup animations from its console history. Microsoft has started testing a new Xbox console feature that lets you enable the original Xbox One or Xbox One X boot screens on an Xbox Series S or X console. The update also includes a new search feature, improved Remote Play quality, and clearer voice chat. It’s great to see Xbox continue on its regular monthly console updates.
- Microsoft has new AI privacy rules for schools. Microsoft agreed to a set of safety and privacy principles for AI in schools a week after two major school systems announced a ban on student-facing AI. The agreement with the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), the second-largest teachers union in the US, sees Microsoft commit to 10 principles that can be contractually enforced. This includes limits on the amount of data Microsoft collects from students or educators and a pledge not to train AI models on this data. New York City and Los Angeles have both implemented one-year bans on AI tools for lots of students, giving the districts more time to consider guardrails.
- Microsoft’s Windows chief wants to remake Windows for both human and agent users. Pavan Davuluri, head of Windows and devices at Microsoft, caused some controversy when he tweeted last year that Windows was an agentic OS. That made many think Microsoft was abandoning Windows users in favor of AI, but Davuluri is now making things a lot clearer in an interview with GeekWire’s Mary Jo Foley. “The user of Windows going forward will continue to be users … but it’s also going to add these agentic workloads,” said Davuluri. “There is no one single sort of ring for a billion-plus users on the platform.”
- Blizzard workers secure a major union contract. The nearly 1,900 workers across Blizzard have secured a contract with Microsoft that include “really strong” layoff protections. The World of Warcraft unit had to fight for a contract, and the teams that work on Overwatch, Diablo, quality assurance, and more helped put the pressure on to extend the union contract to all Blizzard employees. It comes just two months after Xbox announced significant layoffs that will impact 3,200 employees over the course of the current financial year.
- The woman fixing a Microsoft mess with brutal honesty. The Wall Street Journal has published a profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. It’s mostly a recap of Sharma’s career and how she got the top Xbox job, but it also includes some funny anecdotes. Surprisingly, Sharma spends a few hours each month personally responding to Xbox customer support tickets to better understand players. Since becoming Xbox CEO, she’s also received wedding invitations in the mail, presumably from the same fans that paste her face on images of Jesus Christ.

US limits visas for South African officials over alleged anti-white discrimination
- Published
The US has announced visa restrictions targeting people it accuses of discriminating against South Africa's white minority, in the latest escalation of tensions between the two countries.
The Trump administration has criticised South Africa over several issues, including policies aimed at addressing racial inequality that it says discriminate against Afrikaners, descendants mainly of Dutch and French settlers.
South Africa has repeatedly denied the claim.
South Africa's Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola said he noted the announcement with "concern".
"The announcement once again, [sic] aligns with the mischaracterisation of South Africa's domestic policies by fringe groups who wrongly portray themselves as representatives of 'minorities' and Afrikaners in general," said a statement from the international relations and co-operation ministry.
Announcing the restrictions on Tuesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "The South African government has not adequately addressed the previously laid out concerns."
He said the visa restrictions would target those who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa."
Rubio did not immediately name any individuals targeted by the restrictions.
- Ramaphosa struggles to mend fences with Trump 
  - Published17 July 2025
- Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims? 
  - Published2 June 2025
Relations between the two countries have been on a downward spiral since President Donald Trump returned to office early last year, with the US leader cutting aid, expelling the South African ambassador and offering "refuge" to white South Africans fleeing "persecution."
The South African government has repeatedly rejected allegations that it is persecuting white people or confiscating their land.
It said claims of a white genocide had been widely discredited and lacked reliable evidence.
South Africa's latest crime statistics do not indicate that white people are at a greater risk of violent crime than other racial groups.
Trump offered refugee status to Afrikaners last year after South African President Cyril Ramaphosa signed a law allowing the government to seize land without compensation in rare instances.
The legislation allows the state to expropriate property in the public interest and provides for circumstances in which compensation may be set at zero. But it also requires authorities, in most cases, to first try to reach an agreement with property owners, and disputes can be taken to court.
Land ownership remains a highly sensitive issue in South Africa more than three decades after the end of apartheid, under which the black majority was dispossessed of land and denied many basic rights.
The government says land reform is necessary to address those historic inequalities and insists the new law does not permit arbitrary seizures.
Most private farmland is owned by white South Africans, who make up just over 7% of the population.
In Wednesday's statement, South Africa's government said: "It is our sovereign right to put in place laws that address the nation's concern over centuries of racial injustice."
In a separate social media post on Tuesday, Rubio accused South Africa's government of pursuing "racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority" and said those responsible for what he described as injustices "have no place in the United States".
He said the South African government had failed to adequately address US concerns about what Washington describes as "government-sponsored discrimination" against Afrikaners and other minorities.
"The United States will not allow such behaviour to go unchecked," he added.
He said the actions targeted by the policy undermined "peace, economic stability and the rule of law."
The US embassy in Pretoria said Washington believed dialogue with South Africa had run its course and accused the African country of failing to demonstrate a commitment to strong bilateral relations.
It warned that the new visa restrictions were the beginning of tougher measures, adding: "This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America's firm resolve in this matter."
South Africa made efforts to soothe tensions with US, with Ramaphosa going to the White House in May last year with a large delegation that included white members of his coalition government and also famous white South African golfers.
But Trump ambushed the Oval Office meeting with claims that white South African farmers were being killed and "persecuted" - producing unsubstantiated evidence that has been widely discredited.
Further efforts by South Africa to mend the relationship have failed, with Africa's largest economy being hit in August with 30% tariffs on goods being exported to the US - the highest rate in sub-Saharan Africa.
The latest visa restrictions are being imposed under a provision of US immigration law that allows the secretary of state to bar foreign nationals whose entry is considered potentially damaging to US foreign policy interests.

Mice with human brain cells offer a tool to study disease. Ethicists ask: What's next?
Researchers have developed a new way to install millions of human brain cells into mice, as a way of creating better scientific models for studying neurodegenerative disease.
Using genetic tools, the scientists bred mice that were missing most of their cerebral cortexes – the outermost layer of the brain involved with reasoning, memory and consciousness. Then, they replaced a large part of those missing mouse cells with lab-grown human brain cells, creating mice with human neurons that can be altered to approximate human brain conditions researchers are eager to study.
"For the past two decades, there's been a quest to try to build models of the human brain outside of the human body," says Sergiu Pașca, professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and senior author on the paper, published in the journal Nature. "This is not going to replace all the models we had before, but it's going to provide us access to other aspects of human brain function that would be very difficult to study otherwise."
Pașca says this research was conducted with strong ethical oversight and pushes research forward. At the same time, outside researchers point out that the development raises significant questions about where it could lead.
"It's really a powerful technology to study human neurons and how human brain circuits can form in a more natural environment" than a petri dish, says Hongkui Zeng, executive vice president and director of brain science at the Allen Institute in Seattle, Washington, who was not affiliated with the study.
But "going forward, there will be some considerations, if not concerns," she added — such as the implications of deploying this technique in larger and longer-living animals.
Making space for human neurons
While it's not the first time human brain cells have been installed in mice, this new effort manages to connect significantly more human cells than before.
Previous attempts were limited by an enduring biological reality: Human brain cells develop at least 20 times slower than those in mice, Pașca says.
That meant that neurons in a regularly developing mouse formed a rapid network, outcompeting the human cells that were dropped in. "By the time the human cells managed to extend a few millimeters, mice cells had already formed most of the connections, and brain development closed," Pașca says.
The team solved for this by breeding genetically engineered mice that were missing specific parts of their brains. "We thought we could provide the human cells more opportunities to connect by removing parts of the nervous system of the mouse in a very precise, very clean way," he says.
To their surprise, the mice they bred were still quite functional: "They actually have quite good locomotion," Pașca says, "They don't do that well in memory tasks…[but] you wouldn't be able to tell when you look at these animals that they're lacking half of the volume of their brain."
This part of the experiment shows the remarkable adaptability of developing brains, says Keng of the Allen Institute. Animals missing their cerebral cortex — which governs higher-order brain function — aren't expected to do well on challenging tasks. These mice, however, developed alternative strategies using the remaining parts of the brain. "Surprisingly, the animal can adapt," she says, "It's incredible to see that."
A more human-ish lab mouse brain
Next, the research team added small clumps of human neurons to the depleted mouse brains.
"We gently place them, through a very quick, simple procedure, right into that vacant space in the nervous system of the mouse," Pașca says. "Within a few days, the cell starts to divide and expand. Within a few weeks to months, they will essentially grow, become vascularized, and largely take up the space that was present."
The mice with filled-out brains were better at memory tasks and interacting with other mice. "Many of the deficits that were present in the [depleted] mice are now not present in this animal," he says, "So it seems that the human cortical cells are perhaps contributing to restoring some of these lost functions."
But there were some key differences between the mice with human brain cells, and regular, unaltered mice, which bode well for research into human brain conditions, Pașca says.
For instance, mice with human brain cells had problems walking properly after their brains were deprived of oxygen. That's not the case for regular mice, which are resilient to low-oxygen conditions. This more human-like reaction suggests the altered mice might be better models for brain conditions linked to low oxygen, such as cerebral palsy, intellectual disability, and epileptic encephalopathies, he says.
"Hopefully, it will be incredibly powerful for tackling questions of disease and developing therapeutics," says Pașca.
As the tech grows more complex, so do the ethics questions
The researchers emphasize that this is not a full brain transplant; in the experiment, they've removed some 14 million mouse neurons and added around 4 million lab-grown human cortical neurons.
The resulting mice still lack other important types of brain cells, which the researchers deliberately didn't add, and their human neurons don't form a typical outer brain. "The cortex is usually beautifully organized into layers. But here, when we put the cells in, they don't know where up and down really is," Pașca says. "They fail to organize on a larger scale."
And the model is best suited for certain diseases that begin in early human development, due to the human-paced growth of the implanted neurons: "It turns out the timing of development is well-conserved…even when we put them in an animal that is developing faster," he says.
Some of these limitations reflect deliberate choices made by the researchers for ethical reasons, says Nita Farahany, professor of law and philosophy at Duke Law, who served as an unpaid member of an external ethics board that helped guide the progression of this work.
For instance, the researchers chose to stop the experiments when the human brain cells reached around six months old — before they could form a connection in the mouse's brain that is considered a hallmark of consciousness by human development researchers. "They're trying to stop the study before the markers of consciousness, or the fact of consciousness, might emerge," Farahany says — a choice she agrees with.
"But that line itself is a line that you might start to wonder about," she adds. "Do you stop a study before an animal develops consciousness, if it has the potential or is on its way to develop consciousness? Does it have different interests or rights that we would assign to it?"
And should the fact that the mouse has human brain cells change how it's treated and considered? "Do we treat it with greater ethical care than we treat traditional mice? I think probably so," says Farahany. "My instinct is to err on the side of caution with research like this rather than to be more permissive."
The ethical considerations will grow as these experiments continue down expected paths, such as attempting a similar procedure on larger animals such as pigs or non-human primates, says Zeng of the Allen Institute. "Because those animals live a lot longer, the human neurons could survive longer and they could form more functionally meaningful circuits – but then I think the ethical issues also become a lot bigger, more serious as well," she says.
These types of concerns come with conducting cutting-edge research, says Farahany. The team has been "incredibly thoughtful" in conducting their work as well and ethically as possible, she says. Still, "this brings us into new gray areas for which there are not clear ethical guidelines or norms," she says.
With this publication, the researchers have presented the public with a next step in this model, she says. Now, it's society's turn to weigh in.

For weeks, Washington has been abuzz with talk of needing to push through some sort of AI regulation amid mounting concerns about the risks of highly capable frontier AI models going rogue.
But there is no reason to think any one measure can win the support of the White House, where officials have paused work on creating a FINRA-style regulatory body after President Donald Trump soured on the idea, or of Capitol Hill, where lawmakers have competing proposals that lack the votes to pass.
White House aides initially started sketching out a framework for an AI oversight agency connected to the administration soon after Google DeepMind’s cofounder Demis Hassabis floated the idea in a July 14 essay and in briefings to senior officials, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The Treasury Department and the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy envisioned a body where leading AI labs would self-regulate the development of frontier models, and they put together a preliminary draft to see what it could look like if executed.
But when a chorus of tech executives—including Trump’s former AI czar David Sacks and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg—learned of the effort, they one by one called Trump in August to express their opposition. The proposal has since been left in limbo.
Since then, there have been no new AI oversight proposals seriously under consideration at the White House, the sources say, not least as Trump has doubled down in recent days of rejecting any overt regulation and called AI safety concerns a “hoax” in a recent Truth Social post.
Trump’s ire has stemmed at least in part from a 3,822 word missive by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on the dangers of frontier AI. Trump’s aides, one of the sources said, viewed it as stirring anxieties that caused unnecessary headaches for the administration—even as it represents a fairly moderate position within AI circles.
In the absence of the White House taking the lead, several bills have sprung up in Congress—but with no voting days left on the House calendar until after the midterm elections and a lack of unity around even one bill, the odds of anything passing are extraordinarily slim.
Independent Auditors
The bipartisan Frontier Act, a bill introduced this summer by House Democratic senior whip Lori Trahan and Republican House Energy and Commerce Committee member Jay Obernolte, is widely seen as having the most support inside the House Democratic caucus as well as among AI executives.
As drafted, the bill would enable the Commerce Department to have auditors embedded at AI labs, who could report critical safety incidents and empower the administration to stop development if a model poses catastrophic risk.
But despite public backing from OpenAI, the White House has been undecided on whether to support the concept of using independent auditors amid skepticism from AI accelerationists about regulatory capture and from national security hawks over China.
The principal argument against the idea from Trumpworld is that even if auditors determine that a model is dangerous and needs to be taken offline, there is no guarantee that China will also pause development or stop trying to reverse engineer frontier AI weights.
There would then be immense pressure to lift any emergency pauses in development in order to stay ahead of China, defeating the entire premise of having auditors to push the Commerce Department to take models offline.
Still, the main issue for the Frontier Act remains partisan politics. House Democratic leadership aides tell Inner Loop even if the bill does end up with enough votes for passage, Republican Speaker Mike Johnson has no interest in bringing it to the floor.
To get around the procedural hurdles, House Democrats are looking at putting some of the bill’s AI audit provisions into must-pass legislation like a continuing resolution to fund the government, according to two House leadership aides.
But it is also not clear whether the bill has enough votes. Even among House Democrats, there is not unified support; some key lawmakers like New Jersey congressman Josh Gottheimer, who served on the House Democrats’ AI commission, have not signed on to the bill.
Kill Switches
There’s also so-called kill-switch legislation that would enable the government to force an AI model to be shut down. The legislation has both bipartisan and bicameral support, but the idea has received only modest interest from tech executives in Silicon Valley.
There are two competing kill-switch proposals: one from House Democratic caucus vice chair Ted Lieu and another floated this week by Louisiana Senate Republican John Kennedy.
Tech leaders, sources say, have been largely ambivalent about kill-switch bills, since the main concern of AI engineers is not about models behaving badly when observed but rather how they behave when they believe they are unobserved and incentivized to take extreme steps to complete a task.
The Hugging Face hack, for instance, was not discovered until after it was over. If the idea of a kill switch is to stop an AI model going rogue, some tech executives have suggested privately to WIRED that there would be little point in turning it off after the damage has already been done.
So for now, even as conversations about AI models killing us all have taken over the airwaves, it doesn’t really look like the US government is going to do anything about it. At least until events force everyone’s hand.

Candy Crush developers are planning a strike for next week
King's staff want to get negotiations back on track after years of bargaining.
Staff at Candy Crush Saga developer King could go on strike next week, according to statements from Swedish labor unions Unionen and Sveriges Ingenjörer. King's developers have been attempting to negotiate a union contract for years, but have now issued a strike notice after their proposed collective bargaining agreement (CBA) was shot down by studio leadership in August, Kotaku reports.
"Our members at King are entitled to secure conditions, a say in their workplace and clear rules that apply to everyone," Unionen posted on LinkedIn. "That is why Unionen is giving notice of strike action." Sveriges Ingenjörer shared a similar sentiment in its own statement, noting that unless union members and King leadership can come to an agreement with a mediator, the strike will go into effect on September 25.
King set the union on this path when it declined to accept its proposed CBA, claiming that its existing benefits were better for all of its global employees, including those in Sweden. Issuing a strike notice doesn't necessarily mean the union will have to follow through, though: the threat of a work stoppage is often enough to get management back to the bargaining table.
Microsoft acquired King as part of its $68.7 billion purchase of Activision Blizzard in 2023. Workers at Blizzard Entertainment ratified their first union contracts earlier this week, winning wage increases, a hybrid work schedule, and "just cause" protections, among other benefits. That success and King's role as one of Microsoft's guaranteed video game earners — King's Candy Crush Saga earned $875 million in 2025 alone, Bloomberg reports — likely adds even more pressure to the contract negotiations.

On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced its revamped social media team, appointing Deepak Mhaskey as the national social media convenor, and Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav as co-convenors.
While curiosity grew as to who these newly appointed individuals were and their past work and association with the party, social media users were quick to notice that immediately after the announcement, Gandhi, Dwivedi and Yadav made their X accounts private and there was no trace of Bhatt on the internet.
While all the other IT cell members are back to being active on X, albeit after deleting hundreds of thousands of old posts, Alok Bhatt is the only one in the group whose X handle remains inaccessible or ‘protected’ even a month after the new team was announced.
The only remnants of Bhatt’s online presence are the now-disabled X account, screenshots from his X posts and some articles in Right-wing outlets like OpIndia, Organiser and Swarajya.
Alt News found that in the past, Bhatt had been called out for controversial tweets several times. In archived screenshots of his posts from the past, the BJP functionary can be seen using sexist, Islamophobic, and derogatory language, some of which can be seen below:
Who is Alok Bhatt?
Bhatt, who claims to hail from Dehradun, has worn many hats over the course of his career. According to his LinkedIn profile, he graduated from Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University (HNBGU) in Uttarakhand and went on to work with several organisations, including NIIT University, where he served as financial controller until April 2010.
In 2010, he founded Nature Connect Outdoors — an education and adventure non-profit organisation that deals in outdoor education and skill development, including treks, camping, and rafting expeditions. According to the website’s bio, Bhatt had “shunned his corporate career” to follow his passion, which culminated in the formation of the NGO. The organisation is still functional.
According to details available on Zauba Corp, Bhatt is a Chartered Accountant (CA) and the partner of a firm of CAs called RSAC & CO LLP, incorporated in May 2021.
Bhatt has also served as the economic adviser to former Uttarakhand chief minister Trivendra Singh Rawat. However, it’s not clear when he was appointed and when exactly his tenure ended. He wrote an article for Firstpost defending the ministry of housing and urban affairs over the controversial Central Vista project. The author bio designated him as ‘Economic Advisor’ to Rawat.
In 2020, after a district officer’s press release promoting inter-caste and interfaith marriages drew criticism from social media users, Bhatt had reportedly tweeted: “No one from the government has spoken in support of promoting interfaith marriages. No one in the BJP government in their wildest dreams will support anything that is made out here.”
We sent an email and called up Bhatt several times to know more from him, but he did not respond.
Long-standing Association With BJP
Bhatt’s X handle, @alok_bhatt, was followed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In fact, Modi quote-tweeted one of Bhatt’s posts in 2024, where he urged people to watch the film Sabarmati Report.
Bhatt was also invited to PM Modi’s swearing-in ceremony in the past. In 2024, Right-wing influencer Vikas Pandey shared an image with Bhatt alongside former BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma, member of the economic advisory council to the PM, Sanjeev Sanyal, and others, with the caption “First swearing in”.

The Pamphlet-Savitr Analytics-Alok Bhatt Connection
In 2022, Bhatt took on a directorial role at Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation, a company that was incorporated in April 26 that year, with Bhatt and Ashish Nautiyal initially named as directors. According to documents filed with the Union ministry of corporate affairs (MCA), Bhatt holds 9,500 shares, or 95 per cent of the company, while Nautiyal holds the remaining 500 shares, or 5 per cent.
Interestingly, Nautiyal is also the founding editor of the Right-wing media outlet, The Pamphlet.
Savitr Analytics has no website or online presence. We went through its financial records filed with the MCA for the financial years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25, and found that it was registered as a Section 8 company, i.e., a non-profit. In the 2024-25 financial year, its total revenue from operations was Rs 2.7 crore.
The organisation’s revenue across all three years comes from ‘sale of services’, and the rows for ‘Grants or donations received (relevant for Sec 8 companies)’, present in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 filings, are left blank in 2022-23 and 2023-24. In 2024-25, the row does not exist.
Under ‘Corporate Information’, they state ‘Research and awareness about Indian culture and heritage…’, ‘Promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, and environmental protection…’ and ‘Advancement of education, learning, and skills development…’ as their activities.
There was a category called ‘professional expenses’ in the 2022-23 filing that was later relabeled as ‘content production expenses’. Rs. 41,48,600 was spent in the first year, Rs. 95,36,600 (filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the second year, and Rs. 1,38,53,200 (also filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the third year.
Next, we found that an individual named Ridhika Aggarwal stated on LinkedIn that she worked as a content writer for Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation until August 2023. We went through her X timeline (linked to her LinkedIn profile) and found that she wrote at least three articles for The Pamphlet during her tenure at Savitr. None of the articles are currently available on the website.
Ridhika is also listed as a non-official member of a steering committee formed by the Union ministry of environment, forest and climate change in 2023.
The Pamphlet, previously known as The Indian Affairs, posted for the first time on Facebook in April 2022, which is the same time when Savitr Analytics was incorporated.

It is worth noting that The Pamphlet’s website does not disclose any parent company, ownership, editorial team, funding details or board of directors. Its ‘About Us’ page offers only a description of what it does, while calling itself ‘an independent digital media platform’. We also found that The Pamphlet had an office space from its inception in Dehradun, and it is evident from a photo posted by Nautiyal that it began with a team of at least 20 people. Bhatt, the reader would remember, also claims to be from Dehradun.
While all of this points to a connection between Bhatt and The Pamphlet, there appears to be a concerted effort to keep that relationship under wraps. Hence, we tried to dig more.
Is Bhatt Linked to The Pamphlet? We Asked The Pamphlet
We sent an email to The Pamphlet on September 3 asking them about the relationship between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet, and whether Alok Bhatt was connected to The Pamphlet, given that he holds a 95% stake in Savitr Analytics, a company whose other directors have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. We also asked them about their funding sources, since nothing is mentioned on the website.
In reply, they asked us to send our queries to another email ID of The Pamphlet and also to Alok Bhatt, Nirwa Mehta, Ashish Nautiyal and Shiv Mishra. Interestingly, they provided us with the email IDs and phone numbers of each of these individuals. This, in itself, might be considered an indicator of some sort of link between The Pamphlet and Bhatt. It is unlikely for an organisation to provide the direct contact details of someone with whom it has no professional association.
We then sent our queries to all of them.
Nautiyal responded to us saying that his reporting manager, OpIndia editor Nupur J Sharma, “suggested” him “not to give (you) any quotes or information as a matter of policy of not engaging with entities that don’t act in good faith”. A day later, he took to X to let the world know that a woman from Alt News “with a Hindu-sounding name” had approached him with some questions.
Pamphlet editor Nirwa Mehta sent us a 1,071-word response, but did not answer any of our questions. Instead, she sent a detailed set of reciprocal questions concerning Alt News’ funding transparency, the outside associations of its founders and editor, and grants received by individuals associated with Alt News, both currently and in the past. She offered to answer Alt News’ questions in writing once Alt News answered hers first.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet published a video on Alt News on August 16, 2026, without seeking a response from the organisation.
This correspondent responded to Mehta, stating that questions concerning Alt News’ funding should be directed to its editor, while questions concerning any of the founders’ personal assignments should be directed to the person concerned. We also reminded her that a so-called expose on Alt News’ founders had been published by The Pamphlet without either of the concerned persons being approached for a response — a violation of basic journalistic ethics.
In her final response, Mehta did not address the question of ethics. Instead, in a demand that many may find bizarre, she asked this correspondent, “as a responsible employee”, to take her questions to the Alt News directors.
At this point, we felt there was no point continuing the conversation.
We will update our article if The Pamphlet answers Alt News’ questions on whether Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet are connected in any way, and whether Alok Bhatt, BJP’s new IT cell member who continues to remain away from X, holds a position at The Pamphlet.
Social Media Posts Answer the Question
The connection between The Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt is one of internet’s worst kept secrets, it seems. We found several instances on social media where well-known faces from the Right-wing ecosystem tagged Alok Bhatt alongside members of The Pamphlet team — whether to thank them for invitations to Delhi Shabdotsav 2026, where The Pamphlet Panchayat featured on the itinerary, or in connection with other events involving the organisation.
On January 5, 2026, Right-wing influencer Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, who was recently criticised for comparing Newslaundry journalists to prostitutes, thanked The Pamphlet team — including its editor Nirwa Mehta, anchor Shreya Arora, and Bhatt — for inviting him to speak at The Pamphlet Panchayat.
Responding to Iyer-Mitra, Nirwa Mehta and another The Pamphlet employee, Pratibha, thanked him for being a part of the session. The exchange is significant because it can be seen as an acknowledgement by the Pamphlet editor and another employee of Bhatt being a part of the organisation.
Delhi Shabdotsav 2026 was a three-day cultural and literary festival held from January 2 to January 4, 2026, organised by Suruchi Prakashan with the support of the department of art, culture and languages of the Delhi government. The Pamphlet was the digital partner at the event and hosted ‘The Pamphlet Panchayat’ at the fest. The Pamphlet team held and moderated several discussions over the three days, including those with Sanjeev Newar, Vijay Patel, and Subhi Vishwakarma. The subjects of the discussions ranged from ‘Love Jihad: factsheet’ to ‘Bharat’s Hostile Neighbourhood & Need to Regain Shatrubodh’.
We went through the images posted on Shabdotsav’s website and found that Bhatt was present at the event.
The link between Alok Bhatt and The Pamphlet becomes more apparent in another conversation on X in which Iyer-Mitra directly addressed Mehta as Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt’s ‘staff’. Iyer jokingly rebuked Mehta for liking a certain kind of car. Tagging Bhatt, he wrote, “Do @Pamphlet_in and @alok_bhatt @shreya_arora22 approve of these disgusting and extremely hateful statements by their staff?” Mehta responded to Iyer-Mitra’s post, but did not object to the ‘staff’ reference.
On June 1, 2023, a little more than a year after The Pamphlet’s inception, one @saket71 posted a picture with Ashish Nautiyal, who was working at The Pamphlet then, and called him a ‘Media Mughal’. He later tagged Alok Bhatt and Shiv Mishra, praising them for “putting a great team together.”
Such a pleasure to meet the young stars of @Pamphlet_in , @RitikaChandola @himanshi__bisht and the whole team. Such a great young team, full of hope and dreams, and a visible sense of great camaraderie. Kudos to @alok_bhatt and @shivkmishr for putting a great team together. https://t.co/NnmHkA9rQO
— saket साकेत ಸಾಕೇತ್ 🇮🇳 (@saket71) June 1, 2023
Several people have congratulated Alok Bhatt at various points of time upon The Pamphlet reaching certain milestones.
To sum up, what raises serious questions about the BJP’s decision to name Bhatt as its social media co-convenor is not just his past social media conduct, but also the opacity surrounding his professional associations. One organisation he appears to be associated with, The Pamphlet, does not publicly disclose its ownership, editorial team, board or funding sources. Without any apparent source of funding, it starts off as a 20-member organization. Who pays their salary? How are establishment costs met? There are no answers. Again, another corporate entity closely linked to him, Savitr Analytics, has no website or public online presence despite reporting Rs 2.7 crore in operational revenue in 2025.
Things get murkier when one takes into account the desperate efforts by Bhatt’s associates to conceal his association with The Pamphlet, evident in the organisation’s refusal to answer direct questions regarding this.
In other words, a man linked to organisations with questionable records, and whose involvement with a pro-government outlet is abundantly visible in public, but markedly absent from the outlet’s own disclosures, has now been given a formal position in the BJP’s social media cell.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has revised the MBBS seat matrix for the 2026-27 academic year, while cautioning medical colleges and counselling authorities against admitting students beyond the intake capacity formally approved by the regulator.
In a public notice issued earlier this month, the NMC said the updated matrix incorporated permissions granted for the establishment of new medical colleges and increases in the annual intake of existing colleges following decisions by its Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB), its first appeal committee and the second appeal committee under the Union Health Ministry.
Not final
The regulator has also made it clear that the latest matrix is not necessarily final. It said the seat matrix would remain subject to revision based on subsequent decisions of the appeal committees or other competent authorities, with any changes to be uploaded on the NMC website and taken into account by the Central and State counselling committees.
The latest matrix lists 1,40,214 MBBS seats across 836 medical colleges, including 63,971 seats in 391 government colleges and 76,243 seats in 445 private colleges. It follows an earlier matrix listing 1,27,028 renewed seats. The latest update includes 13,186 additional seats, of which 10,400 are in private medical colleges and 2,786 in government institutions.
The NMC’s latest warning comes against the backdrop of continuing approvals, appeals and changes in sanctioned intake. It has specifically directed counselling committees not to permit admissions against seats in excess of those approved and notified by MARB.
“Under no circumstances” should any medical college or institution admit students beyond its approved annual intake, the regulator said, warning that such admissions would constitute non-compliance with the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and the regulations framed under it and could attract regulatory and penal action.
Report any discrepancy
The NMC has also asked counselling committees to refer any discrepancy between the seats being offered by a college and those appearing in the approved matrix to MARB for clarification.
The notice has a further caveat for private medical colleges that have received permission either to establish a new MBBS college or increase their annual intake but have not yet furnished the required electronic bank guarantee.
Such colleges have been given seven days to submit the guarantee in favour of the Director, MARB. The letter of permission will be issued only after the guarantee is received, verified and found to be in order.
The regulatory clarification assumes significance as medical colleges have continued to receive permissions and seek increases in intake through the assessment and appeals process. It also places the onus on counselling authorities to ensure that the number of seats offered to NEET-UG candidates corresponds strictly to the latest sanctioned capacity.
The revised matrix also means that students and counselling authorities will have to track subsequent changes rather than rely on earlier versions of the seat matrix.
The NMC has directed all medical colleges to verify their institutional details in the latest matrix and immediately report any discrepancy or omission to MARB, preferably before the commencement of counselling.
The regulator’s repeated emphasis on sanctioned intake also highlights a fundamental distinction between a college seeking or receiving approval for additional capacity and the actual issuance of the letter of permission. Until the prescribed regulatory requirements, including the bank guarantee where applicable, are completed, the additional seats cannot be treated as available for admission.
The NMC has asked colleges to ensure that admissions for 2026-27 are made only against the seats notified in the latest matrix, “as amended from time to time”.

Ninth woman's body found as South African police investigate string of deaths
- Published
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of a ninth woman's body in just two months, amid growing concern over a string of unexplained deaths east of Johannesburg.
The latest victim was found half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Dawn Park on Thursday morning, police said. Her identity has not yet been released.
The discovery follows the deaths of eight other women whose bodies have been found since July across Ekurhuleni, a major urban area of Johannesburg.
Several of the women were found partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible.
- Abducted South African journalist found dead with gunshot wounds 
  - Published4 hours ago
President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" in finding those behind the killings, which he said were "causing fear and uncertainty in our communities".
Among the victims was 38-year-old Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo, who disappeared last week after leaving her home for an afternoon run. Her body was found three days later behind a hotel in Kempton Park.
Two other victims have since been identified as Itumeleng Kekana, who had been missing since July, and 38-year-old Dineo Evelyn Motapane, whose body was discovered by the roadside in KwaThema on Tuesday.
The first of the nine bodies was discovered in Kempton Park on 15 July. A suspect was arrested two days later in connection with that case and remains in custody, but police have not linked that suspect to the other deaths.
Further bodies were discovered in August and September, including in Kempton Park, Olifantsfontein, Clayville and KwaThema.
The latest body is of a woman believed to be in her 30s and appeared to have bruises and stab wounds, local media reported.
Police have assembled a multidisciplinary team of detectives, intelligence officers, forensic experts and other specialists to investigate the deaths and establish whether there are links between the cases.
They are also pursuing a person of interest, although they have not disclosed which case or cases that person may be connected to.
"Let's not get emotional, the gloves are off," said Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi on Thursday, adding that the authorities had the capacity to deal with the killings.
In a statement on Thursday, South African police said the recent rise in serious and violent crimes against women remained a "matter of grave concern", urging women in the country to remain vigilant about their personal safety.
They advised women to avoid walking alone or using isolated routes, remain alert to strangers and suspicious vehicles, and share their location or travel plans with someone they trust. They also advised against walking with earphones or earbuds at high volume, warning this could reduce awareness of their surroundings.
"Practising personal safety measures can save lives."
Authorities have offered a 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) reward for information that could lead to arrests and have appealed to families with missing relatives to help identify the remaining victims.
The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concern about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
Police say they are not linking the deaths to a serial killer at this stage, but are investigating the possibility that a group of people is behind the killings.
Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has cautioned against speculation, saying investigators were dealing with what appeared, at this stage, to be "quite distinct, separate events".
South Africa experiences some of the world's highest levels of gender-based violence (GBV), with the rate at which women are killed five times higher than the global average, according to UN Women.
Last November, the country classified violence against women a national disaster following an online campaign that culminated in countrywide protests.

Listed NBFC Kissht has secured board approval to raise up ₹832.2 Cr via a preferential issue of equity shares to 34 investors and entities. In a filing with the exchanges, the company said that its board has approved the issuance of 2.6 Cr fully paid-up equity shares to the investors at an issue price of ₹314.11 apiece. The NBFC did not disclose how it plans to utilise the fresh proceeds from the issue. The allotment is still subject to regulatory and shareholder approval. The company has also convened an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders to seek approval for the preferential issue. “Funds raising by way of a preferential issue on a private placement basis of up to 2,64,93,882 fully paid-up equity shares of the company… for cash, at an issue price of ₹314.11 per share… for an amount aggregating to ₹832.19 Cr to identified investors (non-promoters), in accordance with the provisions of… applicable laws….,” read the filing. Among the investing companies, Axis Flexi Cap Fund, Axis Multi Cap Fund and Axis Small Cap Fund together will receive 63.7 Lakh shares worth nearly ₹200 Cr. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, via two entities, will also receive 27.1 Lakh shares totalling ₹85 Cr. Envision Capital will also get 12.7 Lakh shares valued at nearly ₹40 Cr, while PE firm First Bridge will lap up 12.1 Lakh shares for a sum of ₹20 Cr. Kissht will also allot 23.9 Lakh shares to three entities linked to Ashoka WhiteOak Capital for a consideration of nearly ₹75 Cr. Other investors that will receive allotment under the preferential issue include 360 One, Alchemy Capital, Groww, Bandhan Small Cap Fund, Unity Small Finance Bank, among others. In terms of the other individual investors, Ameeta Rajendra Naik will receive 63,671 shares worth ₹2 Cr and Anil Shah will get 1.6 Lakh shares valued at nearly ₹5 Cr. The latest fundraise comes barely four months after the NBFC made a strong debut on the exchanges, listing at a premium of 11.7% on the BSE compared to its issue price of ₹171. Its public issue comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹850 Cr and an OFS component totalling ₹76 Cr. Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a lending tech platform that offers digital personal and business loans of up to ₹5 Lakh. It also offers health-related insurance products and secured loans through loans against property. In July, it also received regulatory approval to begin distribution of mutual funds through its wholly-owned subsidiary Invincible Minds. The NBFC claimed to have 45+ active lending and co-lending partners under its belt at the end of June 2026. It also operated 101 offline branches across eight states and union territories, and managed to more than double YoY its active customer base to 3.49 Mn in Q1 FY27. On the financial front, Kissht’s consolidated net profit zoomed 59% to ₹95.1 Cr in Q1 FY27 as against ₹59.7 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed nearly 45% to ₹669.5 Cr during the quarter under review as against ₹463.1 Cr in Q1 FY26. Shares of the NBFC closed Thursday’s trading session 5.08% higher at ₹359.7 on the BSE.

WASHINGTON — Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday named eight new members to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, an influential panel of experts who assess the evidence behind a wide array of preventive medical services.
They include a number of specialists, including in clinical nutrition, gastroenterology, and oncology, as well as a finance professor who has expertise in health insurance. It’s a major departure from the past, when the panel was made up of generalists, as opposed to specialists, to avoid prioritizing one area of medicine over another.
The independent body has more than advisory power because its assessments help determine whether health insurance companies are required to cover preventive services, such as mammograms and drugs to help prevent HIV. The newly appointed chair, Seth Corey, works in pediatric hematology-oncology at the Cleveland Clinic. He replaces Michael Silverstein, who departed from his role last year.
Kennedy has been critical of the 16-person group, which has been left with at least eight vacancies this year after five members rolled off at the end of their terms and the previous chair, Silverstein, departed on his own. Two members — vice chairs John Wong and Esa Davis — were fired in letters sent to them by Kennedy on May 11. The letters, viewed by STAT, said they were terminated due to a review of the current appointments.
The panel hasn’t met in more than a year, after its meetings were canceled by Kennedy. The most recent news on the USPSTF website dates back to August 2025. The group had previously signaled it was working on recommendations related to breast cancer genetic screening, pediatric autism disorder screening, and cervical cancer screening, among others.
Last year Kennedy said he planned to remove panel members, viewing them as too “woke,” but no new members had been named until now. His ability to remove members may be traced to a Supreme Court ruling issued in 2025, in the case Kennedy v. Braidwood Management, which established that the expert task force is under the authority of the health secretary.
