On dinner timing, weight management, emerging research, pain, disease prevention, healthcare gaps and more
(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Athira Elssa Johnson writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
What we eat, when we eat and how we manage our weight remain important questions in health, even as advice often runs ahead of the evidence. This week,I examine one deceptively simple question: is there a right time to have dinner?
Does eating late really affect our health? Is the time at which we eat more important than what we eat? And how should dinner timing be considered alongside sleep, work schedules, physical activity and the overall quality of the diet? Doctors explain what we know about meal timing, and what it can and cannot tell us about maintaining good health.
Close on the nutrition and weight-management front is a study from the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, which looks at what works better for lasting weight loss. The study finds that combining diet and exercise is more effective for sustained weight loss than either approach alone. The findings are a useful reminder that weight management cannot be reduced to one food, one nutrient or one short-term intervention.
Meanwhile, the focus on protein continues to grow, particularly on social media. But increasing protein intake is not, by itself, a definition of a healthy diet. Ramya Kannan looks at what constitutes a wholesome meal and the importance of considering the overall dietary pattern rather than focusing on individual nutrients or products.
Emerging research
From everyday nutrition, we move to some interesting areas of emerging research.
Researchers are exploring whether material derived from menstrual blood could have applications in the treatment of osteoarthritis. A recent study as reported by Manjeera Gowravaram examined extracellular vesicles derived from menstrual blood stromal cells and their effects on processes involved in cartilage formation. The findings are from laboratory research and do not establish a treatment for osteoarthritis, but they add to growing interest in regenerative approaches to cartilage damage.
Another study reported by Anirban Mukhopadhyay takes a closer look at the genetic basis of cerebral palsy. Researchers found that far fewer genes may have a clear and reproducible association with the condition than some earlier studies had suggested. Understanding which genetic findings hold up is important not only for research but also for how clinicians interpret genetic information in people with cerebral palsy.
Diagnosis and care
There are also important questions about what happens within the healthcare system after patients seek care.
Dr. Suvira Jain writes about why one in three donated corneas is wasted. Eye donation does not automatically translate into transplantation. The cornea has to be retrieved, assessed, preserved and transplanted within the appropriate window. Gaps at different stages can mean that donated tissue is ultimately not used, even as many people continue to wait for corneal transplants.
Pain, too, can persist long after the original injury or illness has apparently healed. Persistent pain may require specialised assessment rather than being dismissed as something a patient simply has to live with. Afshan Yasmeen looks at why persistent pain can be complex and why appropriate pain management needs to go beyond treating the original condition.
Prevention and public health
On the disease prevention front, rabies remains an important public-health concern. Maya C. reports a study from Keralam that looks at the potential impact of dog vaccination in preventing rabies, underlining the importance of controlling the disease in its animal reservoirs alongside ensuring timely post-exposure care for people. Rabies prevention cannot depend on treating people after exposure alone; sustained vaccination and surveillance of dogs are central to controlling transmission.
The issue of counterfeit medicines also highlights why the quality and safety of healthcare products matter. A large stock of suspected counterfeit medicines was seized from a private facility in Bengaluru. Such cases raise concerns that go beyond regulation: a medicine that does not contain what it claims to contain, or does not meet required quality standards, can result in treatment failure and expose patients to further harm.
Air pollution remains another persistent health concern. A study examining winter pollution in north India finds that western disturbances explain a substantial share of the year-to-year variation in winter pollution. Weather systems are only one part of the pollution story, but understanding their role can improve forecasting and help strengthen public-health responses during periods when pollution levels are expected to rise.
Muscle metabolism, healthy ageing
For this month’s Nobel feature we look back at the work of Archibald V. Hill and Otto Meyerhof, whose Nobel-winning research helped establish how muscles generate and use energy. Their independent work helped explain fundamental aspects of muscle metabolism and the relationship between oxygen use, energy production and muscular activity.
And Health Wrap, Episode 50 looks at longevity and the role of racquet sports in healthy ageing, Navin Gnanasekaran, longevity physician and head of radiology, Apollo Hospitals, talk about healthspan, nutrition, sleep, muscle strength, stress, metabolism, inflammation and cognition. The conversation also looks at how racquet sports can bring together physical activity, social interaction and cognitive engagement, making them an interesting part of a broader discussion on maintaining health as we age.
And more:
Shanthi Dass looks at why physiotherapy matters, and the role rehabilitation can play in helping people recover function and manage health conditions.
Dr. Jyoti Bajpai writes about melanoma in India, and why the messaging around this potentially serious skin cancer needs to change to encourage earlier recognition.
Dr. Shivika Gupta looks at what to eat in the weeks before egg retrieval, addressing nutrition in the period leading up to an IVF procedure.
Bindu Shajan Perappadan reports on a WHO-linked study examining smoking and infertility, including the evidence on how quitting smoking can make a meaningful difference.
And in Keralam, health officials have sounded a caution as rising temperatures coincide with a fresh wave of fever cases in Ernakulam, another reminder of how seasonal and environmental changes can intersect with public health.

An enemy that swarmed the battlefield in large groups while under fire, seemingly oblivious to the dangers of drones and fire from automatic weapons. An elite corps of ghost soldiers who chose suicide over surrender. They fought and died in their thousands, then apparently vanished from the battlefield.
North Korea's soldiers were sent to fight by Pyongyang alongside Russian forces as they sought to repel a Ukrainian offensive on Moscow's territory at the end of 2024. They paid a heavy price, as many as 3,000 killed in action from the 13,000 deployed.
Ultimately, they would adapt their tactics, and with Russia would drive Ukrainian forces from its Kursk region. In combat terms, little has been heard of them since, but according to Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelensky, North Korean forces, and their weaponry, are soon to make a dramatic return to Russia's war in Ukraine.
Last month, Zelensky warned that up to 50,000 North Koreans will be deployed in Russia, revising an earlier estimate of 30,000 troops. He called on South Korea to provide support for his country's air defence.
But why, after such heavy losses, would North Korea send more men to fight for Russia, and what happened to its soldiers sent in the first place?
"They're still there", said Dr Yang Uk, research fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, Center for Foreign Policy and National Security in Seoul. "They are defending Russian territory for another counterattack from Ukraine. And we believe that some of the engineer corps or workers might be in [the Russian-occupied] Donbas area but that's not the combat troops."
The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense, HUR, estimates that 8,500 North Korean servicemen are still on Russian territory. They are organised into four brigades, which operate as part of the "North" Group of Forces and are assigned to protecting the state border of the Russian Federation in the Kursk Region from Ukrainian incursions.
"They do not participate in active combat operations. Units of the Korean People's Army have not been observed in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," HUR said in a statement to the BBC.
A first for North Korea
For North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Un, the Kursk deployment was a gamble, its largest combat force ever sent overseas. (In 1973, North Korea sent 1,500 military personnel and instructors to Egypt during the Yom Kippur war with Israel, and in the late 1960s, an estimated 87 North Korean pilots fought for the North Vietnamese against US forces).
And despite the bloodshed, it was a gamble that paid off, reaping countless benefits for the isolated and impoverished country, transforming both its economic and military fortunes. And one that could serve as a blueprint for even deeper military cooperation.
North Koreans, "now know what modern combat is about", said Yang.
The soldiers sent to fight in Russia were from Storm Corps, the elite of the North Korean armed forces. Extremely isolated, totalitarian North Korea is a militarised and heavily indoctrinated state.
At first, neither Russia, nor North Korea, even acknowledged their presence. Ukrainian forces first clashed with them in November 2024, and the first live North Korean prisoners of war wouldn't be captured until January of the following year.
It wasn't until April 2025 that Russia first acknowledged their role, when Valery Gerasimov, chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, described their "heroism" on the battlefield.
Yang continued, "North Korean soldiers are very brave I mean, especially those of Storm Corps. They are willing to die for their country. But the problem is that passion doesn't mean efficient combat skills... [They suffered] a lot of bloodshed in the early stage of the Kursk campaign, but they learned the lessons of modern drone warfare."
"Cannon fodder", is how "Sultan", a soldier with Ukraine's 95th Air Assault Brigade described North Korean troops. He faced them in the battle for Kursk at the end of 2024.
"They would begin with one large assault group, then another 15–20 men would be sent into the same position, and then more after that. The North Koreans operated differently. They kept moving all the time. That gave them a certain advantage, but not a decisive one," he recalled recently in Kyiv.
Communication between them and their Russian allies appeared poor, he said, and their soldiers were inadequately equipped.
After combat, Sultan and his men would search enemy corpses for documents and intelligence information. On the Russian dead they would find personal belongings, identification and equipment. "But when we searched the North Koreans specifically, the only thing we found on them was simply ammo. We checked absolutely all the small pockets - there were no documents, nothing at all," he explained.
Other Ukrainian soldiers reported the North Koreans lacked body armour, winter clothing and helmets.
In one chilling video from a Ukrainian assault, a wounded North Korean soldier lies prone on the snow-covered ground in a wooded area. As the Ukrainians approach, he detonates a grenade under his chin, after calling out, with his last words, the name of his leader, Kim Jong Un.
In April 2025, at a memorial service in Pyongyang at the newly created Museum of Foreign Military Operations, Kim praised heroes who choose suicide over capture.
In a speech to relatives, with Russia's Defence Minister Andrey Belousov in attendance, he said they were "heroes who unhesitatingly opted for self-blasting, suicide attack, in order to defend the great honour".
While North Korea has never officially acknowledged the death toll from the Kursk operation, a BBC Korea analysis of the memorial site estimated that 2,300 soldiers were killed fighting for Russia.
Ukraine's intelligence arm, HUR, puts the figure at 3,000 killed and 1,500 injured.
But aside from the combat experience, why did North Korea sacrifice so many of its best troops in a foreign war?
An economic windfall
The deployment has been a much-needed economic windfall for the country and a geopolitical win, according to Lim Soo-ho, a senior research fellow at the Institute for National Security Strategy, in Seoul.
He estimates that arms sales to Russia and the troop deployment have netted the impoverished country close to $10bn.
"North Korea's annual GDP is estimated at around $30bn (£22bn)," he told me. "That means they earned a third of a year's GDP over two and a half years through weapons exports and troop deployment, which, for an economy as small as North Korea's, is a very significant effect."
In exchange for its manpower, North Korea gets food, oil and hard currency. While China says it complies with sanctions against Pyongyang, Russia does not.
But equally important, the cooperation with Russia has shifted North Korea's long-term dependency on China.
So in Beijing in September last year, Kim Jong Un was able to stand shoulder to shoulder with China's leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in the first public meeting of all three. Not quite as an equal, but no longer reliant on China alone.
This is significant, said Lim, "It's a major geopolitical shift".
"Whenever things got difficult under isolation, North Korea would reach out first toward South Korea, Japan, or especially the US to try to normalise relations, that was the pattern of Korean Peninsula diplomacy. But now that ties with Russia have tightened, Kim Jong Un argues that the world is in a new Cold War, a multipolar system."
The arrangement with Russia, which began as economic and military expediency appears to be developing into something deeper and longer-term. At this year's 9th Party Congress of the Korean Workers' Party, Kim Jong Un was emboldened and spoke of accomplishments that his grandfather Kim Il Sung and father Kim Jong Il never achieved.
But dangers lie ahead. To date, no North Koreans have fought on Ukrainian or Russian-occupied Ukrainian land. If they did so, there would be diplomatic consequences, not least in South Korea, an ally of Ukraine, albeit one which so far has only provided "non-lethal" aid.
This is something that President Zelensky has emphasised as he presses for Seoul to provide advanced military hardware, including air defence systems. He said that since June, preparations have been underway in Russia's Voronezh region to receive fresh North Korean forces and claimed that Pyongyang was preparing to transfer additional ballistic weapons to Russia.
"Russia is helping North Korea learn modern warfare, improve its weapons, and gain real combat experience. This poses a threat to every country in Asia that lies within range of North Korean missiles," he said in a presidential address in July.
Only two North Korean soldiers were captured alive in battles with Ukrainian forces. That's a staggeringly low number, given that between 11,000 and 14,000 fought in the Kursk campaign. (Another was captured alive but died from combat-related injuries, according to the South Korean National Intelligence Service).
Like their comrades who choose suicide over capture, neither man intended to be taken alive.
"For Joseon (North Korean) soldiers, becoming a prisoner of war itself is a crime. That just isn't an option. We can't become POWs," one of the captured men told a South Korean MBC documentary crew who interviewed him in prison in Ukraine.
Baek Pyeong-gang, not his real name, lay wounded from a drone strike for four days before being captured. He was tricked into surrendering when he mistook Ukrainian soldiers for his Russian allies.
The second prisoner, Lee Kang-eun, also a pseudonym, told the journalist Kim Young-mi that he felt guilty he was still alive. Barely conscious, he was found by Ukrainian soldiers on the battlefield with extensive injuries to the arm and jaw.
"I had no grenade or knives on me to self-blast (end my life)," he explained.
He described scores of his colleagues killed by drones, early in the war. The battlefield "reeked of the smell of blood", he said.
Neither man wants to return to North Korea, Lee said he believed that his family members would be "wiped out" as punishment for his capture. Both have said they want to be sent to South Korea, and Seoul is willing to take them.
Only Russia, not Pyongyang, has asked for their return.
But Ukraine, still intent on pressuring Seoul for military aid, has not committed to handing them over to South Korean authorities. Kyiv has said it will honour international human rights obligations which prevent the forced repatriation of prisoners of war.
Their fate remains undecided, but what appears certain is that more North Koreans will join Russia's war. Their service has enormous economic and political value to Pyongyang; but Russia desperately needs them too.
Four and a half years into Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it is facing a desperate manpower shortage. Western and Ukrainian intelligence agencies estimate that it is losing some 6,000 more troops a month than it can recruit. So, Moscow has been forced to turn to foreign fighters, from Colombia, Kenya, Cameroon and North Korea, to sustain its ranks.
For Russia and North Korea, it is a mutually beneficial relationship, a coalition at a price. Ultimately, North Korea will continue to send its soldiers to fight in Russia's war, but only for as long as it is profitable to do so.

An iOS 27 bug can temporarily freeze your iPhone
Here’s how to fix it.
If you're here because your newly updated iPhone suddenly froze while you were using it, don't panic. There's an iOS 27 bug that can temporarily freeze your phone if you happen to do a series of swipes. As 9to5Mac notes, it's not going to ruin your device permanently, and you can get out of by doing a force restart. A force reboot is the first thing you should do when you're troubleshooting issues with any device, as it will clear your RAM and close programs that could be causing you problems.
Since your iPhone is frozen, and you can't access the power icon, you'll have to press and quickly release the volume up button and then do the same with the volume down button. Afterward, press and hold the side button until the Apple logo appears, and you know your phone is going through a restart. Take note that you may have to press on that button for more than 10 seconds.
In case you haven't encountered the bug yet and were wondering how it's triggered, it's by swiping down the Notification Center and the Control Center in quick succession. You'll then see buttons and icons stuck at the top of the screen, and you'll find your iPhone unable to register your swipes and taps. Apple will likely roll out a fix for this in the future, but for now, you may want to memorize our instructions for force restarts above.

In Summary
- New Apple CEO, John Ternus, announced a range of products at the Surprise and Shine event.
- While most of the focus was on the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, there was much more to the event than just devices and a CEO debut.
- We bring you eight takeaways that were buried in the buzz around the new devices, which might have escaped your attention.
It might not have surprised too many people – the leaks messed that up – but Apple did a fair bit of shining at its recent Surprise and Shine event. The event, which also marked John Ternus’ debut as Apple CEO at a launch, went on expected lines, with Apple revealing new AirPods, Apple Watches, new iPhone Pros and, of course, the iPhone Duo, which has grabbed the most attention. There was, however, much more to the event than just the launches. Here are our eight biggest takeaways from the day on which the world saw Apple’s new foldable and the CEO on stage:
Table of Contents
New Era? Presentation-wise, Apple is still Cook-ing (Pun intended)
Yes, it was John Ternus who held the reins at Surprise and Shine. But in terms of presentation style, the template that was followed was still from the menu of the preceding chef, Tim Cook. We had multiple speakers, elaborate backdrops, and a similar race through a number of products, leaving the most time for the star of the show (it was the Air last time around, the Duo this time). Yes, in terms of presentation style, Apple remains well ahead of the competition, although we miss the wit and humor of the past; this launch was more from the Cook manual than the Ternus one.
No surprises (Sigh)…
It’s been a while since Apple surprised the Dickens out of us at a launch, but in recent years, the brand’s product announcements have often been leaked out well in advance. And that was pretty much true this time around. From the iPhone Duo to the shades of Burgundy to the fact that there would be no suffix-less iPhone at the event, the leak community got a lot of things right, which, as we have said in the past, takes some of the mystique and surprise out of the event. Mind you, Apple did pull one rabbit out of its hat.
…except for the AirPods 5
There were no suffix-less iPhones at Surprise and Shine, but there sure were suffix-less AirPods. And while most of the noise was about Apple’s first foldable, the AirPods 5 might have emerged as the silent, value-for-money heroes of the show. While most people had been expecting new AirPods Pro with perhaps a camera built into them, Apple brought in a new version of the classic AirPods, complete with better ANC and battery life, even while retaining the “open” fit and, surprise, surprise, the same price tag as its predecessors. Not too many noticed…until the price of the Duo was announced, and suddenly a device with no price increase became the belle of the tech ball.
Hooray, we will now have TWO iPhone launches every year
Surprise and Shine marked the beginning of a new iPhone era, in which Apple will release its iPhones in two tranches over a twelve-month period. While Apple has released iPhones at two different times of the year in the past, the second launch has generally been a relatively low-profile and soft one (of the SE and ‘e’ mainly). That is set to change now. Even if Apple does a soft launch for the iPhone 18, the iPhone Air 2 and the iPhone 18e, rather than a full-fledged event, the fact is that close to half of the iPhone portfolio will be launched in the second half of the year, and the remainder in the first half of the next year. The iPhone schedules just got tweaked.
Apple is getting REALLY serious about AI (no, really, this time)
Two years ago, Apple launched the iPhone 16 series, saying it had been designed from the ground up for Apple’s avatar of AI, Apple Intelligence. However, AI is one area where the Cupertino brand has been found trailing the competition. So it was not surprising that the brand was clearly out to write a new chapter at Surprise and Shine. Every device it announced – iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods – had a strong element of AI, which different presenters stressed would work wonderfully well, even while preserving the users’ security. Well, we have heard that a few times in the past, but never in such a comprehensive manner. Is Apple finally going to crack the AI puzzle? Based on what we saw, it would be no Surprise if it went on to Shine in that department in the coming months.
Whoop, Whoop, the Apple Watch is now a full-fledged fitness and health device, and is targeting Whoop
It started out trying to be a computer on your wrist, complete with apps, notifications and alerts, but the Apple Watch has of late graduated (or been demoted, depending on your perspective) to being mainly a health and fitness tracking device. And Surprise and Shine saw this trend continuing, with most of the talk about the Apple Watch 4 Ultra and Apple Watch Series 12 revolving around better sensors and measurement. The highlighting of features like Readiness Scores and Health Age seems to indicate that the Cupertino brand now has the screenless Whoop, which popularised these features, in its sights.
The narrative is unmatched, but is now very hardware-driven!
Processors, camera apertures, health sensors, ANC, battery life…these formed the major part of the narrative around Surprise and Shine, showing how Apple’s has shifted from storytelling to specs at its launches in recent times. This might be fine for some, but we do miss the time when an announcer would walk us through nuances of design and amazing (or they called amazing, and often, unbelievable) features on devices.
Yes, Apple remains the lord, master, and commander of product launches, but we prefer tales to tech, and a live presenter on stage to edited videos, no matter how sleekly edited. The fact that the Duo section stood out from the others because of its stress on design and UI only reinforces our belief that Apple might perhaps reconsider going back to its storytelling roots, and leave the specs on the spec sheet, rather than on the speech notes. Everyone else talks specs anyway.
Cosmic orange is out of the Apple cosmos… and Black is back!
This was so typically Apple. After making orange the color of the last twelve months, courtesy of the Cosmic Orange variant of the iPhone 17 Pro series, and making a number of brands come out with orange phones and other devices (JBL even had a pair of headphones in orange), the Cupertino giant pushed the shade out of its color palette. It also brought back the one color that everyone had missed in the Pro series – Black. Henry “Any Color As Long As It Is Black” Ford and AC/DC would approve of the return of the color, and so do we. We are not shedding any tears for orange, although we suspect those orange Pros are going to have great antique value some day.
And one more thing…
Craig Federighi’s hair looks as awesome as ever!

Our immune systems don’t just fight bacteria and viruses invading the body. They are responsible for keeping our own tissues in check, taking out cancerous cells before they have a chance to grow. Once a tumor forms, however, it can create an environment that declaws cancer-fighting immune cells—in some cases even reprogramming them to suppress other parts of the immune system.
Overcoming the oppressive tumor environment remains a barrier for even some of the most promising treatments. “One of the biggest challenges in cancer immunotherapy is that the immune system may be capable of attacking a tumor, but the tumor environment can stop those immune cells from doing their job,” University of Adelaide professor Chunxia Zhao explained in a press release.
In a study published this week in Science Advances, Zhao’s team developed a system that can precisely deliver an mRNA therapy to transform immune cells back into allies. The researchers focused on tumor-associated macrophages, which—when rewired by signals from the cancer—hinder the arrival and activity of T cells, one of the body’s main weapons against cancer. The mRNA carries the instructions for producing CXCL9, a chemical signal for recruiting T cells.
Flipping this switch is the easy part. mRNA technologies have been rapidly advancing, especially in the realm of cancer treatments, since they were first introduced to the public as Covid vaccines. However, you don’t want an immune-activating signal going just anywhere in the body. A risk of any immunotherapy is amping up the immune system too much, which can cause dangerous and potentially deadly side effects.
To make sure the mRNA made it directly to the site of the tumor and nowhere else, the researchers developed a delivery method they dubbed “smart” nanoparticles. In any mRNA therapy, including a standard Covid shot, the mRNA is encased in some kind of nanoparticle, usually a lipid envelope. This fatty structure helps the molecules enter cells. In this case, the researchers took this basic technology and added a targeting mechanism to ensure the mRNA only got into the right cells.
The smart nanoparticles were studded with antibodies that bind to TREM2, a protein present on the surface of tumor-associated immunosuppressive macrophages. A tumor’s environment tends to be a messy place full of many different cell types, so not only does this honing mechanism help get the therapy to the right part of the body, but only into macrophages in that region that need reprogramming.
In addition to the mRNA, the smart nanoparticles also carried a drug called resiquimod, which can stimulate certain immune pathways. Initial laboratory results showed that not the previously lethargic macrophages began producing CXCL9 as well as other markers of an active immune state, such as NOS2, expression of which increased by a factor of 89.5. Signals of a more immunosuppressive state also notably decreased.
The researchers then administered the smart nanoparticles to mice with aggressive breast cancer. After three doses, tumor growth slowed. The concentration of CXCL9 was approximately four times higher than in the control group, and the researchers detected the presence of T-cell activity. The treatment also reduced the proportion of macrophages with immunosuppressive characteristics by 63 percent.
Often, cancer treatments are combined to attack the tumor from different directions. The researchers tested their new therapy in combination with two types of immunotherapy already used called immune checkpoint inhibitors. The combination did not further reduce the tumor size, but it did generate important changes in the immune system. Different types of T cells increased within the tumors and nearby lymph nodes—a finding associated with the potential for a more lasting immune response.
The researchers also did not detect any negative effects to other organs, but they urged caution that more studies are needed to evaluate the safety before human trials can begin.
“This is an important proof of concept that we can use mRNA and nanoparticle technology to reprogram the immune environment of a tumor,” said Professor Zhao. “There is still significant work to do before this approach could be considered for patients, but these results provide an encouraging foundation for developing more targeted cancer immunotherapies.”

India’s senior living market is expected to become a $ 10.1 billion opportunity by 2030, requiring $ 7.7 billion capital investment to meet new supply under a policy-driven scenario, according to a ASLI-JLL report “India’s Silver Economy: From Niche to Necessity”.
“With over 166 million Indians aged above 60 and the number projected to double by 2050, there is a need to build an ecosystem of senior citizens. The organised senior living facility penetration is just 1.5%. The opportunity is about building a strong, accessible, and trusted senior care ecosystem,” G. Rajagopal, chairman of the Association of Senior Living India (ASLI), said in a press release.
The addressable market of urban, financially independent senior households in India is expected to grow from 1.7 million in 2026 to 2.1 million by 2030. The opportunity is not just in senior living friendly properties and communities but includes assisted care, healthcare, specialised care, rehabilitation, and other supporting services, says the report.
The organised senior living sector reached 25,050 dwelling units as of June 2026 (at 1.5 %) compared with 6-7 % in the U.S. and 14-15% in New Zealand. The sector registered 14.2 % CAGR between 2024 and first half of 2026.
“We are looking at a market that could scale from 25,050 units to 74,000 units by 2030, unlocking $ 7.7 billion in capital deployment. But the real story is not just independent living, it is the assisted living crisis. We have barely 2,100 assisted living beds today against a projected need of 11,000 by 2030, while the population of 75 plus years is growing at 7.8% annually,” said Karan Singh Sodi, Senior Managing Director, JLL.
However, despite 80 % – 85% occupancy at well-managed facilities, skilled caregiver shortages and high real estate costs remain key constraints. Affordability is a critical barrier, according to the report.
Rental and service-led models are likely to gain significant traction in the coming years, with rental models expected to overtake outright sales. Financial innovations such as repositioned Reverse Mortgage Loans and insurance-linked products could help convert existing assets into viable funding mechanisms for senior care.
The Maharashtra Housing Policy 2025 has formally recognised senior housing through dedicated planning standards and healthcare linkages, while Haryana’s policy combines licensing clarity with Floor Area Ratio incentives to improve project feasibility. Such policy measures can take the market penetration to nearly 2.4 % within four years.
Operators are also investing in digital health infrastructure, including electronic health records, monitoring wearables and telemedicine, alongside quality and accreditation frameworks, the report said.

How an Aston Villa fringe player became Europe's most prolific scorer
- Published
Just eight months ago, Donyell Malen was struggling to make a significant impact at Aston Villa.
Today, no player in Europe's top five leagues has scored more goals since his Roma debut on 18 January.
The Netherlands international has enjoyed a remarkable turnaround since joining Roma, transforming from a player who struggled to establish himself in the Premier League into one of the continent's most productive forwards.
Europe's hottest scorer
Since his Roma debut, Malen has scored 20 goals, more than Harry Kane (16), Lamine Yamal (15) and anyone else in the Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 during the same period.
He also leads the way for combined goals and assists with 22, ahead of Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes (20), Barcelona's teenage sensation Lamine Yamal (19) and Bayern striker Kane (18).
No player across Europe's top five leagues has made a greater contribution in front of goal.
Why Roma's system suits him?
The contrast with his time at Villa could hardly be greater.
In 46 appearances for the Premier League club, the 27-year-old scored 10 goals and registered two assists. Since joining Roma, he has scored 21 goals and provided three assists in just 25 matches.
His scoring rate has improved from one goal every 149.8 minutes at Villa to one every 96.7 minutes in Rome.
On the surface, the figures suggest two very different versions of the same player. But Roma's success with Malen may owe as much to how he is being used as to any change in confidence or form.
The Dutchman arrived in Italy with a proven goalscoring pedigree and the data suggests Roma have found a role that maximises his attacking instincts.
While confidence and form may have played a part, a change in position appears to be a major factor behind the resurgence.
At Villa, Malen was often used across the frontline and spent only 52% of his league minutes as a central striker. At Roma, 99% of his Serie A minutes have come through the middle under manager Gian Piero Gasperini, making him the focal point of the attack and placing him where he can do the most damage.
The stats are backed up by the eye test. After Roma's 1-1 Champions League draw with Fenerbahce last Thursday, when Malen set up his side's goal, French football journalist Julien Laurens told Match of the Day the Dutchman had become central to Gasperini's plans.
"He has been incredible since January," said Laurens.
"He has been really efficient, super clinical. Malen is at the heart of everything they do with the ball."
Following a familiar Serie A trend
Malen is not the only former Premier League player to have flourished in Italy.
Former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay has thrived since swapping Old Trafford for Naples. Since joining Napoli in August 2024, only five players have scored more Serie A goals than the Scotland international's 22.
His impact has been such that Napoli supporters have even erected a street shrine in his honour.
Former Manchester United striker Rasmus Hojlund has also enjoyed an upturn in fortunes. His time in north west England divided opinion among supporters and pundits alike.
But since his Napoli debut, only Federico Dimarco, Lautaro Martinez and Malen have recorded more goal involvements than the Denmark international (19).
Their success highlights how a move to Serie A can provide players with the opportunity to thrive in a different environment and role.
For Malen, however, the transformation has been particularly dramatic.
Rather than changing Malen's game, Roma appear to have found a role that gets the best out of him. Used almost exclusively as a striker, the Dutchman has responded by producing the kind of form that first brought him to the attention of Europe's biggest clubs.
For a player whose Premier League spell failed to meet expectations, his resurgence in Italy's capital ranks among the most notable revivals in European football this year.

Sources close to Gabriel, who turns 16 on 6 October, feel let down by United, arguing promises around the pathway to the first team have not been kept.
The club say it was anticipated Gabriel would become the youngest ever senior player by playing in Wednesday night's EFL Cup tie with Brighton. Given they lost 3-2 after leading 2-0, it is debatable whether that would have actually happened.

Razer refreshes the one-handed Tartarus Pro keyboard with improved switches
There's also an analog thumbpad.
Razer just introduced the Tartarus V2 Pro, a refresh of its popular one-handed gaming keyboard thingamajig. This is one of those ergonomic designs that features an adjustable palm rest. It's also not quite a keyboard in the conventional sense. It includes over 30 keys and buttons, but they're all programmable. There's no traditional QWERTY layout here.
In any event, the V2 Pro features several upgrades over its predecessor. The optical switches have been upgraded, the keys have a wider actuation (depth) range and the thumbpad is now an analog TMR design.
The device also integrates with some new proprietary input controls. Each button can access something called Snap Flex, which lets users attach two keys to a single press. This should make it easier to pull off multi-key actions with consistency.
There's also Snap Tap, which is pretty much the opposite of Snap Flex. It ensures that two selected keys are never actuated at the same time. This is pretty useful for FPS players who like to strafe, as putting in a reverse directional input at the very moment they stop moving can often lead to both keys accidentally being pushed at once. This can cancel the strafe and leave the avatar standing there motionless like a doofus.
As with the previous version, the Tartarus V2 Pro includes an adjustable wrist-rest. Each key also boasts RGB lighting for custom aesthetics. Finally, each and every of the 31 keys and buttons are fully programmable via the company's Synapse software. It's available right now and costs $200.

Apple's redesigned Health app is available now in the iOS 27.2 developer beta
New features like Health Age bring Apple's app more in line with competitors like Whoop and Oura.
After announcing plans to roll out its redesigned Health app later in 2026, Apple is giving anyone running the iOS 27.2 developer beta a chance to try it out now. The new Health app still acts as a repository for all the data your Apple Watch and other Bluetooth-enabled fitness devices collect, but in a first for Apple, now actually tries to do something with that information.
The current beta version of the app includes the new Insights tab that offers an overview of your daily metrics and trends across categories like sleep, fitness, and readiness (an Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 exclusive); and the Longevity tab, which collects several entirely new features. Under Longevity, you can find things like your Health Age, a score that uses data collected by your Apple Watch to estimate how your body functions relative to its age, and movement assessments that can measure things like flexibility, strength and balance. Apple says written and video commentary from health experts will now also appear dynamically in the app in response to your data.
Other promised features are apparently coming in future beta releases, like personalization for summaries in the Insights tab, personalized recommendations and the ability to order labs from Quest.
Combined, the new features go a long way to making the Health app and an Apple Watch more of a direct competitor to Oura, Whoop and Google. All three companies collect similar types of data to Apple, but use AI and their custom software to package it into unique scores, summaries and recommendations. Up until this point, the Health app has mostly existed as a dumping ground for all the raw information a wearable can collect, but not much else.
Apple hasn't announced a public release date for the redesigned Health app beyond "later this year," but the fact it's already appearing in developer betas seems to suggest it won't be too long.

OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms
- Published
The boss of ChatGPT maker Open AI says people should have more faith in his firm and others like it to do the right thing when it comes to artificial intelligence (AI) development amid rising public concerns about the risks.
"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Sam Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.
However, Altman noted that people were justified in their fears around AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.
Speaking in Washington meanwhile, left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon have both called for greater governance of AI.
Altman's comments came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce.
"It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."
It was the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could kill all humans by the end of the decade if left unchecked.
A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.
The fervour over the claims has led to more scrutiny of AI development in recent days, and in response, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called for the pace of all AI development to slow, external and urged governments to regulate the industry.
The post was applauded by Altman, as well as co-founder of Google's DeepMind Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk, owner of social media site X and AI assistant Grok.
By Tuesday, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement.
Altman said that he felt AI companies like his own were capable of essentially regulating themselves.
"We will get it right, I'm very confident in our company's and industry's ability to do this safely," Altman said, adding that he was sure that they would "keep alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" and if they couldn't, they would "slow down or stop".
Despite the assurances, political figures have cautioned against self-regulation.
Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont who votes with the Democrats, said decisions over AI's development have been made by "a handful of the richest people in the world", naming Elon Musk, Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, among others.
Speaking at a conference hosted in Washington, he said: "The people of this country must make the decisions about AI, and not just a handful of oligarchs."
Bannon, who served as a White House strategist during Trump's first term, also cast doubt on the tech industry's ability to self regulate.
"We can never trust what an oligarch says because... they're disingenuous and they lie," Bannon said at the same conference.
After Altman's comments, Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X that every AI lab has the ability and the incentive "to take its own actions" towards making AI tools and models that are designed for safety.
"Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," Zuckerberg wrote. "Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well."
Jensen Huang, head of Nvidia, also said at the same Tuesday conference that the AI firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released and not be managed by outside forces.
"We don't need new laws or regulations," Huang said, adding that there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products.
Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for the AI computing chips it makes.
"Safety is paramount. However, safety is an engineering problem," Huang said.
He added that if at any time a leader of an AI company lacks confidence in their product they should choose to not release it.
"That's a very obvious thing to do," Huang said. "Run as fast as you can, but if at any time you feel the institution is not in control, take a pause."
- Why doomsday warnings are not the only threat to the AI juggernaut 
  - Published7 hours ago
- Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards 
  - Published22 hours ago
Some industry figures have argued resurgent AI fears were overblown and were being jumped on to generate hype for the industry.
During the conference, Altman addressed a crowd of hundreds of business people, telling them they should use AI tools to aid in their work, but also needed them in order to protect their businesses from potentially AI-enabled cyber attacks.
The idea of AI executives being left to entirely regulate themselves has struck some in the industry as a bad idea.
Jack Clark, an Anthropic executive and co-founder, told the BBC on Monday that leaving AI to be a "totally unregulated industry" was "rolling dice with immense risks".
Patrick Hillman, the chief operating officer of Logical Intelligence, which is chaired by Yann LeCun, a sage of the AI industry, noted Tuesday how little faith people have in tech companies to do anything truly in the public interest, external.
"The only institution that Americans might trust less than Washington these days is Silicon Valley. I have worked and lived in both and I assure you both have earned this scepticism," Hillman said.
"If you believe what you are building is dangerous, show us what you are prepared to stop doing," he added.
Leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic have said they have recently started working towards some sort of industry-wide agreement on safety.
Amodei, during a cameo at the conference on Tuesday, said Anthropic is now in "a dialogue with the rest of the industry" about committing to better safety standards and checks on AI tools and development.
He also said that one of the biggest surprises of the AI boom was not how the technology itself has advanced, but its broader impact.
"We didn't appreciate that it would lead to companies growing so fast, and how quickly they would become central to things," Amodei said.
OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said last week that the company was also working with other AI labs, external "to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support." Those labs include Anthropic and Google Deepmind.
"With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good," Lehane wrote.

Flooding around the city of Malda in the Indian state of West Bengal since Thursday has had a devastating effect. So far, three deaths have been recorded and many areas are still flooded, with numerous villages affected, along with the region of Bhutni. Erosion from the flooding, reported from Khaskol, led to a disruption in river flow which led to a more severe impact in Bhutni. More than 100 boats have been sent out for evacuation.
At East Basudevpur, a 20ft (6-metre) embankment collapsed, reducing the channel from 550ft to under 150ft, which could lead to further flooding unless repaired. This flooding resulted after the Ganges River rose about 75cm above its “extreme danger” level owing to heavy rainfall.
A swell caused by Hurricane Marie led to significant beach erosion across Orange county in California on 7 September. The erosion formed a cliff edge on some of the beaches, along with exposing old asphalt, pipes and even pieces of an old pier. Local people say it is not uncommon to see beach erosion, but this has been one of the most severe cases.

China on Thursday (September 17) rejected the US use of tariffs to pressure countries over their purchases of Russian oil and gas, saying Beijing would not accept Washington’s “long-arm jurisdiction” or interference in its normal trade and economic cooperation.
The warning came after the US House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act 2026, which authorises President Donald Trump to impose sanctions on Russia and steep tariffs on major buyers of Russian energy, including China and India.
The legislation, already passed by the US Senate, cleared the House in a 262-159 vote and will now go to Trump for his signature.
Quick answers to key questions
China opposes US tariffs on Russian oil purchases because it believes such measures constitute 'long-arm jurisdiction' and disrupt its normal trade and economic cooperation with other nations.
China's Foreign Ministry emphasizes that it rejects unilateral sanctions that lack authorization from the UN Security Council, asserting that its trade relations are based on equality and mutual benefit.
US tariffs could significantly affect India's energy imports from Russia by increasing costs and potentially reducing the volume of crude oil purchased, amid India's reliance on Russian oil to meet its energy needs.
India is committed to ensuring its energy security and is exploring diversified sourcing of oil to mitigate the impact of potential US tariffs on its imports of Russian oil.
US sanctions on Russian oil could tighten the supply and increase prices in international energy markets, potentially impacting net energy importers like India, especially amid ongoing geopolitical tensions.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing opposes measures that lack authorisation from the UN Security Council.
“China engages in normal economic and trade cooperation with other countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit,” Guo said at a media briefing.
“Such cooperation does not target any third party and shall be free from disruption or coercion from any third party. China opposes long-arm jurisdiction and unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law and lack UN Security Council mandate,” he said.
The bill seeks sanctions not only against Russia's leadership and energy sector but also against vessels in the so-called “shadow fleet” that allegedly help Moscow evade sanctions on oil shipments.
It also authorises Trump to impose tariffs on countries including China and India in an effort to reduce their dependence on Russian oil and gas, along with additional sanctions targeting Iran.
Beijing's latest warning comes ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping's planned visit to Washington for a summit with Trump, expected on September 24-25.
The meeting would be the second summit between the two leaders this year. Trump visited Beijing in May and held extensive talks with Xi.
China has repeatedly opposed unilateral sanctions and has also continued to purchase Iranian oil despite US sanctions.
China and India are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil and gas. Much of China's Russian energy imports are transported through pipelines across its land border.
Despite the dispute over Russian energy, China and the US are continuing talks on tariffs.
China's Commerce Ministry said Thursday that Beijing and Washington were consulting on a reciprocal tariff reduction framework covering $30 billion worth of products from each side.
India has separately warned that the US sanctions legislation could have implications for New Delhi-Washington ties and the global energy market, particularly because it provides for punitive tariffs of up to 100% on major Russian crude buyers.
The Ministry of External Affairs said India remains “firmly committed” to ensuring the energy security of its 1.4 billion people and would take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests.
India is monitoring developments following the passage of the legislation, the MEA said, adding that the issue has been discussed at high levels with US interlocutors in recent months.
“The government will work closely with Indian trade and industry bodies to deal with the implications of these developments,” the ministry said.

India’s two-wheeler market is seeing a shift towards premium and super-premium motorcycles with more powerful engines, more features, styling, and higher price point growing at more than 22%, a senior TVS Motor Company official said on Thursday (September 17, 2026).
The official, — Head, Business, Premium, TVS Motor Company — was speaking at the launch of TVS Motor Company’s festive-season upgrades across its Apache RTR range, including new safety, connectivity and rider-control features on the RTR 160, RTR 160 4V and RTR 200 4V, as well as updates to the Apache 310 series and TVS Ronin, Vimal Sumbly.
Premium and super-premium two-wheelers account for around 17% of the overall two-wheeler market, they said. However, their contribution is significantly higher when the market is viewed specifically through motorcycles.
“Within motorcycle, 27% of the business or the industry is towards premium and super premium. That’s 150 cc plus,” the official said.
The company said the segment has maintained a high double-digit growth trajectory over the past two to two-and-a-half years, underscoring the shift in consumer preferences.
While premiumisation is being witnessed across consumer categories —from mobile phones and apparel to food and automobiles— it is also becoming increasingly pronounced in the two-wheeler market.
“And hence it’s so important for us to keep on capitalising on this investment that we keep on working on, to build up our portion of customer centricity, our customer obsession, and bringing in technology and disruption with a lot of speed and agility,” said Gaurav Gupta, President India 2 Wheeler Business, TVS.
On the electrification front, TVS Motor Company has seen a sharp increase in the contribution of electric vehicles, with EVs accounting for 10% of its sales last month, compared with 6.7% on a year-to-date basis last year.
The company attributed the increase to a strengthening EV ecosystem as well as growing consumer interest in electric mobility amid the West Asia crisis and its potential impact on fuel prices.

Two Britons among three killed in Swiss Alps light aircraft crash
All three occupants on board were killed when the small plane crashed high in the mountains
Three people have been killed, including two British citizens, after a plane crashed in the Swiss Alps.
The group were on board a light aircraft on Tuesday afternoon when it collided into a mountain slope ten minutes into its journey, killing all occupants on board. The victims have yet to be named and investigations into the incident are ongoing.
Authorities identified the plane as a Cirrus SR22T that had had taken off in Lugano before making a stopover at Sion Airport. It then left Sion to travel to the Rhone Valley and crashed near the town of Leukerbad in the southern canton of Valais at around 4pm.
Police said the plane had been headed towards Buochs Airfield in the canton of Nidwalden.
Signs of smoke were reported in the region raising the alarm, according to a statement by Valais police.
Emergency services including police, firefighters and three helicopters of the Valais Rescue Organisation rushed to the scene of the incident.
Witnesses said that fire and smoke were visible at the site of the crash. An image released by Valais Police show smoke rising from the locations as emergency workers attended the scene.
The reason for the crash is yet to be determined and the Swiss Transportation Board has opened an investigation into the cause.
Valais Police and the Office of the Attorney General have also launched a criminal inquiry following the crash.
The Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office said it was “providing support to the families of two British nationals who died in Switzerland” and is in contact with local authorities, in a statement to the BBC. “Our thoughts remain with the families during this difficult time.”
The incident comes less than a week after a bus carrying 48 Dutch passengers crashed in the Swiss Alps, killing five tourists on board.
The vehicle crashed into a guardrail and overturned before sliding down a slope. At least 40 people were left injured in the incident.
Rescue helicopters airlifted the injured to various hospitals as work began to identify the dead.

How Israel-Palestine broke up Sheeran-Macklemore
The implosion of Ed Sheeran’s ongoing world tour tells us something about shifting attitudes toward Israel.
I logged onto Slack this morning to find an incredible and indecipherable message from one of my coworkers. I briefly thought he was having a fever dream or I had forgotten how to read English. “Even some pro-Israel folks who hate Macklemore are ripshit at Robert Kraft for Streisand-effecting this guy,” the message read.
…included were several links that eventually helped explain why “Macklemore,” “Robert Kraft” and “Israel” would ever appear in the same sentence.
For those of you who have likewise not been following the fantastic implosion of Ed Sheeran’s ongoing tour, let’s break down this wild yarn. It begins with the washed-up millennial-cringe rapper Benjamin Hammond Haggerty, better known as Macklemore, who has lately a) taken up the cause of Palestinian independence and b) been opening for Sheeran on his blockbuster, 59-date Loop Tour.
Macklemore’s advocacy has not sat well with many observers, for reasons general (Gaza is one of the hottest buttons on earth) and particular (the rapper has a documented history of apparently antisemitic behavior, which he has since apologized for). Last Friday, the artist Pink published a lengthy criticism of Macklemore’s on-stage polemic, writing that his comments and use of violent wartime imagery had frightened many Jewish people, including her.
Around the same time, Robert Kraft — the sports magnate and Donald Trump ally who owns Gillette Stadium, outside of Boston — also allegedly notified Sheeran that he would not allow Macklemore to play his late-September show. Macklemore was subsequently dropped from the full tour.
Both he and Sheeran say multiple venues threatened to cancel if he continued to perform. And Kraft, who is Jewish, has also confirmed that he blocked Macklemore from playing at Gillette, citing both his recent advocacy and his “history of antisemitic rhetoric.”
But this is 2026. The backlash couldn’t simply end there. On Tuesday, the remaining opening acts and Sheeran’s backing band all pulled out of the tour in protest of the decision to boot Macklemore.
Go a little deeper
The whole roiling mess has become a cipher of some of the biggest and most explosive topics in American culture and politics: the specter of antisemitism, the limits of free speech and “cancel culture,” and the stark generational differences in Americans’ views of Israel and Gaza.
It’s arguably no coincidence that this particular controversy erupted on the tour of two musicians who are iconic among the 30- to 45-year-old set. American millennials, as a generational and political cohort, have grown sharply more critical of the state of Israel in the past 10 years — laying the groundwork for Gen Z’s high-profile pro-Palestinian activism and driving a larger narrative shift in US politics.
This is, in some ways, an underappreciated dynamic in the debate over American support for Israel. Campus protests, organized by 20-something college students, have come to define young Americans’ growing disillusionment. Speaking on a podcast last year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said “there’s work to be done” to win over Gen Z, in particular. (Macklemore, who is 43, named his pro-Palestinian protest song “Hind’s Hall” in honor of the protests at Columbia.)
But the attitudinal shift on Israel, especially on the left, began long before Gen Z became a major political force. Americans under 30 were, for instance, more likely to blame Israel than Hamas for the 2014 Gaza war. And during the mid-2010s, millennial activists sometimes wrapped Palestinian independence into broader social justice and anti-colonialist causes, including the Black Lives Matter movement. Several of the organizations that mobilized pro-Palestinian campus protests in 2024 had similarly been around for a decade or more.
Today, of course, the shift extends beyond progressive millennials: Sympathy for Israel is down among younger Republicans, as well. It has, in fact, declined sharply across generations.
But over the past two years, the sharpest drop has been among Americans ages 35 to 54. In other words…the exact group of people who might still be jamming to Macklemore.

The discovery of the bodies of seven women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide.
When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral.
Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising.
On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in Olifantsfontein, about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed.
“In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. In the year to 31 March 2024, more than 27,600 people were murdered, 5,578 of them women, according to the latest police data.
For years, women have called on the South African government to take gender-based violence seriously. After hundreds of women protested on the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis.
However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed.
The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas. They should avoid secluded spaces, remain vigilant and, where possible, travel or exercise in groups.”
South African women responded with anger at the idea that they had to be responsible for their own safety, with many runners noting they already took precautions, such as sharing routes. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said the advocacy group Women For Change.
“It should not take a missing woman, a desperate family, runners and communities searching, and a case going viral, before an area is searched with this intensity,” the group said.
Detectives said on Saturday that they were examining a serial killer angle. However, on Monday, a police spokesperson, Athlenda Mathe, told reporters: “For now, nothing tells us that we’ve got a serial killer.”
Mathe added that a suspect in the killing in July of the first woman, her boyfriend, was in custody.
Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations.
Although the gender of the suspect or suspects in the other killings has not been confirmed, campaigners called on men to take responsibility for violence against women and children.
“When some of these things happen in our presence, most of us men tend to look the other way,” said Bafana Khumalo, a co-executive director of Sonke Gender Justice.
“You have excuses like ‘No, it’s not my business’. We feel strongly that violence against women is our business. We need, as men, to begin to face each other squarely and hold each other accountable.”
The identification of Moselakgomo’s body has triggered an outpouring of grief.
Mokoena met her about two years ago, when Moselakgomo joined a running club so she did not have to train alone on Saturdays.
“She’s an amazing woman,” said Mokoena. “She always spoke about her daughter. Tsontso always said ‘Bye guys, I have to go, I have to go to my child’.
“That’s just an example of how close she was with her baby girl. And she was a really light-spirited, funny and joyful woman, who was kind – very, very kind.”
Running clubs around South Africa organised events to remember Moselakgomo and Mokoena said she hoped this would help push the government and police to do more to protect women.
She added: “I’m just happy that the world, or at least our country, was standing still for a moment to acknowledge what is happening. Let’s get this out there and figure out exactly what is happening to women.”

Toward the end of my college days, I harbored a not-so-secret crush. She and I carried on a mild flirtation, dancing around the possibility of more, but it wasn’t until she found out I’d never seen The Fast and the Furious that she gave me an opening.
“What?!” she exclaimed. “It’s my favorite movie!” So we made plans to watch it at her dorm the next day. Even if I didn’t like it, I reasoned, the experience would constitute a worthy reversal of the trope about men forcing testosterone-soaked action movies on their girlfriends. I’ll spare you the details of what happened that afternoon, but it may come as no surprise that I gave the film an enthusiastic five-star review.
In the 25 years since the launch of the franchise, F&F has massively capitalized on such runaway infatuations. The big, bald, sleeveless blockbusters serve as monuments to America’s demented car culture, product placement (Corona, anyone?), and the ambiguously defined bonds of “family”—pronounced “fambly.” With their high-octane set pieces that ignore all known physics, leavened by subpar acting and threadbare storylines, the films invite us to submit to some reptilian part of our brain that cares only for power and speed.
Which is why the series was ideal inspiration for Universal Studios Hollywood’s new foray into cutting-edge outdoor roller coasters. On Wednesday, the long-anticipated Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift opened to the public, offering parkgoers the chance to hop into replicas of the movies’ muscle cars—including Dom Toretto’s 1970 Dodge Charger R/T—that spin and soar along more than 4,000 feet of track at speeds of up to 72 miles per hour. (A different version of the ride is slated to debut at Universal’s Florida park next year.)
The day before, select media and content creators had the chance to experience the attraction without the inconvenience of waiting in line, and I’m pleased to report that it didn't disappoint: I rode it three times in a row and could have gone back for more. Its four launch sections and three corkscrew inversions made for a whip-fast adrenaline rush, augmented by revving motor noise from seat-mounted speakers. In Dom’s lead car, you can even detect the braking resistance as you slide into a drift. I hollered with glee throughout each circuit, making sure to occasionally shout “TOLUCA LAKE,” the name of the affluent neighborhood next door; residents have been very upset about all the screaming.
If you want to feel like you’re a Fast & Furious character within the safer confines of a precisely engineered thrill machine, you can hardly ask for anything better. And despite its innovative design, the overall aesthetic of the ride and its environs demonstrates a welcome nostalgia for the more grounded origins of these movies, when the crew was hijacking trucks full of DVD players instead of launching Pontiacs into space. On your way through the queueing path, you’ll pass garage workbenches littered with tools and LA-style street murals that pay homage to racing culture.
Those welcome simple touches might make you wonder if we’ll ever actually see the conclusion of the increasingly bloated and absurd F&F saga in the perpetually delayed 11th film, Fast Forever. Between the ongoing rewrites and budgetary obstacles, it has yet to even enter production. (The previous film, Fast X, was released in 2023.) Rather than being too big to fail, it’s as though the challenge of topping each successive spectacle has made the Furious brand too unwieldy to push forward.
Could it be that, in the absence of a finale, the F&F rides will cap off the series? In their invitation for Tuesday’s press preview event, Universal noted that Vin Diesel himself would be on hand during a ceremony to help executives cut the ribbon (or, as it happened, a fake plastic chain). But the man synonymous with the franchise was nowhere to be found when the time came to declare the ride officially open. The closest we got was a gaggle of fans in costume as Toretto, complete with bald caps.
When I checked out Diesel’s Instagram account for clues as to what he was up to, I found that he had just posted set photos of himself as Kaulder, his character from The Last Witch Hunter, a 2015 dark fantasy film. Lionsgate confirmed last year that a sequel is in the works, and it appears that Diesel was stoking anticipation with this sneak peek. When this guy isn’t acknowledging a major milestone for the burnt-rubber films that made him a household name, you have to wonder if there’s much gas left in the tank.
Not everything lasts—certainly not college flings that start with stunt-driver flicks. That the Fast & Furious series has earned billions of dollars and spanned a quarter century based on an equally thin premise is a testament to how far this juvenile spirit can take you. Maybe bringing it to life with a really fun roller coaster is the best way to let it roar off into the sunset. When you climb aboard, take a look around at your fellow passengers. You’re the family now.

Amazon MGM Studios’ Phoolan, written and directed by International Emmy Award-winning filmmaker Richie Mehta, received a standing ovation following its World Premiere at the 51st Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) on September 17. The Hindi action drama was screened in the festival’s Special Presentation section at the Princess of Wales Theatre before an audience of more than 2,000.
Richie Mehta’s Phoolan receives standing ovation at Toronto International Film Festival world premiere
Starring Sneha Kumari in the titular role, the film features Anurag Thakur, Vikram Pratap Singh, Aakash Dahiya, Prateek Pachouri and Dev Dutt Budholiya in pivotal roles. The film focuses on a defining period in the life of Phoolan Devi, with its story centred on a 48-hour siege involving an armed group of 2,000 men.
Phoolan is based on Phoolan Devi’s autobiography, I, Phoolan Devi: The Autobiography of India's Bandit Queen, published by Editions Robert Laffont. Rather than covering her entire life, the film focuses on a specific chapter, exploring the experiences that shaped her before she became a widely known figure.
Speaking about the World Premiere, writer-director and producer Richie Mehta said, “Phoolan Devi's story is one that demands to be told with honesty, and without compromise. I was drawn to a very specific chapter of Phoolan's life, the formative years before the world knew her name, contrasted with the period where she was a misunderstood legend. It felt essential to me to strip away the mythology and reveal the human underneath. The themes at the heart of her story — resilience in the face of adversity, the search for dignity, and the courage to claim one's own voice —are timeless. They resonate just as strongly today as they did then, across cultures and geographies. That is why this felt like the right moment to bring her story to the screen. From Poacher to Phoolan, Amazon MGM Studios has been a true creative collaborator, one that backs a filmmaker's vision and gives stories like these the global canvas they deserve. To witness the audience at TIFF rise to their feet, visibly moved, tells me that Phoolan's story has connected in exactly the way we hoped it would. I hope I have done justice to her voice and her story, the way she wanted the world to know.”
Shilangi Mukherji, Director & Head of SVOD Business, Prime Video, India, said, “Our relationship with Richie Mehta goes back to Poacher, a fiercely personal project that became one of our most critically acclaimed Indian Originals. What defines Richie is his unwavering commitment to truth. He doesn't sensationalize; he tells stories with a quiet, unflinching honesty that stays with you long after the credits roll. With Phoolan, backing his vision was instinctive. At Amazon MGM Studios, we believe in the conviction of our filmmakers and their creative freedom to tell stories honestly and Richie exemplifies exactly that. Phoolan is one of those stories carrying a universal theme that transcends borders and languages. We are excited for audiences to experience this film in an authentic way.”
Shareen Mantri, Producer, Namah Pictures, said, "Phoolan is an incredibly special film for all of us at Namah Pictures, and seeing it premiere at TIFF is both emotional and a moment of immense pride. This is a story that has lived in our hearts for a long time, a story of courage and the strength of the human spirit. Richie Mehta has brought such honesty and sensitivity to every frame, and Sneha Kumari has delivered a truly remarkable performance as Phoolan that I believe will resonate deeply with audiences”, said Shareen Mantri, Producer, Namah Pictures. “What makes this collaboration special is how each partner brings something distinct to the table. Namah Pictures' deep connection to Indian stories, Richie Mehta's nuanced and sensitive filmmaking, and Amazon MGM Studios' ability to bring meaningful cinema to a global stage, together, creates the right home for a story like Phoolan's. Watching people at TIFF connect with her story reminded me why we made this film. There are stories that belong not just to one person, but to all of humanity. Phoolan's life, defined by courage, dignity, and an unbreakable will to survive, is one such story. It is this universality that drives us to carry her narrative forward, using her story as a guiding light for storytelling that truly matters.”
The premiere was attended by the film’s cast and creative team, including Sneha Kumari, Anurag Thakur, Aakash Dahiya and Vikram Pratap Singh. Richie Mehta was joined at the event by producers Shareen Mantri Kedia, Kanwal Kohli and Kishor Arora of Namah Pictures, along with Shilangi Mukherji representing Prime Video, India.
Produced by Shareen Mantri Kedia, Kishor Arora, Kanwal Kohli and Richie Mehta, Phoolan is a Namah Pictures production. Following its TIFF premiere, the film is scheduled to premiere on Prime Video in India and across more than 240 countries and territories worldwide at a later date.
