Air pollution spiked after the Trump administration stopped embassy monitoring
Growing up in Shanghai in the early 1990s, Eric Zou remembers the air.
"I lived a couple of miles next to a chemical plant and it was just really bad, really foggy," he says. "It's the middle of the day, but you can't see the sun."
Intensive industrial activity blanketed many cities in China during the 1990s and 2000s with extremely hazardous air. But Zou, now an environmental economist at the University of Michigan, says that many people didn't really understand this smog as air pollution, or something that could harm them.
"When you have a big smog event, people often talk about that as fog, they think it was just like bad weather," says Zou. One big key to changing that sentiment, he says, was information initially provided by the United States.
In 2008, U.S. officials installed an air quality monitor on the embassy in Beijing and began making the information public. Over time, that helped spur demand for cleaner air, says Zou. "Once you have pollution information, it tends to be that it actually helps people to realize, 'Oh, I actually value air quality.' "
Since 2008, the State Department's monitoring initiative has expanded to more than 80 embassies and consulates. Research suggests that monitoring contributed to measurable improvements in air quality, especially across many low- and middle-income countries with limited monitoring systems of their own.
But in March 2025, the Trump administration shuttered that program, citing monetary costs. Research out this week suggests the move had health costs for the people living in those countries. Over the several months following the shutdown, air pollution levels measured via satellite increased by 24-33%, researchers reported Monday in the journal PNAS.
The State Department did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication.
"It's a great study, high quality. And it's a real pity," says Andrea La Nauze, an environmental economist at Deakin University in Australia who has researched the benefits of the program, but wasn't involved in this study. The program "led to sustained improvements in air quality that were continuing to increase after 10 years," she says.
She says this new research suggests those improvements aren't guaranteed if monitoring stops.
Measuring the consequences of not measuring
When Zoe Yiyuan Zhou first heard the news that the Trump administration was shuttering the embassy air quality monitoring, it struck her as a research opportunity.
"It's such a rare case to study this drawback," says the Columbia University climate researcher. While there's ample evidence of the benefits of increased monitoring, she says there aren't many examples of a sudden falloff of surveillance.
Zhou and her colleagues decided to compare air pollution levels before and after monitoring ceased across 46 cities. Since they didn't have on-the-ground measures of air quality for the latter part of that comparison, they used satellite data for both.
The team found no significant trends in air pollution over the 300 days preceding the end of U.S. reporting. But about three to four months after reporting ended, pollution had gone up, on average by about 30%. Satellite data isn't a perfect substitute for monitors that can measure on-the-ground pollution. The researchers estimate their satellite measurements translate to about a 4% increase in PM2.5 — the small suspended particles that can enter the lungs and bloodstream and cause health problems.
"That magnitude is certainly concerning," says La Nauze. "Particulate matter is a serious and dangerous thing, and being exposed to it is not good."
The increase was highest in Southeast Asian cities, including Manila, in the Philippines, Rangoon in Myanmar and Vientiane in Laos, says Zhao. Pollution also spiked more in cities with fewer monitoring alternatives.
The study can't say why pollution increased after monitoring stopped.
For countries with nonexistent or nascent monitoring programs, U.S. data may have prompted more regulatory action, says Zou. "Maybe the U.S. Embassy was a really strong force, in terms of a third-party auditing mechanism, and once that's removed, people are like 'Now I can just pollute, right?'"
In many industries, it costs money to cut down on pollution, says Zhou. When monitoring stops, companies may see it as an opportunity to cut those costs.
But the researchers did find some potentially hopeful news. Pollution levels seemed to go back down somewhat after peaking about three or four months after monitoring stopped.
It's difficult to say why this decrease happened, Zhou says, or whether the trend will continue. She suspects that it may reflect other forms of monitoring, by individuals or local governments, coming online in the wake of the U.S. withdrawal.
But not all areas may have the ability to readily make up for what's been lost, she says, especially in regions where air quality monitoring is new.
"Data is just so important," says Zhou. "Having access to information is necessary to make sure that these previous gains can continue. Public information creates accountability."

In July this year, OpenAI’s models were being tested in a controlled cybersecurity environment and tasked with spotting and exploiting software vulnerabilities. The models found ways around the intended network restrictions and created a “swarm”, with different agents delegating tasks to one another, during an unintended attack on the infrastructure of AI platform Hugging Face. The incident turned longstanding concerns about autonomous AI systems into a more immediate question: what happens when increasingly capable models find ways to operate beyond the restrictions imposed on them? It also became one of the “warning shots” cited by researchers calling for frontier AI labs to coordinate on safety. The debate intensified last week when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon publicly quit the company and accused leading AI labs of racing towards self-improving superintelligence without adequate safeguards. Soon after, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei turned these concerns into a concrete proposal, urging frontier AI companies to “pace” their development. His proposal included independent evaluators, common safety standards, and greater coordination between governments and AI companies. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backed parts of the proposal, saying pacing the frontier has become a primary topic of discussions at OpenAI and that the company would commit to independent evaluations. However, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has rejected calls to slow AI development. “Run as fast as you can,” he said, arguing that companies should continue advancing the technology but hold back products until they know they are safe. The disagreement has sharpened the debate over what pacing means, whether it can work amid intense competition, and who should decide where the brakes are applied. AI’s Shift From Answers To Actions AI has moved from models that largely responded to prompts to reasoning systems capable of using tools, executing code, and coordinating multiple agents to solve complex tasks. Anthropic has warned that agents interacting with codebases, markets, and other digital systems could create a new class of risks, with machine-to-machine interactions eventually outpacing human oversight. Shayak Mazumder, founder of agentic AI venture studio Adya, said newer agents can bypass instructions because they can explore paths developers may not have anticipated, creating a gap between what developers intend and what a system may discover it can do. OpenAI’s own evaluations have also highlighted advances in agentic coding and cybersecurity, prompting it to strengthen network and tool restrictions and monitor risky actions. Ganesh Gopalan, cofounder of Gnani.ai, pointed to jailbreaks, including the Hugging Face incident, and recursively self-improving systems as evidence that the risks are becoming harder to dismiss, even if their precise nature remains unclear. “There is evidence that definitely there is some risk, for sure. But the point is how do you control those risks and what actions will be taken? I think that’s where it’s a completely grey area,” Gopalan said. Who Gets To Write The AI Rulebook? Amodei said pacing does not mean halting AI development. His proposal calls for frontier companies to give embedded third-party evaluators ongoing, employee-like access to assess safety practices and report incidents. He also wants companies in democratic countries to establish common standards before seeking broader international coordination. Pacing could mean slowing the training of more capable models, restricting experiments involving recursive self-improvement, or evaluating models more rigorously before release. However, Gopalan said the lack of a common definition creates a fundamental problem. If some frontier AI companies slow down, it remains unclear whether the same rules would apply to their competitors or to other countries. “If you’re going to say, pacing it, are you going to stop? Are they ready to allow other companies or countries to catch up?” he said. Mazumder believes mandatory checks are needed before frontier models reach users. “We need to come up with global standards and national standards to ensure that LLM has passed those checks before it can be released to the public,” he said. Amitabh Kumar, cofounder of content governance platform Contrails.ai, said frontier companies should have a voice because of their technical expertise, but universities, independent scientists, and policymakers should have an equal seat at the table. He is particularly sceptical of company-appointed evaluators. Could Safety Become A Competitive Moat? Mandatory evaluations, audits, compute controls, and other safety requirements would also increase the cost of developing frontier AI. For Gopalan, the risk is not merely the cost of regulation but the concentration of power it could create around a handful of well-funded companies. “Right now, it’s more of a few companies that are becoming all-powerful,” he said, warning that safety rules should not be used to prevent other companies or countries from catching up. Large AI labs may be able to absorb the cost of audits and repeated evaluations. Smaller companies may struggle, particularly if controls extend to advanced GPUs, computing infrastructure, or training resources. Kumar pushed back against the idea that safety requirements would necessarily become a barrier, arguing that regulation inevitably carries a cost that can become part of doing business in a high-risk industry. Meanwhile, a managing partner at a Bengaluru-based VC firm, who didn’t want to be named, pointed to the gap between private valuations and profitability, along with the capital required to keep developing increasingly powerful models. The investor questioned if the valuations being discussed for the potential public listings of companies like Anthropic and Open AI could be justified, given their profitability timelines and infrastructure spending. “Profitability is far away and infrastructure commitments are out of control,” the investor said. The investor also speculated that safety concerns could give the companies’ CEOs grounds to postpone their listings. However, there is no evidence linking the calls for pacing AI development to their IPO timelines. The more immediate question is whether future safety requirements would constrain the largest AI labs or reinforce their advantage over emerging rivals. While Anthropic is moving towards a possible IPO, Altman has said OpenAI will not go public this year, citing the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems. OpenAI is meanwhile reportedly exploring fresh funding at a $1.2 Tn valuation. The Geopolitics Of Slowing AI Even if US frontier labs agree to pace development, there is no guarantee that companies elsewhere will follow. Amodei argued that failing to build advanced AI could hand the technology to authoritarian powers, while moving too quickly could create uncontrollable risks. The US, therefore, has an incentive to reduce AI risks but also economic and national security reasons to prevent China from overtaking it. Huang’s argument reflects the concern that slowing American labs may only allow rivals to close the capability gap. For countries outside the current frontier, the concern is that safety could evolve into a nuclear-style non-proliferation regime, restricting access to advanced models, chips, or computing infrastructure, according to Gopalan. The issue is relevant for India, where Chinese open-source models have already found significant traction. “If Chinese AI models are cheaper, free, faster, whatever, startups should not be stopped from using them,” the investor quoted above said. Can The AI Race Police Itself? The divide between Amodei and Huang captures the central fault line. One side believes frontier capabilities are advancing too quickly for existing safety mechanisms to keep up. The other believes development should continue at full speed, with companies responsible for ensuring that unsafe products do not reach users. Both approaches carry risks. Voluntary commitments may collapse under competitive pressure, while standards shaped primarily by incumbent labs could raise barriers for smaller competitors and concentrate control over the frontier. Pacing AI development, therefore, is not merely a technical safety question. It is also a contest over who controls the technology, who bears the cost of making it safer, and who gets to participate in the next phase of the AI race. Edited by Vinaykumar Rai

Indian-origin US Congressman 
Raja Krishnamoorthi
 has hit back at a Florida city councilman after he was told to “take your curry and go home”, saying America is his home and that no one can decide who belongs in the country.
Palm Bay City Councilman Chandler Langevin directed the remark at Krishnamoorthi in a post on X, writing, “I won Rajesh. Take your curry and go home.”
Krishnamoorthi, a Democrat representing Illinois, responded: “I’m staying. So is the curry. America is my home. No bigot gets to decide who is American, who belongs here, or what they have for dinner. That’s the America I’ll always fight for.”
The latest exchange came days after Krishnamoorthi criticised a Department of Homeland Security social media post featuring a man identified as “Mr. Singh”. The DHS post, styled as a movie poster, told “Mr. Singh” to “get off our roads” and warned him to “self-deport or find out”.
Krishnamoorthi said the post demonised a name shared by more than 160,000 people in the US and said Sikh and South Asian Americans were “as American as anyone”.
Krishnamoorthi’s remarks came amid renewed attention on Langevin, who has repeatedly made comments about Indian immigrants and the Indian American community.
What did Chandler Langevin say about Indians?
Langevin, a Palm Bay City Council member, came under scrutiny in 2025 over social media posts targeting Indian immigrants. He called for the deportation of Indians and later directed several posts at Krishnamoorthi after the congressman criticised his remarks.
In one post, Langevin described Krishnamoorthi as a “foreign occupier” and mocked his name, while referring to his country of origin as “Tatooine”, the fictional planet from the Star Wars franchise.
Krishnamoorthi responded that he was born in India, raised in Illinois and elected by voters there.
The Palm Bay City Council took action against Langevin in October 2025. On October 2, the council voted 4-1 to ask Florida Governor Ron DeSantis to suspend him from office.
Later that month, it voted 3-2 to censure him. The restrictions included limiting his ability to introduce agenda items, speak during council reports and serve on city-appointed boards and committees.
Langevin subsequently sued the city, arguing that his First Amendment rights had been violated.
The case was settled in February 2026, with Palm Bay agreeing to a USD 55,000 settlement. Court records show the federal case was closed after the parties notified the court of the settlement.
Krishnamoorthi’s recent comments on South Asian Americans
Krishnamoorthi has repeatedly spoken out against social media posts targeting South Asian Americans.
On September 10, he criticised the DHS “Mr. Singh” post, saying the government should not use its power to suggest that someone's faith, heritage or identity means they do not belong in the US.
He also recently criticised a social media post by Texas Republican Railroad Commission nominee Bo French that featured South Asian students at the University of Texas. Krishnamoorthi said the students were being demonised based on their appearance.

Wrexham co-owners Reynolds, McElhenney spoof Southampton 'Spygate' ahead of Championship clash
Sept 17 : Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney are no strangers to mixing football and showbusiness, and the Wrexham co-owners did both in their latest advertisement for internet browser Firefox, playfully lampooning Southampton's "Spygate" scandal ahead of Saturday's Championship clash.
Reynolds, the Canadian-American actor best known for playing the wisecracking antihero "Deadpool", leaned into the controversy in the 59-second video released on Thursday.
Emerging from behind a tree alongside McElhenney, Reynolds says: "Today, for no particular reason, we want to talk about the importance of privacy."

"There's some things that you just don't want any other people to see ..." Reynolds continues, before later adding: "Privacy - that's important to people everywhere," as the pair reference Oxford United, Ipswich Town and Middlesbrough, clubs whose training sessions Southampton were accused of observing last season.
The pair later highlight Firefox's privacy features, with Reynolds remarking: "Refreshing, huh? An organization that actually respects your privacy."
The joke was a nod to the "Spygate" row that erupted in May after Middlesbrough complained of unauthorised filming at their training ground.
The English Football League charged Southampton, who were later expelled from the Championship playoffs after acknowledging they had observed opponents' training sessions within 72 hours of matches.
Middlesbrough, who lost to Southampton in the playoff semi-finals, were reinstated in the final, where Hull City ultimately secured promotion to the Premier League.

Investigation launched into death of Ukrainian activist found dead in the Algarve
Tributes have been paid to Pavlo Sadokha, a leading voice for Ukrainians in Portugal
An inquiry has been launched after a Ukrainian activist and critic of Putin’s Russia was found dead in Portugal.
The body of Ukrainian activist Pavlo Sadokha was discovered in Quarteira, a costal town in the Algarve region, on Sunday.
The 56-year-old was born in the Ukrainian city Lviv, and had lived in Portugal for more than two decades before his death. In recent years he had spoken out against Russian propaganda and Kremlin efforts to militarize young people.
Portuguese newspaper Journal de Noticias reported that while the cause of death had not yet been revealed it was believed to be from natural causes. Sadokha had a history of heart disease and police at the scene found no evidence of foul play, the outlet added.
However, Portugal’s Public Prosecution Service have now opened an inquiry to rule out any third party involvement in Sadokha’s death. According to Portuguese newspaper Correio da Manha, friends and relatives had called for a full autopsy.
Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine Andrii Sybiha paid tribute to Sadokha in a statement on Facebook.
“Pavlo was one of those rare leaders for whom the struggle for Ukraine knew no days off or vacations,” he wrote. “Thanks to his principled stance and tireless energy, Ukraine’s voice in Portugal resonated consistently, clearly, and uncompromisingly.
“His sudden passing is a tremendous loss for the Ukrainian community in Portugal and for Ukrainians worldwide. We have lost a staunch defender of Ukraine, a trusted advisor, and a radiant person with a big heart.”
In 2010, Sadokha was elected chairman of the Council of the Ukrainian Union in Portugal and in 2017, he was awarded the Order of Merit, III Class, by the president of Ukraine.
He served as the Ukrainian World Congress (UWC) vice president for southern Europe, deputy chair of the UWC International Educational Coordinating Council, and president of the Union of Ukrainians in Portugal.
In a statement, the UWC said: “Pavlo dedicated decades of his life to Ukraine and to serving the Ukrainian community in Portugal. He was a key member of the UWC leadership team and was instrumental in establishing the Ukrainian Youth Association (CYM) in Portugal.
“For many years, he was one of the strongest voices for Ukrainians in Portugal. He helped organize Euromaidan solidarity actions in Portugal in 2013-2014 and, following Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, organized rallies, appeals to Portuguese government officials and support for Ukraine’s defenders.
“He also co-organized Lisbon’s annual Peace March and worked to strengthen Ukrainian media and promote Ukraine’s history and culture.”
Paul Grod, UWC president added: “Pavlo was a highly regarded Ukrainian community leader in Portugal and on the world stage. He was a close friend and someone I could always count on.
“He cared deeply and dedicated his life to serving Ukraine and its people around the world. This is a massive loss and he will be missed deeply. May his memory be eternal.”

One dead after torrential rain and flash floods hit Barcelona region
- Published
North-eastern Spain has been hit by torrential rain and flash floods, leaving one person dead and causing widespread disruption across the region.
Spain's national weather agency AEMET issued warnings for heavy rain across eastern regions on Wednesday, including a red alert for Barcelona's coastline.
Rescuers recovered the body of a man on Thursday in Olivella, around 40km (25 miles) west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away by a stream, authorities said.
The deluge has disrupted travel across Catalonia and Valencia, with flights cancelled and roads submerged. Authorities have advised against unnecessary travel, while Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez warned of "very complicated situations".
Emergency services in Catalonia said they received more than 850 calls related to the downpours and catalogued over 500 incidents.
Catalan firefighters said on X on Thursday that they had recovered the "lifeless body of a man" in Olivella, correcting earlier reports that had identified the missing person as a woman.
Videos shared on social media showed partially submerged cars and rescue workers attempting to reach a vehicle trapped in a heavily flooded underpass.
In Barcelona, some metro stations were closed and buses diverted, while regional trains were disrupted and flights delayed or cancelled at El Prat airport.
Neighbouring Valencia had more than 70mm (2.76in) of rain fall in just half an hour in several municipalities, according to AVAMET.
"Rarely have we seen such rainfall accumulations in 30 minutes," the meteorological association said on X.
Emergency services reported 478 incidents in the Valencia province, mostly involving property damage, leaks and traffic disruption.
In the regional capital, all metro lines were suspended and the city's airport shuttered for several hours, causing flights to be diverted.
The downpour comes as Spain emerges from its hottest summer on record and an exceptionally warm start to September.
Scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the Mediterranean storms that typically hit eastern Spain in autumn.
The Mediterranean Sea absorbs heat during summer, increasing evaporation and contributing to heavier rainfall when storms develop.
The flooding comes less than two years after devastating flooding in Valencia killed more than 230 people.

Lunacy, purveyor of fine VST plug-ins like Cube, a synth that you control by moving a ball around a 3D space, has just launched Nova, a platform where creators can build custom music tools using AI and sell them to others. At first, there will be a handful of instruments available, built either by Lunacy or a small selection of partner developers. But eventually, the company will launch Nova Builder, which will let anyone build their own plug-ins or remix existing ones.
Lunacy Audio Nova is a place to build and sell your own AI-powered music plug-ins
It’s a development platform, a storefront, and a plug-in for your DAW.
There are 10 plug-ins available initially, covering everything from crunchy chiptunes to warbly vintage synths and evil ambient drones. None of them do anything particularly unique, but they all sound pretty solid. The lo-fi Drift Cassette synth and Silhouettes are my two favorites right off the bat. The former gets you nostalgic ’80s tones, while the latter is all about sci-fi soundscapes. They all have pretty simple interfaces reminiscent of Native Instruments’ Play series, with bright colors and a handful of controls.
What makes Nova different is that plug-ins aren’t built using code in a text editor. Instead, they’re assembled using premade effects blocks and AI prompts. It’s not unlike Polyend’s Endless, except instead of vibe-coding a guitar pedal, you’re creating music software anyone can use on their computer.
Nova instruments don’t require dedicated hardware. Heck, they don’t even require a digital audio workstation (DAW) and can run directly in a browser. That’s of limited use, though. So there’s also a Nova host plug-in that runs in your DAW of choice. It lets you browse and load any Nova plug-in from your library and swap between them quickly.
Lunacy envisions Nova as a tinkerers’ paradise. Cofounder and CEO Casey Kolb said in a press release that, “Say someone makes a step sequencer and shares it. You open it and wish you could add a custom shimmer reverb to the end of the signal chain. You can add that, then you can share your new version with a friend, and that friend expands it further. The tools are never fixed; they are always evolving.”
So far, though, the response from the music-making community to AI has been rather tepid. Tools like Endless have been met with, at best, cautious curiosity, and at worst, outright hostility. Lunacy is developing Nova out in the open, posting developer diaries and actively seeking customer input, in an attempt to avoid some of the same pitfalls and win over wary musicians.

The world is bracing for a “super” El Niño, and its effects are already being felt in India, where the monsoon has brought less rain than average but more intense downpours.
Meteorologists predict that the current El Niño, which is developing over the Pacific, could be one of the strongest in living memory. India is likely to be heavily affected, particularly later in the monsoon, when El Niño’s influence tends to strengthen.
But, as Ligin Joseph of the University of Southampton explains in The Conversation, its effects on India’s monsoon are not straightforward. A previous study in Science found that El Niño tends to bring more extreme summer monsoon rainfall to India.
This year, the southern state of Kerala has felt the brunt of the building super El Niño, with about a fifth less rain than normal. Yet intense downpours in the first week of August triggered flash flooding and landslides, killing 26 people.
The super El Niño is expected to peak after India’s monsoon season, but Indians are already keeping an anxious eye on the skies, wondering where and when the next deluge may come.

This story appeared in The Logoff, a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here.
Trump’s failed Fed takeover
The Fed is raising interest rates, despite Trump’s best efforts.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s Fed gambit has officially failed.
What happened? On Wednesday, the Federal Reserve voted to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percent, citing ongoing inflation. The rate hike was widely expected, and normally it would be largely unremarkable (at least for this newsletter, which doesn’t generally cover monetary policy).
In this case, however, it’s also a direct rebuke to Trump, who has spent the last year-and-a-half-plus demanding rate cuts — and plotting a Fed takeover to get them.
How has Trump gone after the Fed? It’s a long list, but the two most significant episodes are Trump’s efforts to force Fed governor Lisa Cook from her seat to stack the Fed board in his favor (still ongoing) and the Justice Department’s coercive criminal investigation against former Fed chair Jerome Powell (since ended).
Neither succeeded, but Trump likely thought his goal was in reach when the Senate confirmed his nominee for Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, in May. On Wednesday, however, Warsh — several months into a four-year term as Fed chair — bucked Trump’s persistent demands by voting for the rate hike.
Why does this matter? Trump successfully exerting political control over the Fed would be extremely bad news for just about everyone. Lowering interest rates is a great way to juice the economy in the short term — exactly what he might want as his party faces down a potential midterm wipeout. But it could seriously damage the economy’s long-term health too, which is why the Fed is designed — successfully, as it turns out — to be insulated from partisan politics.
What else should I know? So far, Trump’s response to the hike has been muted, at least by his standards.
He’s threatened to take more drastic action, however: Earlier this month, he said he would suspend trade relations “WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT” if the Fed went through with its rate hike.
It’s not clear whether he’ll make good on that threat — but one way or another, we likely haven’t heard the last of Trump’s Fed vendetta.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Judge orders Trump to give 30 days notice before any steps to demolish Kennedy Centre
The order came after US President Donald Trump said the Kennedy Centre could be "ripped down" if his plans for the venue were not carried out.
WASHINGTON: A federal judge ordered US President Donald Trump's administration on Thursday (Sep 17) to provide at least 30 days' notice before taking any steps to demolish the Kennedy Centre, the landmark performing arts venue that has become a flashpoint in his efforts to reshape the US capital.
US District Judge Christopher Cooper issued the order after lawyers for a Democratic congresswoman who is suing to keep the venue open and Trump's name off its facade submitted new evidence citing the Republican president's comments on Wednesday referring to demolishing the Kennedy Centre.
"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down," Trump told reporters in North Carolina, referring to putting his name on the facility established by Congress and opened in 1971 as a memorial to slain President John Kennedy.
Matt Floca, the Kennedy Centre's Trump-backed executive director, said in a court filing earlier on Thursday that the building was being temporarily closed to assess safety risks in areas "exhibiting severe structural deterioration."
Democratic US Representative Joyce Beatty, who sued Trump last year over his Kennedy Centre plans, responded in a filing in federal court in Washington that the closure "is a recipe for defendants extending their shutdown forever and closing the Kennedy Centre for the next two years - the very thing this court said they could not do without its permission."
Beatty's lawyers also cited a photo circulating on social media that depicted the president aboard Air Force One looking at a poster they said appeared to be titled "Kennedy Centre DEMOLISHED." The photo has not been independently verified by Reuters.
Trump last year had the White House's historic East Wing demolished to make way for a ballroom project he has pursued.
EMERGENCY HEARING DENIED
Cooper turned down a request by Beatty for an emergency hearing on her lawsuit after the Kennedy Centre's board, including Trump and his hand-picked appointees, voted this week to close the venue for up to two years for a US$257 million renovation project.
Beatty, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center's board, said the venue is no longer accessible to the public during normal operating hours. New barriers were visible outside the building on Wednesday.
Beatty and other critics have accused Trump of seeking to place his name on the Kennedy Centre out of vanity. Trump's name had been placed on the building's facade until the judge in May ordered it removed, saying only Congress can change the name.
Cooper earlier directed the board to explain by Thursday whether the administration's plan violates an earlier order he issued limiting its ability to shut its doors. The board said on Thursday morning that it was not in violation of the order, and the seven-day emergency closure was separate from the larger renovation plans.
The Trump administration said it would ask the judge by Friday to dissolve the prior order to allow for what the government called "closure necessary to complete the restoration and renovations."
Cooper, in a ruling on Tuesday, rejected the center's latest effort to put Trump's name on the building to reflect his role in the planned renovation. The administration has appealed, and Trump said on social media the Kennedy Centre "is destined to doom" if it is not permitted to close for repairs.

Since the beginning of the Iran war in late February 2026, people have shared a video allegedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump in 1987 advocating to "go in" and take the Middle Eastern country's oil.
In the purported clip, Trump says of Iran, "You take their oil. That's what I'd do," adding, "You go in." Journalist Barbara Walters asks how he would take the oil, inquiring, "Would you take a chance in a war?" Trump responds, appearing to say a war would be inevitable even if the U.S. did nothing, telling her: "You're going to have a war. … You're going to have a war by being weak."
Users shared (archived) the video (archived) on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived) and X (archived), among other platforms.
In sum, the decades-old clip is authentic, meaning that it was not created with artificial intelligence or other digital fakery. Trump truly advocated for going into Iran in 1987, saying, "You take the oil. That's what I'd do."
Trump posted the video on Truth Social on March 30, as some users accurately pointed out (archived). The video in his post begins with him saying, "because I'm running for the presidency." A longer video shows he fully says, "I'm not here today because I'm running for the presidency."
The clip originates from an episode of ABC's "20/20" featuring a profile of Trump by Walters. Newspaper archives pin (archived) the segment's apparent air date as Dec. 11, 1987.
Snopes emailed the White House to ask whether the Trump administration wished to respond to users sharing the video and will update this article if we receive further details.
Days after reposting the clip, on April 3, Trump posted a message matching his stance from nearly 39 years before, saying he wanted to take Iran's oil:
With a little more time, we can easily OPEN THE HORMUZ STRAIT, TAKE THE OIL, & MAKE A FORTUNE. IT WOULD BE A "GUSHER" FOR THE WORLD??? President DONALD J. TRUMP
(Donald Trump via Truth Social)
Transcript of Trump's 1987 remarks on Iran
A lengthier video from the "20/20" segment appears on Vimeo and YouTube, with the part about Iran beginning just after the two-minute mark.
The longer clip features more details, including journalist Charles Bremner remarking on Trump's stance:
WALTERS (
voice-over ): But does Donald Trump want to be president? TRUMP (speaking to the Portsmouth, New Hampshire, Rotary Club): I'm not here today because I'm running for the presidency. I'm here because I'm personally tired of seeing this great country of ours being ripped off.
WALTERS (voice-over): But as far as Trump is concerned, our allies are only part of the problem. The real culprit is Iran.
TRUMP (speaking to the Rotary Club): Why couldn't we go in and take over some of their oil, which is along the sea?
WALTERS (speaking to Trump): How would you do that? Would you send in the Marines? Would you take a chance in a war?
TRUMP: Let 'em have Iran. You take their oil. That's what I'd do.
WALTERS: But how?
TRUMP: How?
WALTERS: I mean, do we want a war? What do you mean, we take their oil?
TRUMP: You go in… you go in…
WALTERS: How do we go in?
TRUMP: You're going to have a war. Barbara… You're going to have a war by being weak.
WALTERS: OK. How do we go in? What do we do?
TRUMP: Excuse me.
WALTERS: Yeah.
TRUMP: You're going to have a war, and it's going to start in the Middle East.
WALTERS: What if the Soviet Union said, "You do this to Iran, we're going to come in?"
TRUMP: I don't believe they'd do it. The next time Iran attacks this country, go in and grab one of their big oil installations, and I mean, grab it and keep it, and get back your losses, because this country has lost plenty because of Iran.
BREMNER (speaking to off-camera interviewer): Donald Trump seems to have a Clint Eastwood approach to foreign policy.
WALTERS (voice-over): Charles Bremner is the New York correspondent for the London Times. He wrote this article that appeared in the Times the week following Trump's New Hampshire speech.
BREMNER: He recommended strikes at Iranian oil fields. This obviously would create a great chain reaction across the area if it ever took place. And obviously, European allies would be appalled by any such behavior.
We messaged Bremner on X to ask whether he wished to share any new comment about the parallels of the video from the past lining up with the war and will update this article if we receive a response.
The report also notes that Trump took out a full-page advertisement in The New York Times (archived) and other newspapers in September 1987 with the title "There's nothing wrong with America's Foreign Defense Policy that a little backbone can't cure." The International Meteor Organization, the nonprofit that coordinates and publishes amateur and professional observations of meteor phenomena, said its infrastructure has suffered a “critical blow” from a cyberattack.
“We recently suffered a cyberattack that dealt a critical blow to aging infrastructure, taking much of our site offline,” a static page on its website on Wednesday said. “We expect several weeks of partial downtime as we transition to new infrastructure and services.”
“I am very sad to see the site down”
In the meantime, the IMO said it’s prioritizing the reporting of fireball observations, which can be reported here. The organization is also providing some information on its Facebook page.
The IMO has helped forge unified standards for reporting meteor observations. Its databases of reported meteor and fireball observations—made up of text, photos, and videos—are also considered essential by many in the field. The IMO also publishes the bimonthly WGN journal, which in English is short for Working Group News. The body was formally founded in 1988.
It’s unclear why an organization that tracks large, fiery space objects hurtling toward Earth would be the target of a damaging cyberattack. It’s equally unclear why someone would want to steal its data (assuming that was the motive), which is mostly public.

International students, 'visa hoppers' and backpackers targeted in Australia migration crackdown
- Published
International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will be targeted under stricter rules announced by Australia on Thursday in a bid to curb immigration.
Foreign students will no longer be able to bring their families with them and those who want to extend their stay must choose a higher qualification.
Rules will also be stricter for working holiday visas - commonly used by backpackers and a crucial labour source for the agricultural sector - with a ballot system although these changes will not affect the UK.
The new rules were revealed by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke who said that while immigration was a "strength" of Australia, there needed to be a "high level of control".
For international student and graduate visas, Burke said: "We will no longer be adding to the stock of students automatically being able to bring family members over."
There would be exemptions for foreign students already in Australia as well as applicants from the Pacific and South East Asian countries, he said.
PhD students would also be able to bring their families as they were in different life circumstances to undergraduates, Burke said.
In a speech titled "The work of managing the migration program: who arrives, who stays, who leaves", Burke revealed a raft of changes as the government aims to bring net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.
On student visas, he said the government would clamp down on "visa hopping" - where a student finishes a course, then applies to do another course which is often a lower qualification and sometimes with a "not so legitimate provider".
Students who want to go "up the scale" will be allowed, Burke said, for example, if a student finishes a bachelor's degree and then wants to complete a masters.
He also announced major changes to working holiday visas for those aged 18 to 30 years old who can work in Australia for 12 months, but can extend for a second and third year.
Currently, these visa holders must work for three months in regional Australia during their first year to qualify for a second year, and then six months to qualify for a third year.
Under the new changes, those who qualify for a second year will have to go into a ballot with a cap of 45,000, down from the 57,000 who qualified last year.
For the third year, the ballot will be limited to 5,000, down from 31,000 who qualified last year. British working holidaymakers will not be affected by these changes due to the UK's free trade agreement with Australia.
New figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday showed Australia's population grew 1.4% in the 12 months to March 2026 to 27.9m.
That total figure included births and deaths as well as a net overseas migration of 292,100.
Migration remains a major political issue as debate around Australia's population grows amid rising living costs, housing affordability and increased strain on public services.
One Nation, a populist right-wing party known for its anti-immigration stance and which has seen a surge in support in recent months, detailed its migration policy earlier this week, proposing to cut temporary migrant visas by 750,000 over three years.
The party, which won its first lower house seat in May, also wants to cap net overseas immigration to 130,000, drawing a rebuke from Burke who said such a proposal would risk "smashing parts of the Australian economy".
In July, the government introduced a policy to prioritise applications for family visas lodged onshore - where the applicant is in the country already - over those submitted overseas.
Skilled migrants already in Australia who applied for permanent visas were also prioritised over those applying from overseas.
It also paused applications for working holiday visas from 24 countries, not including the UK.
Violet Roumeliotis, from Settlement Services International which helps new arrivals to Australia, says the migration debate was increasingly driven by "short-term politics rather than what is best for the country".
"The proposed changes to family visas for international students is a good example of this," she said, adding that it would make it harder for Australia to compete for "future talent".

iOS 27 focuses on useful refinements, with better Liquid Glass controls, smarter Siri AI, natural-language Shortcuts, Safari web-change alerts, separate alarm volume, improved Photos tools, AirPods EQ, smarter password handling, and several everyday quality-of-life upgrades.
Apple has finally started rolling out iOS 27 to all eligible devices after testing it in beta for months. If you are reading this article, the update is already rolling out. If your iPhone supports it, you can go to Settings, General, Software Update, and update to the latest version.
iOS 27 isn’t a significant jump from what we have seen from iOS 18 to iOS 26. For those who are not aware, Apple has changed the version names to match the year. So instead of iOS 19, they moved it to iOS 26 to match the year 2026.
This year’s iOS 27 is more about refinement and fixing the issues that came along with iOS 26.
One of the biggest updates for most people, at least based on our insight, is the ability to refine the liquid glass design. Apple is now offering a separate setting to make your liquid glass look more frosted or transparent, and also allowing you to set different volumes for the alarms.
Plus, there is a new Siri and plenty of other Siri AI features, such as creating your own shortcuts using natural prompts. Let your password app fix compromised passwords, monitor website changes for free using Safari, and much more.
I have been testing iOS 27 for a few months now, testing its wide variety of features. In this guide, you will learn about the 27 best iOS 27 features that everybody should know and use for a better quality of life.
Table of Contents
Best iOS 27 Features You Should Know and Use
There are tens of new feature additions and improvements in iOS 27. However, not every new feature deserves your attention. There are a few features that really stood out for me and are genuinely useful in day-to-day life that everyone should be aware of. So here are my ten favorite picks before going to the comprehensive list of features.
Adjust Liquid Glass Design Transparency
It is evident that most people hated the new liquid glass design Apple introduced in iOS 26. Apple made the entire UI transparent overnight with a glossy effect, which made text hard to read and was resource-heavy.
Additionally, a few apps failed to adapt to this design perfectly, resulting in a bad user experience. However, Apple didn’t back off from the decision. Since the launch, Apple has continued to refine the liquid glass design to make it better and more usable.
In the latest iOS 27 update, Apple is offering a separate setting that lets you adjust the transparency of the liquid glass design. This setting is different from what we have covered in our TechPP videos, and here is how to use it.
Build Your Own Shortcuts Using Natural Prompts
Extensions and shortcuts are the two easiest ways to add missing features, whether it’s on your iPhone or in any browser. However, creating shortcuts isn’t always an easy task. It involves dealing with plenty of elements and actions, which can be hard for a casual user.
But that’s changing with iOS 27. The new Siri AI will now let you create a new shortcut based on simple, natural prompts. Now you can simply describe a shortcut using natural language, highlighting what it can do. For instance: A shortcut that automatically changes your iPhone wallpaper every morning or a shortcut that reminds you to drink water every two hours.
Since it uses AI behind the scenes, the possibilities are endless. You can describe whatever problem or feature you want to add through the shortcuts, and it will do it for you. However, the current implementation is not reliable for complex extensions. But it is a good start, and it will only get better in future versions.
I found using Claude or Codex to create iPhone shortcuts is the most reliable way, and it works much better for me than using Siri to create shortcuts, which often don’t get the desired results I wanted.
Let Your Password Apps Handle Your Compromised Passwords
When Apple first introduced the Passcodes app in iOS 18, it was super basic and missed a lot of the features found on other passcode management apps at the time. However, Apple continues to add new features, and the recent iOS 27 brings the ability to fix your compromised passwords automatically.
In simple words, if any of your passwords are compromised, your password app will automatically renew them into new passwords without you having to do it manually.
Password management apps are very good at finding your compromised passwords in data breaches. However, previously you had to manually visit every site and change the password yourself. But that’s going to change with iOS 27, where you can simply tap to auto-change the password, and it does it for you.
Monitor Any Web Changes in Real Time
This is my favorite addition to the Safari browser. Probably a feature that can kill many third-party apps. Apple has added a new Notify Me feature to the Safari web browser in iOS 27. It lets Siri AI monitor real-time changes on the website and notify you. Whether it’s an e-commerce price drop, real-time stock changes, or even a new article addition to any webpage, Safari can monitor it for you.
The best part is, you can describe what changes you want to get notified about in a natural prompt, and it does it for you. Also, there are no hard limits on how many trackers or websites you can track, and it lets you track changes every hour. Weekly, monthly, or even daily. The only requirement is that your device should support the Apple Intelligence feature.
Set Separate Volume for Your Alarms
Another feature that Apple should have introduced years ago is the ability to set custom volumes for your alarms in iOS 27. Previously, Apple used to have a single volume for all sounds, including alarms, calls, media, and notifications. In iOS 27, Apple is splitting that up, letting you set separate volume levels for alarms, media, and notifications.
One-Tap Access for Your Wi-Fi and Mobile Data Toggles
If you are someone who frequently adjusts the mobile and Wi-Fi toggles on your iPhone, iOS 27 is getting a very big, useful upgrade. Now, without needing to open the toggle or the entire panel, you can just individually turn your Wi-Fi toggle on and off directly from the toggle. It is enabled by default.
If you have customized it, you can just drag and drop the new network panel to get access to these features.
Auto-Paste Suggestions on Top of Your Keyboard
Another feature that Android users have enjoyed for years is now finally available on iPhone starting with iOS 27. Once you copy text or take a screenshot, the iOS keyboard now automatically suggests the recently copied clipboard text and images, which you can simply tap on and paste wherever you want.
Previously, it required you to long-press, select, and tap on the paste option to do that.
New Custom Equalizer for Your AirPods
Apple is rolling out a custom equalizer in the settings for AirPods. Now, iPhones with iOS 27 have a native AirPods equalizer in Settings to help you customize the audio output.
The new custom equalizer allows you to adjust lows, mids, and high frequencies separately. However, it is only available for devices running on H2 or later Pro devices, and for older devices, users need to rely on Apple’s Adaptive EQ.
Quickly View Photos Captured by You
One of the biggest downsides of iOS Photos is that the images captured from your iPhone are mixed with screenshots, memes, and other downloaded images saved from third-party apps. This makes it extremely hard for you to find the photos captured particularly from your iPhone. In iOS 27, Apple has added a new “Captured by Me” folder to the Photos app. It only shows the photos and videos taken with your iPhone camera, letting you easily find them.
Let Your Earbuds Automatically Pause When They Detect You Have Fallen Asleep
If you use AirPods, Apple has added another useful feature in iOS 27: your AirPods can automatically pause music, podcasts, or whatever you are listening to when they detect that you have fallen asleep.
Most apps these days offer sleep timers that automatically pause after a certain time. However, Apple’s implementation is more dynamic and doesn’t rely on a set time limit. Based on your movement, the AirPods automatically detect when you have fallen asleep and pause the music. This can be extra useful if you are someone like me who falls asleep, and it also eliminates the need for you to set a sleep timer every night.
The Phone App Automatically Shows Relevant Information While You Are on the Call
How many times have you searched for specific information during a call with a service agent? If your answer is often, then Apple has added a very useful feature for you.
With iOS 27, the Phone app on your iPhone now automatically shows relevant information when you are on a call in real time. These include your reservation numbers, order details, confirmation codes, and much more, which Apple can fetch from other Apple services. This eliminates the need for you to search through emails, messages, or other apps while speaking to customer support or during a business call.
Apple’s Mail App Is Now Better at Finding Information
If you use Apple Mail, it is getting a useful update. Starting with iOS 27, Apple says Mail search is upgraded to find more relevant information based on your search.
Now, instead of remembering the exact subject lines, names, or even words in your email, you can just use your natural tone and search for the exact information you want. Apple says the Mail app can now display more relevant information at the top of the search results, and it’s also smarter, as it can automatically identify the query and find the relevant information.
Now, You Can Set an Exact Expiry Time for Your Find My Sharing
If you use Apple’s Find My for location sharing, it is getting a useful update. You can select the exact time when your location sharing should stop. Previously, Apple only allowed you to share your location for an hour, until the end of the day, or until you manually turn it off.
But with iOS 27, Apple is giving you more flexibility, letting you choose a custom time. Now you can set a combination of days along with the hours to share your location. This also eliminates the need for you to manually remember to turn off location sharing if you have set it to indefinitely.
Now, You Can Turn Your Physical Cards Into Digital Passes
Apple Wallet app in iOS 27 lets you convert your physical cards into digital cards and store them in your Apple Wallet. Carrying a physical card can be a hassle, especially if you have multiple cards. It not only makes your wallet bulky, but also makes it hard to find the right one when you need it.
Moreover, there is a high chance that you can forget it, and it could get lost. Now, with the ability to convert your physical cards into digital ones, the Apple Wallet app eliminates all of these pain points. Plus, even if you want to carry a physical card, I would highly suggest converting it into a digital one, which can come in handy sometimes.
Improved AI Writing Tools Across the System
AI writing tools were the first Apple Intelligence features Apple introduced in iOS 18. However, Apple left them out and forgot to update them in iOS 26.
But in iOS 27, with the overall improvements in the AI features and getting close to what it has promised, Apple has also upgraded AI writing tools throughout the system.
Now, these writing tools are more advanced and improved. The best part of these AI writing tools is that they are integrated directly into the workflow.
So if you want to summarize, shorten, or fix spelling mistakes, you don’t need to switch apps. You can generate, rewrite, or correct text directly from your iPhone keyboard. Plus, Apple is also integrating these AI capabilities across the system, including Mail and the Notes app, letting you easily access them anywhere.
Easily Create Calendar Events Without Specific Details
Creating a calendar event requires you to fill in separate details for title, date, time, location, and other details. However, with iOS 27, Apple is making it easy for you to create or edit calendar events.
Now, without needing to fill everything manually, you can just create a calendar event using natural prompts.
For instance, you can ask Calendar to create a birthday event at 4 a.m. tomorrow, and it will do it for you. Calendar app can now understand details such as important keywords, dates (such as tomorrow at 4 PM), a person’s name, and other key details, and automatically create a calendar event. Plus, you can also edit using natural language.
Connect an iPhone Directly to Gym Equipment
If you own an iPhone and want to track your workout data, pairing it with an Apple Watch is the most sensible decision. However, it is expensive and can be overkill for users looking for basic fitness tracking features who don’t need distraction on their wrist.
However, the Apple Watch has this nifty feature where they connect to your gym equipment and receives live workout data, such as your speed, distance, pace, resistance, and the duration of your workout, which you can then measure and analyze in your Apple Health app.
If you do not own an Apple Watch or don’t want to carry it during your workout, Apple in iOS 27 has added the same GymKit functionality directly on your iPhone. So now your iPhone can directly connect to your compatible gym equipment and receive the live workout data. Plus, if you have an Acura Pro 3, you can also connect and track your real-time heart rate information.
Pause Location Sharing Without Disabling It Permanently
If you use Find My to share your location with others, iOS 27 is adding the ability to temporarily hide your location without permanently ending location sharing completely.
In previous versions, if you wanted to temporarily stop sharing your location, whether it’s because your iPhone battery is running out, or if you are planning a surprise, or if you don’t want to reveal your destination, you needed to permanently stop location sharing.
With iOS 27, you can temporarily hide your location from a person. The best part is that the person does not need to be removed, and you also do not need to remember to turn the location back on after the situation has ended.
New Improved Cleanup Tool for Your Photos
I personally hate AI photo editing features inside the Photos app. Recently, both Apple and Google have added several features that are designed to alter and convert your photos into AI-generated ones. However, one feature that I found very useful is the ability to remove unwanted people or objects from a photo directly in the Photos app without relying on third-party tools.
However, Apple’s initial version of the Clean Up Tool isn’t as great as expected. It struggled to remove unwanted distractions from an image. However, with iOS 27, Apple has significantly improved it. Now it’s on par with other clean-up tools that perfectly edit the image naturally, without leaving smudges or empty patches.
Automatically Organize Safari Tabs by Subject
With iOS 27, Apple’s Safari browser can now automatically organize tabs for you. Many other browsers have adopted this feature, but it took some time for Apple to implement it.
If you use the Safari browser and have many tabs open, you can enable the Auto-Organize feature so that it automatically organizes your tabs. This lets you easily find them or close all of them at once.
Generate Your Own Extensions for Safari
Similar to iOS Shortcuts, you can also generate your own extensions using natural prompts in Safari. If you have an Apple Intelligence-supported iPhone, you can just visit the extension tab and give it a natural prompt about what exact features the extension might have, and Apple Intelligence will create a fully working extension for you.
You can just use this extension for an individual web page, or for all the web pages in your Safari browser.
New Siri for Agentic Tasks
Apple is finally close to delivering the Siri it promised two years ago. With iOS 27, Apple is introducing the new Siri, called Siri AI, which is now better at answering your questions and also better at agentic tasks. Plus, it can now search across your Apple apps, including Mail, Messages, Photos, Notes, and all other supported apps, and get information for you.
You can create a reminder, edit a message, organize details, or complete another task. Plus, Siri can also have better context, which means it can remember the information that it gets from other apps. Although at its current stage it is not as advanced as Gemini or other intelligent or agentic AI tools, it is a good start for Apple to deliver what it promised.
It will only get better from now on. Plus, Siri is directly integrated into the system. You can activate it from any screen. Plus, it is free to use without any limitations, except for a few features that Apple might put behind a subscription paywall in the future.
New Wallpaper Extensions
If you customize your iPhone and set a new wallpaper often, this can come in handy. Apple is introducing a new wallpaper extension feature in iOS 27, which expands your wallpaper so it fits correctly based on your iPhone dimensions.
In most cases, if your iPhone wallpaper doesn’t match your iPhone screen dimensions, it can look blurry and pixelated. Plus, if you want to set it as a lock screen wallpaper, it can also affect the depth effect, making the overall wallpaper look blurry and clumsy.
With this new extension wallpaper, Apple now extends the wallpaper to perfectly fit your iPhone’s aspect ratio. The best part is it preserves the main subject and only generates the matching scenery at the image’s edges, so that the subject stays in the middle without being cut off.
Reply Inline to the Messages From Android Users
With the iOS 27 update, Apple is putting an end to another discussion of blue and green bubbles and Apple’s tactics to limit RCS messaging.
Apple iMessage now supports inline replies, where you can directly reply to a specific message sent from your Android friend. This is like a nested reply where you can long-press on any message and tap on Reply. Along with your reply, the other person’s message appears on top, making it easy for them to spot and understand.
New Siri Visual Intelligence
Siri is also now upgraded with better visual intelligence, and it is now live inside your camera app. Now you can spot objects inside your camera and ask Siri to describe them. This can be especially useful for visual intelligence tasks, such as translating the text from a photo, identifying a specific object or food, or extracting the details from a flyer.
Plus, the best part is that, since it is being done by Siri, you can also ask follow-up questions and even delegate tasks, such as adding the extracted information to your calendar or splitting and storing it in any app. Now, adjust your lock screen clock to make it look smaller.
This can be small, but useful for people who often customize their lock screen.
Apple is now letting you adjust the clock size on your iPhone lock screen. Now you can adjust the size of the lock screen clock even smaller. If you feel your clock is covering the important details of your wallpaper, or if you want it to take up less space, you can simply use the smaller clock feature to adjust its size and make it look smaller.
Organize Your Photos Better
While Apple’s Photos app search is smart enough to find the relevant image you are looking for using just natural prompts, Apple is also letting you add individual star ratings and keywords to the photos. Starting with iOS 27, you can rate the photos up to 5 stars and add keywords.
Photos app displays these details while you are browsing your media library, letting these photos stand out from the rest. This makes them easy to spot instead of manually comparing photos to find the best ones from your extensive media library.
Save Photos Directly From Videos
With iOS 27, Apple also introduced the ability to save any frame from a video. You can simply use the Save frame as a photo feature, and the video frame will be saved as a photo. You can save multiple frames as photos.
Here is how:
- Open the Photos app on your Phone
- Play any video and tap on the three-dot menu at the top
- From here, tap on the Save Video frame as a photo option
Get the Most Out of iOS 27
Those are the 27 best iOS 27 features that everyone should know and use.
