“First they destroyed our farmland. Then they demolished our homes. Now they are trying to take away our voting rights,” said 74-year-old Sheela Devi, as she stood in front of her jhuggi underneath a bridge near Delhi’s Raj Ghat. The ‘they’ she referred to comprises the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) and the state Election Commission. She was one of the over 47 lakh voters left out of Delhi’s draft SIR roll.
One hot afternoon in March 2023, the DDA’s bulldozers tore through standing crop of rice, herbs, and vegetables in Bela Estate after having demolished hundreds of houses of farmers living in the eco-sensitive Zone O floodplains of the Yamuna. The community protested and filed a petition for rehabilitation, but did not get any relief. Their livelihood taken away, the marginalized community has been living since then in tarpaulin covered make-shift shanties under the Geeta Colony bridge and nearby elevated roads.
The slum cluster falls under Part No 38 of Chandni Chowk assembly constituency (Lal Quila Yamuna Bridge). Total 729 enumeration forms were generated as the first step of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise from this Part. The ASDD (Absent-Shifted-Dead-Duplicate) list threw up a shocker as it listed 728 voters, leaving just one name — that of a priest at a local temple — in the draft roll.
In other words, 728 voters out of 729 were excluded from the draft SIR roll — an unprecedented 99.8% deletion rate. The deletions include 42 deaths, and the biggest category is ‘permanently shifted’, which has 632 names. In Chandni Chowk constituency of Old Delhi district, the overall SIR exclusion rate is 38%.
It is deeply ironic that after forcing them to relocate again and again, the State has now moved to strike their names off the electoral roll, marking them as ‘permanently shifted’.
The anxiety now engulfing Sheela Devi and hundreds like her is shaped by what voter-roll deletions have meant for people elsewhere in the country. In West Bengal, for instance, being left out of electoral rolls has been accompanied by questions over citizenship and difficulties accessing government welfare schemes and other entitlements. For a community that has already lost its farmland and homes, the prospect of being deleted from the voter list raises fears that they could be pushed further to the margins, with their identity, access to state benefits and their whole existence called into question.
‘Have Lived here for Generations. This is our Home’
Bela Estate is a large slum cluster on the western bank of the Yamuna, comprising five sub-areas informally known as China Colony, Malla Gaon, Bela Gaon, Moolchand Basti and Kanchan Puri. Residents say the settlement has existed for more than 70 years and is home to over 700 households.
The construction of a bridge in 2009 separated Malla Gaon and China Colony from Bela Gaon, Moolchand Basti and Kanchan Puri. While the latter areas now fall under the Jungpura assembly constituency, Malla Gaon and China Colony are part of Chandni Chowk — and it is here that the mass exclusion of voters occurred during the SIR.
The entire Bela Estate falls within the first phase of the Yamuna Riverfront Development Project, under which the DDA plans to develop a biodiversity park and a lake across 189 acres.
The settlements have faced multiple demolitions over the years. In the months preceding the SIR, residential settlements along the Yamuna floodplains in several parts of Delhi also witnessed a spate of demolitions, carried out by the DDA as anti-encroachment drives.
Among those excluded from Bela Estate are dozens of Sheela Devi’s family members, including her seven sons and their wives. “We have been voting from here for a long time. We have four generations of family here. Our elders lived and died here. We had a house here, we had farmland, everything is gone now,” she said, pointing to a now-grilled boundary that separates the bridge area from the green floodplains.
Janaki Devi (52), standing beside her mother-in-law Sheela Devi, said the booth level officer (BLO) came to give them forms, which they filled and submitted. “We are old voters. I don’t know why we were left out.”
“They can demolish our makeshift houses, but we still stay back here,” she said. “When we could farm, we were fine. Now we hardly get any work. Some in our family are daily-wagers, some others do odd jobs in the market. Some sell vegetables from the cart. Our children have to walk several kilometres to get to the nearest school. But we don’t want to leave. This is our home, we don’t have any village to go back to.”
Octogenarian Ram Charan, who says he arrived here as a toddler with his father, sat on a chaar-payi outside his jhuggi in another cluster of settlements, some distance from where Sheela Devi’s family lives. He cannot walk more than a few meters due to old age, but Ram Charan says he still goes to vote every year. “This is the first time this has happened,” he added.
“We have lived and farmed here in Bela Estate since pre-independence days. Earlier, we had our houses; after those were demolished, we made jhuggis; now we live under these tarpaulin sheets,” the elderly man said, adding, “Since 2004, we have been repeatedly rendered homeless. We have been beaten up by police as well. And now, they have taken away our voting rights.”
“Modi ji had said, ‘Jahan jhuggi wohi makan’. Where is that promise now?” added Pushpa as she came out of her room with her Voter ID card.
A few Jhuggis away, Dulari sits with her friend, chatting. “I have all the documents. I met the BLO here in our settlement, and also provided details of my name from the 2002 voter roll,” she said. Alt News verified her papers and found that her name was indeed there in the last revised list of 2002.
Fifty-five-year-old Kantara Devi, who lay on a chaar-payi, had her midriff bandaged. She cannot sit or walk. She said she fell down amid the chaos and confusion over the draft roll, as people jostled to find out what had gone wrong. “I am worried my widow pension might stop since my name has been struck off. I don’t have any other source of income. That Rs 2,500 is what I live on. I also have to marry my daughter off this month,” she said in a low, broken voice.
The Fight to Prove They Live Here
Kamal Lal, a daily wage worker who is marked ‘permanently shifted’ on the ASDD list, said, “I helped the residents here fill and submit more than 500 enumeration forms. I have taken the BLO to where the voters were residing. She even acknowledged the help I provided. But she said she could not do anything about the exclusions as she was under pressure from higher authorities who wanted to delete votes here. When we went to officials, they said it was DDA’s land and our jhuggi was kachhi (temporary), it won’t be recognised. They asked us whether we had land registration papers, water or electricity bills? I told them there was no rule requiring such documents for voter enumeration.”
Kamal said most people in Bela Estate had their names, or those of immediate relatives, on the 2002 roll. Those who did not have a link to the 2002 roll, had several of the 12 documents listed by the Election Commission, including birth certificates, bank documents and Aadhaar. “We could have been included based on those. But they removed all of us,” he added.
Many residents of Bela Estate belong to the Mallah community (traditional boatmen and fishermen tribes), a notified Scheduled Caste in Delhi, who have been living on the banks of the Yamuna for generations. An ethnographic Census study from 1961 traces the Mallahs as boatmen and fishermen staying in Bela Estate and parts of Mayur Vihar, among other settlements along the Yamuna.
The National Green Tribunal banned vegetable cultivation on the Yamuna floodplain in 2015 citing the river’s toxicity, while the DDA acquired parts of the floodplain for a biodiversity zone and park. In 2019, NEERI found lead levels above FSSAI safety limits in vegetable and soil samples, while a CPCB study flagged fertiliser and pesticide use as a source of pollution. The NGT subsequently ordered the DDA to stop cultivation there. Farmers, however, disputed the findings, saying they primarily used groundwater and manure rather than Yamuna water.
“Our ancestors came here in the 1910s from Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and other neighbouring places. The floodplain lands were used during the British times to grow grass for horse grazing. Slowly, people started farming vegetables there. The DDA came much later,” Kamal asserted.
Several families claimed they used to have pucca houses before a 2015 DDA-led demolition. Fearing future demolitions, they stopped trying to build permanent structures and started living in huts and shanties, scattered across the floodplains near Raj Ghat, in the marshes, under bridges, wherever they could find a little space. In the same vain, they never received formal electricity and water connections. Some have gas connections, as this correspondent checked, and use solar batteries to run small fans and lights and charge their phones.
“In this round of SIR, the Election Commission had said that you should only be able to map yourself to the 2002 voter list. And you can show 12 documents including Aadhaar, that should suffice, which they all have,” said Anjali Bharadwaj, a social activist who is the co-convenor of the National Campaign for People’s Right to Information, and founding member of Satark Nagrik Sangathan.
She added, “Their settlements at Bela Estate were broken, and they are living in the same area, But the ERO apparently told them they did not have any proof of electricity and water bills and hence, they can’t be included.”
Deletion Directly Flouts ECI Provisions
According to court submissions during a hearing in August on a petition demanding special provisions for including the homeless and those living precariously in the electoral roll, the counsel for the petitioner argued that since the SIR process “proceeds on the premise that Booth Level Officers would be able to physically locate existing electors at their recorded addresses”, “persons who are homeless or have been rendered homeless or displaced pursuant to demolition drives are at serious risk of systematic exclusion from the electoral rolls, thereby infringing their right to franchise and casting doubt upon their citizenship…”
The court said the ECI’s submission sufficed to address the matter. The counsel for ECI submitted that “there is no requirement to pass a direction as sought by the Petitioner in view of the provisions contained in Manual on Electoral Rolls (“Manual”) published in March, 2023, which provides in Chapter 8 thereof the procedure for determination of ordinary residence.
Clause 8.5 of the manual provides as under:
“Homeless/pavement Dwellers – Homeless/the persons living in sheds/pavement dwellers, who do not possess any documentary proof of ordinary residence are eligible for enrolment in electoral roll, provided they are ordinarily residing there, irrespective of the fact whether that is a private property or pavement or an encroachment on government land. In such case the Booth Level Officer will visit the address given in Form 6 for more than one night to ascertain that the homeless person actually sleeps at the given place…””
The said procedure prescribes such homeless (including those rendered homeless by demolition) persons to fill Form 6 for inclusion in the electoral roll.
When Alt News spoke to sub-district magistrate Manoj Kumar, who is also the electoral registration officer (ERO) of Chandni Chowk, he claimed these voters were excluded because they had moved from their earlier residence. “These people used to do illegal cultivation there. There was a case in 2022 which they lost. After that, the illegal cultivation was stopped. After their houses were demolished, they now stay here and there. In SIR, our BLO visits the registered address. When she did not find them, she marked them on ASDD.”
However, Alt News saw hundreds of copies of enumeration forms which were signed by the BLO upon receipt.
When Alt News called the BLO, Garima Arya, to check whether she could not find the people residing in the area, a woman picked up the phone and claimed it was not Arya’s number. However, residents confirmed the number as belonging to the BLO and the Delhi CEO’s office lists the same phone number for her.
“Just because somebody does not have a residence, that cannot be a ground for remove the name of the person from the voter list,” observed Supantha Sinha, a Supreme Court advocate and member of the Delhi-based citizen’s forum Voter Adhikar Manch.
SDM Kumar also alleged that several voter cards from Bela Estate mentioned ‘agricultural land’ as their address, which Alt News found to be the case, as well. The residents explained that they lived around the land they farmed on and there has never been formal house numbers and streets there, and thus no conventional address.
He also said that his team would set up a camp soon to let the residents submit Form 6 and required declarations for re-enrolling. According to the Manual of Electoral Rolls, they will be registered from the address where they have moved, he added.
When asked whether a person needs proof of residential ownership to be included in the electoral roll, former chief election commissioner Om Prakash Rawat said, “There is no need of property and title. You should not be even asked about these documents because it is not a case of title being judged or checked, and hence proof is to be obtained for that. Electoral roll is for your ordinary residence — that you are ordinarily residing here, that’s good enough.”

SAPPORO – Hokkaido Railway (JR Hokkaido) has said it will withdraw a proposal to ask local municipalities to share the cost of maintaining loss-making sections in the prefecture.
JR Hokkaido made the announcement Wednesday after it faced opposition from municipalities to the proposal, which concerned eight sections it considers difficult to maintain on its own.
The company will instead seek to establish a new council led by the central government to discuss measures to keep the sections in service, and has asked the Hokkaido Prefectural Government to join the council.
The central government has asked the company to draw up fundamental measures to improve the financial situation of the eight sections by the end of fiscal 2026, which ends in March next year.
In April, JR Hokkaido announced four reform proposals, including one under which the company would continue train operations while municipalities would own and manage the tracks and other facilities.
The proposal drew strong opposition from the municipalities along the sections over concerns about increased financial burdens.
JR Hokkaido President Yasuyuki Watanuki said at a news conference Wednesday, “I would like to offer my apologies having received harsh criticism from various parties after making the proposal a topic of discussion.”
The new council will aim to formulate improvement measures by examining possible strategies to enhance the value of the sections, through the use of tourist trains as well as the transfer of railway assets, such as station buildings, to local governments.
Also on Wednesday, Watanuki and Tomoyuki Ishizuka, head of the Hokkaido District Transport Bureau at the transport ministry, held talks with Hokkaido Gov. Naomichi Suzuki and asked the prefectural government to participate in the council as its secretariat.
Suzuki said, “Frankly, I must say it will be difficult to compile (improvement measures) within the remaining six months.” He called for the compilation process to proceed carefully so as not to reach a hasty conclusion.
Some municipalities along the sections took the announcement positively.
An official of Kitami said the city welcomed the withdrawal of the earlier proposal, which did not make clear how financial burdens would be shared. “We hope the central and prefectural governments will carefully consider improvement measures in light of the significance of the sections,” the official said.

By the early 1880s, bacteriology was emerging as a rigorous science. Within the circle of German microbiologist Robert Koch in Berlin, investigators were attempting to isolate specific disease-causing organisms. The logic was to prove that a microbe caused disease, one had to grow it in pure culture, separate it from contaminants, and study its properties systematically. The available solidifying agent was gelatin. It provided a temporary structure to the nutrient broth, allowing colonies to form on the surface. But gelatin was fundamentally flawed: It liquefied at temperatures approaching 37 degrees Celsius, precisely the temperature required to culture many human pathogens. Even worse, several bacteria secreted enzymes that digested gelatin itself. The medium collapsed, colonies merged, and experimental clarity dissolved into formless fluid. For scientists attempting to establish causation of individual species in infectious disease, this was not a minor inconvenience: it was a structural limitation.
Who was Fanny Hesse?
Fanny Angelina Hesse was not formally appointed as a scientist. She assisted her husband, Walther Hesse, who worked in Koch’s laboratory. She prepared materials, maintained cultures, and drew meticulous illustrations of bacterial forms for publication. She was present, not as an investigator, but as a quiet labourer in daily experimental work. It was in that proximity that she repeatedly encountered the gelatin problem. Failed plates, melted surfaces, cultures lost at incubation temperatures. The frustration was practical and persistent. At home, however, she handled another substance entirely. Agar jellies prepared in her kitchen remained firm even in summer warmth. They did not soften as gelatin did. They did not seem to degrade. One evening, in what history records only briefly but imagination can render vividly, the domestic and the scientific converged. The problem of the laboratory and the memory of the kitchen overlapped. She suggested that if agar could withstand heat on the dining table, why would it not withstand incubation in the laboratory?
Before the laboratory
Agar is a complex polysaccharide extracted from the cell walls of certain red algae, mainly species of Gelidium and Gracilaria. Chemically, it consists primarily of two components: agarose and agaropectin. Agarose is a linear polymer made up of repeating units of galactose and 3,6-anhydro-L-galactopyranose, and it is this fraction that gives agar its remarkable gelling property. Agaropectin contains sulfate groups and contributes to viscosity and charge characteristics. The word “agar” is believed to derive from the Malay term agar-agar, meaning jelly.
Long before bacteriologists struggled with melting cultures in Berlin, agar had already lived a quiet life in kitchens. Extracted from red seaweed and known in parts of Asia for nearly two centuries, it was used to set desserts into firm, translucent gels. Unlike gelatin derived from animal tissue, agar did not collapse in warm weather. It held its structure. It was stable. It obeyed heat differently. In the nineteenth century, European cooks encountered agar as an exotic culinary thickener. But in scientific circles, its potential was invisible. The laboratory and the kitchen were separate worlds, divided by sex, habit and hierarchy. No one imagined that a domestic ingredient could resolve a foundational problem in bacteriology.
Thus, Fanny Angelina Hesse’s suggestion to replace gelatin with agar, was out of the box.
Moment of trial
When agar was introduced into nutrient media in Koch’s laboratory, the transformation was immediate and decisive. The medium remained solid at incubation temperatures. It did not liquefy. Most bacteria lacked the enzymatic machinery to degrade it. Colonies appeared as discrete, visible units, each derived from a single organism. For the first time, bacteriologists possessed a surface that was chemically inert, thermally stable, and optically clear. The ability to isolate pure cultures became reliable rather than tentative. Within months, the method was embedded in the experimental practices that led to the identification of the tuberculosis bacillus and other pathogens in the decades to come.
To understand why agar transformed medicine, one must first grasp the idea of culture. A culture medium is an artificial nutrient environment that allows bacteria to grow outside the human body under controlled conditions and at a controlled temperature. Individual bacteria are invisible, but when placed on a suitable medium, such as agar, they form individual visible colonies. This enables laboratories to isolate the exact organism from samples like blood, urine, or sputum. Once identified, the bacteria are tested against different antibiotics to determine which drugs are effective and to detect resistance. Imagine culture is like switching on a floodlight in a dark room. Agar becomes the illuminated stage where hidden microbes step forward, enabling precise diagnosis and rational treatment.
The breakthrough was not dramatic in spectacle. It was a shift merely in material. Yet that shift altered the trajectory of microbiology.
Aftermath and recognition
The scientific practice and literature of the period absorbed agar rapidly, but credit did not travel with equal speed. The technique became standard practice. Petri dishes were designed to accommodate solid media. Textbooks described agar plates as routine apparatus. The name of Koch became synonymous with bacteriological rigour. Fanny Hesse’s contribution receded into footnotes. For decades, the laboratory bench carried her insight without carrying her name. Only later did historians of science begin to recover her role and situate it within the broader narrative of microbiology.
Agar today
More than a century later, agar remains foundational. In every microbiology laboratory, from district hospitals to advanced research institutes, agar plates are prepared daily. Blood agar to detect haemolysis, MacConkey agar to differentiate lactose fermenters, chocolate agar for fastidious organisms. Selective and differential media, all structured upon the same seaweed-derived matrix. Antibiotic susceptibility testing depends on agar diffusion methods. Colony counting for public health surveillance relies on agar surfaces. Molecular biology workflows begin with bacterial colonies grown on agar plates before plasmid extraction or genetic analysis. Even in the era of automated diagnostics and genomic sequencing, agar persists as the primary tool for culturing living microbes.
Today, major production occurs in countries such as Japan, Spain, Chile, China, Indonesia, and Morocco, where seaweed is cultivated or harvested. Beyond microbiology, agar is widely used in the food industry as a vegetarian gelling agent, in confectionery and desserts, in pharmaceuticals as a stabilizer and laxative, and in biotechnology for gel electrophoresis to separate DNA and RNA fragments.
Its properties remain unmatched. It melts at high temperatures but solidifies at lower temperatures, allowing sterile preparation and convenient pouring. It is largely resistant to microbial digestion. It forms a clear, stable gel that supports nutrient supplementation without chemical interference.
Firming up microbiology
Without that transition from gelatin to agar, the systematic isolation of pathogens would have been delayed. The architecture of modern microbiology would have developed more slowly, along a more convoluted path.
Fanny Angelina Hesse recognised continuity between her kitchen and her laboratory. Today, when a microbiologist streaks a plate and waits for colonies to appear, the act is routine. Yet beneath that routine lies the insight of Fanny Hesse. Without her intervention, the discipline might have remained uncertain at its foundation, its cultures unstable, its conclusions tentative.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

Lifeguard Greg Wilfert was swimming off the coast of Scarborough, Maine, in August when he was yanked underwater by a force tugging on his rescue buoy. Wilfert, a lifeguard of 55 years, told local news outlet WFSB that he first thought he’d gotten caught on a boat propeller, but the real culprit was a great white shark.
The incident is one in a long line of great white sightings off the coast of Maine this year. It was a busy summer for shark sightings along the rest of the East Coast, but Maine, in particular, seems to have had a great white bonanza. A dozen sightings were reported in a two-day period near Pine Point Beach in southern Maine in August. Beaches were temporarily closed all over the state following multiple sightings throughout July and August. The sharks followed beachgoers through the end of summer: A great white was spotted off Wells Beach over Labor Day weekend, while a fisherman caught another on the holiday about 30 miles down the coast.
The waters off the coast of Maine are some of the world’s fastest-warming, and the Atlantic has seen a series of marine heat waves. The El Niño weather phenomenon is only boosting global heat further. But experts told WIRED that the reason for our recent glut of shark encounters is a lot more complicated than just attributing them to climate change, especially when it comes to great whites. Instead, a successful conservation effort decades ago is likely starting to pay dividends, coupled with more people bringing technology that can spot sharks to the beach.
When Steven Spielberg’s classic movie Jaws came out in 1975, great whites were in trouble. The species had declined in waters off both the east and west coasts of the US thanks to overfishing, bycatch, and trophy hunting. In the 1990s, federal protections were instated for both the sharks and for gray seals, one of their key prey species.
Maine’s state shark monitoring system uses a technology called acoustic telemetry, which outfits the animal with a tag that emits a unique electronic signature. Underwater stations can then pick up on that signal and log the tagged sharks, helping track their movement up and down the coast. Maine’s program is less than a decade old, and “not every shark is tagged,” says Matthew Davis, a shark expert at Maine’s Department of Natural Resources. That makes pinpointing exactly what is going on with this uptick in sightings a little more challenging.
But Davis and Walter Golet, an associate professor at the University of Maine School of Marine Science who collaborates on shark research, both believe that there were more great whites off the coast this summer compared to decades past. They attribute it in part to federal protections working. Great whites males take 26 years to reach adulthood, while females can take up to 33 years. That timeframe aligns with when federal protections were put in place and could help explain why more sharks are showing up off of Maine. Research generally backs this up: Multiple studies have found that protections for both sharks and seals helped to increase populations along the East Coast.
While climate change has driven massive changes in the ocean, including pushing many species northward as waters warm, its direct effect on great white sharks is a little more murky. Some research has suggested that great whites could suffer from very hot ocean temperatures by causing them to overheat and forcing them to slow down or move to colder water to seek food. But James Sulikowski, the director of the Coastal Oregon Marine Experiment Station at Oregon State University, emphasizes that great whites can control their body temperature, which enables them to withstand much larger ranges in ocean temperatures than other shark species.
“They’re not so subject to these huge fluctuations—they’re really good regulators,” he says.
Davis says that the knock-on effects of climate change—like warmer ocean temperatures changing certain prey species’ habitat range—are more likely to impact great whites than the hotter ocean temperatures do. Prey species may “hang around a little bit longer because the water is going to be a little bit warmer,” he says, which could mean great whites spend more time in areas they previously would’ve been in for only a few months.
Another indirect impact of climate change: more people at the beach during hot days. And, since it’s 2026, more and more people bring equipment, from iPhones to hobby drones, that can capture high-quality footage of marine life. All three experts say that the raft of shark sightings in Maine this summer may just be a result of people going outside with better, more technologically advanced eyes on the ocean.
“There are more of them, but they are also easier to see, so you have to untangle that,” says Golet. “I think we’re all sort of a prisoner of our own timeline.”

Judge orders Kennedy Center to give 30-day notice before any major changes — including demolition
Ruling comes after board voted to close center after losing bid to put Trump's name back on it
A U.S. federal judge on Thursday ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30-day notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it as President Donald Trump has threatened to do.
U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper said his ruling would "avoid any confusion on that score given more recent events," including the sudden closure of the building to the public on Wednesday.
Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center's executive director and chief operating officer, said he closed the iconic performing arts centre temporarily due to "acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration" of the aging building.
The building will be closed for at least seven days to "assess existing safety risks in those portions of the main building exhibiting severe structural deterioration," Floca said.
The temporary closure, which occurred without notice Wednesday, is separate from a vote Tuesday by the Kennedy Center's board to close the performing arts centre indefinitely for repairs, Floca and other officials said. The closure was based on an inspection of the roof terrace canopy and a partial ceiling collapse earlier this month, Floca said. The closure may be extended after evaluation next week, he said.
The announcement of the closure came in response to a court case filed by a Democratic congresswoman who is a trustee and sought an emergency court hearing to prevent what she called the building's "unlawful closing."
Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, has led efforts to block Trump's name from being added to the building. Beatty had a verbal confrontation with the Republican president Tuesday during a virtual board meeting.
Beatty's lawyers said in a court filing Thursday that the board members' "rationale that they are only temporarily closing the Kennedy Center is a plain pretext to justify shutting down the Center permanently. The facts before the Court are deeply concerning."
Cooper denied a request by Beatty's legal team to hold a hearing to clarify the board's actions and intent. But he agreed to their request "to make crystal clear" that his order prohibits demolition of the building.
The Trump-aligned board, chaired by the president, voted to close the centre after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning Trump's name to the building.
Trump, who was named the Kennedy Center's chairman last year by loyalists on the board, said Wednesday that his efforts to restore the aging building deserve recognition, "because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape."
Congress has allocated $257 million US to cover the repairs, but Trump said they only would happen if the board was permitted to move forward with plans to add his name to the building.
Barbra Streisand, a Kennedy Center honoree in 2008, on Thursday questioned the closing of the centre for repairs and called the controversy surrounding its operation "galling and painful to witness."
- Fencing goes up around Kennedy Center as activists worry it will be demolished
- Kennedy Center board votes to close after judge again blocks efforts to add Trump name to it
The Kennedy Center board voted in August to inscribe Trump's name on the Kennedy Center's facade so it would read "The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump." If the Trump Kennedy Center Fund reached $100 million US, another inscription would be added reading "Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."
The plaza in front of the Kennedy Center would also have been renamed in Trump's honour.
All of those proposals were shot down Tuesday by Cooper, who ruled that nothing could happen "without Congress's blessing."
Cooper ruled in May that the Kennedy Center illegally added Trump's name to the building, ordering it removed. The institution's leaders complied in June but left a tarp and scaffolding in place where Trump's name was once displayed.

It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.
Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance – a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.
They were talking about creatine.
Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.
But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' – even if it was legal.
From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.
Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.
"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.
"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."
So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?
While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.
Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.
"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.
Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.
Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.
During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 – effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".
In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.
According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".
The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research., external
Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.
"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.
"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.
"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."
Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.
"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.
"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating – all of those things – before we add in all of the extras."
Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.
Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.
Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.
"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.
"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.
"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."
Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.
So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?
"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.
"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.
"So creatine is a good example.
"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."
But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.
"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.
And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.
There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.
One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.
While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.
If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.
In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.
"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.
Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".
There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."
He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.
"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.
There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge – and some are going back to basics.
For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative – from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.
It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.
The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.
Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.
In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.
These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.
British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.
"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."
As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.
She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."
Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.
"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."
She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".
"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."
And then there is taste.
"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.
"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

Data center developer sues city after requiring company to supply renewable energy on-site
Critics of the data center in St. Louis, Missouri, worry about its water usage, the impact on the city’s air quality and utility costs
The developer of a proposed $3.1 billion data center in St. Louis, Missouri, has sued a board that handles city zoning after the five-member panel required the company to supply renewable energy on-site.
David Lambiaso, a partner at data center developer TerraWatt, claimed in a lawsuit filed Wednesday that the St. Louis Board of Adjustment imposed illegal conditions when it upheld a permit for the 120-megawatt facility in July, according to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, which reported on the filing.
The lawsuit argues that requiring his company to supply a minimum of 2.4 megawatts of renewable energy at the data center exceeds the board’s authority.
The rapid development of data centers across the country to power the AI boom has often led to friction between cities and developers, with locals citing environmental and quality of life concerns.
Some St. Louis residents have complained that the proposed data center in the Midtown neighborhood would use too much water, worsen air quality and raise utility costs, the Post-Dispatch reported.
Lambiaso also claimed the renewable energy requirement is “practically impossible” given the size of the 11-acre site.
The Independent has reached out to TerraWatt and the St. Louis City Counselor’s Office for comment.
TerraWatt did agree to use renewable energy for at least 50 percent of the data center’s energy load within five years of the facility’s opening in a community benefits agreement.
That amounts to about 60 megawatts — far more than the 2.4 megawatts mandated by the board. But there are other ways to generate that energy, rather than producing it on site, such as buying power from energy providers.
Local environmentalists have argued the community benefits agreement does not actually represent residents’ wishes.
Elyse Schaeffer with the Missouri Coalition for the Environment told local outlet KSDK, “I'm reluctant to call this a community benefits agreement at all because at base level a community benefits agreement should involve conversations with feedback from and input by community members. And that's not the process that we saw happen with this.”
“‘Community Benefit Agreement’ — which community does it benefit? It should be called a Developers' Benefit Agreement,” Kerry McCullen with the Eco-Socialist Green Party of Eastern Missouri told the outlet. “The community did not and does not consent to this. It is being forced upon us. It's disgusting that we have no say in the matter.”
The St. Louis Board of Adjustment has also required aldermen to approve the community benefits agreement, which Lambiaso argued in the lawsuit exceeds the board and aldermen’s authority.

Bushra Bano cleared the Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission examination in 2017 with Rank 6, becoming a PCS Officer and later a sub-divisional magistrate. She studied on her own, without coaching, while working full-time and raising two children with her engineer husband. She sat for the UPSC exam twice — in 2019 and 2021 — before securing Rank 234 and clearing the Indian Police Service.
On September 14, 2026, she was transferred from her post as additional SP of Kharagpur in West Bengal’s Paschim Medinipur district, a day after propaganda news channels and Right-wing accounts targeted her for using the Arabic words, ‘Assalamu Alaikum’, ‘Jazakallah’, and ‘Inshallah’, in a video.
In the clip, Bushara is heard commending a government-aided residential coaching academy for minorities, women and SC/ST students at Aligarh Muslim University. While she spoke, she said the three phrases in Arabic. She said, “Assalamu Alaikum. My name is Bushra Bano… ” at first. Towards the end, she said, “…If they (the students) stay and study through the RCA then Inshallah many more people will move forward like me and get the opportunity to serve their country.” At the end she ended her video by saying, “Thank you, Jazakallah”.
“Assalamu Alaikum” is a common greeting which means “Peace be upon you”; “Inshallah” translates to “God willing”, and the phrase “Jazakallah” means “May God Reward You”. The reader might note that these are not religious phrases but greetings and wishes.
A simple video, made by a Muslim IPS officer who used a few Arabic phrases, sent ripples across the Right-wing ecosystem. On September 13, propaganda outlet Sudarshan News, which has its own national TV channel, shared the video on X and said, “Starting with ‘Assalamualaikum,’ slipping in ‘Inshallah’ midway, and wrapping up with ‘Jazakallah’, Bushra Bano… shared how she came from Saudi Arabia and became an IPS officer in India… She made full use of the scheme being run by the government at Aligarh Muslim University.”
“अस्सलाम वाले कुम” से शुरू कर बीच में “इंशाल्लाह” कहते हुए “जज़ाकल्लाह” पर किया खत्म,
खड़गपुर में एडिशनल एसपी के तौर पर तैनात बुशरा बानो ने बताया कि सऊदी अरब से आ कर वो कैसे भारत में बनीं IPS..
सरकार द्वारा अलीगढ़ मुस्लिम यूनिवर्सिटी में चलाई जा रही स्कीम का उठाया भरपूर फायदा.… pic.twitter.com/foYKjihMV2
— Sudarshan News (@SudarshanNewsTV) September 13, 2026
Soon, a barrage of online trolls started targeting Bano. An X handle called @HinduLegalFund posted on X that a complaint had been filed with the West Bengal home secretary regarding the video. “She began with Assalamualaikum, used Inshallah, ended with Jazakallah — and did not use Vande Mataram or Jai Hind…” the post read. Additionally, it stated that a serving officer should maintain “neutrality and national expressions in public communication”.
Complaint filed with West Bengal Home Secretary regarding IPS Bushra Bano’s official video statement.
She began with Assalamualaikum, used Inshallah, ended with Jazakallah — and did not use Vande Mataram or Jai Hind.
A serving officer representing the Indian state should…
— Hindu Legal Fund (@HinduLegalFund) September 13, 2026
Several Right-wing accounts, including @JaipurDialogues and @MeghUpdates, also shared the video and complained that no ‘Vande Mataram’ or ‘Jai Hind’ had been used by the IPS officer.
A notification issued by the government of West Bengal on Monday stated that Bano, alongside two other WBPS officers, was being transferred to a different posting “in public interest”. She has been made the deputy commandant of the state armed police 4th battalion. The notification does not state any reason behind the transfer.
West Bengal Government reshuffles 3 police officers with immediate effect; Partha Ghosh appointed as Addl SP, Kharagpur, Paschim Medinipur.
Subhendu Mandal posted as Addl DC, Chandannagar
Dr. Bushara Bano, transferred as Dy. CO, SAP 4th Bn. pic.twitter.com/MHu5WK4De1
— ANI (@ANI) September 14, 2026
It should be common knowledge that Arabic is a language and Islam is a religion. Muslims use Arabic extensively for religious purposes, but Arabic is not synonymous with Islam. In other words, none of these expressions is simply a ‘Muslim word’ in the narrow linguistic sense. They are Arabic phrases whose meanings and histories intersect with Islamic religious usage, but they are not exclusive to Islam. The tradition of greeting a person with ‘Peace be upon you’, for example, exists in other languages and religious traditions — the Hebrew expression ‘shalom aleichem’, for example, literally means ‘peace be upon you’ and is common in Jewish religious literature. None of this, however, came in the way of pro-BJP handles slamming the officer for her alleged religion posturing.
Sudarshan News editor Suresh Chavhanke, whose history of peddling misinformation and communal propaganda is well documented, called Bano’s case ‘UPSC Jihad’.
Even if one were to accept this as an instance of religious posturing, it would hardly be the first time a police officer has done so. What stands out, however, is how differently such conduct is received depending on the community to which the officer belongs.
In May 2026, IPS officer C V Anand invited priests to perform a puja in his office on the day he took charge as director general of police of Telangana.
Senior IPS officer CV Anand taking charge as Telangana DGP. pic.twitter.com/5ZSSAT6K3w
— Piyush Rai (@Benarasiyaa) May 2, 2026
He himself posted about this on X. No one batted an eyelid. Anand is still serving as the DGP of Telangana.
Anand wrote, “As per the muhurtham , I reached the DGP office at Lakdikapul with my family , took the salute and followed the pujari into the dgp chambers where the puja and blessings were done.”
It was a very busy and perhaps the biggest day for me and my family . As per the muhurtham , I reached the DGP office at Lakdikapul with my family , took the salute and followed the pujari into the dgp chambers where the puja and blessings were done.
Then at 11:05 AM , signed… pic.twitter.com/wlkJX8hszp
— CV Anand IPS (@CVAnandIPS) May 1, 2026
More such instances are not difficult to find.
In Uttar Pradesh’s Sambhal, a circle officer named Anuj Chaudhary, who was an accused of firing during the violence at the Shahi Jama Masjid in November 2024, was pictured joining a Hindu religious procession in January 2025. He was accused of participating in religious rituals while on duty and violating service conduct rules. A complaint was filed by retired IPS officer and Azad Adhikar Sena president Amitabh Thakur, following which a probe was launched.
The same year, on Holi, Chaudhary had stated: “Holi comes once a year, Jumma comes 52 times. If you want to serve sevai, you must also eat gujiya.” Again, an investigation was initiated, and Chaudhary was eventually given a clean chit.
In May 2025, he was transferred from Sambhal to Chandausi, some 30 km away. Three months later, in August, Chaudhary was promoted to the role of additional superintendent of police (ASP). His colleagues and senior officers, including SP K K Bishnoi and ASP Rajesh Kumar Srivastava, marked the occasion with a felicitation ceremony.
Was there no outrage when Anuj Chaudhary carried a mace and marched in a religious procession in uniform? There was, from one section, but he went on to be promoted. Bano’s case panned out differently. The principle, presumably, is that the same rules apply to everyone. In practice, however, some seem to be considerably more equal than others. And if Bushra Bano’s transfer was, as the government put it, “in public interest”, one is left wondering exactly which ‘public’ that interest was meant to serve.
Bano’s transfer set off a series of critical reactions from the Opposition. Several politicians alleged that the transfer was a direct fallout of her use of Arabic phrases. Comparing the incident with Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s inauguration of the Parliament “with sengol & bare chested sadhus”, Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra remarked, “…We are a nation gone mad, poisoned with hate & bigotry. God Save India”.
For a country whose Prime Minister inaugurated new Parliament with sengol & bare chested sadhus, transferring a Muslim IPS officer for saying Assalamalaikum & Inshallah is ridiculous. We are a nation gone mad, poisoned with hate & bigotry. God Save India.
— Mahua Moitra (@MahuaMoitra) September 15, 2026
Former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Mehbooba Mufti also criticised the move, saying the transfer, which was followed by the West Bengal CM “calling an election a ‘test’ of Muslim loyalty”, was “a veiled threat to the community”. “…First our food, clothes and marriages , now even our vocabulary and our votes are being policed”, she added.
Congress MP Imran Pratapgarhi took to X to condemn the move. “A hate-mongering TV channel first sensationalized that video by posting it and incited online trolling against the female IPS officer, and instead of standing by her, the state government transferred her the very next day. What kind of India are you building, @narendramodi ji? @IPS_Association, are you watching this?”, he wrote.

VC firm Peak XV Partners has sold 9.17 Cr shares of fintech major Groww in a bulk deal today. As per NSE data, the firm, via its holding entity Peak XV Partners Investments VI-1, sold the shares at a price of ₹191.49 apiece, 1% higher than Groww’s closing price today. The investor raked in ₹1,756.2 Cr via the transaction, with the shares sold amounting to around almost 1.5% of the company’s equity. The identities of the buyers couldn’t be immediately ascertained. Peak XV is Groww’s largest institutional shareholder, with the firm owning around 98.4 Cr shares in Groww, equivalent to 15.7% stake, as of June 30, 2026. Hence, the investor has offloaded only about 9% of its shareholding in the company. Notably, the listed fintech startup has seen several major investors offloading stake in bulk over the past few months. Earlier, Ribbit Capital offloaded 11.31 Cr shares worth ₹2,217.3 Cr via two bulk deals. Y Combinator also sold 7.47 Cr shares worth ₹1,435.2 Cr through a bulk deal last month. Additionally, US-based early stage investor Friale dumped 1.13 Cr shares in a block deal worth ₹210.4 Cr back in June. Notably, Peak XV had earlier offloaded 15.82 Cr shares as part of the offer for sale (OFS) component of Groww’s IPO, securing a 52X return on its investment. The investor is cashing in at a time when Groww has been delivering strong returns to investors. Its stock has surged nearly 35% on a year-to-date basis. The strong stock performance is in line with the company’s financial health. On the financial front, Groww’s consolidated net profit zoomed 94.3% to ₹735 Cr in Q1 FY27. The startup’s revenue from operations also jumped 66% to ₹1,501.4 Cr during the quarter. However, the last few weeks have seen up and down swings in the stock price amid multiple bulk/block deals. Groww shares slid nearly 4% on the NSE today, ending the day 3.89% lower at ₹189.76.

Since the release of the Steam Deck, Valve fans have gotten very familiar with the idea of the Proton compatibility layer that allows games written for Windows to run capably on the Linux-based SteamOS (though Valve’s efforts in this realm date back further than that). To get more games running on the SteamOS-powered Steam Frame, though, Valve is relying on two additional compatibility layers that are new to the Steam architecture.
The first, FEX, is Valve’s port of fex-emu, an open source project that emulates x86 processor instructions on an Arm chipset. Since 2018, what started as a small cross-platform emulation project has grown to include “an advanced binary recompiler that supports all modern extensions of the x86(-64) instruction set,” according to the Fex website. The emulator can also make calls to graphics libraries like OpenGL and Vulkan to reduce overhead and uses “code caching to minimize stuttering as much as possible,” according to Steam’s own developer documentation.
While Proton was based on the pre-existing Wine conversion tool, Valve engineer Pierre-Loup Griffais told The Verge last year that the company has been funding Fex lead developer Ryan Houdek since the project was just a prototype. Back then, Valve was already anticipating that “close to a decade of work [would be] needed before [Fex-emu] would be robust enough people could rely on it for their libraries.”
“I want to thank the people from Valve for being here from the start and allowing me to kickstart this project,” Houdek wrote last November while marking the seventh anniversary of the project. “They trusted me with the responsibility of designing and frameworking the project in a way that it can work long-term; not only for their use cases but also keeping it an open project that anyone can adapt for their own use cases.”
Now that Fex is finally ready for integration into the Steam Frame headset, Valve says it’s actively exploring versions of SteamOS for other Arm devices. “I think one of the things that we want to do, and that the Frame is kind of paving the way for, is just more general SteamOS for Arm, right?” Griffais recently told Rock Paper Shotgun. “There’s a bunch of devices where you could have a great experience running SteamOS on there, that are currently kind of this adjacent ecosystem that’s just a little bit different. But not really that different, in our opinion.”

Hyper Light Drifter dev at risk of closing after laying off 'nearly everyone'
A tough end for another indie darling.
Making games can be a brutal business, and another studio may have fallen victim to those struggles. Heart Machine Founder Alx Preston posted on LinkedIn today that the maker of Hyper Light Drifter has cut most of its team:
"We had been working on an unannounced title, funded by a publisher. This week, they decided to no longer move forward with it. Without this key income for the studio, any other immediate prospects or other funds, nearly everyone at the studio had to be laid off. It's devastating."
Heart Machine both developed and published Hyper Light Drifter, which launched to critical acclaim in 2016. However, the studio began working with external publishers beginning with its next effort, Solar Ash, and it announced plans in 2022 for Hyper Light Breaker. Work on the sequel to its debut game continued at the same time as the team also embarked on making Possessor(s), which may have stretched the team's resources thin. Although Possessor(s) did come out last year, Heart Machine ended development on Hyper Light Breaker and laid off workers in October 2025. Some of its remaining employees opted to unionize in March 2026.
Preston added in his missive today that "Navigating an increasingly challenging industry has been extremely difficult, and I'm not sure yet what's next for Heart Machine to survive." It's a sad possible end for a studio that won so many fans ten years ago.

The Delhi High Court on Thursday (September 17, 2026) cautioned that it could stay the counting of votes and declaration of results of the Delhi University Students’ Union (DUSU) elections if it was not satisfied with the action taken by the authorities over alleged violence and hooliganism during the campaign.
The warning came after the court was informed of alleged violence, vandalism, entry of outsiders and other violations during campaigning, which ended on Wednesday (September 17, 2026). Voting is scheduled for Friday (September 18, 2026) and counting for September 19.
A Bench comprising Chief Justice D.K. Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia directed Delhi Police and Delhi University to submit status reports by Friday and asked lawyers representing various student organisations to appear before it.
“No excuses will be accepted by the court. We are making it very clear that though we are not staying the election or postponing the election, if we are not satisfied by your action, tomorrow we can pass harsher orders, including staying the counting and declaration of results,” the Bench said.
The court said criminal conduct could not be justified in the name of democracy and called the material before it indicative of a “complete failure” by the authorities and students.
Campus violence
A group of Delhi University teachers has written to Vice-Chancellor P.C. Joshi seeking urgent intervention against alleged assaults, threats and misconduct towards teachers, following an incident at Motilal Nehru College (Evening) in which a teacher was allegedly assaulted by a group of students during the DUSU election campaign.
According to the teachers, the group of students attempting to enter the college for campaigning allegedly assaulted a teacher who tried to stop them. The students have not been identified, and their organisation is unclear.
The teachers called the incident “a matter of serious concern” and said similar instances of threats, intimidation and physical altercations involving teachers and students had been reported across the university.

Delhi has reportedly bucked the broader rainfall trend this monsoon, receiving 8% more rain than its seasonal normal as of September 16, even as neighbouring regions recorded rainfall deficits. The unusual contrast has raised the possibility that changing weather patterns linked to a strengthening El Niño, along with climate change, may have influenced the capital’s rainfall, according to a report by Times Of India. While Delhi recorded above-normal rainfall, its meteorological subdivision, Haryana, received 23% less rainfall, while northwest India as a whole was 10% below normal. The contrast becomes more striking when district-level rainfall is considered. Delhi sits close to a large belt of rainfall-deficient districts stretching across Haryana and Punjab. Neighbouring Sonipat has recorded 32% less rainfall than normal, while Rohtak is at a 47% deficit. Further north, Hoshiarpur has received 53% less rainfall and Kapurthala is facing a 69% shortfall. More than 30 districts across Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh and western Uttar Pradesh have recorded significant rainfall deficits this season. One possible explanation lies in the changing movement of low-pressure systems originating over the Bay of Bengal, the report noted. This season, these systems appear to have followed a different trajectory, potentially influenced by El Niño conditions, bringing more rainfall towards Delhi-NCR. The interaction of these systems with western disturbances may have further boosted rainfall over the capital, helping Delhi emerge as an unusual pocket of above-normal rainfall amid a wider rain-deficient region. Meanwhile, India could face an extended disruption to its monsoon as a potentially record-strength El Niño develops, while unusually warm Pacific Ocean temperatures are also raising concerns about an exceptionally hot summer in 2027, The Telegraph reported. The climate pattern is expected to reach its peak sometime between late 2026 and early 2027. However, scientists say its influence could continue even after the phenomenon begins to weaken, as heat accumulated in the Pacific can take months to dissipate. This could have prolonged effects on India's monsoon, temperatures and wider weather patterns. The outlook comes as India's monsoon rainfall is already 13% below normal, according to the report. About 40% of the country has received rainfall at least 20% below the average, potentially creating risks for agricultural output and the wider economy. The UK Met Office said on Friday that the El Niño event now taking shape could become the strongest observed since the 1800s. Some projections indicate that sea surface temperatures in the Pacific could rise to more than 3°C above the average by late 2026 or the beginning of 2027. “I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts,” Adam Scaife, head of the long-range forecasting division at the UK Met Office, said in a statement on Friday. A video is viral on social media platforms, which shows Prime Minister Narendra Modi appearing to present the Chinese President Xi Jinping with his own portrait.
Users have shared this clip with the claim that it is from the Chinese President’s current visit to India for the ongoing BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12 and 13.
An X user named Priya Purohit (@Priyaa_Purohit) posted the clip on September 12, which garnered close to 800,000 views at the time of this article being written. (Archive)
Modi gifted Xi Jinping his own portrait. 😭
Self-Love Level : PMO Edition 😤 🤣 pic.twitter.com/rNjUpL6J9w
— Priya Purohit (@Priyaa_Purohit) September 12, 2026
Another X user with the handle, @LancerFlying, also posted the clip. (Archive)
Kaun apni hi photo kisi ko gift karta hai??
I mean apni girlfriend ke ilawa that is🤣😂 pic.twitter.com/Uu5RVbTAaM
— Flying Lancer Полковник Раджен Bhaduri (@LancerFlying) September 11, 2026
Others, such as @MeIndian03 and @HenrySingh_x also posted the viral clip. (Archives: 1, 2)
Fact Check
To check whether Modi had indeed presented Xi Jinping with his own portrait, we broke down the clip into keyframes. A reverse image search on one such keyframe led us to this article published by Asia News Network on August 11, 2025. It features a photo which shows the leaders posing with the portrait, with the description clarifying that it was taken on October 12, 2019, during a meeting between Narendra Modi and Xi Jinping in Mahabalipuram in Tamil Nadu.
Taking cue from this, we ran relevant keyword searches on Google, which led us to more reports about the Chinese President’s visit to India in 2019.
We found that on October 12, PM Modi had gifted his Chinese counterpart a handmade silk shawl. An NDTV report noted, that in return, Xi Jinping had gifted him a “…porcelain memento, which had PM Modi’s image.
The Times of India, in a report from October 12, 2019, wrote in detail about the meeting between the two leaders on the concluding day of the summit, corroborating that a porcelain plate, made of traditional bone China, with a portrait of the Indian Prime Minister on it, had been presented to Modi at Mamallapuram, or Mahabalipuram.
Other news outlets like Economic Times and WION, too, reported on the exchange of gifts between the two leaders.
We also found a video of the meeting, uploaded by VOA News China, where it can be clearly seen that the Chinese President is offering Modi the porcelain plate with his portrait on it.
The Press Information Bureau (PIB) had also posted photos of the two leaders meeting on the concluding day of the summit.
PM @narendramodi exchanging gifts with Chinese President #XiJinping in #Mamallapuram #ModixijinpingMeet pic.twitter.com/nE4RIze35M
— PIB India (@PIB_India) October 12, 2019
To sum up, a video is viral with the false claim that PM Modi presented Xi Jinping with his own portrait, during the 2026 BRICS summit in New Delhi. Alt News found that it was in fact the Chinese President who had presented Modi with a porcelain plate carrying his portrait, during an informal summit at Mamallapuram in October 2019.

DJI's new SDR Transmission II beams 4K 60 fps HDR video up to 2.5 miles
The new system will benefit professional multi-camera shoots for sports and more.
An underrated part of DJI's success is in the area of video transmission, with the company's drones and camera systems offering wireless video quality and range that rivals can't match. Now, the Shenzhen-based company is significantly upping its game in the area of pro video with the its new SDR Transmission II system. It boosts both image quality and range, giving multi-camera productions more options in tricky environments.
Where the original SDR Transmission system was limited to 1080p video at a 20Mbps bitrate and range of 1.8 miles (3 km), the SDR Transmission II ("SDR" means "software defined radio") in TX mode can send 4K 60 fps HDR video at 50Mbps to transceivers (RX mode) as far away as 2.5 miles (4 km). That means for pro productions, "a reliable link can be established in various environments from open stadiums to dense mountain forests, and through demanding car-to-car shots or challenging FPV drone work," DJI said.
A single transceiver can connect to up to eight others with each supporting remote control. On top of providing monitoring for directors, producers and set personnel, it "lets camera operators and focus pullers remotely adjust settings and control the camera," DJI said. For larger productions, it supports up to five transmitters and 40 receivers working simultaneously for complex multi-camera shoots.
Another key feature is the ability to tap to switch between camera feeds without the normal re-booting, disconnecting and searching required. Latency is as low as 35 milliseconds for more responsive commands for things like focus pulling and gimbal movement. Along with smartphone monitoring, it supports assist tools like LUTs, focus peaking and waveforms. It also supports PTP control to change functions like capture, aperture, shutter speed and ISO on compatible cameras.
Though this tech is professionally oriented, it uses the same foundational wireless tech as DJI's OcuSync system for drones. It would be nice if DJI boosted OcuSync transmission to 4K 60p as well, as that would provide a better backup in case of on-board drone memory problems. The DJI SDR Transmission 2 transceivers start at €349 or £309, and you can a Combo two-pack for €629 (£559). There's no US availability yet, likely due to a ban on certain DJI products.

Heavy rain and floods in northern Vietnam submerge homes and disrupt economy
Heavy rain has caused widespread flooding across northern Vietnam
HANOI, Vietnam -- Heavy rain caused flooding across parts of northern Vietnam on Thursday, disrupting travel, inundating homes and pushing several rivers above dangerous levels, authorities and state media said.
Rain has fallen across northern and north-central Vietnam this week, with some areas receiving more than 50 centimeters (19.7 inches), according to the disaster prevention department said.
More than 2,000 homes have been submerged, many key transportation routes blocked and more than 1,000 households isolated. Ninh Binh and Thanh Hoa provinces, which include lowland and hilly areas south of the capital Hanoi, have been among the hardest hit.
Vietnam is among the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries and prone to flooding. A series of severe storms last year spurred the country to find new ways to prepare for and manage floods.
In Thanh Hoa province, authorities told students to stay home because flooding had made travel to school dangerous, state media said.
Heavy rains and flooding have submerged or damaged about 10,014 hectares (24,745 acres) of rice and other crops, with the largest losses reported in Ninh Binh, Thanh Hoa and Nghe An provinces. Thousands of livestock and poultry also have been killed.
“The flood happens every year,” Ninh Binh resident Tran Ngoc Tai told national broadcaster VTV, adding that people were prepared with fresh water and food.
Many streets in Hanoi were deeply flooded Thursday morning, with water nearly a meter (3.2 feet) deep in some places, disrupting traffic and making it difficult for residents to get to work, take children to school or leave their homes.
Rainfall from Wednesday night to Thursday morning exceeded 15 centimeters (5.9 inches) in some areas, state media said.
Many high schools and universities in Hanoi remained closed or switched to online classes Thursday afternoon as heavy rain caused widespread flooding.
The rising waters of Bui River in the southwest outskirts of Hanoi threatened to flood homes, prompting authorities to deploy hundreds of soldiers to help residents move belongings to higher ground, state media said.
A cold air mass moving south is expected to bring five days of heavy rain to southern Vietnam including flood-prone Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam’s financial capital, starting Sept. 17, according to the Southern Regional Hydro-Meteorological Center.
Forecasters predict widespread rain through Sept. 21. Authorities have warned of flooding in low-lying areas and along waterways. Ho Chi Minh City is forecast to receive 10 to 20 centimeters (4 to 8 inches) of rain, with some areas getting more.
Vietnam experienced repeated severe flooding in 2025. Tropical Storm Wipha brought heavy rain and flooding in July, followed by more flooding and landslides in August when Tropical Storm Kajiki struck. Typhoon Bualoi killed at least 26 in September. In October, the historic cities of Hue and Hoi An in central Vietnam flooded, along with much of northern Vietnam.
