Indonesian police are investigating the deaths of three Australians who died in Bali over the weekend, with initial reports suggesting a father killed his two young children before taking his own life.
The man, 57, and his two children, seven and four, who are also Indonesian citizens, were discovered deceased in a bungalow in Kuta on Sunday morning.
According to Denpasar police, a witness, 51-year-old Nur Khamid, received a phone call from someone claiming to be the victim’s wife at about 8.30am on Sunday. She was in Jakarta, and asked Khamid to check on the condition of her husband and family, who she had been unable to reach.
Khamid went to their bungalow and tried to look inside through a window, but “no activity or people were visible inside”, Denpasar police said in its statement.
The witness then met the bungalow owner and both returned to perform a check before contacting the “neighbourhood head”, Kelian Lingkungan. Residents “knocked and pounded” on the door before it was forcibly opened, and the three bodies were located.
“Police officers arriving at the scene conducted a crime scene investigation and preliminary examination alongside the Denpasar Police Identification Team,” the statement read.
“From the initial external examination of the three victims, it is suspected that the two children died as a result of acts of violence, while [the father] is suspected to have died by hanging.”
The bodies are at Prof Dr IGNG Ngoerah Central general hospital for further examination and handling.
The Denpasar police chief, senior commissioner Leonardo D Simatupang, said Kuta police officers were investigating the incident.
“Investigators are still conducting inquiries, including crime scene processing, examining CCTV footage at the scene, and questioning witnesses – including the victim’s wife – to determine the cause of death,” he said.
Simatupang said Kuta police had taken a statement from the man’s wife and reviewed CCTV footage. They had also coordinated with the Australian consulate.
A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the family of the three Australians.
“We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment,” they said in a statement.

It’s a big year for Nintendo of America — and it’s about to get bigger.
On the heels of the one-year anniversary for the launch of the Nintendo Switch 2 gaming console and amid the 40th anniversary celebrations for “The Legend of Zelda” franchise, Nintendo of America president and COO Devon Pritchard warns fans this is just the start of the video game giant’s multiyear master IP plan.
“We’re working with Sony Pictures. We are going to have a movie come out in the end of April,” Pritchard told Variety co-editor-in-chief Cynthia Littleton during a panel at the Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY on Thursday. “We’re very excited about that. And ‘The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.’”
Pritchard is referring to the upcoming “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” remake coming to Switch 2 in November, which will be out ahead of the release of “The Legend of Zelda” live-action film next spring. That game is one of the most anticipated releases by Switch 2 fans, but it’s far from the last for this console.
Popular on Variety
“We’re at the beginning of Nintendo Switch 2,” Pritchard said. “This is just beginning and we’ve already had some really wonderful experiences, both ours and third party come to the table and I can’t wait to see what the system is going to do and what our talented developers will bring to the table. But again, those partnerships and touchpoints with companies like Sony and Sony Pictures around how we can bring those experiences more broadly to not only our current players and fans but to new ones, I think that’s one of the most exciting things for us over the next few years”
While Nintendo has no shortage of dedicated fans, Pritchard said that the Japan-based company is just as concerned about the surplus of content problem facing all media companies these days. But Nintendo is trying to attack that problem with a different solution than its competitors.
“There are more channels for content than ever before,” Pritchard said. “Content is available 24/7. So I think you hear a lot of times, people saying, we are competing for consumers’ time and I think what’s unique is that Nintendo is focused instead on building experiences that create relationships that last generations and I think that’s a different kind of focus for us. But that really is where we put our time and our energy is, how do we create those fun experiences? And that becomes the test: is something fun? It sounds simple, of course it’s not.”

Anthropic said Thursday it has blocked efforts by bad actors to use its artificial intelligence models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance, and research that could have led to biological weapons.
As AI models grow more powerful, elaborate cyberattacks no longer require sophisticated skills and even lone individuals can create threats that would not have been possible even a year ago, Anthropic said. The company said it has added stronger safeguards in its latest models to restrict biological research that could also be used to make weapons.
“The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic said in its third report since March 2025 describing AI misuse. The report includes snippets of the malicious code and AI prompts Anthropic said it found, and urges governments and AI competitors to identify and prevent similar abuse.
“We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services. As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” the company said.
The lengthy report by the AI startup, which is planning an initial public offering this fall, was published two days after one of its researchers announced he's resigning over concerns that Anthropic and its competitors are not acting responsibly in AI development. He echoed concerns raised inside and outside of the industry about the technology’s potential to elude human control.
Between December 2025 and August 2026, researchers at Anthropic found misuse by actors ranging from spyware vendors and “politically motivated individuals” to state-sponsored groups spreading propaganda.
Among the findings in the company's report are unnamed actors attempting to use its models for research that could have led to biological weapons. In one instance, Anthropic said its systems blocked a request for Claude’s assistance in authoring a grant application for scientific funding.
“The work discussed in the application involved gain-of-function research (that is, research that genetically alters an organism to create a new or enhanced biological property) on the chikungunya virus. This gain of function research was aimed at the virus’ transmissibility and immune evasion properties,” the report said.
Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus that causes debilitating symptoms such as severe pain and fever. The request involved a grant proposal for research seeking to enhance mutations to make the virus progressively more harmful. While such research could “certainly” be used to develop better vaccines and treatments, Anthropic said, “it could also be used to make the pathogen more dangerous.”
None of the cases Anthropic included in its report were found to be using its newer, more powerful Claude Fable or Mythos-class models, with the exception of one illicit distillation case that Anthropic described as “an industrial-scale, covert campaign to extract a model’s capabilities and replicate them in another model without authorization.”
Anthropic said its older models, such as Claude Opus 4 and Claude Sonnet 4.5, from 2025, “were well below the threshold where they could meaningfully assist a sophisticated user in carrying out dangerous biological research.”
“As a result, safeguards on these models were less stringent, directed mostly at preventing access to content that might uplift novices in recreating known bioweapons,” the report said. “But for today’s models — which are capable of assisting in a range of complex scientific research tasks — the evidence is no longer certain, and we cannot make that same assurance.”
Because of this, Anthropic has applied “stronger safeguards that restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries” in its more recent models, such as Claude Fable 5, the report said.
As companies introduce increasingly powerful AI models, experts have called on governments to regulate the technology, rather than relying on the industry to police itself.
John Thickstun, an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University, said it is an uncomfortable position for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to be in when they are expected to determine what is safe vs. unsafe behaviour and make "value judgments at societal scale without any kind of democratic or deliberative oversight.”
Anthropic also found groups that created hundreds of social media accounts that look like they belong to ordinary people and then posted material amplifying the same political view over the course of a week. The company outlined nine such cases it found, originating in Russia, Iran, Turkey and across the Persian Gulf, South Asia, Africa and Europe.
While social media companies can detect influence operations on their platforms once posts are circulating, “we may see it on Claude while the operation is still being built.”
Anthropic released this report after one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, announced he's resigning amid fears the company and its chief rival OpenAI “are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Coxon's post warned that some of his colleagues now believe AI could threaten human life by the end of the decade.
But Anthropic said it has blocked each of the malicious activities it identified, used the experience to strengthen safeguards and shared information with government authorities and industry partners.
“We hope that the findings in this report will help other developers recognize similar patterns on their own platforms, give governments and civil society a clearer view of how emerging threats take shape, and strengthen collective defenses,” Anthropic said.

Half a year after Iranian drone strikes knocked out multiple Amazon data centers, the US tech company has acknowledged the permanent loss of some customer data that was hosted in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.
Amazon Web Services was “unable to restore access to the resources and data” hosted in some of the war-damaged data centers, according to an AWS dashboard update posted on September 15. The development was first reported by Reuters and suggests that the Iranian strikes inflicted catastrophic damage on the data centers.
Customer data was irretrievably lost in one of three AWS availability zones in the United Arab Emirates region, specifically the mec1-az2 availability zone. Each availability zone is serviced by one or more Amazon data centers.
The company is still working on “recovering regional resources” and restoring resources hosted in the other two availability zones in the United Arab Emirates. The AWS update described ongoing work to replace “affected infrastructure” and promised to update customers on a restoration of services in the coming months.
But the destruction was apparently even more widespread for the data centers in the Bahrain region, because Amazon said it was unable to restore access to resources and data across all three availability zones there.
“The damage to our infrastructure spanned multiple availability zones and exceeded what our regional and multi-AZ services are designed to withstand,” the AWS update said.
The company had already suspended customer billing in the affected AWS regions in Bahrain and the UAE and has spent the past six months attempting to restore normal operations.
The Iranian drones first struck the Amazon data centers on March 1 in the opening days of the ongoing war that began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28.
AWS immediately urged customers to migrate resources to other cloud regions and use remote backups to restore any “inaccessible resources.” The cloud service also reportedly issued $150 million in customer credits following the initial Iranian strikes in March.
A follow-up Iranian strike focused on Amazon’s data centers in Bahrain on April 1. The latest AWS update acknowledged this “disruption” of a second availability zone in the Bahrain region in April but described most affected customers as having already followed the company’s recommendations to migrate their cloud computing workloads elsewhere.
On July 24, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched yet another strike using missiles that specifically targeted a remaining Amazon data center structure in Bahrain. That damage was independently confirmed by satellite imagery.
“We remain committed to supporting our customers in Bahrain in the long term and will share a further update in early 2027,” the latest AWS update said.
Meanwhile, the US-Israeli war with Iran has since spiraled into a broader regional conflict and growing global energy crisis because of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. One of the few silver linings has been the surging interest worldwide in renewable power generation, such as solar rooftop panels.

Buddhi Clinic and The Hindu will host a webinar, “Alzheimer’s Dementia: The Promise of Brain Stimulation,” on September 20 at 11.30 a.m. as part of events organised to observe World Alzheimer’s Day on September 21.
For decades, patients and families living with dementia were often told that treatment could largely focus on managing symptoms. Today, however, earlier diagnosis, advances in disease-modifying therapies, rehabilitation, lifestyle interventions and emerging approaches to brain stimulation are opening up new possibilities in dementia care.
At the heart of the discussion is an important question: Can stimulating the brain help preserve cognitive function and change the way Alzheimer’s disease is managed?
Ennapadam S. Krishnamoorthy, Founder, Behavioural Neurologist and Neuropsychiatrist, Buddhi Clinic, will begin by looking at Alzheimer’s disease and dementia beyond the commonly understood symptom of memory loss. He will discuss why recognising the early signs and arriving at an accurate diagnosis can make a significant difference to care and long-term planning. He will also examine the role of multidisciplinary assessments, including those undertaken at Buddhi Clinic, and how the treatment landscape is evolving — from symptomatic medications and rehabilitation to newer disease-modifying therapies.
The discussion will then move to one of the emerging frontiers in dementia care: neuromodulation and brain stimulation.
Vivek Misra, Senior Consultant – Neuromodulation & Clinical Neurosciences, Buddhi Clinic, will explain how Alzheimer’s disease affects not only individual regions of the brain but also the networks that connect them. As these interconnected networks become disrupted, researchers are exploring whether stimulating specific areas or key hubs could help support cognitive function. The session will examine the science behind these developing approaches and what they could mean for the future of Alzheimer’s care.
The changing landscape suggests that the future of dementia care may not depend on a single drug or technology. Instead, it could involve a more integrated approach that brings together early diagnosis, disease-modifying and symptomatic treatments, lifestyle and vascular risk management, cognitive rehabilitation, and emerging techniques aimed at modulating the brain’s networks.
As research continues to expand the possibilities, the webinar will examine where the science stands today, which approaches remain promising but experimental, and how these advances could shape the future of Alzheimer’s care. The discussion will also explore how earlier intervention and a more comprehensive approach to treatment could help patients and families navigate an evolving landscape of dementia care.
Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, The Hindu, will moderate the session. To register, please visit https://newsth.live/THBCAE or scan the QR code

In June 2026, numerous Chinese news media outlets reported on updated international guidelines advising researchers not to independently respond to extraterrestrial signals. English-language news outlets also reported on these updated guidelines, which came from an international scientific organization. It was not possible to find any evidence of the Chinese government sending a nationwide alert telling people not to communicate with aliens, nor of the existence of a U.N. "alien hotline."
In September 2026, a rumor circulated online that the Chinese government broadcast a warning to the country's population of roughly 1.4 billion people, instructing them not to communicate with aliens and to instead contact the United Nations if extraterrestrial life reaches out to them.
For example, one Instagram user posted a video making the claim (archived), during which the user said the alleged warning was distributed through several channels:
Broadcast was made as if it were a giant emergency. They did it through the radio, they did it like the way that you get Amber Alerts on your phone, they did a television broadcast and they had messengers going into rural communities to tell people this and give them this information.
The supposed announcement said, "If you are contacted by aliens, do not attempt to communicate with them. Call this phone number, which will send you to the United Nations desk of the alien communications specialist, and they will take care of it for you." The Instagram user later referred to the supposed number as an "alien hotline" and said similar messages circulated in Japan and South Korea.
The claim spread spread elsewhere on Instagram as well as on Reddit and Facebook. Readers also contacted Snopes to ask whether it was true.
In short, it was not possible to find any evidence the Chinese government issued the nationwide warning described in the posts, and a spokesperson for China's embassy in Washington, D.C., said no Chinese government agency issued such a warning. The real guidance behind the rumor also did not instruct ordinary people to call a U.N. "alien communications specialist" if extraterrestrials contacted them. As such, we have rated the claim as false.
Warning did appear in Chinese media
There is a real story behind the rumor. On June 1, 2026, the International Academy of Astronautics, a Paris-based nongovernmental scientific organization, published updated guidelines for people and organizations involved in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI. The document says possible signals should be independently verified and that researchers should not send a reply before international consultation.
These guidelines did receive attention in China. For instance, on June 7, IT Home, a Chinese technology news website, published an article titled (translated using Google Translate) "Do not respond to aliens without authorization! The International Academy of Astronautics updates eight guidelines." China Science Daily, Shanghai-based digital newspaper The Paper and national television broadcaster CCTV News also reported on the updated declaration.
The article on The Paper's website appeared in its "Government Affairs" section, which could make it seem like an official government message.
English-language news media outlets similarly reported on the IAA's updated guidelines.
Graphic may explain how rumor spread
A blue graphic with yellow text in Chinese circulated alongside the rumor in some social media posts. Jingchu Network (荆楚网) — which is part of CnHubei, a news website in Hubei province — posted the graphic on its Douyin account (shown below). The message, translated using Google Translate, reads:
Do not reply to extraterrestrials on your own initiative; the International Academy of Astronautics recommends immediately notifying the United Nations upon the discovery of extraterrestrial life.
(Jingchu Network Douyin account)
The Douyin post cites Red Star News as its source and explains that the message concerned the IAA's guidelines. On June 7, Red Star News published an article about the IAA update.
Jingchu Network is a state-backed news outlet. According to its website, it is supervised by the Hubei Provincial Party Committee Propaganda Department and the Hubei Provincial Cyberspace Administration. "It is the only national key provincial news website in Hubei Province approved by the State Council Information Office," the website reads.
The graphic later circulated on English-language social media platforms, where users described it as an announcement posted in China. This may have contributed to claims that the Chinese government itself issued the warning.
Government website also links to the story
The story also indirectly appeared on at least one official Chinese government website.
On June 10, Fushun Municipal Science and Technology Bureau — a government department of the city of Fushun, in Liaoning province — listed (as shown below) a webpage titled, "Do not respond to aliens without authorization! Why did the International Academy of Astronautics call for a halt?" in the "Science and Technology Work Updates" section of its website.
(fskjj.fushun.gov.cn)
However, that webpage originated from outside the department's website. It was not presenting the message as a new government policy or warning.
Liu Chang, a spokesperson for China's embassy in Washington, D.C. said via email that the Chinese government issued no such warning:
Based on publicly available information to my knowledge, no Chinese government agency issued such a warning, distributed it through national alert channels, or instructed the public to contact the U.N. about extraterrestrial contact.
The claim may stem from confusion over a revised SETI protocol issued by the International Academy of Astronautics and reported by Chinese media. It was not a Chinese government notice.
Snopes also contacted the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Guidance is for researchers, not ordinary people
The IAA document explicitly says it was written for people and organizations taking part in scientific SETI research. It does not tell ordinary people what to do if an alien personally contacts them.
The declaration says that after a confirmed detection, researchers should take part in international consultations over whether a response should be sent. Until those talks are finished, "no reply should be sent." It also says those discussions should include the United Nations and other international bodies.
Chinese Science Daily interviewed Zhang Tongjie, a Beijing Normal University professor who took part in discussions about the revised declaration. He reportedly said the cautious approach was based on uncertainty about whether an extraterrestrial civilization would be friendly, hostile or neutral. He was also quoted as saying the declaration was not legally binding.
There is no UN 'alien hotline'
Social media posts also claimed Chinese citizens were given a phone number for a U.N. "alien communications specialist," but no such a number is in the IAA declaration. The document directs questions about its principles to the IAA itself.
Searching Google for a United Nations "alien communications specialist" returned no results (archived) suggesting that such a role exists.
Though the declaration says consultations about whether to respond to confirmed extraterrestrial intelligence should involve the United Nations and other international bodies, it also says the specific procedures for such consultations still need to be established in a separate agreement or arrangement.
The idea of an official U.N. representative for alien contact has appeared before. In 2010, a report in British newspaper The Times claimed astrophysicist Mazlan Othman, then-director of the U.N. Office for Outer Space Affairs, was appointed as Earth's contact person for extraterrestrials. Othman denied this and said no specific U.N. response role had been decided, while further action would be up to member states.
Therefore, the IAA declaration's reference to international consultation through the United Nations does not mean there is a U.N. "alien hotline."
Snopes has contacted the U.N. and, specifically, its Office for Outer Space Affairs to ask whether such a hotline exists. We will update this article if we receive any responses.
Bottom line
All in all, there is a kernel of truth behind the story. In June 2026, Chinese news media outlets did publish messages saying people should not "respond to aliens" without authorization, and an official municipal government website did link to a webpage on the topic.
However, that information came from guidelines for SETI researchers issued by the International Academy of Astronautics. The guidelines say a possible extraterrestrial signal should first be verified and that no response should be sent before international consultation.
Finally, it was not possible to find any evidence that China sent a nationwide emergency alert or gave people a phone number for a U.N. "alien communications specialist."

Is Canada about to join the EU?

Both sides seem to be seeking closer ties, and in his speech today, Carney said he welcomed the EU's "ambition" for Canada to become an "associate member".
The president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors.
US President Donald Trump has threatened to take action against the EU if it makes Canada its first "associate member".
The BBC's Europe editor Katya Alder looks at the EU's future relationship with Canada and what it really means.

Here is a story that on the face of it seems so wildly unlikely it can only be true. Indeed, the very concept of a romantic documentary sounds almost oxymoronic, an indication of how much nonfiction films have become synonymous with grim histories full of suffering and injustice. Let’s hope this sweet work, directed by Orlando von Einsiedel (who’s made his share of hardcore, suffering-intensive docs including Oscar-winning short The White Helmets) launches a new trend in nonfiction film-making for stuff that makes you happy-cry.
The basic meet-cute happened in 1975, when PK (played by Chirag Lobo in the film’s extensive re-enactments) met Lotta (Mina Dale) in Delhi. He was a poor street artist, a Dalit, the lowest possible caste, once called Untouchables. The real PK Mahanandia appears on screen to explain how he had left his rural village for Delhi in order to get away from all that caste hierarchy. When he met Lotta he pretty much knew he’d met the woman of his dreams because he’d been carrying a horoscope his father had commissioned for him when he was a baby that prophesised he’d fall in love with a woman whose family owned a jungle. Lotta, a backpacker from Sweden, hailed from a clan back home that owned a forest, so that was good enough for PK to believe he’d met his fate. After a chaste holiday romance bloomed between these two crazy kids, she went back to Sweden and he decided to bicycle the 6,000 miles all the way there from India to prove his love.
As we hear the now elderly young lovers describe what they were thinking at the time, we watch Lobo and Dale act out the journey, with poor PK getting into a few scrapes that set him back a few steps as he plods his way westward. Some of the most touching interludes are the interactions he has with strangers along the way that seem incredibly naturalistic and semi-improvised. Cynics might quibble that one can’t help wondering what darker parts of the story have been left out, and note that the actors chosen to play the lovers are a few notches more conventionally beautiful than the actual people – but every love story has its soft focus, flaw-concealing fudges so we’ll let it slide here.

In September 2026, roughly a year after Charlie Kirk's assassination, a rumor recirculated on social media claiming the conservative activist once called George Floyd a "scumbag."
"Charlie Kirk about George Floyd a few years before scumbag KKKirk himself was murdered in public," read one Facebook post (archived) with the claim. The post included purported comments Kirk made about Floyd.
(Facebook page Community Independent Journal)
Since Kirk's assassination in September 2025, the claim has spread on X, Facebook and Instagram, as well as via outlets such as Black News, Arkansas Times and India Times.
It was true Kirk called Floyd a "scumbag" during a 2021 public appearance in Mankato, Minnesota, a video of that event shows. He apparently made the comment in reference to Floyd's alleged criminal history and the circumstances surrounding his death.
Kirk's exact words were: "I am also going to offer some context and some nuance about the death of George Floyd that no one dares to say out loud. Which is that this guy was a scumbag. Now, does that mean he deserves to die? That's two totally different things — of course not."
The event took place on Oct. 6, 2021, at Minnesota State University as part of Kirk's "Exposing Critical Racism Tour." Turning Point USA, Kirk's political organization, streamed (archived) the event live on YouTube under the title "LIVE: Charlie Kirk at Minnesota State University - Mankato." (Kirk made the "scumbag" remark around the 15:28 mark in the video.)
Below is our transcript of the relevant portion of Kirk's speech (emphasis ours):
On May 25, 2020, up in Minneapolis, a cellphone video changed the trajectory of our entire nation. In this state.
The reason why our tour is called the CRT [Critical Racism Tour] Tour is because of George Floyd's death and the misinterpretation of that. And I'm not going to go on this endless soapbox defending Derek Chauvin, I think he's kind of not a great person.
But I am also going to offer some context and some nuance about the death of George Floyd that no one dares to say out loud. Which is that this guy was a scumbag. Now, does that mean he deserves to die? That's two totally different things — of course not.
After that comment, Kirk listed a series of accusations about Floyd's background, criminal history and cause of death — all with varying degrees of legitimacy. The Associated Press, reporting on the event, described that section of the speech as "an avalanche of aspersions and debunked claims about Floyd."
Kirk claimed protests and debates following Floyd's death were based on a "misinterpretation" of the event.
At the time, several media outlets reported on the event and Kirk's comments about Floyd, including the Minnesota Reporter and University of Alabama student-run publication The Crimson White.
The "scumbag" statement is just one of many purported quotes by Kirk that circulated after his death. For example, social media users shared an authentic quote he made about some prominent Black women not having "the brain processing power to otherwise be taken really seriously," as well as a false rumor about him saying gay people should be stoned to death.

SC awards ₹12 lakh to Haryana woman denied Indian Oil Corporation job in 1988
Haryana woman was denied helper’s job at an LPG bottling plant in 1988 because the company considered the work of carrying gas cylinders unsuitable for women
The Supreme Court on Thursday directed Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) to pay ₹12 lakh in compensation to a Haryana woman who was denied a helper’s job at an LPG bottling plant in 1988 because the company considered the work of carrying gas cylinders unsuitable for women.
“It is an affront to womanhood and that too by a Government of India undertaking,” a bench of justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi said, pulling up the government entity for “disrespecting” women.
As the woman had attained the age of 63, well beyond the age of superannuation, the court noted that she had litigated for decades and directed IOC to pay a lump sum of ₹12 lakh in compensation.
“Day in and day out, when men are not at home, it is the women who lift gas cylinders in the house and change it. And you denied her appointment just because she is a lady. This is disrespect to womanhood,” the bench said.
The woman petitioner, Sumitra, was a resident of Karnal in Haryana and belonged to the Scheduled Caste community. She had sought employment as a helper when the LPG bottling plant opened in Karnal in 1988. She was one of the 49 persons shortlisted for the job. Although educationally qualified and meeting all the requirements, she did not figure among the 43 selected candidates. Later, she was told that she had been refused employment because she was a woman.
The IOC, in its response before the top court, said, “As the nature of the job and atmosphere and odd working hours in the company of the males was such that petitioner being lady was not considered fit for the job.”
Sumitra had first approached the trial court, where she won a decree in 1990 directing IOC to absorb her in any post other than that of a labourer. This judgment was challenged by the IOC before the Punjab & Haryana high court, which overturned the decision in October 2025. It was this order that Sumitra challenged in the top court.
The court noted the long litigation that the woman had to endure, in addition to the discrimination at the hands of IOC. The petition, filed through advocate Surya Nath Pandey, stated that gender was the only ground for denying her employment.
The bench observed, “In India, every day we say a woman is a goddess, respect her. This is a fit case for compensation.”
At one point during the hearing, the IOC lawyer was even willing to agree to mediation. However, the court was not interested in keeping the matter pending after going through the facts of the case and noting the considerable delay of over three decades since the litigation began.

LONDON — English health authorities on Thursday agreed to provide a breast cancer drug from AstraZeneca through the National Health Service, ending a years-long dispute that stoked questions about how committed the pharma company was to the U.K.
Notably, the move — one that will extend the drug, called Enhertu, to an estimated 1,000 people in England — is in part a result of a U.S.-U.K. drug pricing deal reached late last year. Under the pact, a U.K. health agency agreed to raise the thresholds for what would be considered a cost-effective drug and worth paying for on the NHS.
Now, women with metastatic breast cancer whose tumors have low levels of the protein HER2 will be eligible to receive Enhertu, a type of next-generation chemotherapy known as an antibody-drug conjugate. AstraZeneca noted that Scotland has covered the drug since 2023, and it’s paid for in 26 other European countries. (Patients with HER2-positive cancers have been able to get Enhertu in England.)

The story uses screenshots and not the actual viral video in view of its sensitive nature.
A 12-second long video is going viral on social media where a woman is seen bathing in river water while wearing a bikini.
The video was posted on September 15 by X user Barkha Trehan, who describes herself as ‘Activist | Voice Of Men | President, Purush Aayog’. She wrote, “Location : Haridwar. Madam: My Body My Choice. Your take ??” The video garnered over 1 million views. (Archive)
In her X bio, Trehan identifies herself as a “men’s rights activist” and the “president of Purush Aayog”. She also claims to be a TEDx speaker and a “Hindu entrepreneur”; she apparently also “directed a documentary titled The Curse of Manhood”.
Media outlet News 18 Hindi published a report with screenshots from the video pointing out that it had angered social media users. (Archive)
This same video was posted by content creator Piyali Banerjee, where she questioned the “basic decency” and “knowledge of clothing” of the woman.
Other social media users also shared the same video with similar captions, questing the woman for wearing a bikini in Haridwar, with misogynistic comments about her character.
The video is also viral on Instagram.
Fact Check
To verify its authenticity, we ran a reverse image search on a few keyframes from the viral clip. This search led us to a reel posted on Instagram on August 18. The 21-second long reel was uploaded by an account named ‘ishika_pandit’. It showed the same woman bathing at the same spot, but wearing completely different clothes.
This video matched the background of the viral clip with the steel railing on the river and the foundations of a bridge clearly visible in the background. The woman’s hand gestures also mirror the viral video, and the same two men are visible in both videos.
Based on these similarities, it can be concluded that the video uploaded on August 18 is the original footage. The woman in the original video is seen wearing a yellow suit, and not a bikini. Thus, the viral clip is a doctored version of the original video, manipulating the attire of the woman.
Some social media users highlighted the possibility of the viral clip being an AI-generated deepfake, claiming that the woman’s clothes had been purposely changed from a suit to a bikini. (Archive)

The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but was unlikely to name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

Just over a year ago, Dylan Borland—a former Air Force geospatial intelligence specialist—told a House Oversight task force that he'd watched a roughly 100-foot triangular craft lift silently off the flight line at Langley Air Force Base in 2012. But there were some questions he couldn’t answer.
Nearly half a dozen times during the hearing, he told members of Congress he could only answer their questions, such as whether a private company he worked for was reverse engineering nonhuman technology, inside a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF. He said he was concerned whether he was “legally even allowed to answer” some questions and at one point cited a fear of being charged under the Espionage Act.
A year later, on September 14, the Defense Department announced it had lowered that risk, though it falls short of what some in the unidentified anomalous phenomena research community say is needed to achieve broad transparency.
The Pentagon said on Monday that it had issued a "targeted legal waiver" allowing all current and former “service members, civilian personnel, and contractors" holding UAP-related national defense information to disclose it to the White House–directed effort that has been dumping UFO files on war.gov since May.
The waiver, which hasn’t been made public, "supersedes civil and administrative enforcement provisions" of NDAs and special access program agreements, "strictly for communications directed to the PURSUE team," a reference to the White House program. Basically, if you signed a secrecy agreement and know something about UFOs, you can now tell PURSUE without being sued or losing your clearance, though the same protections don’t extend to speaking with Congress, the press, or the public. The release announcing the waiver says nothing about criminal law, and only covers agreements "previously executed within the United States."
President Donald Trump telegraphed the move over the summer when he reportedly directed the Defense Department and the intelligence community to waive UAP-related NDAs. It was reinforced on July 31 when Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence Aaron Lukas sent a memo to 18 intelligence chiefs declaring that any NDAs “prohibiting disclosure to the President, or designees like PURSUE, are no longer in force.” The memo cited a “Presidential Direction” it never quotes and gave the intelligence community 30 days to set up its own procedures. That deadline passed in August. The White House directed a request for comment to the Defense Department. An agency spokesperson said it had no additional comment outside the press release and referred further questions to the White House.
Borland, the kind of person all of this was written for, is unmoved.
“Bad-faith actors are talking about, ‘Oh, this allows whistleblowers to go and talk to the public.’ No, it doesn't. It changes nothing,” he tells WIRED. “It's one more place to go.
“Those of us who already became whistleblowers, we already were told that our NDAs were waived. We were legally allowed to talk to AARO,” he says, referring to the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, created in 2022 to investigate UAP reports and serve as the official channel for whistleblowers. He adds that the new directive essentially “just repeated what we've been told for three, four years.”
A provision Congress passed in December 2022 already states that an authorized UAP disclosure—meaning one made through AARO—"shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement," complies with classification rules, and "is not a violation" of the relevant section of the Espionage Act. The channel was AARO and Borland used it.
But AARO has little credibility with the people it was built to hear from, especially after its former director publicly questioned the credibility of whistleblowers, and its March 2024 historical report found no evidence the government had ever recovered alien technology. Borland told Congress that he met with AARO in March 2023, but that he withheld sources and methods because he considered the agency's public assessments up until then, "a misrepresentation of the truth." That August, after a former intelligence officer testified about an alleged decades-long crash-retrieval program, Borland filed a complaint with the intelligence community's inspector general over what he says he knew and the retaliation he says he’d faced.
Since then, he wrote in his statement to Congress, he has "been prevented from resuming my prior employment" and remains “blacklisted from certain agencies within the Intelligence Community.”
Other UAP whistleblowers have faced similar issues after coming forward, from break-ins at their homes to leaked personal details.
The new waiver also only covers those who have worked with the Pentagon, leaving a CIA-sized hole in it.
“I'm glad that they're waiving NDAs for everybody who was on the [Defense Department] side,” Borland says. “It doesn't change the [Intelligence Community] side.”
He pointed to the need to offer similar protections to the alphabet soup of intelligence agencies beyond just the CIA, including the National Security Agency, FBI, and others, as well as science agencies like NASA.
Marik von Rennenkampff, a former State Department analyst and Obama-era Pentagon appointee now at the Sol Foundation, a UAP research nonprofit, agrees with that sentiment because of where whistleblowers say the secrets about nonhuman technology are kept. He points to a specific unit in the CIA that’s “allegedly—allegedly, allegedly, allegedly, I can't stress that enough—the quarterback for this alleged legacy effort.”
“What has been announced publicly does not cover the core of the alleged legacy program yet,” von Rennenkampff tells WIRED.
There's a second gap that no memo can close. Many of the people alleged to hold this information work for private contractors, and the government can't waive an NDA it isn't party to. Only the 2022 statute addresses those types of agreements, and only for disclosures made through the official AARO channel.
Despite these shortcomings, UAP researchers and whistleblowers point to, von Rennenkampff argues this week’s announcement is still important.
“After 80 years of government denial, obfuscation, and ridicule on this topic, there's now true political capital invested in this,” he says. Unlike AARO, PURSUE is a “presidentially directed initiative” that is reporting ultimately to political appointees in the White House, “versus career bureaucrats.”
“It shows that the Trump administration is taking extraordinary claims about retrievals of a craft of nonhuman origins seriously,” he says. There’s a phrase in the release that von Rennenkampff says is another curious detail, particularly given how “wordsmithed to hell” government statements about UAP generally are. The Pentagon wrote that “individuals with direct knowledge of UAP-related programs” have historically feared legal liability for speaking.
“It doesn't say people with partial knowledge, half knowledge, alleging knowledge,” he says. “It says people with direct knowledge.”
Borland's hope is that PURSUE answers to someone with the power to act on what it hears. He points to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller—who Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed is working on the UAP portfolio—as someone who would signal the White House is doing more than paying lip service to the topic.
Beyond that, Borland has an offer.
“There's enough smoke, and there's enough people behind the scenes,” he says, referring to himself and other whistleblowers. “If Stephen Miller and Trump wanted to actually know some stuff, they could call us into the White House right now, and I can throw down, and so can the rest of them.”

Ending child marriage requires dismantling the patriarchal norms that perpetuate it. Rockstar has officially announced the GTA 6 music album, including a physical vinyl release, but instead of getting excited, I got frustrated reading about it. What bugs me about Rockstar’s latest announcement is that the album has a physical CD and vinyl, but the game doesn’t come on a disc. Instead, GTA 6 physical copies have a code in the box, and frankly, that’s baffling.
I grew up collecting GTA games on PC, whether it was San Andreas or Vice City, and I always appreciated how Rockstar included physical goodies like a map, exclusive posters, and whatnot. Likewise, I was looking forward to what goodies GTA 6 would have, but that ship never sailed. And now, with Rockstar revealing the GTA 6 albums with a disc, they’re playing in my face.
GTA 5 Had 7 Discs, While GTA 6 Has None Outside the Music Album
When I bought GTA 5 on PC back in 2015, I couldn’t believe how many discs Rockstar packed into the box, along with a manual and a double-sided poster of Los Santos and Blaine County. Since it was 7 dual-layer installation discs, it felt like opening a new book, only much better because it was Grand Theft Auto.
PC discs haven’t been a thing in quite a while, so naturally, I moved to PlayStation to grow my physical collection. I was looking forward to the GTA 6 physical release on PS5 since the first GTA 6 trailer dropped in 2023. However, Rockstar decided to go the all-digital route with GTA 6, and I couldn’t, for the life of me, understand why.
I initially thought Rockstar might have delayed GTA 6’s physical release to avoid spoilers, as that did happen with Red Dead Redemption 2 months before its release, but a prominent leaker single-handedly debunked that theory. CyberLeek posted multiple GTA 6 leaks on social media platforms, even though the game is skipping a physical release.
And now, looking at the GTA 6 music album editions, all of which include a physical CD or a vinyl disc, I wonder what went wrong. Did Rockstar make this decision to please shareholders, or because Sony is killing physical PS5 discs starting in January 2028, and they just wanted to be ahead of the game? They do have a marketing deal with Sony, so maybe I don’t have the full picture just yet.
Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick previously said that GTA 6 discs don’t make sense for consumers, but their argument falls apart with the official physical vinyl release on November 19, 2026. A PS5 disc is generally cheaper to produce than a vinyl disc, so this decision really makes me wonder. I doubt Rockstar would even include a map in the GTA 6 “physical” release,
I Would Easily Spend More to Own GTA 6 on a Disc
This is a hot take, but I definitely would’ve spent more on a true GTA 6 physical edition with a disc; that’s not an album or a vinyl release. I’m already paying $80 for GTA 6, So, paying an extra $10–15 for a physical disc edition doesn’t seem unreasonable to me, especially given the circumstances.
Honestly, I would’ve even paid more if Rockstar had made the disc exclusive to the GTA 6 Ultimate Edition. Regardless, Rockstar has already locked five features with the GTA 6 Ultimate Edition, so including a physical disc would have made the $100 price tag feel even more worthwhile.
Rockstar not offering a physical disc for what is probably the biggest game ever made is pretty wild to me. They have already made a fortune, with GTA 5 selling over 230 million copies worldwide, as revealed by Take-Two in an earnings call. GTA 6 pre-orders are soaring too, so would it really have been that hard to give physical fans a disc, just like it’s doing with the GTA 6 album vinyl?
No physical disc not only limits options, but also sets a dangerous precedent for future physical releases, which is unfortunately what Sony is doing too. Even with all the backlash surrounding Marvel’s Wolverine, PlayStation’s newest release, it still comes with a physical disc containing the full game. I have to give Insomniac credit for at least doing that.
There are still 2 months left, so I’m holding out hope for an eventual GTA 6 physical disc, even though the chances are slim. Truthfully, if Rockstar doesn’t give GTA 6 a proper physical disc release, then maybe it should’ve kept the album strictly digital, too.

- Valor Mortis prices and editions have been announced on the official X account of the game.

The Allahabad High Court has set Ayush Malik, a 31-year-old man from Shamli who said he had voluntarily converted to Islam, at liberty to live at a place of his choice, observing that an adult’s decisions regarding faith, residence and marriage cannot be overridden by family objections.
Justice Sandeep Jain passed the order on Wednesday while hearing a habeas corpus petition alleging that Malik, who changed his name to Mohammad Ali, was being illegally confined by his family following his religious conversion.
The court said Malik had categorically stated that he embraced Islam voluntarily and that his decision was not influenced by any threat, coercion, undue influence or pressure.
“Nothing has been brought on record which may persuade this Court to disbelieve the statement made by the corpus in the course of his interaction with the Court,” the Bench observed.
The court said there was no lawful justification for continuing any restraint on Malik’s personal liberty after he expressed his wishes before it.
It directed that he be allowed to reside wherever and with whomever he chose, profess and practise the religion of his choice, and take an appropriate decision regarding his matrimonial relationship in accordance with law.
Father opposed conversion
The court was informed that Malik had embraced Islam in 2014 and had been following the essential practices of the faith. He told the Bench that his decision was not acceptable to his parents and other family members.
Malik also expressed his intention to marry Chandni Qureshi, a Muslim woman, and alleged that he had been subjected to threats and unlawful confinement at his home since June 4.
His father, Devraj Singh Malik, disputed his son’s account, claiming that he had been influenced or brainwashed by certain persons and had not converted voluntarily.
The court noted that the father’s concern for his son’s welfare was understandable but said it could not override the constitutionally protected autonomy of an adult capable of making decisions about his own life.
Court cites individual autonomy
The Bench said a person who has attained majority is ordinarily entitled to determine their faith according to their conscience.
“Such a choice, being an expression of individual autonomy and freedom of conscience, cannot be displaced merely because it is not acceptable to his family members,” it observed.
The court also said the right to choose a person with whom one wishes to establish a matrimonial relationship is an integral part of the right to life and personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution.
It added that the mere fact that an adult’s choice may go against the wishes or expectations of family members cannot, by itself, provide a legitimate basis for restricting that choice.
“Once an adult person has unequivocally expressed his free will and choice before the Court, such choice is ordinarily entitled to be respected,” the Bench said.
Background of the case
The court had on September 9 directed authorities in Uttar Pradesh to produce Malik before it.
His conversion had earlier led to the arrest of Chandni Qureshi and her father under the Uttar Pradesh Prohibition of Unlawful Conversion of Religion Act, 2021, in a case registered by Shamli police.
Malik had previously told the media that he converted voluntarily. His father, a businessman, had alleged that the woman and her family coerced him in an attempt to gain control over their property. Malik had reportedly later returned to Hinduism.
The latest habeas corpus petition, however, alleged that he was being illegally confined by his family.
The court said that in exercising its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution, it was not required to substitute its own perception of what would be beneficial for the considered choice of an adult.
It accordingly set Malik at liberty to make decisions concerning his residence, faith and matrimonial relationship.

In December 1892, Lizzie Borden was arrested on suspicion of killing her father and stepmother with a hatchet in their Fall River, Massachusetts, home.
Nearly 10 months after her arrest, Borden was acquitted of the crimes, in part because prosecutors lacked physical evidence linking her to the killings. No one else was charged in connection with the murders, and more than a century later, the case remains unsolved.
The crime has inspired countless adaptations, including Netflix's "Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story," the fourth installment of Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan's anthology series, which premieres September 17.
While the story continues to draw audiences, the Borden home has become an attraction in its own right. Last listed for sale in 2021 for $2 million, the property now offers ghost tours and operates as a bed-and-breakfast, with rooms starting at $259 a night.
Take a look inside the site of one of America's earliest true-crime stories.
The Borden family house is in Fall River, Massachusetts.
Fall River is about 52 miles south of Boston, near the border between Massachusetts and Rhode Island.
Andrew Borden was a well-to-do businessman.
According to the Lizzie Borden House's bed-and-breakfast website, although Andrew Borden was born into a prominent New England family, he grew up middle-class.
He began his career as a carpenter and cabinetmaker, later amassing a considerable fortune through a mix of real estate investments, mill ownership, and banking. At the time of his death, his net worth was reportedly over $300,000, equivalent to roughly $10 million today, according to the website.
Andrew carefully selected their Massachusetts home.
The house was built in 1845 and purchased by Andrew Borden in the 1870s, local news outlet WJAR reported.
Borden chose the home in part for its practical location — a short walk from his Main Street businesses in a bustling part of town —according to the Borden bed-and-breakfast's website.
Over a century later, the Borden home has become a popular tourist attraction.
Donald Woods and Leann Wilbur operated the Lizzie Borden Bed & Breakfast Museum for more than 15 years before selling it in 2021.
Lance Zaal, founder of US Ghost Adventures, bought the property for $1.8 million and has continued operating it as an inn and museum, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The home looks as though it were pulled straight from the pages of a history book.
While some of the home's furnishings have been replaced over the years with replicas, its original doors and hardware remain intact.
Period details are scattered throughout the home, including sewing machines, lanterns, and mannequins dressed in floor-length, era-appropriate gowns.
The home is spread out over three levels.
Altogether, the home occupies a little over 3,600 square feet.
The spacious home can be booked in its entirety and accommodates groups of up to 20 people.
Floor plans of the home shared with Business Insider show it has 8 bedrooms and 3.5 bathrooms.
The second and third floors are almost exclusively devoted to living quarters.
All of the bedrooms have floral wallpaper, ornate dressers, and large wooden headboards.
For an additional $30, guests can also arrange to have an axe placed on the beds.
Most of the bedrooms are on the second floor, and some are on the third.
The primary bedroom includes an en suite bathroom with a tub, according to The Seyboth Team, the brokerage that handled the property's most recent sale.
You can stay in one of the home's rooms for $249 a night.
Though the home operates as a bed-and-breakfast, it also remains a museum and tour site. Guests staying more than one night must vacate the property between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m.
This is the John V. Morse Suite.
This room is where Abby Borden was found after her murder. Eerily, a photograph of Lizzie Borden hangs in the bedroom.
According to the bed-and-breakfast's website, guests have reported paranormal experiences in rooms throughout the home.
This was Andrew and Abby's bedroom.
It's the only suite in the entire home that has its own bathroom.
The kitchen is located on the first floor.
The home has an old-fashioned wood-burning stove that certainly looks like a throwback to the 1800s.
It also has modern appliances like a coffee maker and a dishwasher.
Despite modern appliances, the room still feels historical.
The first floor has several rooms dedicated to entertaining.
At first glance, this unassuming sitting room appears rather ordinary. But it conceals a dark history: Andrew Borden was killed here while sitting on the large black couch.
There's a less eerie space for entertaining.
For couples drawn to the home's spooky history, the Borden house hosts several weddings each year. This room would make an intimate setting for a cocktail hour.
The home also has a separate gift shop.
The gift shop sells items including a Lizzie Borden coloring book, a collector's miniature hatchet, and a mug modeled after Lizzie's mug shot.

Trump seen with image of apparent Kennedy Centre demolition
The US president has threatened to tear down the famed arts venue because he has been blocked from renaming it after himself
A photo of Donald Trump examining a depiction of Washington’s Kennedy Centre apparently being demolished sparked widespread attention on Thursday after the US president threatened to tear down the revered arts venue because he has been blocked from renaming it after himself.
In the image captured by Agence France-Presse photographer Brendan Smialowski late on Wednesday at Joint Base Andrews, the Republican leader was seen through the windows of Air Force One holding a placard with visible text in red declaring: “Kennedy Center DEMOLIS …”
The rest of the word was obscured by the plane’s window frame but Trump has mused repeatedly about razing the Washington arts venue.
Below the words is a large picture showing a yellow heavy construction vehicle scooping rubble from a torn-down building.

The Santa Fe International Film Festival will present its Visionary Award to Dark Winds actor Zahn McClarnon on Friday, Oct. 16 at the Lensic Performing Arts Center in Santa Fe, NM.
McClarnon plays Lieutenant Joe Leaphorn in the AMC series Dark Winds executive produced by George R.R. Martin and the late Robert Redford. McClarnon also serves as an EP and Director (season 4 episode 2) for the series, which just wrapped its fifth season. Based on Tony Hillerman’s Leaphorn & Chee novels, Dark Winds follows two Navajo police officers in the 1970s as they investigate numerous seemingly unrelated crimes in the American Southwest. The series is shot in Santa Fe.
The actor also played Officer Big in the FX series Reservation Dogs, earning him a Film Independent Spirit Award for Best Ensemble Cast in a New Scripted Series.
Watch on Deadline
Other standout roles include Officer Mathias in Longmire, Akecheta in HBO’s second season of Westworld, and Hanzee Dent in the second season of FX’s Fargo. McClarnon was a series regular on National Geographic’s Barkskins, opposite Marcia Gay Harden and David Thewlis. He also starred on AMC’s The Son. His film credits include The Silencing, with Nikolaj Coster-Waldau, and Mike Flanagan’s adaptation of Stephen King’s Doctor Sleep. On television, he has recurred on Disney+ and Marvel Studio’s Hawkeye and Echo.
Additional credits include Hulu’s History of the World, Part II, the Jennifer Lawrence comedy No Hard Feelings, and Tony Tost’s Americana. He also voiced Olrox in Netflix’s animated series Castlevania: Nocturne.
“Zahn McClarnon brings authenticity and excitement to each of his roles. His entrée into directing makes him an exemplary person to receive the Visionary Award,” said Santa Fe International Film Festival Executive Director Liesette Bailey.
Previous recipients of the Santa Fe International Film Festival’s Visionary Award include Giancarlo Esposito, Sterlin Harjo, Wes Studi, and Catherine Hardwicke.

An F-16 fighter jet from Texas crashed in rural Michigan on Thursday during a routine training exercise, with the pilot ejecting safely before being taken to a local hospital, a military spokesman said.
The aircraft was taking part in exercises at a National Guard base in Alpena, about 190 miles (305 km) north of Detroit, when it went down. Sgt. Derek Gutierrez, a public affairs specialist with the 149th Fighter Wing, said the pilot was receiving medical treatment but declined to provide the pilot’s name or details about any injuries, citing military policy.
The crash sent a plume of dark smoke into the air and prompted reports of explosions from people living nearby.
The fighter jet was among several F-16s from Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland in Texas participating in the Michigan exercises, Gutierrez said.
Wendy Sobeck, who lives in the area with her husband, said they initially believed a vehicle had crashed near their home. “We thought there was a car accident outside our house. We saw big billowing black smoke. We couldn’t tell what it was, so my husband got into his pickup truck and saw what happened,” she said. 
“You could see the plane debris in the field. Explosions kept happening," she said, as quoted by AP.
Her husband, Fred Sobeck, 65, said he saw flames after driving toward the crash site. “Police told me to get out of there because of explosions,” he said, recalling a “big fireball in the field” near a house and a camper. Neither structure was hit, he said.
The US military began operating F-16s in 1979. The Air Force Safety Center records at least 14 Class A mishaps involving the aircraft since 2000. The designation generally applies when an incident results in more than $2 million in damage, destroys an aircraft or causes a service member’s death.
Another F-16C Fighting Falcon crashed in California’s desert in December while flying with the US Air Force Thunderbirds. The pilot also ejected safely in that incident.

US-based semiconductor equipment and materials-engineering company Applied Materials has announced a $5 Bn (₹47,980.8 Cr) investment commitment as part of its Applied Materials India Vision 2035. Prabhu Raja, president of the semiconductor products group at Applied Materials, made the commitment while addressing the SEMICON India 2026 at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi, today. This investment will be used over the next decade to accelerate and integrate India's semiconductor ecosystem into the global value chain, with a three pillar approach — to deepen its research and development (R&D) in India, to accelerate the semiconductor ecosystem in India and to foster talent in India. “Today, we are committing to a new 140-acre advanced semiconductor research park, bringing together cleanroom capabilities, engineering expertise, and collaborative R&D with customers and suppliers on one side. Second, accelerate the ecosystem in India. Inventions done here must scale globally,” Raja said. He further added that the company aims to grow its India-based supply chain capacity 10X by 2035, creating opportunities for Indian suppliers and bringing global suppliers here. Industry Expansion Targets Under Semicon 2.0 Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted commercial production launches of two new semiconductor plants at Mohali and Surat today at the SEMICON India conference. In late August, the Union Cabinet approved the second phase of the Indian Semiconductor Mission, Semicon 2.0, with an outlay of ₹1.28 Lakh Cr, which will focus on six areas — chip design; semiconductor equipment and materials; fabrication plants (fabs); assembly, testing, marking and packaging (ATMP)/ outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) units; research and development; and talent development. Setting targets for the second phase, Modi said that the government expects least 200 chip-design startups and companies to participate in India, up from 105 that participated in the first phase, and 1 Lakh factory-floor and clean-room workers to be trained, alongside the existing chip-design talent goal with new 3D packaging unit coming up in Odisha. Semicon 2.0 is eyeing to attract more chipmakers to set up facilities in India, including silicon fabs, compound semiconductor fabs, discrete component fabs and display fabs. The government has received investment commitments of over ₹1 Lakh Cr ($11-12 Bn) since launch of Semicon 2.0 and has created 1 Lakh jobs, union minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said. PM also called for building a stronger domestic semiconductor supply chain by backing fabless chip companies, developing homegrown intellectual property and integrating silicon photonics into AI infrastructure. He urged players across semiconductor equipment, chemicals, gases and materials to tap the opportunities created by the 12 approved projects and the country’s growing chip demand.

The big questions for Tuchel's first England squad since World Cup
- Published
Sixty-five days after England's semi-final defeat by Argentina, Thomas Tuchel will name his first squad since the World Cup on Friday.
While the tournament ultimately ended with a spectacular 6-4 win over France in the bronze-medal match, the Three Lions left the United States with a long list of what ifs.
Now, with four games in the space of 11 days coming up during the extended international break, fans will get a glimpse of what Tuchel's next England side might look like.
Could players like Trent Alexander-Arnold be recalled? Will others like Alex Scott make their debut? And how might we expect them to play?
BBC Sport senior football correspondent Sami Mokbel, journalist Jess Anderson and BBC Radio 5 Live's John Murray go through the big questions facing Tuchel.
Are some of the players overlooked for the World Cup likely to return and which new names may feature?
Sami Mokbel: Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Hall are among the players to have been named in England manager Thomas Tuchel's provisional squad for the forthcoming Nations League internationals, though it remains to be seen whether they make the final cut.
Liverpool winger Ngumoha was part of a contingent of young players that flew with the England senior squad for their pre-World Cup training camp in Palm Beach.
He was unexpectedly handed his debut in the warm-up game against New Zealand, impressing in a second-half cameo.
But the 18-year-old is yet to be picked in a full senior England squad - although he is in with a chance of being selected by Tuchel for the forthcoming games against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia.
Hall's World Cup omission raised eyebrows given England entered the tournament without a natural left-back.
Before naming his full squad on Friday, Tuchel is required to submit a preliminary squad of players from which he will name his final party.
It is understood Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott, Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly and Everton's Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall are also among the names selected in Tuchel's extended list.
Attacking duo Cole Palmer and Phil Foden are on there too, after being two of the biggest omissions from Tuchel's squad for the World Cup.
That decision was deemed a mistake from certain circles, given they are two of English football's most creative players.
Meanwhile, Tuchel is expected to omit Jordan Henderson, Dean Henderson and John Stones because of injury.

  - Published4 September
Who is in the running to be back-up to Harry Kane?
Jess Anderson: One of the most talked-about issues surrounding England is who they turn to in the absence of captain and star striker Harry Kane. At the World Cup, Tuchel simply did not turn to anyone. Kane started all seven of England's matches up to the semi-final and was substituted only twice - both times late on with the game already won.
Kane was rested for the bronze-medal match, with Ivan Toney the preferred option, although the Al-Ahli striker did not score in the 6-4 win over France. Toney will not be an option this international break as he has since been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear in court later this month.
Ollie Watkins' shock summer move to Saudi Arabia puts his England future into question, while Dominic Calvert-Lewin is the man in form with four goals in four games for Leeds United.
This could be the moment for Tuchel to start to further integrate Liam Delap, who is improving at new club Nottingham Forest and has yet to make a senior England appearance. He scored his first goal for Forest in last weekend's win at Aston Villa.
What can we expect from England?
John Murray: In the immediate aftermath of the semi-final in Atlanta, Tuchel and the players spoke of being too passive. At the squad announcement it will be interesting to hear what conclusions Tuchel has reached on why that was the case, and how they came to surrender the initiative to Argentina from 1-0 up with just over half an hour to play.
Head of the queue for a recall is Cole Palmer, who seems to have recaptured the form he was missing last season, which resulted in his omission from the World Cup squad.
What England fans will want to see against Spain at Wembley, is Palmer and his like taking the initiative and imposing themselves on their opponents in a way that was so lacking in the latter stages against Argentina in July.
Will England be happy they have such tough matches lined up?
John Murray: Happy or not, that's what they've got - but this has to be better than another group of qualifiers such as the one they had for the World Cup, against teams way below them in the world rankings.
In those matches last autumn England played some of the best football they have so far produced under Tuchel.
But, while that helped establish patterns of play and build confidence, you never really know until you face the best. That clearly will be the case from the outset in the Nations League, with this opening match against the new world champions.
These matches will also provide preparation for the next Euros in 2028 when, assuming they qualify, England will be playing opponents like this at Wembley. And, lest you forget, this tournament does provide an opportunity to win a trophy which would be the best possible way for Tuchel and his team to step on from their third place at the World Cup.
What do we know about the mood in the camp after the World Cup?
Sami Mokbel: This will be a key theme to watch over the next three weeks. The spirit was high in the England camp during the World Cup - as evidenced by their brilliant victory against Mexico in the last 16 with 10 men.
But the devastating semi-final defeat by Argentina, and questions over England's approach as a 1-0 lead became a 2-1 loss late on, led to some form of an inquest in the England camp into what was to blame.
Away from the height of those emotions in July, the Football Association is completing a review into England's World Cup campaign. The FA has been keen to stress that this assessment is a standard process, rather than an indication of wider concern or alarm about England's third-place finish.
Indeed, key figures at the FA view the tournament in which England achieved their best finish since 1966 as a success, and the organisation has already backed Tuchel before the Euro 2028 qualifying campaign.
Tuchel and members of his backroom team gave their contributions to the review at St George's Park in late August. England players' opinions are also being gathered before a report is presented to senior bosses at the FA.
The ongoing review will also look into the impact of the team's permanent Kansas City base during the tournament. After every game, they returned to Kansas City - and the effects of the travelling will be analysed.
The content of the review won't be made public, but the next three weeks will give an indication of whether the camp is still as together as that night at the Azteca.
