Chimpanzees are known to use rudimentary tools when foraging for food. According to a new paper in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, this learned behavior is passed down from adults to offspring through social learning. Specifically, adult chimps deliberately model the behavior, then turn their tools over to the youngsters so they can mimic the same motions.
“Receiving food and tools from experienced individuals, which we call food or tool transfer, may help chimpanzees learn to use technology to extract foods that are difficult to access,” said co-author Andreu Sánchez-Megías, a graduate student at the University of Barcelona and the Jane Goodall Institute Spain in Senegal. “Tool transfers thus appear to be a form of teaching, together with observation and supervised practice. It appears that mothers are the main models and teachers for young chimpanzees in this manner.”
As we have previously reported, tool use was once thought to be one of the defining features of humans, although Charles Darwin observed chimpanzees using stones to crack nuts in 1871. In 1960, the late primatologist Jane Goodall observed a chimp named David Greybeard bend a twig, strip off the leaves, and use it to spoon termites out of a nest and into his mouth. When he learned of the behavior, Goodall’s mentor, Louis Leakey, famously observed, “Now we must redefine ‘tool,’ redefine ‘man,’ or accept chimpanzees as humans.” Since then, chimps have been observed making sponges out of leaves to soak up liquids, shaping sticks to collect algae, and sharpening rudimentary spears for hunting.
Other examples of tool use have been observed in various species, although the behavior seems to have evolved more frequently among monkeys and apes. Dolphins can toss objects as a form of play, which some scientists consider to be a type of tool use, particularly when it involves another member of the same species. Potential purposes include communication, social bonding, or aggression. (Octopuses have also been observed engaging in similar throwing behavior.)

Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft
- Published
The head of Microsoft AI has warned that without adequate safeguards, the development of AI could lead to the emergence of a new "silicon species" wich competes with humans.
Mustafa Suleyman said rival firm Anthropic is treating AI like it is human, an approach he called "misguided" which could create technology that humanity cannot control.
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, the chief executive said it was "right" for people to be concerned about AI, but there were "very practical things that we can do" to control it.
The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers. Anthropic has been approached for comment.

- OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms 
  - Published22 hours ago
Speaking to the Today programme on Thursday, Suleyman warned against firms continuing to create AI systems capable of setting their own objectives, earning money and owning assets.
That would mean "essentially seeding a new silicon species", he said, which could "no doubt compete with us for resources, no matter how much it cares about humanity and loves us".
Suleyman's comments to the BBC follow an essay he published earlier this week, external, in which he questioned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude, despite praising boss Dario Amodei and his team as "intellectually honest people".
In it, he criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self.
He also warned tech firms risk creating something "impossible" to control by treating the technology like a human.
"AIs are not conscious," he wrote.
"They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.
"They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans."
The Microsoft boss said greater transparency was needed around how AI systems are trained and evaluated.
This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology.
"We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote.
Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone".
'Humanist' superintelligence
The question of how much autonomy AI systems should have is increasingly dividing the industry.
Speaking to the BBC about an upcoming AI summit, Suleyman called for "alignment" to create technology that must be "subordinate" to humanity.
Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.
"I think that the good news here is that everybody who is human is going to have a very strong interest in making sure that the systems that we all create and... are used around the world in every nation are safe and controllable and subordinate to humanity," he said.
"Everybody must be aligned."
Microsoft founded its own superintelligence team in October 2025 and the company, much like its rival Anthropic, is also pursuing efforts in advanced AI development.
Suleyman's comments reflects Microsoft's initial draft of its Humanist AI Code of Conduct, external, a "training manual" published on Monday for how the company is developing its AI, which sets out the idea of "humanist superintelligence".
This, the code states, is "very advanced AI that always works for people, stays within limits, and remains under human control".
The company's vision of a "humanist" AI highlights the central challenge facing the technology - how to make it more powerful, without losing sight of the values it is meant to serve.

Pennsylvania’s Measles Outbreak Is Enormous
The two latest deaths suggest that the true number of infections is much larger than reported.
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.
Following America’s recent measles deaths, anti-vaccine activists have cast doubt on the virus as the culprit. They’ve pointed to a victim’s underlying health conditions or, as they did last year in Texas, blamed hospital error. But the two latest measles deaths in Pennsylvania—bringing the state’s total to four since mid-August—have made the United States’ measles crisis undeniable.
Last month, the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-associated deaths; both cases were later revealed to be infants too young to have been vaccinated. In response, Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—who was an anti-vaccine activist for decades before becoming health secretary—wrote on X that the deaths might have been “altogether fabricated.” (He later acknowledged a coroner’s conclusion that one of the deaths had been caused by measles.) Then, last weekend, an unvaccinated 40-year-old woman died in Jefferson County; immediately, people on Reddit and X insisted that her death wasn’t really caused by measles, because she’d had asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, both of which can make breathing difficult. Yesterday, state officials revealed that an unvaccinated 18-year-old died from a rare inflammatory condition of the brain and spinal cord that can be triggered by measles. Some commenters online deemed that death suspicious too.
What the armchair epidemiologists miss is that vulnerability to the infection doesn’t make a death less real. The two infants both tested positive for measles. The Lancaster County coroner’s office determined that one infant died of a ruptured spleen; however, when I spoke with that child’s parents, they told me that the mother had been extremely ill with the disease when she gave birth, the baby was not breathing when he was born, and they believed measles had killed their son. The other infant was born with a rare neurological condition, but the coroner found that measles was ultimately the cause of death. Greg Furlong, the Jefferson County coroner who investigated the 40-year-old woman’s death, told me that although the woman had conditions that made her vulnerable to measles, and was on supplemental oxygen, she was active before she contracted the virus. She cooked for her family and cleaned the house. Measles killed her in about a week. “If she wouldn’t have got the measles, would she still be alive today? I say yes,” Furlong, a Republican who is also the mayor of Summerville, said.
Four deaths in roughly four weeks suggest that the state is in the midst of an enormous outbreak. The Pennsylvania health department lists total cases at 693, with 99 in the past week. But considering that measles kills about one to three of every 1,000 children it infects, the actual number is likely much larger. Milder cases are going unreported. Many who fall ill, particularly in the Amish community, aren’t getting tested; the Amish parents of the infant who died with a ruptured spleen told me that their 13 living children had all caught the virus, but they never got swabbed.
These deaths are occurring after three unvaccinated people, including two young girls, died of measles in Texas and New Mexico last year. Those were the first measles deaths in the country in a decade. The last time the United States experienced four measles deaths in a calendar year was in 1992, at the tail end of a years-long outbreak that killed more than 100 Americans. That resurgence led to a recommendation that children receive two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, and prompted a nationwide push to increase vaccination rates. It worked, and measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000. But overall kindergarten vaccination rates started declining during the coronavirus pandemic, and some areas, including Lancaster County, have fallen well below the 95 percent needed to maintain herd immunity.
Now, in the face of a new increase in measles deaths, Kennedy appears more interested in scoring political points than boosting national vaccination rates. He has accused Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, of “the weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain”; Shapiro, in turn, charged Kennedy with “playing games with public health” after the CDC declined to update its measles statistics to include the deaths in his state. Kennedy’s stated reason for the omission is that the agency is “applying a consistent national standard.” But the delay marks a shift in policy: Last year, the CDC counted both Texas girls’ deaths and the death of the adult in New Mexico after the states announced them. (In a post on X, Kennedy wrote that the National Center for Health Statistics will determine if measles is the true cause of the deaths in Pennsylvania after examining death records; a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to questions about that investigation. In a statement, Pennsylvania’s health department said that its investigation had determined that all four deaths met the criteria for measles-associated fatalities.)
Tomorrow, Kennedy is scheduled to be the keynote speaker at the annual conference for Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization that he founded before becoming health secretary. Children’s Health Defense has a long history of ginning up fears about the vaccine for measles, mumps, and rubella while downplaying the seriousness of the diseases. Kennedy does, too. In July 2021, Kennedy told attendees at an Amish country fair in Pennsylvania, “The cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A.” In fact, no known cure for measles exists; vitamin A has shown some promise in people with severe vitamin A deficiency, which is exceedingly rare in the United States. Since becoming health secretary, he has stated publicly that vaccination is “the most effective way to prevent measles infection,” but as I’ve reported, he also undercut that message by telling the father of a girl who died in West Texas that “you don’t know what’s in the vaccine anymore.” Kennedy has been a stronger advocate for measles itself, which he’s falsely credited with boosting resistance to cancer and cardiac disease, than he has for the vaccine that prevents it.
As cases and deaths rise, the reality becomes harder to ignore: Measles, a disease the country seemingly overcame 30 years ago, is once again killing Americans.

Stellar performance and cooling. Great battery life. Excellent and fun cameras with a customizable camera app. Bright, responsive screens with a smaller Dynamic Island.
TIRED
Pricier than ever. No base model (yet). Living in the iPhone Duo's shadow.
There is no iPhone 18 this year. If you were hoping to upgrade your smartphone right now, Apple is only offering the new iPhone 18 Pro models (and a very expensive folding iPhone coming next month). Don't let that be a reason to spend extra money on a phone you might not need.
Apple hasn't confirmed the next base-model yet, but the iPhone 18 is expected in spring 2027 alongside a mid-tier iPhone 18e. If you've historically been more than satisfied with the base iPhone model, you should absolutely wait to upgrade. Don't let the hype machine sway you.
That said, if you're a Pro connoisseur, the iPhone 18 Pro ($1,199) and its bigger sibling, the 18 Pro Max ($1,299), are very good phones, despite the $100 price hike over last year’s Pro models. No, you don't need to upgrade if you're coming from an iPhone 17 Pro, 16 Pro, or even a 15 Pro—hold onto your devices for longer!—but Apple's flagships deliver where it matters, even if they feel eclipsed by the spectacle of the foldable iPhone Duo.
Minor Refresh
Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro models have significant upgrades, but let's be a little more measured here.
Battery life has been stellar on the Pro models over the last few years, and that remains true here. The Pro Max is the more notable of the two because it packs a denser battery. With average use (around 5 hours of screen-on time), I hovered around 50 percent by the end of the day, and easily made it through day two on a single charge. I spent a little less time with the smaller Pro, but so far it has also comfortably gotten me through a day with around 40 percent left by bedtime. Safe to say, most people will very much enjoy the battery life, but the update doesn't feel drastic.
Next, there's the processor: the A20 Pro chip. I hardly run into problems with Apple's flagship silicon, and that hasn't changed. The phones run every app fluidly, and my benchmark tests show a surprisingly sizable leap over the A19 Pro in the 17 series.
It runs Control—a AAA game from 2019 ported to iOS earlier this year—decently well. However, aggressive upscaling makes the graphics look grainy, and character movements can feel a little sluggish. (I maxed out the graphics settings.) It's certainly not perfect, but I still can't believe I'm playing such a demanding title on an iPhone.
More impressive is Apple's thermal management on these phones. The company has expanded the vapor chamber's surface area by three times—the phone's cooling technology that helps spread heat around—meaning the entire phone felt toasty after close to an hour of gameplay in Control, with no uncomfortable localized hot spots. This larger vapor chamber also lets you game longer before phone’s thermal throttling kicks in and slows everything down.
The iPhone 18 Pro models come with iOS 27 out of the box, which features the all-new Siri AI. Yes, Siri AI is infinitely more capable than any version of Siri that Apple has offered before. It still doesn't quite have the spark or versatility of other AI assistants, but you might be fine with that. If you throw Siri AI a question, there's a good chance it can actually give you a satisfactory answer now. Remember that Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features aren't exclusive to the latest models, though you do need an iPhone 15 Pro or newer to access them.
The Dynamic Island, the pill-shaped bar housing the selfie camera and Face ID sensors, is noticeably smaller this year. To take full advantage of it, you can now view three live activities—like a DoorDash order status or your Uber ETA—simultaneously inside the Island, up from two. I was navigating in Apple Maps, chatting on a phone call, and had a DoorDash order en route to my home, and it spaced out all of these activities neatly.
Speaking of the iPhone 18 Pro design, I do like the new burgundy color, though I miss brighter, more playful options like last year's Cosmic Orange. But the real headline feature is almost invisible—embedded into the main camera on the back of the iPhone.
Aperture Priority
Apple is debuting a variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro models. This is by no means the first time we've seen a smartphone with a variable aperture—Samsung and Huawei both launched phones with the capability years ago. While Samsung abandoned the tech, Huawei and Xiaomi still ship it on their flagships.
What is a variable aperture? Simply put, the aperture is the physical opening that lets light reach the camera sensor. A wider aperture lets in more light and has a lower “f-stop” number, while a narrower aperture restricts light. Most smartphones rely on fixed apertures—the iPhone 17 Pro's main camera, for example, is locked at f/1.78. A variable aperture gives the lens mechanical blades that physically expand or contract in a circular shape, adjusting how much light hits the sensor. Apple gives you four f-stops to select from: f/1.48, f/1.78, f/2.8, and f/4.
Open the aperture to f/1.48 on the iPhone 18 Pro and more light floods in, delivering cleaner low-light shots and faster Night Mode captures. This also creates a real optical bokeh—the soft blurred background effect phone makers have spent years simulating with computational Portrait modes. Step it down to f/4, this blur recedes, keeping more of the scene and background in crisp focus. All of this can be very confusing for people unfamiliar with these camera terms, which is why Apple defaults the aperture to “Auto.”
I love it. I shoot manual on my mirrorless camera, so I immediately took to the new customization features in the Camera app to show Shutter Speed and Lens Aperture as easy-to-access settings. Shooting at f/1.48 delivers a nice bokeh effect—especially in low light—so I stopped using Apple's Portrait mode altogether. (Some parts of the image may look less sharp than on an iPhone 17 Pro because the plane of focus is narrower.) Apple will point out that Portrait mode is still useful, as you can always add more bokeh post-capture.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
iPhone 18 Pro Max, main camera with a one-second shutter speed.
Move to f/4 for group shots when you want everyone in the frame to be in focus. (Or if you want a very fun starburst effect with light sources!) As you change between the four aperture settings, you can see the blades moving on the main camera—it's very cool. In auto mode, the camera largely sticks to f/1.78, or f/1.48 in low light. It chooses the other two apertures for specific, usually brighter, scenes.
I have also enjoyed the ability to adjust the camera’s shutter speed. Yes, you can already do this with a third-party camera app, but now it's baked in! With a one-second shutter, you can capture some fun shutter drag to accentuate motion in a photo. However, you'll definitely need to buy a neutral density filter for super-bright scenes to balance exposure. It's fun to play around with.
I compared several of the 18 Pro’s photos with shots from Google's Pixel 11 Pro, and I do have to note that the iPhone tends to over-brighten scenes that should be very dark. So much so that it can misrepresent the dark mood you might be chasing. The Pixel tended to preserve more of those shadows, though it delivered more lifted blacks that made the image appear more matte. The iPhone can also struggle with backlit scenes, more so than the Pixel.
Apple has added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles, and this is a fun element to sink your teeth into and explore. Phone makers have realized that ultra-clean, sharp, “perfect” shots are perhaps not what most people want, and these stylings—like the new Camera Looks on Pixel phones—offer a new degree of “authenticity.”
The iPhone 18 Pro's camera system is fun without feeling overwhelming. You can pick and choose what degree of control you want, tweak Photographic Styles to your tastes, and add more depth after the fact, whether it's for videos or photos. Who knew people liked having more control? There aren't any sweeping improvements to the camera lenses or sensors, but this is a system that shutterbugs will love to experiment with, and that's what the Pro iPhone is all about.

Rescuers dig 4 bodies from a Nepal hydropower tunnel as families demand answers
Rescuers in Nepal have recovered four bodies from a hydropower plant tunnel three weeks after a devastating flash flood
KATHMANDU, Nepal -- Rescuers in Nepal have recovered four bodies from the tunnel of a hydropower plant as search operations continued for those still missing three weeks after the devastating flash flood last month that killed hundreds and left thousands missing.
Families of the thousands missing, meanwhile, are seeking answers from authorities on their whereabouts.
Nepal's army said that four bodies were recovered Wednesday from the Chilime Hydropower plant, which was situated on the Trishuli River that flooded on Aug. 26.
Nepal's disaster management agency said five more bodies were located in a different location and equipment was being sent to recover them.
The number of bodies that have been recovered since the flooding has reached 1,403 while 6,150 people are still missing, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
Families of the missing have been pressuring the government to speed up the rescue and recovery process from the tunnels.
They have held rallies and many have called on the government to declare the missing as dead because they want to receive death certificates, which would allow them to move forward with legal proceedings and religious rites and give them some emotional closure.
At the Tribhuvan University Teaching hospital in Kathmandu, the lobby walls have been pasted with photos of hundreds of missing people. Relatives go there seeking news of their loved ones.
Usha Khatri's husband Indra Bahadur was working as a cook with a group of pilgrims when the flood hit the Nepal-China border. Since then she has been searching for him in many of the towns where the river flows and where bodies have been recovered.
“The government has not done much for us. They have not met us or given any information or any assurances. I am by myself searching for my husband,” Khatri said.
There were 13 hydropower plants that were damaged by the flooding and many workers were either swept or trapped by the raging water or debris.
Finding the workers who were trapped has been a priority for the government and rescuers. But access to the tunnels has been hampered by thick mud, debris and damaged infrastructure, making it difficult for rescue teams to reach the areas.
Two Nepali workers were found alive by rescuers on Sept. 4, days after the flooding. A day later a Chinese worker was pulled out alive from a separate area.
The government estimates the country's reconstruction costs at around $4.78 billion.

Our basic understanding of core-collapse supernovae hasn’t changed in decades. Large stars burn through all the fuel at their cores and start creating heavier elements in reactions that consume energy. The lack of energy from these reactions allows gravity to pull the interior of the star in on itself, collapsing it into a neutron star or black hole. The energy released by this process then blows the remainder of the star apart.
And, generally, that’s right. But there’s an entire busload of devils in the details. The statistics of supernovae that we’ve observed indicate that the model may be seriously incomplete. And on the theoretical side, there are still plenty of uncertainties, including over some of the basics, such as whether all core collapses actually result in a supernova.
A paper being released by Physical Review D provides what might be a potential explanation for the discrepancy: flavor-changing neutrinos. Neutrinos play a key role in our current models of supernovae, and right now, those models don’t take into account one of neutrinos’ most striking features: their ability to change identity.
Supernovae and their discontents
We’ve observed plenty of supernovae, so it would seem like there would be little mystery left. But a number of observations suggest there are some subtleties that we might be missing. For example, if we compare the rate of star formation in the Universe to the frequency of supernovae, there’s a discrepancy; it appears we’re forming enough stars to fuel a much higher frequency of supernovae than we actually observe. Also, in cases where we can identify the progenitor star that exploded, we find too few red supergiants, indicating that they may be contributing to this discrepancy.
Other problems come from observations of gravitational waves generated by mergers of the black holes left behind after a supernova. These mergers suggest there’s a “mass gap” in black hole formation—a range of masses where there are fewer black holes than you’d expect from an even distribution. But that data is complicated by the fact that theorists haven’t definitively identified the conditions that determine when a neutron star tips over into a black hole instead.

Combining healthy dietary practices with regular physical activity is the most effective non-drug strategy for achieving sustained weight loss and improving key metabolic health indicators among adults with overweight or obesity, according to a major review by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) here.
The findings, published in the international journal Obesity Pillars, are based on an umbrella review that analysed evidence from 112 systematic reviews and meta-analyses covering 2,332 randomised controlled trials and more than 5.07 lakh participant observations across over 50 countries.
The review, led by ICMR-NIN scientists Mahesh Kumar Mummadi and Samarasimha Reddy, compared the impact of dietary interventions, physical activity, lifestyle changes and combined approaches on weight management and cardiometabolic health.
Researchers found that all major non-pharmacological interventions produced statistically significant, though generally modest, reductions in body weight and Body Mass Index (BMI). However, the combination of diet and physical activity delivered the most sustained results, with participants losing an average of 3.68 kg beyond 12 months compared with control groups.
Low-calorie diets were found to be the most effective for short-term weight loss, resulting in an average reduction of 2.64 kg within the first three months. Physical activity alone led to smaller reductions in body weight, but its benefits increased over longer follow-up periods.
Lifestyle interventions such as behavioural counselling, goal-setting, self-monitoring and health education also showed positive outcomes, with their effectiveness improving over time. Beyond weight loss, the study highlighted significant improvements in metabolic health. The combination of diet and physical activity produced the greatest benefits in blood sugar control, reducing fasting blood glucose levels and insulin resistance after 12 months.
Physical activity emerged as the most effective strategy for lowering blood pressure, reducing systolic blood pressure by about 6.1 mmHg between six and 12 months. Intermittent fasting showed the largest short-term reduction in diastolic blood pressure and supported weight loss for up to a year, although these benefits were not sustained beyond 12 months.
ICMR-NIN director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings underscore the importance of an integrated approach to tackling obesity. “Healthy dietary practices, regular physical activity and behavioural support each have a role, but their combination can provide broader and more sustained benefits. This is particularly relevant for India, where scalable and sustainable approaches are needed to address the growing burden of overweight, obesity and related non-communicable diseases,” she said.
Mr.Mummadi noted that although the review drew evidence from more than 50 countries, most studies originated from high-income and upper-middle-income nations. India and other lower-middle-income countries remained under-represented, highlighting the need for more locally relevant research, said a press release on Saturday.

Cooking gas distributors are evaluating the likely impact of the flat ₹5 Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) that the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has proposed on transactions above ₹2,000 from October 15.
Commercial liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) cylinder sales coming under the purview of the levy is a given since the 19-kg refills priced nearly ₹3,000 each. But what is not clear to the distributors is whether they will end up attracting MDR on the domestic refills sales, to households, too.
Though the 14.2 kg cylinders come for less than ₹1,000 each, the common practice of permitting delivery personnel to collect payments from customers and remit the same to the agency subsequently may trigger the charge. “Delivery boys collect payments on their individual UPI account for the refills they supply through the day to the households. In the evening, they transfer the sum collected to the distributor. But from October 15, such bulk remittance are likely to attract the MDR,” Telangana LPG Distributors Association president Jagan Mohan Reddy said.
Stating the practice has become common with distributors not sharing QR code with each of the delivery personnel, he said the LPG distributors are studying the likely impact and plan to approach government soon seeking exemption from the MDR. Like the petroleum dealers, the cooking gas distributors are expected to flag the impact of the charge citing the fixed, thin margins on which they operate.
While announcing the MDR framework, the NPCI said for specific merchant categories such as railways, telecom services, insurance and fuel, among others, a flat MDR of ₹5 per transaction will be applicable for transaction above ₹2,000. The fixed fee instead of a 0.4% variable rate, for the specified sectors, will prevent cost escalations in critical public services, utility bill collection and thin-margin sectors like fuel retail. It ensures essential consumer services remain low-cost and digitally efficient, NPCI had said.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is prepared for encapsulation inside the payload fairing of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket. Roman's grapple fixture, installed for a potential future refueling mission, is visible at bottom right.
Credit:
SpaceX
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is prepared for encapsulation inside the payload fairing of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket. Roman's grapple fixture, installed for a potential future refueling mission, is visible at bottom right.
Credit:
SpaceX
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is gliding toward its distant observation post on a pinpoint trajectory so precise that engineers estimate the spacecraft’s fuel load will last twice as long as their initial expectations, the space agency confirmed Monday.
The $4.3 billion observatory’s designers originally planned to load enough propellant into Roman’s four fuel tanks for a minimum lifetime of five years, plus a potential five-year mission extension. That was a conservative estimate. NASA officials knew an on-target launch and perfect execution of the observatory’s first post-launch course correction maneuver would leave Roman with a hearty fuel reserve.
“As a result of exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team, brilliant execution by the operations team, and a precise launch from SpaceX, Roman has fuel for at least 22 years of potential science operations,” Jamie Dunn, center director at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, said in a press release.
The Roman telescope launched August 30 from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, kicking off a mission to widen our view of the Universe. Roman’s telescope and scientific instruments will provide astronomers with images of the sky at the same resolution as NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, but with 100 times the field of view. It would take Hubble a century to observe what Roman will see in a month.
Astronomers hope Roman’s broad vision will reveal insights into the largest structures in the Universe. Roman’s Wide Field Instrument, fitted with 18 near-infrared detectors, will produce images equivalent to those of a 300-megapixel camera. Its wide viewing area will allow Roman to map galactic clusters, along with the filaments of matter and dark matter that string through the cosmos. Mapping so much of the sky could help astronomers study the nature of dark energy, scientists’ name for the elusive force driving the acceleration of the Universe.
A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket lifts off on August 30 from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, with the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
Credit:
NASA/Joel Kowsky
A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket lifts off on August 30 from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, with the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
Credit:
NASA/Joel Kowsky
Right on the money
The Falcon Heavy released Roman on a trajectory that will take it a million miles from Earth, where the spacecraft will loop into a “quasi-halo” orbit around the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point, a point of balance between the gravitational pull of Earth and the Sun. It will take Roman about three months to reach L2.
The launch was so accurate that the first big burn with Roman’s control thrusters, executed one day into the mission, consumed just 40 pounds (18 kilograms) of hydrazine fuel, down from the preflight allocation of 441 pounds (200 kilograms), NASA said.
“I do thank SpaceX for putting us down the middle. It’s going to help us in terms of long-duration performance, how long we can stay at L2, as well as our positioning capability,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA’s associate administrator, during a talk Tuesday at the American Astronautical Society’s Glenn Space Technology Symposium.
Roman launched nine months ahead of the schedule set by NASA during the mission’s confirmation review in 2020. It also launched lighter than planned. Both are rather unusual in the annals of NASA science missions.
The observatory’s actual weight at completion was 17,760 pounds (8,056 kilograms), approximately two tons less than its maximum allowable weight. This allowed ground crews at Kennedy Space Center to load 290 gallons of hydrazine into Roman’s fuel tanks, more than engineers anticipated early in the mission’s design phase. The hydrazine feeds 24 thrusters scattered around the outside of the observatory.
At launch, the fully fueled Roman observatory weighed 20,224 pounds (9,173.5 kilograms), still a half-ton below its weight limit, a NASA spokesperson told Ars. In addition to the extra fuel, Roman’s lower mass meant its thrusters did not have to fire as long for the course correction maneuver the day after launch.
“A spacecraft’s mass changes throughout the design and build process, so we base the propellant budget on a set maximum value so we won’t come up short,” said Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard. “We track the propellant needed based on actual mass throughout integration and testing as well, to make sure we have wiggle room. Since Roman’s was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed to for the 10-year requirement.”
A second course correction planned for later this month will give Roman the last tiny boost to get into position for another maneuver in early December to slip into its final orbit at L2. “According to current projections, both maneuvers will use less fuel than planned, potentially saving even more for future science,” NASA said.
Roman’s thrusters will perform additional station-keeping burns roughly every 28 days. The observatory will also use its propulsion system to periodically unload momentum from its six reaction wheels, which normally control Roman’s pointing.
Artist’s illustration of thrusters firing on the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
Credit:
NASA
Artist’s illustration of thrusters firing on the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
Credit:
NASA
Refueling deferred
The mission’s exceptional fuel savings lower the likelihood of NASA having to send a refueling mission to Roman anytime soon. The observatory’s life-limiting resource will likely be propellant, and NASA set a requirement early on in Roman’s development that the spacecraft be refuelable.
NASA has serviced a space telescope before. Astronauts on five Space Shuttle flights visited Hubble to carry out a range of tasks, including repairs of the telescope’s aberrant vision, maintenance work, and the installation of more powerful science instruments. Hubble does not have a propulsion system, so visiting Space Shuttles also boosted the observatory’s orbit around Earth.
Officials prepared Roman to receive a potential uncrewed servicing mission. NASA attached a grapple fixture on the bottom of Roman similar to those used by the robotic arms on the International Space Station and the Space Shuttle. Roman also has navigation aids—a retroreflector and external reference points—to help guide a servicing mission on final approach.
“While Roman is nowhere near as serviceable as the Hubble Space Telescope was, we do have everything that’s necessary to enable the rendezvous and capture and docking with a hypothetical servicer; that’s the point of the grapple fixture,” said Jackie Townsend, Roman’s project manager at NASA Goddard. “Then, in 2020, when we were baselined, we were told that we would focus on refueling. So the blanketing around the fueling port has been designed especially so that it’s easier for a robot to get in there if we needed to refuel.”
The blanketing around the fueling port also has a magnetic closure to simplify opening and re-closing by a robotic servicer, Townsend told Ars.
There are no servicing spacecraft currently available that could travel out to Roman’s position a million miles from Earth. Several US companies are developing refueling satellites for use in low-Earth orbit and geosynchronous orbit, primarily for the US Space Force. Two Chinese spacecraft docked last year to conduct the first satellite-to-satellite refueling in geosynchronous orbit.
Everything else onboard Roman has been working well for more than two weeks since launch, according to Kshatriya, NASA’s highest-ranking civil servant. The telescope opened its aperture cover on September 1, allowing starlight to fall on its primary mirror for the first time.
“All the preliminary checks are good,” Kshatriya said. “In fact, we got some data on the Wide Field Instrument just a couple days ago. All the mirrors, all the CCDs are chilling down in the right way. We do false current tests to make sure that we’re getting the right connectivity, etc. All that’s green across the board on all 18 (detectors), which is awesome.”
Roman’s other instrument, a coronagraph designed for direct imaging of exoplanets, also performed well during preliminary checkouts.
“When we get first light, it’s going to be a big party,” Kshatriya said.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

- Social media users alleged in September 2026 that U.S. truckers planned to strike over high fuel costs beginning on Oct. 1, leading to food and supply chain shortages.
- There was no evidence to support this unfounded rumor.
- Searches indicated the claim largely spread because of a video one social media user originally posted on Sept. 15. Other users then reposted his clip without first looking for credible evidence.
- A spokesperson for the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association said they had no knowledge of an upcoming strike. We also emailed the International Brotherhood of Teamsters and the man from the video, and will update this article if we receive more information.
In mid-September 2026, social media users alleged U.S. truckers had announced a plan to strike beginning on Oct. 1 to protest record-high diesel fuel costs of more than $6 a gallon. The posts claimed the stoppage of transportation would lead to nationwide food and supply chain shortages.
There was no evidence to support this unfounded rumor. Queries of DuckDuckGo, Google and other search engines found no news media outlets or other authoritative sources reporting about truckers planning to strike. Reddit's r/Truckers subreddit, a forum with hundreds of thousands of weekly visitors, featured a post with commenters saying they had heard nothing of a strike.
We emailed the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association to ask about this rumor. The organization's website says it has over 150,000 members in the U.S. and Canada operating more than 240,000 trucks and truck fleets. A spokesperson responded, "Our awareness is consistent with yours in that it seems to be social media chatter at this point in time."
We also emailed the International Brotherhood of Teamsters to ask about the rumor. The labor union has a freight division it says is made up of tens of thousands of Teamsters. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Where the unfounded rumor spread
Searches of social media websites indicated a video, first posted on Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived) on Sept. 15, was potentially the most-popular content promoting the rumor. Users have since reposted the same video across platforms, including Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and X (archived). Others also generally shared the rumor of a trucker strike.
In the video, which ends with a request for users to buy paid subscriptions, a man tells viewers about the purported strike and subsequent food shortages:
In the trucking world, they put out a deal to strike until the fuel prices drop. Shut down Oct. 1. Park it. Stand together. Make their voices heard. Truckers are done.
You know what that means if they do that? Food shortages. Food's not getting to grocery stores. Nothing's getting anywhere.
What have I been telling you? Make sure you've got enough f***ing food for a month to three months, even six months. S***'s gonna hit the fan. S*** is hitting the fan, currently. And with this deal, this is huge.
A lot of people don't understand if trucks aren't moving, you're not getting anything. Grocery stores aren't getting a f***ing thing. Nobody's getting a thing. Just FYI.
That should probably freak you out a little bit because that happened basically during COVID. Remember when you couldn't find anything in the f***ing stores. This'll be a lot worse, if it comes to fruition. Just FYI. 
Please like, share, follow. Share my s***. Subscribe for a buck. 
We messaged the man in the video on Facebook and Instagram to ask for evidence, and will update this story if we receive more information.
A TikTok user's video (archived) also promoted the rumor with the caption "50,000 Truckers Threaten Strike: What It Means For America." In the video, the user claims, without evidence, that 50,000 truckers "are reportedly said to" no longer drive as of Oct. 1.
The unfounded rumor potentially originated out of a previous strike claim (archived) appearing to pertain to the dates of Oct. 1-10, 2025.
For further reading, we previously reported the truth of a story regarding truckers banding together to save someone from jumping off an overpass.

Snap Specs hands on: Standalone AR glasses are here
The $2,195 glasses are Snap's biggest AR bet yet.
Snap has been experimenting with glasses for a decade and AR-enabled frames for the last five years. I've tried every pair, and it's always been clear that the company was working towards something bigger. Specs, the company's first consumer-ready AR glasses are exactly that.
The $2,195 glasses are able to replicate much of the functionality of a mixed reality headset without a separate puck, controller or tethered connection. But that also comes with some trade-offs, like the size. But after trying out Specs for myself, I think there's a lot to like. The operating system feels more polished than previous versions, and Snap has more apps that feel like they would actually be useful. But I still have a lot of questions about the product and who it's ultimately for.
Look and fit
Specs come in two sizes: 47 mm and 52 mm. I tried both and the smaller frames (pictured above) were a much better fit for my face. And look, as someone who regularly reviews smart glasses, I'm very aware that people have strong opinions about how these look! I'm not here to say that Specs can pass for "normal" glasses, and I don't think they are supposed to. They're chunkier than the bulkiest smart glasses I've worn, but they are also far more capable than something like the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses.
Given Specs' capabilities, I actually think they look okay. I likely wouldn't wear them as my everyday glasses, but I don't think they look any goofier than other AR products I've tried, like Xreal's Aura headset. I will say I have something of an advantage, though, since I have long hair that can cover the thick arms that would otherwise stick out past my ears.
Specs also don't feel nearly as heavy as they are. At 132 grams, they're almost twice as heavy as Meta's display-enabled frames, but the weight felt more evenly distributed around my head. The fit was surprisingly snug and the glasses never slipped down my nose, even if I shook my head. I only had them on for about 20 minutes, so I can't speak to how they would feel after longer periods, but I never felt uncomfortable during my demo. And, as someone who frequently struggles with glasses not fitting tightly enough, it was nice to never have to adjust their position.
Hand tracking and AR
Specs are equipped with two cameras, which enable the hand-tracking controls. The interface is similar to the last generation: you point with your index finger to move a cursor around the display and pinch your thumb and index finger together to select. You can also access the main menu and some other controls by opening your palm and tapping on the relevant shortcuts.
The hand tracking was intuitive and responsive. The only issue I experienced was when some hair fell in front of one of the cameras, which caused the cursor to jump around the display somewhat erratically, but it resolved as soon as I pushed my hair back.
The actual display was bright and easy to see, though there was some variation based on the lighting conditions of my space. Content looked a bit sharper when I was in a darker environment. Specs also have an adjustable dimming function that can help with brighter environments, but I wasn't able to use it extensively.
One significant improvement from the last generation of glasses is that the AR content can now "follow" you around as you physically move around your space. When I tried the last generation of Spectacles a few years ago, I noted that it was at times frustrating to have to look around to find the AR content I knew was there but couldn't quite see. But Snap OS now has the ability to "anchor" a window so it can move around your view as you physically move in your surroundings.
It also helps that Specs have a slightly wider field of view than their predecessor. At 51 degrees, it felt big enough to be useful, even though there were still times when content was cut off. I could often address this by rearranging the size and position of the windows, but that also takes away from the immersiveness.
Evan Spiegel has described Specs as a "wearable computer" that's suitable for doing actual work in augmented reality. I didn't get a chance to try out too many productivity-focused apps, but I was able to open Google Docs in a browser window and type with a Bluetooth keyboard, as well as the built-in AR keyboard. I think the AR keyboard would only be suitable for a few words at a time, but typing with a physical keyboard felt pretty natural.
A lot of the AR experiences I've seen on past versions of Spectacles have felt somewhat gimmicky, so I was happy to see that Snap has invested in some utility-focused apps. I tried out a Mapbox-powered navigation app for walking directions, and a translation app that was able to project an English captions of someone speaking Italian. Snap also has an AR measuring tool and a "whiteboard" app for sketching out ideas, though I didn't get to try these.
One of the more interesting aspects of Specs is how they can enable shared experiences between two people. I got a taste of this by playing a quick game of dominoes with a Snap representative who was also wearing a pair of Specs. It reminded me a little of some of the tabletop VR games I've tried with Meta's Quest headsets. While dominoes is much simpler than an interactive RPG, the form factor of Specs feels like a more natural way to play a game with someone sitting next to you than a bulky headset. Overall, it seems like there's a lot of potential for casual, social games.
Another addition Snap has made is "travel mode," for viewing streaming content when you're in a moving vehicle (as a passenger). When enabled, you can watch streaming content via Specs' browser and the window will track to the movements of the vehicle rather than the movements of your head. It's a subtle difference, but it's meant to make viewing feel more natural in these situations. I only tried it while slowly driving around the parking lot of Snap's HQ, but I could see it being useful for streaming content while on a plane or a train. (I tend to get a little motion sick when sitting in a backseat so I don't think in-car viewing is for me, even though I didn't feel unsettled during my demo.)
Battery life and other questions
Watching YouTube videos and HBO shows in an AR window is a cool experience, but also one I suspect will drain Specs' battery rather quickly. The company has said Specs will have up to fours of battery life with "mixed use" but I still don't have a sense of how quickly the apps I tried might drain the battery. I did notice that the arms of the glasses, which house Qualcomm processors, were warm to the touch after about 10 minutes of use, though they didn't feel uncomfortably hot.
I also suspect that connectivity could be a limitation in some situations. Certain Specs experiences, like streaming video or navigation, require some kind of connection, which could limit their utility when you don't have Wi-Fi available or don't feel like hotspotting from your phone.
Snap is selling a dedicated charging case with a cellular connection that will address potential battery and connectivity concerns. The $200 case holds up to four additional charges, and will enable a standalone cellular connection when on the go (Snap is partnering with Verizon and other carriers on the plans, but no word on pricing yet). But the accessory and extra data plan will add significant cost to an already pricey device.
All that makes me wonder who Specs are for. There's clearly growing excitement for augmented reality, and I think enthusiasts will see the appeal of Snap's approach. The company is also launching a dedicated enterprise program for businesses that want to take advantage of the platform. But Snap seems to want to appeal to the consumer market as well; the company has been promoting the glasses with a splashy celeb-fueled ad campaign. But given the size and price of the glasses, I have some doubts that the current version of Specs will be appealing to anyone but AR enthusiasts.
Specs are available now for pre-order and are expected to ship "later this fall" in the US, UK and France.

USA midfielder sues doctors after on-pitch cardiac arrest
- Published
United States women's national team player Savannah DeMelo is suing a hospital and two doctors after she suffered a cardiac arrest on the pitch last year.
Midfielder DeMelo, who has seven senior caps for the USA, has filed a lawsuit against University of Louisville Health (UofL Health) for negligence.
The 28-year-old, who plays for Racing Louisville, collapsed in the first half of a National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) match on 14 September 2025.
According to documents, external seen by BBC Sport, the case was filed on Tuesday morning with Jefferson Circuit Court in Kentucky, where her club is based - a year and a day after her on-field collapse.
DeMelo's filing claims UofL Health and two doctors, Dr Sarabjeet Suri and Dr Jennifer Daily, "failed to act as a reasonably prudent and competent medical practice, and such negligence was a substantial factor in causing DeMelo to suffer severe physical injuries, including, but not limited to, her cardiac arrest".
Dr Daily, according to her online UofL biography, external, is Racing Louisville's chief medical officer. The lawsuit states DeMelo was under the care of Dr Daily from January 2024 to July 2026.
It states that in March 2025, Dr Daily referred DeMelo to Dr Suri for "evaluation and treatment" after she had been complaining of chest pain, dizziness and shortness of air; Dr Suri obtained a history, performed a physical examination and ordered diagnostic tests.
Nearly six months later, DeMelo suffered the cardiac arrest.
"She was subsequently diagnosed and treated for ventricular tachycardia [an abnormal heart rhythm]," the suit states.
DeMelo, who has spent her entire professional career with Racing Louisville, has not played since her collapse.
In a post to her Instagram page, external on Tuesday, De Melo - who was picked in the USA squad for the 2023 Women's World Cup and started their first two games - marked the anniversary of the incident.
"A year ago today, while playing soccer, I collapsed due to an undiagnosed cardiac arrhythmia, that caused me to go into cardiac arrest," she wrote.
"I respect and appreciate the privacy everyone has met me with while going through everything I have this year. I'll never be able to fully put into words how emotionally hard this year has been. There has been a lot of uncertainty and emotions intertwined with it all."

Srinagar, Sep 17: The Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly has formally accepted the Private Member’s Resolution moved by MLA Aga Syed Muntazir Mehdi on Hokersar Wetland. The Speaker has admitted the Resolution under Rule 179, clearing the path for it to be taken up in the House.
MLA Aga Syed Muntazir Mehdi will table this Resolution after the balloting scheduled for 18 September 2026 at 3:00 P.M. in the Office Chambers of the Secretary, Legislative Assembly.
Key Demands of the Resolution:
Demarcation of Wetland and Adjoining Areas: The resolution demanded clear examination of the present and historical extent of Hokersar Wetland and adjoining habitation/agricultural lands to protect genuine rights of the people and check arbitrary expansion.
Operation of Flood Gates and Water Levels: The resolution emphasized on thorough review of the operation of flood gates and the practice of maintaining high water levels throughout the year that has caused repeated inundation of residential and agricultural areas.
Impact on Habitations and Farmland: It demanded detailed assessment of how current water-level management is damaging homes, crops and the daily life of the surrounding population.
Condition of the Seven Nallahs: The resolution sought assessment of the present condition and carrying capacity of the seven Nallahs connected to the wetland, which directly affect flooding and drainage.
Compensation for Losses Suffered: It also sought recognition of the losses already suffered by residents and agriculturists and demanded for appropriate compensation for damage to property and livelihood.
Balance Between Conservation and People’s Rights: The resolution impressed upon to ensure conservation of Hokersar Wetland without compromising the legitimate rights and interests of the people living in its vicinity.
The resolution is a decisive political intervention. For years, the voices of the people living around Hokersar were ignored while their fields remained submerged and their homes faced constant threat. By forcing the Assembly to constitute a House Committee, Aga Syed Muntazir Mehdi has converted public pain into legislative action. The move sends a clear message: conservation cannot become a cover for injustice, and the rights of ordinary citizens will no longer be sacrificed in the name of environmental management. It is a strong assertion that the Assembly must stand with the people, demand accountability, and deliver justice, the resolution added.

Why dealing with defeat is key for Lampard at Coventry
- Published
Managing a newly-promoted team in the Premier League is very demanding, as Frank Lampard is finding out at Coventry.
It's the highest level, not just for the technical ability of the players that your team faces but also the sheer physicality that these players possess, and it feels like the gap to the Championship is getting greater every season.
From my experience in the same situation, you have to be really smart in the way you approach each game and recognise the importance of preparation for each specific opponent, because your team has to be organised in possession, and definitely out of possession.
Teams in the Premier League counter-attack with greater efficiency so being solid behind your own attacking play is absolutely vital.
But the real advice I would give to managers in Frank's shoes is to manage yourself, and your own time, as well as your players.
By that I mean you have to try to stay fresh and positive, because invariably you are going to go on bad runs of defeats like Coventry are on, which can drag your mood down.
Find a way of getting everyone back on track
I can tell you now that, whoever you are playing, if you get beaten - and especially beaten heavily like Coventry were by Brighton on Sunday - then it resonates with you. It's the same for every manager.
For Frank, whether it is losing at home to Hull or Brighton, or against Arsenal and Manchester City, then it will hurt.
But it is how he deals with those defeats that will decide what happens next.
Being the leader of a group of young men, you cannot look washed out and empty on a Monday morning after a heavy loss.
Yes, inside you will be hurting and your pride will be taking a bashing but everyone at the club will be waiting for your reaction, and will act accordingly.
Walking into the training ground in a dark mood and with your head around your backside just does not work, irrespective of what you are feeling inside.
I've been in that situation many times myself as a manager and what you have to do is puff your chest out and find a way of getting everyone back on track and working even harder with a set focus on the next game.
That's what all good leaders do. It is draining at times, but that is why managing your time and prioritising the issues that you can resolve is so important.
When I took Stoke up to the Premier League in 2008, I was learning on my feet.
We did not make a great start and I had to roll my sleeves up and get on with what I'd got in my squad, and really focus on getting results.
But away from that I was always forward thinking and I was quick at recognising what was needed to improve our chances of staying up.
When the window opened again in January, we were already in discussions with Tottenham for Matty Etherington, to supply us with crosses and chances from the wing.
We needed more goals too, so I took James Beattie from Sheffield United. They were a Championship side but that didn't matter because he had a record of scoring goals in the top flight.
We have heard so much about recruiting the right players in the right positions, and it is true today as it was in my day. Both lads played a significant role in keeping us up.
Coventry haven't scored a goal yet, and people might look in from the outside and feel the forward areas are an issue for them because the usual thinking is that the centre-forward has to lead the scoring charts, or a wide player or the number 10.
But the emphasis is on everyone to chip in and I would also reinforce one of the points I made in this column last season, about the importance of defending properly too.
On average, clean sheets earn you more points than scoring a goal, which is something I always stressed to my players. Nailing down the importance of both ends of the pitch is the narrative, whatever kind of run of results you are on, because games are won and lost there.
Why I was confident Stoke would stay up
Coventry have made a poor start but what has happened in their first four games does not have to become the story of their whole season.
With Stoke, we got a win in our first home game - against Aston Villa - but that was our only victory in our first seven league matches after getting promoted.
The thing I remember most from that time is that Hull had come up with us and, after seven games, they had won at Newcastle, Arsenal and Tottenham and were in the top five in the table, while we were third or fourth from bottom.
I went out for dinner with my chairman, Peter Coates, and he said how Hull had made a wonderful start. I replied by telling him I bet you now that we finish above Hull... and we did.
The reason I thought that was because of the mindset of the team, and the fans.
I was confident my players were not going to go weak at the knees, and the togetherness we needed was already there in the squad, while the support was just off the scales, which helped us enormously at home.
Every defeat was taken on the chin, and accepted, but the lads were always ready to go, again and again.
Survival is success for every promoted team
It was Steve Coppell who said to me how you have to deal with the fact you are going to lose a lot of games - or at least not win a lot of them - when you take a team up into the Premier League.
It is a very unusual situation, to go from being in the Championship and winning regularly week after week, to dealing with defeat after defeat.
Steve told me to get ready for going on runs where we would not win for five or six games on the bounce, but then if we could win two or three games in the same period after that, we would fly up the table.
But getting your head around that is hard, and it is the same for the players who were part of that promotion - especially if you were dominant like Coventry were last season.
They were expected to challenge at the top of the Championship, but in my opinion over-achieved by finishing clear at the top.
It was different for Hull, who achieved a promotion under Sergej Jakirovic that no-one outside that club believed was possible.
They have started the season on fire, just like the Tigers did in 2008 when Phil Brown was in charge, and now they have to try to sustain it.
They are third at the moment but if they are 17th come the end of May, which is where they finished under Brownie, then that will be a successful season.
I will be taking a closer look at Hull's progress in this column in the weeks to come, as well as the other promoted team, Ipswich.
Gary O'Neil has a really tough gig at Portman Road but it is one he will relish. I gave Gary his senior debut with Portsmouth in the Championship in 1999 and he's a smart lad who was always football mad.
Ipswich are a great club and I hope both are successful this season. Gary has experience of the Premier League with Bournemouth and Wolves, and he is going to need it.
New season, nine new managers - which appointments make sense?
Including O'Neil, there are nine new managers starting with clubs in the Premier League. It's a bigger number than usual and I wanted to quickly run through all of them.
Enzo Maresca at Manchester City seemed like common sense to me, even before they started the season with four league wins out of four, because he has worked with Pep and the club before.
City had a large turnover of players with their ins and outs over the summer, but I'd expect them to be in the mix for all the trophies again this season.
Another place where lots of changes have taken place is Stamford Bridge. Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has experience of playing in England and will understand that no game in the Premier League is a shoe-in - as Saturday's draw with Hull showed us again.
Andoni Iraola did an amazing job at Bournemouth but he will need all of his managerial ability and acumen to succeed at Liverpool.
At Liverpool, teams will drop deep and rely on counter-attacking situations. At Bournemouth that did not happen very often.
So, Andoni has to prepare his coaching philosophy to overcome teams who will definitely play deeper and be much more defensive-minded against Liverpool than they were against Bournemouth.
In my opinion, given time he will a great success but as he prepares to take his new team back to face his old one at Vitality Stadium on Sunday, we are already seeing that Liverpool will need more changes to develop into the title-winning side that their fantastic supporters demand.
At Nottingham Forest, Oliver Glasner did a wonderful job at Palace and I am sure we will see more of the same at the City Ground.
At the moment I know less about Marco Rose, Matthias Jaissle, and Pierre Sage, at Bournemouth, Newcastle and Crystal Palace.
Unlike the other managers I have mentioned, they have no experience of the Premier League but they are all joining established top-flight sides which is a huge help.
Finally, there is Alvaro Arbeloa at Fulham. He had a fantastic playing record at Real Madrid and Liverpool and coached in the Real Madrid academy and their B team before taking charge of the first team for the second half of last season.
While he has not had much experience in the dugout, he has worked with many top managers and players.
Fulham will be a real test for him, as we've seen from the way they have started the season, so again they are a club I will be keeping a close eye on - but there are plenty of those!
I got stuck into lots of topics in this column last season, at all levels of the game and covering every aspect of management, but I'd love to know what you would like me to talk about over the next few weeks.
Please make any suggestions in the comments section below - and also feel free to ask me any questions too.
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Bose announced a new version of its Ultra Open Earbuds that helped kick off the industry trend of clip-on wireless earbuds nearly two-and-a-half years ago. The new Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) feature a subtle redesign with improved performance in both sound quality and battery life. They’re also joined by a new cheaper alternative called the Bose Sport Open Earbuds designed to provide a more secure and stable fit during physical activities.
Bose’s next open earbuds have more bass, more volume, and more battery life
The second-gen Ultra Open Earbuds are joined by a new sport option providing a more secure fit when you’re active.
The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) will be available for preorder on September 19th for $299 with availability starting on October 1st. Color options include black, white smoke, cherry chocolate, olive green, and sky pink. Preorders and availability for the Bose Sport Open Earbuds are the same, but they’re $100 cheaper at $199. Colors include black, white smoke, and eucalyptus green.
Like the original version, the new Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) feature a design that clips to your outer ear with a transducer that directs audio into your ear canal with “minimal sound leakage,” Bose claims. There’s still no ANC because these are designed to do the exact opposite and let you hear what’s going on around you while enjoying music or a podcast.
In addition to a refreshed design with a new beveled finish on each earbud’s metal cap, the 2nd Gen feature a new driver delivering higher volume with automatic adjustments and deeper bass. A new Cinema Mode simulates a “wider, more immersive soundstage” using Bose’s TrueSpatial technology while keeping dialogue clear and centered. Battery life with the buds alone has been boosted to up to nine hours (from seven hours) with an additional 19.5 hours of playback from the redesigned case that can now stand upright for use on a wireless charger.
The Bose Sport Open Earbuds take a similar approach with a design that clips to your ear to project sounds inward, but they feature a thinner cuff with a “soft silicone matte finish” providing more grip to keep them in place. Bose says the Sport version will stay secure during head shakes, cartwheels, and running. They also feature automatic volume adjustments that adapt to ambient noise levels to ensure what you’re listening to isn’t drowned out, and the customizable shortcut button on the end of each battery barrel has an added texture, so they’re easier to find while working out. Battery life is rated at up to seven hours of playback plus an additional 22 hours with the wireless charging case.

The Election Commission has frozen Mamata Banerjee’s Trinamool Congress name and party symbol. Separate meetings were held today with the "Kalighat Trinamool" and "Ritobroto Trinamool". Following these, an interim order was issued tonight, Anandabazar Online has reported. It has been clearly stated that, for now, the name of the All India Trinamool Congress party and its twin-flower symbol have been frozen, the publication added. By-elections are coming up soon in Nandigram and Rejinagar. For these, both camps will have to choose from among the Election Commission's "free symbols". After leaving the Congress, Mamata formed her own new party in 1998. She built the Trinamool with her own hands. It is also known that the party's symbol was drawn by Banerjee herself. Now, for the time being, the former Bengal CM has lost control of even the party's name and symbol. TMC MP Kalyan Banerjee earlier raised sharp questions during the EC hearing. He challenged the rival faction's claim about the party's existence. According to him, they say TMC ceased to exist in 2025. But the same group got recognised as a legislative bloc in 2026. Banerjee called this claim contradictory and confusing. Speaking to ANI, he explained the timeline in detail. The hearing lasted nearly 90 minutes. He said Mamata Banerjee had issued the party symbol earlier. The rival group approached the Speaker on 3 June. They claimed to be the AITC's official bloc that day. This meant they had accepted TMC's existence until then. Suddenly, on 22 June, they denied TMC had even existed. Banerjee also made a personal allegation in this matter. He claimed Ritobroto Banerjee was behind the entire dispute. This happened after Ritobroto had missed the opposition leader's post. “You can't approve it and disapprove it. African greats inspired by the potential of Nairobi 2029
- Published
The decision to award the 2029 World Athletics Championships to Nairobi has prompted an outpouring of celebration across Africa.
Ethiopian great Haile Gebrselassie, a two-time Olympic 10,000m champion, congratulated the whole continent on the "wonderful news" following the announcement by World Athletics on Tuesday morning.
The Kenyan capital saw off former Olympic Games hosts London and Rome to secure a slice of history, with the event set to be held in Africa for the first time.
Unsurprisingly, news that the globe's top athletes will descend on the 48,000-capacity Kasarani Stadium in three years' time has gone down well with some of East Africa's biggest track and field stars.
Given the passionate following the sport has in Kenya, several commenters have stated that athletics will be "coming home".
'Huge for Africa'
Julius Yego, javelin world champion in 2015, said winning the bid is "a huge thing for Africa".
"I'm so happy that the world will come to Kenya," the 37-year-old told the BBC World Service.
"Africa has produced the best of athletes but we've never had a chance to witness such a big championship.
"It is something that will bring people to Africa. And people will know Africa."
Kenyans are known for their love of athletics, with 68% of people from the country who were surveyed by World Athletics rating their interest in the sport as high.

Gebrselassie expects the atmosphere inside the Kasarani Stadium, which is undergoing redevelopment ahead of the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, to be "very different".
"This is something very big in front of your people, in front of your city," he said.
"Many spectators can fly to Nairobi, many people can watch their athletes.
"It's going to be wonderful. I myself will be there to watch.
"Like in soccer, playing at home and then playing [away] is different. It's a big chance for Kenyans, it's a big chance for Ethiopians, in 2029, to win a race."
Inspiring the next generation
Janeth Jepkosgei, who won the women's 800m title at the 2007 World Championships in Osaka, thinks the "really exciting" decision will inspire the next generation of athletes.
"It means a lot for the youth and the juniors because it makes the dream really big," she said.
"This is the time where the youth and juniors should begin dreaming of winning at home."
Jepkosgei, who has moved into coaching since retiring from competition, says aspiring stars now have a very firm target in mind after being given a chance to challenge for world titles on home soil.
"We have been dreaming with these young ones, setting their goals," she said.
"This is where the young ones we have now can showcase their talent.
"Because we have three years [for] those athletes who are really promising. It is a good way to make them stay dedicated to it, focused and disciplined to the event.
"I've been speaking to my athletes and they're saying 'It has come home, we have to be there, on that starting line'."
Kenyan sprinter Ferdinand Omanyala, the holder of the African 100m record, was himself inspired by Nairobi hosting the Under-18 World Championships in 2017.
The 30-year-old expects the 2029 event to give a "big boost" to both current athletes and the generations to come.
"I can imagine what this is going to do to up-and-coming athletes," he said.
"They're going to see all these stars coming into the country and they'll be having this chance to watch them warm up and compete. That will be a huge motivation."
Capitalising on hosting
Africa will stage several big events over the next four years, with the first of those the upcoming Youth Olympics in the Senegalese capital Dakar from 31 October to 13 November.
South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia will host next year's men's Cricket World Cup, while the men's Fifa World Cup will return to the continent for the first time since 2010 when Morocco co-hosts alongside Spain and Portugal in 2030.

"Let's dream of hosting the Olympics and bring the best of the world in sports to Africa - to feel Africa, to enjoy Africa."
Both Egypt and South Africa have previously said they want to host the 2036 Olympics.
Yego's positive view is shared by Gebrselassie, who also hopes other cities will gain the confidence to bid for global events.
"This is a big chance, not only in sport, in economy, politics. Now Africans can do anything they want," the 53-year-old said.
"If Nairobi can host this championship, why not Addis Ababa? Why not Lagos or South Africa, Uganda, Rwanda?
"In 2029, I think the whole world will be surprised at how well they (Kenya) host."
