The farming lobby’s claim that immigration rule changes will increase food prices for households is wrong, Tony Burke has said, describing moves to speed up processing of backpacker visas as a positive step for agriculture.
Burke unveiled Labor’s long-awaited reforms at the National Press Club on Thursday, flagging that the plan was more limited than the government would like, due to a lack of support for wider legislation from the Coalition.
But the package has received mixed reviews, with business groups and the Coalition saying it did not do enough to lower net overseas migration levels, while refugee advocates said it showed migrants remained “political punching bags”.
The National Farmers Federation’s chief executive, Mike Guerin, said farmers would see an immediate economic impact from restrictions on working holidaymakers and other temporary migrants. He warned producers were already struggling to get workers for the harvesting season.
Backpackers seeking to stay in Australia for more than a year will be subject to a new ballot, with places severely restricted for years two and three.
“We will see a lift in the price of food,” Guerin said. 
 “We will see emptier supermarkets ... And while it’s yet to play out directly for consumers, for people in the cities, it’s very close. We will not be able to finish the harvest this year, before Christmas.”
But Burke told Guardian Australia the plan was carefully formulated, reducing demand driven settings and giving the government great control, while not damaging the economy.
He said healthcare, construction and aged care all relied on overseas workers, and broader cuts would hurt essential services.
“The economic contribution matters in terms of services that people rely on.
“The announcement we made today is about getting the processing moving again for those backpacker visas that have an obligation, if you want the extra years, to work in the regions. That’s a significant advantage … the department getting moving on the processing of those again at a faster pace.”
Burke said the agriculture sector could utilise workers from the Pacific Australia labour mobility scheme, and producers had legal responsibilities to pay staff adequately.
“I don’t think consumers believe their pathway to paying less should rely on worker exploitation.”
The government’s changes include new compliance measures to deal with people overstaying their visa, but Burke said enforcement would be measured and sensible.
About 100 new additional compliance officers will be added, along with 250 additional beds in immigration detention.
Burke said the changes were not like hardline immigration enforcement in countries overseas, such as the approach used by Donald Trump’s administration.
But the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre said the planned increase in enforcement would leave Australia “smaller, meaner and more divided”.
  “How much of its soul is the Labor party prepared to sacrifice chasing people who will never be satisfied,” founder Kon Karapanagiotidis said.
  The Greens deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi, criticised the increased immigration detention and bar on foreign students bringing family members to Australia.
  “Labor’s move to force people to choose between their family and a chance to study in Australia is soulless mimicry of One Nation tactics,” Faruqi said.
“Pauline Hanson and her billionaire backers might as well be ghostwriting Labor’s immigration policy.”
 Major employers welcomed the reforms, with the Minerals Council of Australia praising the government’s prioritisation of mining workers.
 Big business lobby group the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry said the government had avoided a damaging overcorrection and the plan would help rebuild public confidence. But its chief executive, Andrew McKellar, warned its execution via ministerial directives meant policy was being held together by “the stroke of a pen”.
 The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, accused the government of using farmers and regional industries as “whipping boys for their failure to bring down migration”. 
 Cuts to the working holidaymaker program would lead to staff shortages, the Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association chief, Wes Lambert, warned.
 “A chef, cook or hospitality manager filling a genuine shortage is valuable too,” Lambert said.
“Australia absolutely needs a sustainable migration system. But migration policy cannot simply be a numbers exercise. It must recognise where the workers are actually needed.”

Healthtech startup Practo has overhauled its top leadership, appointing former COO Jagnoor Singh as CEO, while cofounder and former CEO Shashank ND Singh has moved to the expanded role of MD and executive chairman. Singh’s appointment took effect on September 1. He will lead Practo’s overall strategy, growth, and operations across its global markets, the startup said in a statement. Meanwhile, Shashank will focus on Practo’s long-term vision, product and strategy, innovation agenda, capital strategy, inorganic growth, and corporate development initiatives. Singh joined Practo as COO in January 2025 and has since worked on its growth strategy, operational execution, and entry into new markets. Before joining Practo, he held senior positions at Bharti Airtel, Unacademy, and OYO. Practo has also expanded the responsibilities of three senior executives as part of the leadership reshuffle. Cofounder Siddhartha Nihalani has taken on the additional responsibility of COO – B2C and will oversee Practo’s consumer businesses. Rowel Coelho, previously its head of monetisation, has been appointed COO – B2B and will lead the soonicorn’s enterprise and corporate businesses. Meanwhile, cofounder Abhinav Lal has been named chief scientist. In the research-focused role, he will lead Practo’s exploration of AI applications in healthcare, build research partnerships, and develop an innovation hub focused on emerging technologies. Practo’s IPO Preparations The leadership changes come as Practo steps up its international expansion and prepares for a proposed public listing. Earlier this year, the startup appointed former Union health secretary CK Mishra as an independent director as part of efforts to strengthen its board. Inc42 previously reported that Practo was in advanced discussions to raise $100 Mn to $125 Mn in a pre-IPO funding round at a post-money valuation of around $700 Mn. The startup is reportedly targeting a public listing in 2027. Practo claimed that it is currently growing at 40% YoY and has remained profitable for the past two-and-a-half years. The startup turned EBITDA profitable in FY25, reporting an operating EBITDA of ₹15 Cr on revenue of ₹234 Cr. This marked a turnaround from FY24, when it posted an EBITDA loss of ₹17 Cr on revenue of ₹240 Cr. Founded in 2008 by Shashank and Lal, Practo operates a digital healthcare platform that allows patients to find doctors, book appointments, consult physicians online, order medicines, and schedule diagnostic tests. It also offers practice management software for doctors, clinics, and hospitals, and operates 40 co-branded dermatology clinics across India. Its platform connects patients with more than 7 Lakh doctors and healthcare providers across over 2,400 cities globally. Practo also operates Insta, a hospital information management system used by more than 500 clients across over 1,200 facilities. Besides India, Practo has expanded into the US and the UAE. It entered the UAE last year and launched a pilot in the US, where it claims to have onboarded more than 2 Lakh doctors and built an annual GMV run rate of over $75 Mn. It has raised a total funding of about $230 Mn to date from investors like Peak XV Partners, Sofina, Thrive Capital, and Capital G. The leadership reshuffle also comes months after Shashank launched preventive healthcare startup Cent alongside former Ola CMO Anshul Khandelwal and sales executive Arpit Garg. Cent raised $5 Mn in seed funding from OneFlow Holdings, Shashank’s family office, and South Park Commons.

Newcastle players see Jaissle's angry side - can they respond?
- Published
Newcastle United players had previously experienced an unhappy Matthias Jaissle in training in the opening weeks of his reign.
But the head coach was especially forthright in the away dressing room at Elland Road on Monday.
It was a night the visitors suffered a chastening 4-1 defeat against Leeds United.
"There was all clarity in the room that the learning curve needs to be really fast," Jaissle said a few days on.
Even during the course of a previous five-game unbeaten run, there was a recognition within the club that this was "always going to be a work in progress" following a summer of huge change.
Newcastle have gone from having one of the most experienced starting line-ups in the Premier League last season to the second-youngest this time around.
Yet the manner of Newcastle's first loss of the campaign still came as a jolt.
It already feels like much will be learned from how Jaissle's team respond against in-form Hull City on Saturday.
"If you're tougher in the duels, if you're more aggressive, if you're more sharp and hungry to collect the second balls, then it will be automatically a huge step already," he said.
"That means that you're more dominant, that you have more possession, and then that leads also to the fact that you threaten the opposition much more.
"So they will be the elements where we will focus on and there will be a reaction."
A bruising night at Elland Road
Jaissle was parachuted into the hot seat just three weeks before the start of the season after predecessor Eddie Howe stepped down.
He is still adapting to the Premier League and injuries to, among others, Dan Burn, Joelinton, Anthony Elanga and William Osula have hardly helped in that regard.
That being said, no team have faced more shots (76) in the opening weeks of the season in the top flight, while at the other end Newcastle have been averaging little more than three efforts on target per game in the league.
The visitors struggled to gain a foothold against an aggressive Leeds side, even before influential midfielder Nico Gonzalez went off with a concussion in the 19th minute.
Vertical football is Jaissle's trademark, in an effort to "stress" the opposition, but too often Newcastle's main tactic appeared to be punting the ball forward for Yoane Wissa and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to chase hopefully at Elland Road.
Leeds' three towering centre-backs outnumbered the pair and Newcastle were also swarmed in midfield after Jaissle stuck with his preferred two-man pivot.
However exposed Jaissle's system was, though, that does not excuse those on the field failing to do the basics from the off against one of the most physical sides in the league.
Meek Newcastle lost 56% of their duels in the first half against Leeds and defenders Malick Thiaw and Sven Botman were bullied by Dominic Calvert-Lewin, who scored twice.
A warning had previously been sounded when Newcastle failed to match Bournemouth's intensity and found themselves 2-0 down after just 35 minutes earlier this month.
Jaissle's team showed admirable grit and spirit to come back and draw that game at St James' Park, but a similar response was never on the cards in West Yorkshire.
No wonder one or two Newcastle players threw out their palms apologetically as they trudged over to the away end at full-time.
'He's still in a phase of figuring things out'
Jaissle repeatedly stressed his "fundamentals" - being physical, intense and competitive in duels - were "non-negotiable" and how his players needed to take losing a duel personally.
He spent the bus journey home digging into the detail behind the defeat with his analysts.
However, just as Jaissle has not allowed himself to get too high following positive results, he has not tended to emotionally rip up the foundations after a setback, either, as former Red Bull Salzburg midfielder Zlatko Junuzovic explained.
"They analysed the situation and, where necessary, made one or two adjustments, but nothing drastic," he said of his approach to defeats during their time in Austria.
"I think he's still in a phase of figuring things out [at Newcastle], where he has to see for himself which players fit his system and which ones don't."
Jaissle, 38, may still be a relatively young manager but he has experience to fall back on in that regard.
It was a different level, a different sort of capitulation and a different squad, but Jaissle also suffered a bruising away defeat at a similar point of his reign at Al-Ahli after the Saudi Pro League side were hammered 5-1 by Al-Fateh in 2023.
Could that difficult night in Leeds prove a similarly valuable learning experience or will this campaign be characterised by further ups and downs?
"We don't search for excuses, even with a young squad," Jaissle said. "We need to learn fast."

US to allow Iran delegation to attend UN meetings in New York as war passes half-year mark

The US government has granted visas to Iranian officials so they can travel to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, as the war between the two countries grinds into its seventh month.
The BBC understands the core delegation permitted to attend includes Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
A spokesman for the US State Department confirmed the decision on Thursday, saying that the delegation will be placed under travel restrictions and will be banned from purchasing certain American products.
The move comes as the war shows no sign of ending. Since it began in February, it has driven up global energy prices, and expanded into neighbouring countries.
"Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week," a spokesman for the US State Department told the BBC.
"The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year."
Last year, diplomats attending from Iran were banned from shopping at wholesale stores like Costco. They also were required to seek permission from the US before purchasing luxury goods, including jewellery, alcohol and cars.
The 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) is currently underway. The General Debate - the centrepiece of the annual event - is due to begin on Tuesday.
Tuesday will include speeches from US President Donald Trump, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and France President Emmanuel Macron.
Wednesday is expected to see speeches from the leaders of Ukraine, Syria and Iran.
Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.
Since the war began, Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.
The BBC recently learned that the US denied a visa to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and the Palestinian delegation to attend UNGA.
The White House, which does not recognise the legitimacy of the Palestinian delegation, denied them visas for a second year in a row.

Thousands of patients in India are diagnosed with melanoma, a type of skin cancer, each year. While melanoma is far less common here than in Western populations, it is far from rare and the way it presents in our patient population makes it uniquely difficult to detect early. Too many patients come to us when the disease is already advanced, precisely at a time when treatment options have never been more powerful or more personalised. This contrast between available therapies and the stage at which patients are diagnosed defines one of the most pressing challenges in melanoma care in India today.
Why melanoma gets missed
The warning signs most people associate with skin cancer come from research developed for fairer-skinned populations, where melanoma tends to appear on sun-exposed areas as an irregular or darkening mole. That picture does not reflect what clinicians see in India.
Melanoma here, most commonly presents on the soles of the feet or beneath the nails, sites that are rarely examined and even more rarely associated with cancer. This condition is called acral lentiginous melanoma, a subtype that accounts for 35 to 60% of cases in dark-skinned individuals. Such lesions are frequently mistaken for bruises, fungal infections, or diabetic ulcers, and by the time a biopsy is taken, the disease has often progressed.
Mucosal melanomas, a rare type of cancer that starts in the mucous membranes, are highly aggressive with a very low chance of recovery and produce few early warning signs. Most are diagnosed only after spread has occurred.
Any pigmented lesion that changes or persists, wherever it appears on the body, deserves investigation rather than reassurance.
A decade of transformation
When I began my oncology career, managing advanced melanoma meant offering patients limited and rarely durable options. That has fortunately changed significantly.
The foundational shift came from James Allison and Tasuku Honjo, whose discoveries on CTLA-4 and PD-1 earned them the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Their research established the principle of immune-checkpoint blockade: rather than attacking a tumour directly, we can sometimes release the biological brakes that stop the patient’s own immune system from doing so. The results can be extraordinary. Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter was diagnosed at 91 with melanoma that had spread to his liver and brain. Surgical resection of liver disease, stereotactic radiation for the brain, and immunotherapy with the checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab produced a durable remission, and he lived to 100.
Precision medicine has reshaped the approach in parallel. Some melanomas carry specific mutations, particularly in the BRAF pathway, that can be directly targeted with molecularly designed therapies. This is where next-generation sequencing, or NGS, becomes critical. In simple terms, it reads the genetic blueprint of a patient’s tumour and identifies the alterations that should guide treatment, turning what was once a single clinical decision into a detailed, individualised process.
The melanoma story is not over; it is only becoming more exciting. TIL therapy takes tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, expands them in the laboratory, and reinfuses them in far greater numbers, a step toward truly personalised cellular treatment. In August 2026, intismeran, a personalised mRNA vaccine built from the patient’s own tumour sequence, was combined with pembrolizumab in high-risk melanoma patients after surgery. The results were striking: a significant reduction in recurrence compared with pembrolizumab alone, making it the first positive late-stage trial of a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine, though survival data remain pending.
What still needs to change
All of these advances deliver their best results when treatment begins early. The more sophisticated our therapies become, the more clearly we see that they work best before the disease has spread. In India, awareness and referral gaps continue to push diagnosis toward advanced stages.
Recalibrating public health messaging to reflect how melanoma actually presents in Indian patients is a start. Faster pathways from primary care to specialist centres matter equally. More fundamentally, India needs a national melanoma registry, stronger epidemiological and genomic data, more clinical trials in Indian patients, and deeper international collaboration. The advances of the past decade are genuinely extraordinary. Whether they reach the patients who need them comes down to one thing: a diagnosis early enough to act on.
(Prof. Jyoti Bajpai is director – medical precision immuno-oncology, Apollo Hospitals, Mumbai & Western Zone. drjyoti_ba@apollohospitals.com)

Shehzad Poonawalla set to join Prime Video's 'Rise and Fall' Season 2 after BJP exit
The politician's participation in the Prime Video show was confirmed after a trailer for the second season aired online on social media.
Former BJP spokesperson Shehzad Poonawalla is set to join reality TV show ‘Rise and Fall.’ The politician's participation in the Prime Video show was confirmed after a trailer for the second season aired online on social media.
Poonawalla's participation in the reality TV show also comes after his exit from the Bharatiya Janata Party.
The political commentator quit the BJP earlier this year in August. Speaking to reporters, the spokesperson said he submitted his resignation after “long and hard contemplation."
“Due to pressing emergency financial and personal circumstances, I will move into the private sector, but wherever possible and in whatever format possible, I will continue to support the vision and work of Prime Minister Modi and the BJP,” he said. “I am only leaving the Vyavastha (organisation) not the Vyakti (people) or Vichar (ideology),” Poonawalla added.
Tehseen Poonawaalla also took to X to congratulate the former BJP spokesperson on his "new chapter."
"Dearest Shehzad, here is wishing you all the best as you embark on your new journey in "Reality Television entertainment!". May you have all the "Rise" & may you never "Fall!". You genuinely were the best Spokesperson that I came across, much much better than me & may you RISE, RISE, RISE and do much better than me on Reality TV. (that's not difficult!)," Poonawaalla wrote on X.
Rise and Fall Season 2 to air Sept 26
The new season for Prime Video's Rise and Fall is set to air on September 26, 2026.
Produced by Banijay Asia, the series will stream daily at 12pm on Prime Video and the MX Player Android app.
Along with Poonawaalaa, actress Swara Bhasker, reality television veteran Priyanka Chahar Choudhary and television actor Karan Patel will also be joining the show.
The second season will be hosted by cricket legen Virender Sehway, replacing Asheneer Grover.

Senior Congress leader and former Union Minister E.M. Sudarsana Natchiappan passed away at his residence in Sivaganga on Thursday (September 17, 2026). He was 78, and is survived by his wife, daughter, two sons, and two elder brothers.
Tamil Nadu Congress Committee (TNCC) president Manickam Tagore, a nephew of Natchiappan, said his uncle had died in his sleep. “When he did not get up in the morning, his driver went to his room, only to find he was no more,” he told The Hindu.
A Congressman since 1969, Natchiappan rose through the ranks from his early days as the Singampunari Regional Youth Congress president to become the vice-president of the TNCC in 2002. He also served as the party whip in Parliament.
Student leader
Born in Eriyur in Sivaganga district, Natchiappan was active in the Students’ Congress while studying at the Law College. “Later, he worked in the Youth Congress and became its general secretary. He was elected chairman of the Sivaganga Panchayat Union in the 1986 local body elections, which showcased a lot of talented Congress leaders in Tamil Nadu,” Mr. Tagore said.
After practising law in Sivaganga, Natchiappan shifted his practice to the Madras High Court in 1991 and to the Supreme Court in 1995.
A staunch Congress loyalist and admirer of former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and Congress leader Sonia Gandhi, Natchiappan remained with the Congress when the late G.K. Moopanar launched the Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) in 1996 in protest against the Congress high command’s decision to align with the AIADMK.
Victory in 1999 LS polls
Before making his mark in national politics, he gained widespread attention in the 1999 Lok Sabha elections by winning the Sivaganga parliamentary seat against senior Congress leader P. Chidambaram when the latter was in the TMC.
After Mr. Chidambaram returned to the Congress, Natchiappan could not secure the Sivaganga Lok Sabha constituency again. He was later nominated to the Rajya Sabha by party leader Sonia Gandhi and represented the House for two terms. He served as the Congress Lok Sabha member from the Sivaganga constituency from 1999 to 2004 and as a Rajya Sabha member from 2004 to 2016.
He also served as Union Minister of State for Commerce and Industry for a brief period between 2013 and 2014. He made significant contributions as chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice between 2004 and 2009.
Natchiappan, an expert in the Sri Lankan Tamils issue, fishermen’s rights, and the Katchatheevu islet, had addressed the United Nations General Assembly on two occasions.
He had been receiving medical care for his declining health in Sivaganga for the past few days, but passed away at his residence after the treatment proved unsuccessful.
Leaders condole death
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, and Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar condoled the death of Natchiappan.
Mr. Gandhi recalled Mr. Natchiappan’s commitment to public service, Tamil Nadu and the Congress party, while Mr. Birla extended condolences to his family, friends and supporters.
Mr. Shivakumar remembered his long and dedicated service to the people of Tamil Nadu and the Congress movement. Mr. Tagore recalled his association with the Youth Congress from his early years and his contributions as Sivaganga MP, Union Minister and in various organisational positions in the party. He also said Mr. Natchiappan’s death was an irreparable loss to the Congress.
Meanwhile, Congress leaders and functionaries paid floral tributes to Mr. Natchiappan’s portrait at Sathyamurthy Bhavan in Chennai. AICC general secretary and Tamil Nadu in-charge Ghulam Ahmad Mir, former Tamil Nadu Congress Committee president K.V. Thangabalu, Peter Alphonse, AICC secretary Nivedith Alva, IT and social media department head and MP Vijay Vasanth, among other State and district-level leaders, functionaries and party workers, participated.
VCK president Thol. Thirumavalavan said his demise was a great loss to Tamil Nadu. On behalf of the Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi, he expressed his condolences to Mr. Natchiappan’s family and paid homage to the former Union Minister.
TVK leaders, including party spokesperson Arunraaj and C.T.R. Nirmal Kumar, also condoled the death of the senior Congress leader.
Veteran political activist and former member of the central committee of the Eelam People’s Revolutionary Liberation Front (EPRLF), Sritharan Thirunavukkarasu, also known as Sugu, recalled that when Sri Lankan government, headed by Mahinda Rajapaksa, made an attempt to dilute the 13th Amendment to its Constitution in violation of the spirit of the 1987 Indo-Lanka Accord, the Congress leader took the initiative of hosting a meeting of Tamil leaders from the island-nation in New Delhi and got a resolution adopted that any such endeavour to weaken the letter and spirit of the Amendment should be stopped and powers, intended for provincial councils in Sri Lanka, be transferred.
The Amma Makkal Munnetra Kazhagam (AMMK) general secretary T.T.V. Dhinakaran expressed sadness over the death of the former Union Minister.

If you felt a gust of wind late on Friday, it came from hundreds of immigration lawyers who simultaneously exhaled after the Supreme Court announced it would not hear a case known as Genalo v. Black. That case asked whether certain immigrants could be held in immigration detention facilities indefinitely without ever receiving a bond hearing or other opportunity to seek temporary release. And if the Court had decided this case, its recent immigration decisions suggest that most of the justices may have blessed indefinite detention.
The successful campaign to make a terrifying Supreme Court immigration case disappear
For now…
The Black case originally concerned two lawful permanent residents of the United States who were arrested during the first Trump administration because of crimes the two men committed years before, and that they had already served prison sentences for committing.
These immigrants were arrested because of a federal law, which provides that the federal government “shall take into custody” noncitizens who committed certain crimes or who are accused of involvement with terrorism so that the government may begin deportation proceedings against these individuals. This law does not allow these noncitizens to challenge their detention while their deportation case is pending. (Notably, the relevant federal law sometimes allows an immigrant to be detained without hearing if they are merely suspected of terrorism, which means the person could be detained indefinitely based on false allegations.)
Both men sued, claiming that it is unconstitutional to hold them for too long without some kind of hearing to determine whether they should be released after paying a bond. And a federal appeals court agreed, holding that “due process bars the Executive from detaining such individuals for an unreasonably prolonged period…without a bond hearing.”
Thus, Black was more than just another flash point in America’s debates over immigration. It was a test of one of the most fundamental protections that a liberal society provides to its residents — the right not to be locked up, forever, without any way to challenge the basis of that detention.
Now that the Supreme Court has removed the Black case from its own docket, this appeals court decision will not be formally repudiated by the Supreme Court. So immigrants who are detained indefinitely may still ask courts to give them a bond hearing — at least for now.
Still, the Court’s nondecision in Black leaves a cloud of uncertainty hanging over similarly situated immigrants. The Trump administration will no doubt continue to detain people for prolonged periods of time (most of whom won’t be able to obtain a gubernatorial pardon, like one of the men was in this case). And the question of whether these immigrants can be detained forever will remain unresolved until the Supreme Court takes up another case involving a similarly situated immigrant.
Why the case was dismissed
Both men at the heart of the Black case spent significant amounts of time in immigration detention facilities years after serving sentences for crimes. One, a Jamaican citizen named Carol Williams Black, spent seven months in an immigration detention facility. The other, Keisy Guerrero Mariano, spent 21 months in detention without a bond hearing or other procedure that could allow him to seek release while his case was pending. These 21 months in immigration detention more than doubled the time he spent in New York state prison for his actual crime — he pled guilty to second-degree assault after he got into a fight outside a New York City restaurant.
But there is no longer a legal dispute about what should happen to either man — in the words of the law, both cases are now moot. Black has since been released from detention and says that he “made the difficult decision to leave the United States” and has no intention to return. And the Trump administration’s case against Guerrero Mariano went up in smoke in late August, after New York Gov. Kathy Hochul gave him a pardon — thus wiping away the conviction that allowed the Trump administration to detain Guerrero Mariano in the first place.
Guerrero Mariano is one of six individuals that Hochul pardoned at the time. In her official announcement, she said that she did so because these six people “have demonstrated remorse, exemplified rehabilitation and displayed a commitment to improving themselves and their communities.”
There’s also a great deal of evidence indicating that Hochul pardoned Guerrero Mariano in order to resolve his immigration case — and potentially keep the Supreme Court from deciding Black. Among other things, the actual pardon document signed by Hochul specifically states that it will grant Guerrero Mariano “relief from removal.” Guerrero Mariano’s lawyers had sought this pardon, and Hochul granted it mere days before his brief was due in the Supreme Court.
That brief’s very first sentence, moreover, states that Hochul “granted Respondent Keisy G.M. a full and unconditional pardon of the state criminal conviction that is the sole basis for his removal,” and it urges the justices to dismiss the case as moot.
Last Thursday, Trump’s Justice Department joined a stipulation calling for the justices to dismiss the case against Guerrero Mariano, most likely because even they recognized that a lawful permanent resident with no conviction may not be detained. The Court granted that request on Friday.
So that’s good news for Guerrero Mariano, who presumably will now be able to live freely in the United States.
Guerrero Mariano’s lawyers were right to fear a trip to the Supreme Court
It’s possible that the Supreme Court might have agreed with the lower court’s holding that immigrants who are detained for an “unreasonably prolonged period” have a constitutional right to a bond hearing — this Court has, on rare occasions, broken with the Trump administration in immigration cases. But those decisions are few and far between.
Among other things, this Court has allowed President Donald Trump to deport immigrants back to war zones. The Court’s Republican majority effectively nullified the Convention Against Torture, a treaty that is supposed to protect immigrants from being deported to nations where they will be tortured. The Court also blessed so-called Kavanaugh stops, which permit suspected immigrants to be racially profiled so long as their race or ethnicity isn’t the sole reason why they are stopped by law enforcement.
Moreover, while the US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit’s decision in Black — the one holding that immigrants like Guerrero Mariano may receive a bond hearing if their detention is “unreasonably prolonged” — reached a plausible legal conclusion, this conclusion was not a slam dunk under the Supreme Court’s previous precedents. And that means that the justices could have easily come up with a reason to reverse that decision if they wanted.
On the one hand, the Court said in Zadvydas v. Davis (2001) that “a statute permitting indefinite detention of an alien would raise a serious constitutional problem.” On the other hand, the Court held in Demore v. Kim (2003) that an immigrant similarly situated to Guerrero Mariano may “be detained for the brief period necessary for their removal proceedings.”
Read together, these decisions suggest that the government does have some power to detain people while their immigration case is pending. While Zadvydas indicates that this detention can go on for too long, the Court has never established when an immigrant’s detention has stretched too long. So that means that the justices would have a fair amount of leeway to allow prolonged detentions without defying any of their previous precedents.
So it’s clear why everyone from Guerrero Mariano’s lawyers to Hochul seemed concerned about what would happen if the Court decided this case. In the worst-case scenario for immigrants, Trump could have gained the power to lock many people up for years without any meaningful way to challenge their detention. In the best case, the Supreme Court may have reached the same conclusion as the Second Circuit — but even that decision was vague about how long an immigrant must be detained before they must receive a bond hearing.
In any event, the bottom line is that the Court’s decision to dismiss the Black case is good news for Guerrero Mariano. But that dismissal merely delays a reckoning for other immigrants who face prolonged detention while their case is pending.

Manitoba adopts permanent daylight time after survey suggested overwhelming opposition to clock changes
More than 90% of 72,000 Manitobans who voted in online survey wanted to ditch twice-yearly changes: province
Manitobans no longer need to remember to spring forward or fall back one hour on their clocks.
Daylight time will be in place permanently, Premier Wab Kinew announced in a news release Thursday.
This change means clocks will not revert to standard time on Nov. 1.
Manitoba joins several other provinces and territories that have adopted or are moving toward a permanent time, including British Columbia, Yukon, the Northwest Territories, Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Just six months ago, Kinew said his government was too busy with more important matters to consider changes to the clocks.
He was asked about it in early March, shortly after B.C. announced it intended to remain on daylight time permanently.
He later softened his stance, suggesting it may be time to revisit the issue for Manitoba.
In April, Alberta announced plans to table legislation to cement a move to permanent daylight time. Days later, the Northwest Territories said it will also end time changes. Yukon has been on permanent time since 2020 and Saskatchewan since 1966.
In May, Manitoba launched a survey, asking the public to weigh in the issue. For those who did want to see the twice-annual changes halted, the survey asked if they preferred to stay on standard or daylight time.
In its news release at the time the survey launched, the province included a link to an analysis by Manitoba Health, which concluded that eliminating the time change would be better for population health.
On Thursday, the province said nearly 72,000 votes were submitted in its survey, with 92 per cent of respondents saying they wanted to see an end to seasonal time changes. Among respondents, 58 per cent preferred permanent daylight time and 34 per cent sided with standard time.
Permanent daylight time is good for health, business and families with young kids, whose routines, especially sleep cycles, can be disrupted for days with those one-hour time changes, Kinew said in Thursday's news release.
The province is working with organizations, businesses and industry partners to adapt to the change, he said.
Manitoba enacted the Official Time Act, bringing provincewide daylight time into official effect on May 12, 1963. However, some cities, like Brandon and Winnipeg, had been experimenting with daylight time off and on since as early as 1916.
Under the Official Time Act, daylight time began on the first Sunday in April and went until the last Sunday in October, when clocks fell back to standard time.
Daylight time was extended in 2007, starting the second Sunday in March and continuing until the first Sunday in November, to match U.S. changes.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi reshuffled her Cabinet for the first time on Thursday, focusing her changes on less prominent positions while keeping key figures intact.
While the reshuffle saw more than half the Cabinet replaced, almost every senior Liberal Democratic Party executive remained, as did the prominent Cabinet members. The most noteworthy changes were the addition of a Japan Innovation Party member to the Cabinet, the removal of the LDP’s Upper House secretary-general and the departure of a future prime minister hopeful.
This was not what many observers anticipated. Takaichi has faced discord within the party ranks, the specter of a declining public approval rating and a looming LDP leadership race. Traditionally, Cabinet reshuffles have been tools for managing intraparty competition, so it would not have been unusual to see substantial personnel changes as the prime minister managed allies and rivals.

Russia’s parliamentary vote features no real opposition to Putin's policies
Russia’s parliamentary election features the main Kremlin’s party and nine others that all back President Vladimir Putin’s policies
Russia’s parliamentary election features the Kremlin's main party, United Russia, and nine others that all support President Vladimir Putin’s policies. The only party that dared to oppose the war in Ukraine has been barred from the ballot.
The absence of genuine opposition all but assures the Kremlin will keep tight control of the Russian political scene amid mounting economic costs and increasing Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries and online retailers. Those drone strikes have made Russians feel the pain from the war more than 4½ years after its start.
The Kremlin wants the election — the first since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022 — to underline public support for the war and give a veneer of legitimacy to its action. It has sought to avoid any political risks by stamping out even the slightest sign of dissent.
Here's what to know about the election and its main parties:
Starting Friday and lasting through Sunday, Russians will elect members of the lower house, the State Duma. They also will cast ballots in local elections. Voters in 11 regions will elect their governors, and 39 regions will elect members of regional legislatures.
The balloting is spread over three days in a bid to boost turnout among the 111 million eligible voters and includes areas that Russia illegally annexed in Ukraine. Electronic voting is allowed.
Half of the Duma's 450 seats are filled by party lists and the other half are contested in single-ballot races. The main Kremlin party, United Russia, is set to retain its overwhelming control of the Duma, while other “systemic opposition” parties that vote in sync with the government on all key issues also are expected to retain their presence.
The liberal Yabloko Party, the only registered political party that opposes the war, initially was on the ballot but the Supreme Court in August ordered it removed. It cited, among other reasons, that the anti-war stance was akin to seeking the violation of Russia’s territorial integrity. Yabloko now only has candidates in single-ballot races.
United Russia, whose symbol is a bear prowling beneath the Russian tricolor, won more than two-thirds of the Duma’s seats in the 2021 election. It is again poised to dominate the body.
Even amid growing public fatigue, recession and stagnating living standards, the massive state propaganda machine and tight control over the election all but assure United Russia's victory.
The party's list is led by political heavyweights: Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, 76, who has been Russia’s top diplomat for 22 years, and Sergei Sobyanin, 68, the powerful mayor of Moscow.
In an apparent bid to add fresh faces in what is widely seen as a party of bureaucrats, its No. 3 official is war correspondent Yevgeny Poddubny, who was badly wounded by a Ukrainian drone.
Members of United Russia have vowed to back the war effort and Putin's maximalist goals in what the Kremlin calls the “special military operation” in Ukraine.
At the same time, Sobyanin, who is widely seen as a pragmatist, has rebuffed calls by Russian hawks for a broad mobilization of conscripts and putting the entire economy on a war footing.
“To destroy a normal economy is to destroy the country altogether,” he said in remarks reflecting Kremlin hopes to win the war without risking a broad, unpopular mobilization.
The Communist Party has been a leading force in parliament since the 1990s, led for more than three decades by 82-year-old Gennady Zyuganov, a former Soviet official.
Throughout Putin’s rule of over a quarter-century, the Communists have criticized some aspects of government policy but carefully avoided any criticism of him. They steadfastly support the war in Ukraine.
“We strictly adhere to President Putin’s directives,” Zyuganov said last month while overseeing a shipment of military supplies.
The party is increasingly active on social media as it seeks to shift from relying on elderly voters to expand its base to a younger generation.
The misleadingly named Liberal Democratic Party is an ultranationalist force that has been a significant presence in parliament since the early 1990s. Founded by Vladimir Zhirinovsky, an outspoken firebrand who frequently called for reclaiming former Soviet lands and threatened to use nuclear weapons against Russia’s enemies, it competes with the Communists by trying to cater to voters nostalgic for the USSR.
After Zhirinovsky’s death in 2022, the party has been led by Leonid Slutsky, an uncharismatic former professor who weathered sexual harassment allegations.
Like the Communists, the LDPR staunchly supports the war and boasts of having multiple veterans as members. Among its candidates is Viktor Bout, a former arms trader nicknamed the “Merchant of Death.” He was serving a 25-year prison sentence in the U.S. before being exchanged in December 2022 for WNBA star Brittney Griner, who had been arrested 10 months earlier in Moscow for possession of cannabis oil.
The party known as A Just Russia has been on Russia’s political scene for two decades. A social-democratic party, it competes with the Communists for older and middle-aged voters nostalgic for the Soviet past, and it supports the war in Ukraine.
Its leader, Sergei Mironov, 73, once gained headlines by posing with a symbol of brutality — a sledgehammer given to him by Yevgeny Prigozhin, the late Wagner mercenary leader shortly before his failed 2023 mutiny. The Wagner group purportedly used sledgehammers to kill people it deemed traitors.
The New People Party was founded shortly before the last parliamentary election in 2021, seeking to position itself as a liberal voice representing younger voters and technocrats. It won just over 5% of the vote, allowing it to form a small faction.
Even though it once cast itself as an opposition force, it embraced Putin’s policies after the vote, disappointing many of its backers. Led by Alexei Nechayev, the head of a cosmetics firm, the party was widely seen as a product of the Kremlin, intended to cater to the liberal audience and to present a semblance of political competition.
Among the other parties seeking seats are Communists of Russia, a small rival of the main Communist Party; the Party of Pensioners; the Green Party; the Party of Direct Democracy; and the Motherland Party.
Motherland, a hard-line nationalist party, has repeatedly changed its structure and leadership since its start in the early 2000s. It's led by Alexei Zhuravlev, who holds its only seat in the Duma and is known for vociferous attacks on the West on state TV. It was Zhuravlev who went to the Supreme Court to remove Yabloko from the ballot.

Why reshaping memories may hold the key to raising self-esteem
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
"You're an idiot." "You're weak."
Have you ever said critical things to yourself when you feel any emotions? If so, it may be a sign you struggle with self-worth, says psychologist Marisa Franco. That means feeling good about yourself and "treating your emotions like they matter."
Life Kit
Feeling insecure? Try this memory-update exercise
The good news is that self-worth is a skill that you can learn and get better at, says Franco, author of Worth: The New Science of Self-Esteem and Secure Attachment, published in September. Drawing on the latest research in psychology and neuroscience, the book offers insights and exercises on how to build a stronger sense of value for yourself.
One effective way to do that is to revisit difficult memories, Franco says. This approach is based on memory reconsolidation theory, based on the work of behavioral neuroscientist Karim Nader.
"It's about looking back at these memories, giving yourself catharsis and allowing those feelings to move through you more so they don't continue to shape your sense of self right now," Franco says.
In a conversation with Life Kit, Franco explains the benefits of good self-esteem — and shares an exercise to boost your sense of self-worth. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Let's talk about memory reconsolidation. Researchers have found that we can transform our memories, and that can make us feel more worthy.
The thing about memories is they don't just record the past, they predict the future.
When you return to a memory and envision yourself intervening as an adult and saying, "You're safe, I care about you and I'm never going to leave you," it can be quite transformative.
That leads to higher self-esteem, less symptoms of trauma, and also changes in the hippocampus, which is the part of our brain where our memories are stored.
In your book, you explain how to do a memory reconsolidation exercise called reparenting (see instructions above). It asks you, as your current self, to provide reassurance to your younger self as a way to work through a troubling past event. Can you share an example?
One of the memories I reconsolidated was the experience of being a kid whose mom showed up late to soccer practice. I was one of the only kids of color [on the team]. When I go back to that memory, I can viscerally experience how I felt ashamed, embarrassed and different from everyone else.
I picture my current self showing up before my mom gets there. Adult me looks so excited to see younger me. Adult me gives younger me a hug and says, "Oh my gosh, I'm so happy that I get to pick you up. Even though your mom is late, she loves you."
How does this exercise make you feel?
It allows me to see the good in the world, to not evaluate things based off of the negativity eclipsing everything good about it. [It makes me] feel more valued, more enthusiastic, less afraid, bolder.
Why is it worth addressing low self-esteem?
All the beauties of life slip off of you when you have lower self-esteem. You can experience great success and still feel like a failure. You can find great love and still feel unlovable. So your ability to internalize the good is disrupted by your own sense of self.
If we're able to feel good about ourselves, we are able to receive all the good happening in our lives more deeply.

US interest rates raised for first time in three years
- Published
US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices.
Rates were hiked to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% by the Federal Reserve in a unanimous decision despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".
However, Trump said rates "should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World - BY FAR".
Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for people wanting to secure loans, mortgages, and credit cards, but can lead to better returns on savings.
Warsh said during a press conference on Wednesday following the decision that, while there was "an attitude of optimism" within the Fed leadership, inflation remained a problem.
Central banks tend to increase rates when inflation is high to discourage spending and encourage saving in the hope this will reduce the pace of price rises.
But it's a balancing act, as higher rates can also encourage businesses to hold off on investing and hurt economic growth.
Like many central banks, the Fed has a target of keeping inflation at 2% or below. Warsh. Warsh noted that US inflation has been above that target "for more than five years".
Ahead of the midterm elections in November, affordability is one of the top concerns of American voters, who have seen diesel prices hit an all-time high and petrol rise above $4 (£3) a gallon on average.
Global oil prices have surged since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, driving up the price of car fuel as well as the cost of goods and services generally.
Warsh said the decision to raise interest rates that the Fed "cannot affect any individual price whether it be oil prices, whether it be food stuffs at the grocery store", but could ensure price rises do not broaden across the economy.
He added that the strong jobs market and wider economy meant the Fed was focused on stabilising prices, adding that those least well off had most to gain from lower inflation.
Disagreement with the White House
Asked about the message the decision sent to Trump, Warsh chuckled before saying "I have got nothing for you on a discussion with the president".
The Federal Reserve is independent of the government, but has faced sharp criticism from Trump over its decisions on rates in recent years.
Trump was heavily critical of Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell for not cutting rates.
The US president appointed Warsh to take over as Fed chair after Powell stepped down at the end of his term earlier this year.
Following Wednesday's announcement, Trump said on social media: "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"
Earlier, White House Press Secretary Kush Desai told Fox News the president and White House had reiterated their "commitment to the independence of the Federal Reserve on numerous occasions" but said that did not prevent Trump being able to voice his opinions.
Warsh said at Wednesday's press conference that "part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane".
The Fed's hike is the first rate move in any direction since they were cut in December 2025. The last time they were raised was in July 2023.
The increase will likely add to increasing mortgage rates for homebuyers, as the rates set by banks and other lenders are heavily influenced by the Fed's policy rate.
Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp, and BNY all raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday to 7% from 6.75%, which will affect rates charged on credit cards and personal loans.
Mortgage costs have climbed over the past year but remain below peaks seen in 2023. A 30-year fixed deal is 6.76% on average, while a 15-year deal is 6.09%, according to figures from Freddie Mac.
Due to many US homeowners having 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, changes to interest rates will not impact many Americans monthly repayments, though they could affect those looking to secure a loan for a home or refinance.
Warsh declined to provide his own view on where he saw interest rates going, but the majority of his fellow policymakers said they believe rates would be hiked again before the end of this year to between 4-4.25%.
A small majority said rates could rise further to the 4.25-4.5% next year, before cuts begin in 2028 and 2029.
The forecast suggested price rises will ease in the coming years, with inflation, the measure used to assess the cost of living, predicted to fall steadily to the Fed's 2% target by 2029.
The US Fed is not alone in facing rising inflation since the Iran war, with the European Central Bank raising rates last week and the Bank of England set to make its own decision on Thursday.
